items.text: משנת הפתיחה: הפרשת הכהן הגדול והכנת כהן חלופי
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Separation of the High Priest
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that seven days before Yom Kippur, the High Priest is separated from his home to the Parhedrin chamber, and a substitute priest is prepared in case he becomes disqualified. Rabbi Yehuda adds that a substitute wife is also prepared in case his wife dies, citing the verse 'and he shall atone for himself and for his house'—'his house' meaning his wife. The Sages object that this would have no end.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שמפרישים את הכהן הגדול שבעה ימים לפני יום הכיפורים ללשכת פרהדרין, ומכינים כהן אחר תחתיו למקרה שייפסל. רבי יהודה מוסיף שמכינים גם אשה אחרת למקרה שתמות אשתו, והחכמים דוחים זאת מפני שאין לדבר סוף.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that seven days before Yom Kippur, the High Priest is separated from his home to the Parhedrin chamber, and a substitute priest is prepared in case he becomes disqualified.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בקביעה שמפרישים את הכהן הגדול שבעה ימים לפני יום הכיפורים ללשכת פרהדרין, ומכינים כהן אחר תחתיו למקרה שייפסל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda adds that a substitute wife is also prepared in case his wife dies, citing the verse 'and he shall atone for himself and for his house'—'his house' meaning his wife.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מוסיף שמכינים גם אשה אחרת למקרה שתמות אשתו, ומביא ראיה מהפסוק 'וכפר בעדו ובעד ביתו' שביתו זו אשתו.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object that if a substitute wife is prepared, there would be no end to the matter.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מוסיף שמכינים גם אשה אחרת למקרה שתמות אשתו, ומביא ראיה מהפסוק 'וכפר בעדו ובעד ביתו' שביתו זו אשתו.

items.text: Gemara: Parallel to the Red Heifer
items.text_en: Gemara: Parallel to the Red Heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah: seven days before the burning of the red heifer, the priest who burns it is separated from his home to the chamber called 'the stone chamber,' located northeast of the Temple Mount, where all work is done with vessels of dung, stone, and earth.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of a parallel Mishnah
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of a parallel Mishnah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah about the separation of the priest who burns the red heifer (פרה אדומה) seven days before the burning, and the special chamber called לשכת בית האבן where all work is done in vessels of dung, stone, and earth.

items.text: Reason for the Vessels and Separation
items.text_en: Reason for the Vessels and Separation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason for using non-absorbent vessels: since a tevul yom is valid for the red heifer (to counter the Sadducees who insisted on sunset), the Sages instituted vessels that cannot become impure, to prevent disrespect. The separation itself is derived from a verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages used vessels of dung, stone, and earth for the red heifer, and explains it was to counter the Sadducees who insisted the heifer be performed after sunset.
The Gemara answers that the Sages instituted these non-absorbent vessels so that they would not become impure, thereby preventing disrespect toward the heifer.

items.text: טעם מיקום הלשכה בצפון מזרח
items.text_en: Location of the Chamber: Northeast
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the chamber is specifically northeast, and answers: because the red heifer is a sin-offering, which requires the north side, and the verse 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting' indicates a recognizable location, so the Sages placed it northeast.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע הלשכה ממוקמת דווקא בצפון מזרח, ומשיבה מפני שהפרה היא חטאת הטעונה צפון, וכתוב 'אל נוכח פני אוהל מועד' המכוון למזרח, ולכן קבעו לשכה בצפון מזרח כדי שיהיה היכר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the chamber was specifically in the northeast, and answers that since the red heifer is a חטאת (sin-offering) which requires the north side, and the verse says 'אֶל נֹכַח פְּנֵי אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' (toward the front of the Tent of Meeting), the Sages instituted the chamber in the northeast to provide a recognizable distinction.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע הלשכה ממוקמת דווקא בצפון מזרח.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: because the red heifer is a sin-offering (חטאת) requiring the north side, and the verse 'toward the front of the Tent of Meeting' demands a recognizable location, so the Sages placed it northeast.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע הלשכה ממוקמת דווקא בצפון מזרח.

items.text: פירוש 'בירה'
items.text_en: Definition of 'Birah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the term 'birah' in the Mishnah: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that it is a specific place on the Temple Mount called Birah. Reish Lakish says the entire Temple is called Birah, citing the verse 'the birah which I have prepared.'
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במשמעות המונח 'בירה': רבה בר בר חנה בשם רבי יוחנן אומר שמדובר במקום ספציפי בהר הבית, וריש לקיש אומר שכל המקדש נקרא בירה, על פי הפסוק 'הבירה אשר הכינותי'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'בירה' (the fortress) refers to, and cites two opinions: Rabbi Yochanan says it is a specific place on the Temple Mount called 'בירה', while Reish Lakish says the entire Temple is called 'בירה', as the verse says 'the fortress which I have prepared'.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש המונח 'בירה' המוזכר במשנה.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish argues that the entire Temple is called Birah, citing the verse 'the birah which I have prepared.'
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש המונח 'בירה' המוזכר במשנה.

items.text: מקור ההפרשה מהפסוקים ומהקשר לפרה
items.text_en: Derivation of Separation via Verbal Analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the separation. Rav Minyomi bar Chilkiyah in the name of Rav Machseya bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'as he did on this day, so the Lord commanded to do to make atonement for you'—'to do' refers to the acts of the red heifer, 'to atone' to Yom Kippur. The Gemara objects that the verse could apply entirely to Yom Kippur, but resolves with a verbal analogy: 'commanded' here and 'commanded' there (in the red heifer passage) teach that just as there it is the red heifer, so here it is the red heifer, and just as here there is separation, so there there is separation.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'כאשר עשה ביום הזה צוה ה' לעשות לכפר עליכם' ללמד שההפרשה נוהגת גם בפרה וגם ביום הכיפורים. לאחר קושיה שהפסוק כולו עוסק ביום הכיפורים, הגמרא מתרצת בגזירה שווה 'צוה' 'צוה' מהפרה, ומכאן לומדים שגם בפרה יש הפרשה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the separation of the High Priest) derived?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמדת ההפרשה של הכהן השורף את הפרה ושל הכהן הגדול ביום הכיפורים.

sub.text_en: Rav Minyomi bar Chilkiyah in the name of Rav Machseya bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Minyomi bar Chilkiyah cites a verse: 'as he did on this day, so the Lord commanded to do to make atonement for you' — 'to do' refers to the acts of the red heifer, 'to atone' to Yom Kippur.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמדת ההפרשה של הכהן השורף את הפרה ושל הכהן הגדול ביום הכיפורים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Granted, the entire verse cannot apply to the red heifer because 'to atone' is written and the red heifer is not a means of atonement; rather, say the entire verse is written about Yom Kippur.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הפסוק כולו אינו יכול לעסוק בפרה, כי כתוב 'לכפר' ופרה אינה מכפרת; אלא יש לומר שהפסוק כולו נאמר על יום הכיפורים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'צִוָּה' (commanded) — just as there (in the red heifer passage) it is the red heifer, so here (in the Yom Kippur verse) it is the red heifer; and just as here (in the Yom Kippur context) there is separation, so there (in the red heifer context) there is separation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת בגזירה שווה 'צוה' 'צוה': כשם שבפרה כתוב 'צוה ה' לאמר', כך כאן 'צוה ה' לעשות' – ומכאן לומדים שגם בפרה יש הפרשה, וכשם שבהפרשת יום הכיפורים יש הפרשה, כך בפרה יש הפרשה.

items.text: Rejecting derivation from Yom Kippur's 'tzivah' and from sacrifices
items.text_en: Rejecting derivation from Yom Kippur's 'tzivah' and from sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers deriving the separation from the word 'tzivah' written regarding Yom Kippur, but rejects it because that 'tzivah' is after the action, while the one in Leviticus 8 is before. It then considers deriving from 'tzivah' in the context of sacrifices, but rejects it because the form is different ('tzavoto' vs. 'tzivah').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the separation from the word 'צִוָּה' (commanded) written regarding Yom Kippur, but rejects it because that 'צִוָּה' is after the action, while the one in Leviticus 8 is before.
The Gemara then considers deriving from 'צִוָּה' in the context of sacrifices, but rejects it because the form is different ('צַוֹּתוֹ' vs. 'צִוָּה').

items.text: Defending the method of verbal analogy
items.text_en: Defending the method of verbal analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for a verbal analogy at all, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael that similar words can be equated. It answers that this principle applies only when there is no closer parallel, but here there is a closer parallel (the dedication of the Tabernacle).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for a verbal analogy, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael that similar words can be equated.
The Gemara answers that the principle of equating similar words applies only when there is no closer parallel, but here there is a closer parallel (the dedication of the Tabernacle).

items.text: Rejecting derivation from sacrifices via 'lekhapper'
items.text_en: Rejecting derivation from sacrifices via 'lekhapper'
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests deriving from the word 'lekhapper' which refers to Yom Kippur, but then considers sacrifices. It argues that for sacrifices we do not know which priest will perform the service, so a separation for the entire watch would be needed, but Yom Kippur is a fixed time, unlike daily sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests deriving from the word 'lekhapper' which refers to Yom Kippur, but then considers sacrifices as an alternative source.

The Gemara rejects the derivation from sacrifices because we do not know which priest will perform the service, so a separation for the entire watch would be needed, but Yom Kippur is a fixed time, unlike daily sacrifices.

items.text: Rejecting derivation from festivals
items.text_en: Rejecting derivation from festivals
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers deriving from festivals, but rejects because festivals occur multiple times a year, while Yom Kippur is once a year. It then considers a single festival, but notes uncertainty which one (Passover or Sukkot) should be chosen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the requirement of separation from the festivals (רגלים), but rejects this because festivals occur multiple times a year, unlike Yom Kippur which occurs once a year.

The Gemara then considers deriving from a single festival, but notes the uncertainty of which festival to choose—Passover (חג המצות) because the Torah begins with it, or Sukkot (חג הסוכות) because its mitzvot are numerous.

items.text: Deriving from the dedication of the Tabernacle and rejecting Shemini
items.text_en: Deriving from the dedication of the Tabernacle and rejecting Shemini
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes a derivation from the dedication of the Tabernacle, which also required a seven-day separation for a single day. It then considers the eighth day of the dedication (Shemini), which also had a seven-day separation for one day, but rejects it because Shemini had prior sanctity (the seven days of dedication), unlike Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the derivation must be from a case of a seven-day separation for a single day, matching the Tabernacle dedication.
The Gemara objects that the eighth day of the dedication (Shemini) also had a seven-day separation for one day, so it could be the source.
The Gemara rejects Shemini because it had prior sanctity (the seven days of dedication), unlike Yom Kippur which has no prior sanctity.

items.text: Rejecting a kal vachomer and final resolution
items.text_en: Rejecting a kal vachomer and final resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer: if something without prior sanctity requires separation, something with prior sanctity certainly does. Rav Mesharshiya rejects this because the verse says 'hazeh' (this one), limiting the derivation. Rav Ashi adds that the main festival (Sukkot) does not require separation, so its appendage (Shemini) cannot require it either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if something without prior sanctity requires separation, something with prior sanctity certainly does.
Rav Mesharshiya rejects the kal vachomer because the verse says 'הַזֶּה' (this one), limiting the derivation to this specific case.
Rav Ashi adds that the main festival (Sukkot) does not require separation, so its appendage (Shemini) cannot require it either.

items.text: Opening statement: Yom Kippur's makeup offering is like the first festival day
items.text_en: Opening statement: Yom Kippur's makeup offering is like the first festival day
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that for makeup offerings, Yom Kippur is considered like the first day of the festival, citing the Mishnah that one who did not celebrate on the first festival day may celebrate throughout the entire festival, including the last day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that for makeup offerings, Yom Kippur is like the first festival day, citing the Mishnah that one who did not celebrate on the first day may celebrate throughout the entire festival.

items.text: First objection: Shavuot as a counterexample
items.text_en: First objection: Shavuot as a counterexample
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps Shavuot, which is only one day, should also be considered like the first day? Rabbi Abba answers by deriving a gezerah shavah from 'one bull and one ram' to exclude Shavuot, which has two rams.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Shavuot (עֲצֶרֶת) is not considered analogous, since it is a single day separated by seven weeks.
Rabbi Abba answers that Yom Kippur is derived from the first festival day via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'one bull and one ram', excluding Shavuot which has two rams.

items.text: Challenge: Dispute about the number of rams on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Challenge: Dispute about the number of rams on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works for the opinion that Yom Kippur has one ram, but for Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon who says there are two rams, the objection stands. A baraita is cited: Rabbi says one ram, Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon says two rams.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the analogy works for the opinion that Yom Kippur has two rams, citing the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi says there is one ram (the same in both places), while Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon says there are two distinct rams.

items.text: Resolution: Even for two rams, one is for the day's obligation
items.text_en: Resolution: Even for two rams, one is for the day's obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon, one ram is for the day's obligation and one for the additional offerings, so the gezerah shavah still excludes Shavuot where both rams are for the day's obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon, one ram is for the day's obligation and one for the additional offerings, excluding Shavuot where both rams are for the day's obligation.

items.text: Second objection: Rosh Hashanah as a counterexample
items.text_en: Second objection: Rosh Hashanah as a counterexample
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection: perhaps Rosh Hashanah, which is also a one-day festival, should be included? Rabbi Avahu answers by deriving a gezerah shavah from 'his bull and ram' to exclude communal offerings like those of Shavuot and Rosh Hashanah. This works for the opinion that 'take for yourself' means from your own property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rosh Hashanah (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה) is not considered analogous, since it is also a single day separated by seven days.

Rabbi Abahu answers that Yom Kippur is derived from the first festival day via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'his bull and his ram', excluding Shavuot and Rosh Hashanah which are communal offerings.
The Gemara questions how this works for the opinion that 'קח לך' (take for yourself) implies from one's own property.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan regarding 'take for yourself' and 'make for yourself'
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan regarding 'take for yourself' and 'make for yourself'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'make for yourself' in the context of the High Priest's bull. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yoshiya holds that 'take for yourself' and 'make for yourself' mean from your own, while 'and they shall take for you' means from the community. Rabbi Yonatan argues that all phrases mean from the community, but 'take for yourself' indicates God's preference for the individual's contribution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'make for yourself' in the context of the High Priest's bull, noting that according to one view it means from one's own, but for the one who says it means from the community, what can be said?

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yoshiya holds that 'take for yourself' and 'make for yourself' mean from your own, while 'and they shall take for you' means from the community; Rabbi Yonatan argues that all phrases mean from the community, but 'take for yourself' indicates God's preference for the individual's contribution.

items.text: Abba Chanan's proof from the Ark
items.text_en: Abba Chanan's proof from the Ark
items.desc_en: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar brings a proof from contradictory verses about the Ark: one says 'make for yourself' and another says 'they shall make'. He resolves that when Israel does God's will, it is from their own; when not, from the community.

sub.desc_en: Abba Chanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar resolves a contradiction between two verses about the Ark: when Israel does God's will, the Ark is from their own funds; when not, from the community.

items.text: Proofs from the dedication and Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Proofs from the dedication and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the dispute only applies to general 'takings' and 'makings', but specific verses clarify that the High Priest's offerings must be from his own. It brings proofs from the dedication (milu'im) where Aaron is told 'take for yourself' and from Yom Kippur where the verse says 'the bull of the sin-offering which is his'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute only applies to general 'takings' and 'makings', but specific verses clarify that the High Priest's offerings must be from his own.
The Gemara brings a proof from the dedication (milu'im) where Aaron is told 'קַח לְךָ' (take for yourself), indicating it must be from his own.
The Gemara brings a proof from Yom Kippur where the verse says 'פַּר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לוֹ' (the bull of the sin-offering which is his), indicating it must be from his own.

items.text: Rav Ashi and Ravina's derivations
items.text_en: Rav Ashi and Ravina's derivations
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives the requirement from a gezerah shavah comparing the bull and ram of Yom Kippur to those of the dedication, excluding Rosh Hashanah and Shavuot which are both burnt-offerings. Ravina derives from a gezerah shavah comparing service by the High Priest, excluding all other services. Another version of Ravina's statement compares the first service in the place.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives the requirement from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) comparing the bull and ram of Yom Kippur to those of the dedication, excluding Rosh Hashanah and Shavuot which are both burnt-offerings.
Ravina derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) comparing service by the High Priest, excluding all other services.
Another version of Ravina's statement compares the first service in the place, with the gemara clarifying that 'first' means first in the place, not first in the High Priest.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi regarding the seven-day separation
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi regarding the seven-day separation
items.desc_en: When Rav Dimi came, he reported that Rabbi Yochanan taught one derivation from the verse 'la'asot lechaper' referring only to Yom Kippur, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught two: 'la'asot' for the red heifer and 'lechaper' for Yom Kippur. The Gemara questions this, citing a mishnah that mentions seven days before both Yom Kippur and the burning of the red heifer, and a statement from Rabbi Yochanan himself that 'la'asot' refers to the red heifer. It resolves that the latter was his teacher's tradition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan taught one derivation from the verse 'לַעֲשׂוֹת לְכַפֵּר' (to do, to make atonement) referring only to Yom Kippur, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught two: 'לַעֲשׂוֹת' (to do) for the red heifer and 'לְכַפֵּר' (to make atonement) for Yom Kippur.

The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's position by citing the mishnah that mentions seven days of separation before both Yom Kippur and the burning of the red heifer, and answers that the red heifer separation is merely a higher standard (מעלה בעלמא).

The Gemara objects further by citing a statement from Rabbi Yochanan himself that 'לַעֲשׂוֹת' (to do) refers to the red heifer and 'לְכַפֵּר' (to make atonement) to Yom Kippur, and resolves that this was his teacher's tradition, as Ravin reported that Rabbi Yochanan said this in the name of Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Reish Lakish's challenge and the derivation from Sinai
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's challenge and the derivation from Sinai
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan: if you derive the seven-day separation from the dedication (milu'im), then all details of the dedication should be required, but the mishnah does not mention 'setting aside' a replacement priest. Rabbi Yochanan responds that he derives it from Sinai, where Moses was separated for six days before entering the cloud.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan: if the seven-day separation is derived from the dedication (milu'im), then all details of the dedication should be required for Yom Kippur as well.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's objection from the mishnah
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's objection from the mishnah
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish objects that the mishnah does not use the term 'מפרישין' (setting aside) for the replacement priest, only 'מתקינין' (designating), showing that the separation is not a strict requirement.

Rabbi Yochanan responds that he derives the separation from Sinai, where Moses was separated for six days before entering the cloud, establishing a paradigm for anyone entering the camp of the Divine Presence.

items.text: The objection from the mishnah requiring seven days
items.text_en: The objection from the mishnah requiring seven days
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishnah requires seven days, not six. It answers that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who is concerned for an additional factor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishnah explicitly requires seven days of separation, not six.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who is concerned for an additional factor requiring seven days.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the High Priest is separated for seven days before Yom Kippur, and that he is sprinkled with all the sin-offerings that were there.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the High Priest is separated for seven days before Yom Kippur and sprinkled with all the sin-offerings that were there.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish debate the source
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish debate the source
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that the separation is derived from the milu'im, while Reish Lakish derives it from Sinai. Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish that there was no sprinkling at Sinai. Reish Lakish counters that the milu'im involved blood, while here it is water, but Rabbi Chiya resolves that water replaced blood. Reish Lakish then concedes that the Sinai derivation is merely a stringency.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish: according to my view deriving from the milu'im, the baraita about sprinkling fits, but according to your view deriving from Sinai, was there sprinkling at Sinai?
Reish Lakish objects: according to your own reasoning, is it satisfactory? The milu'im involved blood, but here it is water.
Rabbi Chiya resolves the objection: water replaced blood in this context.
Rabbi Yochanan repeats his challenge: according to your view, was there sprinkling at Sinai?
Reish Lakish concedes that the Sinai derivation is merely a stringency (מעלה בעלמא).

items.text: Baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's view: the verse 'With this Aaron shall enter the sanctuary' refers to the milu'im, where Aaron separated for seven days and served one day, and Moses taught him. This applies to all future High Priests, who separate for seven days and are taught by two Torah scholars, excluding Sadducees. The baraita then states that the High Priest is separated seven days before Yom Kippur, and similarly the priest who burns the red heifer, and both are sprinkled with all the sin-offerings.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan: the verse 'בְּזֹאת יָבֹא אַהֲרֹן אֶל הַקֹּדֶשׁ' refers to the milu'im, where Aaron separated for seven days and served one day, and Moses taught him.
The baraita extends the rule to all future High Priests: they separate for seven days and are taught by two Torah scholars, excluding Sadducees.
The baraita concludes that the High Priest is separated seven days before Yom Kippur, and similarly the priest who burns the red heifer, and both are sprinkled with all the sin-offerings.

items.text: Addressing the blood-water objection and extending the law
items.text_en: Addressing the blood-water objection and extending the law
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the objection that milu'im involved blood while here it is water, citing that water replaced blood. It then cites a verse to show that the law applies to all Yom Kippurim and all High Priests, not just the first one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the objection that the milu'im involved blood while here it is water, and answers that water replaced blood.
The Gemara cites a verse to show that the law applies to all Yom Kippurim and all High Priests, and resolves a potential redundancy in the verse.
The Gemara explains that the additional verse teaches that the requirement of separation applies to all Yom Kippurim and all High Priests, not just the first.

items.text: Baraita supports Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Baraita supports Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Reish Lakish's view: Moses ascended in a cloud, was covered, and sanctified to receive the Torah, based on a verse. Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva debate the timing of this event.

items.text: Debate on the purpose of the cloud and the call to Moses
items.text_en: Debate on the purpose of the cloud and the call to Moses
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents three opinions on why the cloud covered the mountain and God called to Moses: Rabbi Nathan says it was to honor Moses, Rabbi Matya ben Charash says it was to instill awe, and an earlier view suggests it was to purify Moses like an angel.

sub.desc_en: The anonymous first opinion explains that the cloud covered the mountain and God called to Moses to honor him, as Moses and all Israel were standing.
Rabbi Nathan says the cloud and call were to purge Moses of food and drink, making him like ministering angels.
Rabbi Matya ben Charash says the cloud and call were to instill awe, so the Torah would be given with fear and trembling.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Mattana citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana in the name of Rav explains the verse 'עבדו את ה׳ ביראה וגילו ברעדה' to mean that in a place of joy there should be trembling.

items.text: Introduction to the dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Introduction to the dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva regarding the date of the giving of the Torah, linking it to a Tannaitic debate about whether it was on the sixth or seventh of Sivan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva, and answers that it stems from a Tannaitic debate about whether the Torah was given on the sixth or seventh of Sivan.

items.text: Rabbi Yose HaGelili's position explained
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili's position explained
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds like the first Tanna that the Torah was given on the sixth, so the cloud and call occurred after the Ten Commandments, not before.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds like the first Tanna that the Torah was given on the sixth, so the cloud and call occurred after the Ten Commandments, not before.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's position and the chronology of the tablets' breaking
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's position and the chronology of the tablets' breaking
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Yose that the Torah was given on the seventh, which allows for the tablets to be broken on the seventeenth of Tammuz. Rabbi Yose HaGelili responds that the forty days on the mountain include the six days of separation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Yose that the Torah was given on the seventh, which allows for the tablets to be broken on the seventeenth of Tammuz.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Yose HaGelili, the tablets would not have been broken until the twenty-third of Tammuz.
Rabbi Yose HaGelili responds that the forty days on the mountain include the six days of separation.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Elazar's view on the call to Moses
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Elazar's view on the call to Moses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita supporting Rabbi Elazar that the call was only for Moses, not all Israel, and resolves a contradiction between verses about who heard the call.

sub.desc_en: Mar cites a baraita stating that the call 'וַיִּקְרָא אֶל מֹשֶׁה' was directed to Moses while all Israel stood, supporting Rabbi Elazar's view that the call was only for Moses' honor.
The Gemara raises an objection from verses that say 'קוֹל לוֹ' and 'קוֹל אֵלָיו', implying only Moses heard the voice, not all Israel.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the revelation at Sinai, where all Israel heard, and the Tent of Meeting, where only Moses heard.
An alternative resolution distinguishes between the call (קְרִיאָה), which all Israel heard, and the speech (דִּבּוּר), which only Moses heard.

items.text: Resolution of a contradiction about Moses entering the cloud
items.text_en: Resolution of a contradiction about Moses entering the cloud
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika raises a contradiction between verses about Moses entering the cloud, and Rabbi Elazar explains that God brought him in. The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds a gezerah shavah to show there was a path.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika raises a contradiction before Rabbi Elazar: one verse says Moses could not enter the Tent of Meeting because the cloud rested on it, while another says he entered into the cloud.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Holy One, blessed be He, grasped Moses and brought him into the cloud.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'בתוך' (within) used at the sea, where a path was made, to show that here too there was a path for Moses in the cloud.

items.text: Lesson from the order of 'call' and 'speak'
items.text_en: Lesson from the order of 'call' and 'speak'
items.desc_en: The Gemara learns from the verse that one should not speak to another without first calling him, supporting Rabbi Chanina, and derives that one must be told 'go say' before speaking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse places 'call' before 'speak', and answers that the Torah teaches proper conduct.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Chanina's statement that one must not speak to another without first calling him.

sub.text: Rabbi Musya bar brei d'Rabbi Masya in the name of Rabbi Rabbah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Musya bar brei d'Rabbi Masya in the name of Rabbi Rabbah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Musya bar brei d'Rabbi Masya derives from the word 'לֵאמֹר' that one must be told 'go say' before speaking.

items.text: Dispute about whether all details of the miluim are indispensable
items.text_en: Dispute about whether all details of the miluim are indispensable
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina about whether all details written in the miluim (consecration offerings) are indispensable, and concludes that Rabbi Yochanan holds they are, based on Reish Lakish's challenge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that both Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina agree that the details of the miluim (consecration offerings) are indispensable, introducing their dispute.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan holds that all details are indispensable, based on Reish Lakish's challenge to which Rabbi Yochanan did not respond.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions.

items.text: Rav Yosef: Semikhah is the difference
items.text_en: Rav Yosef: Semikhah is the difference
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asserts that the dispute between those who hold that everything written in the inauguration is indispensable and those who hold that what is not indispensable for generations is not indispensable in the inauguration revolves around semikhah (laying of hands). He then cites a baraita proving that semikhah is not indispensable for generations, as it is merely a 'remnant of a mitzvah' that does not affect atonement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asserts that the dispute between the two positions about indispensability in the inauguration revolves around semikhah (laying of hands).
The gemara asks: from where do we know that semikhah is not indispensable for generations?
A baraita is cited, showing that semikhah is only a 'remnant of a mitzvah' (שיירי מצוה) that does not affect atonement, proving it is not indispensable.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: Tenufah is the difference
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: Tenufah is the difference
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak argues that the practical difference is tenufah (waving). He similarly cites a baraita showing that tenufah is not indispensable for generations, as it does not effect atonement but is a 'remnant of a mitzvah'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asserts that the dispute revolves around tenufah (waving).
The gemara asks: from where do we know that tenufah is not indispensable for generations?
A baraita is cited, showing that tenufah is only a 'remnant of a mitzvah' (שיירי מצוה) that does not affect atonement, proving it is not indispensable.

items.text: Rav Pappa: Separation of seven days is the difference
items.text_en: Rav Pappa: Separation of seven days is the difference
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa proposes that the difference is the requirement of a seven-day separation (פרישת שבעה) before the inauguration. He proves it is not indispensable for generations because the Mishnah uses the term 'prepare' (מתקינין) rather than 'separate' (מפרישין).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asserts that the dispute revolves around the seven-day separation (פרישת שבעה).
The gemara asks: from where do we know that the seven-day separation is not indispensable for generations?
The gemara infers from the baraita's use of 'מתקינין' (they prepare) rather than 'מפרישין' (they separate) that the separation is not indispensable.

items.text: Ravina: Seven days of investiture and seven days of anointing is the difference
items.text_en: Ravina: Seven days of investiture and seven days of anointing is the difference
items.desc_en: Ravina argues that the difference is the requirement of seven days of investiture (ריבוי שבעה) and seven days of anointing (משיחה שבעה). He cites a baraita that derives these from a verse, and then explains that for generations, the requirement is only initial (לכתחילה), not indispensable, using two alternative proofs: one from the need for a verse to exclude it, and another from a juxtaposition (היקש) of anointing to investiture.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asserts that the dispute revolves around the seven-day investiture (ריבוי שבעה) and seven-day anointing (משיחה שבעה).
The gemara asks: from where do we know that the seven-day investiture and anointing are not indispensable for generations?
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse that the anointing and investiture are not indispensable for generations, as they can be performed in various combinations.
The gemara asks: we found that seven-day investiture is required לכתחילה (ideally), but from where do we derive that seven-day anointing is also required לכתחילה?
The gemara provides two answers: either from the fact that a verse was needed to exclude it, or from a verbal analogy (היקש) linking anointing to investiture.

items.text: Source for the position that everything written is indispensable
items.text_en: Source for the position that everything written is indispensable
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of the opinion that everything written in the inauguration is indispensable. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna cites the verse 'And you shall do for Aharon and his sons thus' (ככה), which implies that doing it 'thus' is indispensable. The daf breaks off mid-discussion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: what is the reasoning of the one who holds that everything written in the inauguration is indispensable?
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna answers that the verse 'וְעָשִׂיתָ לְאַהֲרֹן וּלְבָנָיו כָּכָה' (and you shall do thus to Aaron and his sons) uses the word 'כָּכָה' (thus), which indicates indispensability.

items.text: Deriving missing details from the consecration narrative
items.text_en: Deriving missing details from the consecration narrative
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that details not explicitly written in the current context are required. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, Rav Mesharshiya, and Rav Ashi each offer a different derivation: a verbal analogy on 'opening', or the word 'keep' or 'for so I was commanded' indicating a requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we derive details not explicitly written in the current context.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives the requirement via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'פתח' (opening).
Rav Mesharshiya derives the requirement from the word 'ושמרתם' (keep), indicating a mandatory condition (עכובא).
Rav Ashi derives the requirement from the phrase 'כי כן צויתי' (for so I was commanded), indicating a mandatory condition (עכובא).

items.text: Baraita on the phrases 'for so I was commanded' etc.
items.text_en: Baraita on the phrases 'for so I was commanded' etc.
items.desc_en: A baraita explains three similar phrases: 'for so I was commanded' refers to eating the sin-offering in mourning; 'as I was commanded' indicates he told them at the time of the act; 'as the Lord commanded' means he did not speak on his own authority.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces three similar phrases and explains each: 'כי כן צויתי' refers to eating the sin-offering in mourning; 'כאשר צויתי' indicates he told them at the time of the act; 'כאשר צוה ה׳' means he did not speak on his own authority.
The baraita resolves: 'for thus I am commanded' means they eat in mourning; 'as I commanded' means at the time of the act he told them; 'as Hashem commanded' means not from myself I say.

items.text: Deriving the inclusion of the linen breeches and the tenth of an ephah
items.text_en: Deriving the inclusion of the linen breeches and the tenth of an ephah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina notes that the linen breeches are not written in the parashah of the consecration, but the verse 'this is the thing that you shall do to them' includes them and the tenth of an ephah. The Gemara explains that the tenth of an ephah is derived via a verbal analogy on 'this' from the passage about Aaron's daily offering.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוסי בר חנינא (Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina) states that the linen breeches are not written in the parashah, but the verse 'וזה הדבר אשר תעשה להם' (and this is the thing that you shall do to them) comes to include the breeches and the tenth of an ephah.
The Gemara asks: Granted, the breeches are written in the context of the garments, but from where do we derive the tenth of an ephah?
The Gemara answers: It is derived via a verbal analogy on 'זה' (this) from the verse 'וזה קרבן אהרן ובניו... עשירית האיפה' (and this is the offering of Aaron and his sons... a tenth of an ephah).

items.text: Even the reading of the parashah is a requirement
items.text_en: Even the reading of the parashah is a requirement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches that even the oral recitation of the parashah is a requirement, derived from the verse 'this is the thing that the Lord commanded' — even speech is a requirement.

sub.text: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחאי (Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai)
sub.text_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחאי (Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai)
sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) states in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחאי (Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai) that even the oral recitation of the parashah is a requirement, derived from the verse 'וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל הָעֵדָה זֶה הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה ה׳' (And Moses said to the assembly: This is the thing that the Lord commanded), teaching that even speech is a requirement.

items.text: Debate on the order of dressing Aaron and his sons
items.text_en: Debate on the order of dressing Aaron and his sons
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially misunderstands a question about how they were dressed, then clarifies it refers to the order of the verses. The sons of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yochanan disagree: one says Aaron was dressed first, then his sons; the other says they were dressed simultaneously. Abaye explains that all agree regarding the tunic and turban that Aaron precedes, but they dispute regarding the sash, each citing different verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how they were dressed, then rejects a literal reading and clarifies that the question is about the order of the verses.

sub.text: Sons of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Sons of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute between the sons of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yochanan: one says Aaron was dressed first, then his sons; the other says they were dressed simultaneously.
Abaye explains that all agree regarding the tunic and turban that Aaron precedes, but they dispute regarding the sash, each citing different verses.

items.text: The belt of the High Priest vs. ordinary priest
items.text_en: The belt of the High Priest vs. ordinary priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a challenge: according to the view that Aaron was anointed first and then his sons, the verse says 'and you shall gird them with belts' (plural), implying the same belt for all. The answer is that this teaches that the High Priest's belt is the same as the ordinary priest's belt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse about the High Priest's belt is not the same as the ordinary priest's belt.
The Gemara objects: according to the view that Aaron was anointed first, the verse says 'and you shall gird them with belts' (plural), implying the same belt for all.
The Gemara resolves that the verse teaches that the High Priest's belt is the same as the ordinary priest's belt.

items.text: Proof that Aaron was anointed before his sons
items.text_en: Proof that Aaron was anointed before his sons
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse repeats 'and he girded him with a belt' and 'and he girded them with belts' — this teaches that Aaron was anointed first, then his sons. It clarifies that this is not done simultaneously but sequentially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse repeats 'and he girded him with a belt' and 'and he girded them with belts' — what does this teach?
The Gemara answers that this teaches that Aaron was anointed first, then his sons, and clarifies that this is not done simultaneously but sequentially.

items.text: Why separate the High Priest?
items.text_en: Why separate the High Priest?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that they separate the High Priest. The Gemara asks why, and answers that it is according to the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding the reason for separation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that they separate the High Priest.
The Gemara asks why the High Priest is separated.
The Gemara answers that the reason follows the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, each according to his own view.

items.text: Why separate from his house?
items.text_en: Why separate from his house?
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the question is why the High Priest separates from his house. A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: lest his wife be found to be a safek niddah and he have relations with her. The Gemara corrects: lest he have relations with his wife and she be found to be a safek niddah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the question is not why they separate the High Priest generally, but why he separates from his house.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's explanation: lest his wife be found to be a safek niddah (doubtful menstruant) and he have relations with her.
The Gemara objects: are we dealing with wicked people who would intentionally have relations with a safek niddah?
The Gemara corrects the baraita's wording: the concern is lest he have relations with his wife and she be found to be a safek niddah after the fact.

items.text: The dispute about niddah contaminating her husband
items.text_en: The dispute about niddah contaminating her husband
items.desc_en: The rabbis before Rav Chisda suggest that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira follows Rabbi Akiva, who says niddah contaminates her husband. Rav Chisda responds that even according to the Rabbis, they only dispute about after the fact (achar achar), but in the immediate case (chad achar) they agree.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis before Rav Chisda propose that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's ruling aligns with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a niddah (menstruant) contaminates her husband, unlike the Rabbis who deny this.
Rav Chisda responds that even according to the Rabbis, they only dispute about a case of 'achar achar' (delayed contact), but in 'chad achar' (immediate contact) they agree with Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Proof that one who has relations with a niddah is not like a niddah
items.text_en: Proof that one who has relations with a niddah is not like a niddah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira infers from the separation that one who has relations with a niddah is not like a niddah, because if he were, he would need to immerse at night and would not be able to perform the Temple service the next day due to the need for sunset. Thus, he must be able to immerse during the day.

sub.desc_en: רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) opens by stating that one can learn from the mishna's separation that a בועל נדה (one who has relations with a menstruating woman) is not like a נדה (menstruating woman) with regard to immersion, and immerses during the day.

רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) supports his claim with a conditional argument: if a בועל נדה (one who has relations with a menstruating woman) were like a נדה (menstruating woman), he would have to immerse at night and then require sunset before serving, which would prevent him from performing the Yom Kippur service; therefore, he must be unlike a נדה (menstruating woman).

items.text: Alternative answer: separation close to sunset
items.text_en: Alternative answer: separation close to sunset
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi from Nehardea offers an alternative: even if one who has relations with a niddah is like a niddah, we separate him one hour before sunset so that he can immerse at night and still serve the next day.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi from Nehardea offers an alternative: even if one who has relations with a niddah is like a niddah, we separate him one hour before sunset so that he can immerse at night and still serve the next day.

items.text: Challenges to Rav Shimi's view
items.text_en: Challenges to Rav Shimi's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that all obligated in immersions immerse by day, except niddah and yoledet who immerse at night. This implies that a ba'al keri (one who has a seminal emission) immerses by day, but a bo'el niddah is not mentioned. The Gemara answers that niddah includes all derived from it. Another baraita compares ba'al keri to one who touches a sheretz, and bo'el niddah to one who is tamei met — but this refers to their impurity, not immersion. The Gemara questions this, as their impurity is explicitly written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Shimi's view by citing a baraita that all obligated in immersions immerse by day except niddah and yoledet, implying that a ba'al keri immerses by day but a bo'el niddah is not mentioned.
The Gemara answers that the baraita's mention of niddah includes all derived from it, including a bo'el niddah.

The Gemara brings another baraita comparing ba'al keri to one who touches a sheretz and bo'el niddah to one who is tamei met, and the Gemara initially suggests this refers to immersion, but then answers it refers to their impurity.
The Gemara objects that the impurity of both is explicitly written in the Torah, so the comparison is unnecessary.

items.text: Challenge from immersion times
items.text_en: Challenge from immersion times
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier distinction between corpse impurity and other impurities by citing a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya that lists the immersion times for various impure persons, including a zav, zavah, metzora, and one who engages with a niddah, all of whom immerse during the day, while a niddah and a woman after childbirth immerse at night. This contradicts the earlier claim that the distinction is based on the severity of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier distinction by citing a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya that lists immersion times for various impure persons, showing that a zav, zavah, metzora, and one who engages with a niddah immerse during the day, while a niddah and a woman after childbirth immerse at night.
The Gemara declares this a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of the earlier position.

items.text: Interpretation of the separation from corpse impurity
items.text_en: Interpretation of the separation from corpse impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the phrase 'separate him from corpse impurity' to indicate that corpse impurity is permitted for the community. Rav Tahleifa bar Rav Huna in the name of Rava states that this implies corpse impurity is permitted for the community. Ravina adds that even if it is only deferred, the reason for separating from corpse impurity is that it is uncommon, while impurity from his house is common.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's phrase 'separate him from corpse impurity' as a prooftext.

sub.text: Rav Tahleifa bar Rav Huna in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Tahleifa bar Rav Huna in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Tahleifa bar Rav Huna citing Rava states that the baraita implies corpse impurity is permitted (הותרה) for the community.
Ravina objects that even if corpse impurity is only deferred (דחויה) for the community, the baraita's logic still holds because corpse impurity is uncommon while house impurity is common.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: Rav Nachman says corpse impurity is permitted for the community, while Rav Sheshet says it is only deferred. This sets up the framework for the subsequent discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet regarding whether corpse impurity is permitted (הותרה) or merely deferred (דחויה) for the community.
Rav Nachman states that corpse impurity is permitted (הותרה) for the community, meaning it is entirely allowed.
Rav Sheshet counters that corpse impurity is only deferred (דחויה) for the community, meaning it is temporarily set aside but not fully permitted.

items.text: Practical implications: bringing pure individuals from another family
items.text_en: Practical implications: bringing pure individuals from another family
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical difference between the two views: when there are both pure and impure individuals in the same family, all agree that the pure ones perform the service and the impure do not. The dispute is about whether to bring pure individuals from another family. Rav Nachman, who holds it is permitted, says we do not bring them; Rav Sheshet, who holds it is deferred, says we do bring them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes the agreed-upon case: when both pure and impure individuals exist in the same family, the pure serve and the impure do not.
The Gemara identifies the point of dispute: whether to bring pure individuals from another family.
Rav Nachman, who holds that impurity is permitted (הותרה) for the community, rules that we do not bring pure individuals from another family.
Rav Sheshet, who holds that impurity is merely deferred (דחויה) for the community, rules that we do bring pure individuals from another family.

items.text: Alternative version: Rav Nachman allows impure to serve
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Nachman allows impure to serve
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that even when there are pure and impure in the same family, Rav Nachman holds that the impure may also serve, implying a more lenient view that corpse impurity is permitted.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Nachman holds that even when there are pure and impure priests in the same family, the impure may also serve, implying a more lenient view that corpse impurity is permitted (הותרה) in the Temple service.

items.text: Opening principle: impurity permitted in communal offerings
items.text_en: Opening principle: impurity permitted in communal offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that all impurity of the dead is permitted by the Torah in communal offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that all impurity of the dead is permitted by the Torah in communal offerings.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's proof from the Omer
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's proof from the Omer
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita about the Omer offering: if it becomes impure, they bring another; if none other exists, they tell him to be silent. This implies impurity is not permitted in all communal offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita about the Omer offering becoming impure, where they bring another if available, otherwise tell him to be silent, implying impurity is not permitted in all communal offerings.

items.text: Rav Nachman's distinction: when there are remnants for eating
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's distinction: when there are remnants for eating
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the baraita refers to a case where there are remnants of the Omer for eating, implying that impurity is not permitted when the offering can still be consumed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that the baraita's leniency applies only when there are remnants (שיריים) of the Omer available for eating, so impurity is not permitted when the offering can still be consumed.

items.text: Objection from bulls, rams, and lambs
items.text_en: Objection from bulls, rams, and lambs
items.desc_en: A baraita about bulls, rams, and lambs becoming impure is brought as an objection. The Gemara assumes these are the festival offerings, which are communal, yet they require replacement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita about bulls, rams, and lambs whose meal-offering became impure, and assumes these are the festival offerings (חַג), which are communal, yet they require replacement.

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution: each case is individual or non-fixed
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution: each case is individual or non-fixed
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the bulls refer to the bull for idolatry (non-fixed time), the ram is Aaron's ram (individual), and the lamb is the lamb of the Omer (has remnants for eating). Thus none are standard communal offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rejects the objection and explains that the bulls refer to the bull for idolatry (non-fixed time), the rams to Aaron's ram (individual), and the lambs to the lamb of the Omer (has remnants for eating), so none are standard communal offerings.

items.text: Objection from impure blood sprinkled
items.text_en: Objection from impure blood sprinkled
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if impure blood was sprinkled, if done unintentionally it is accepted, but if intentionally it is not. The Gemara deflects this as referring to an individual offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if impure blood was sprinkled, if done unintentionally it is accepted, but if intentionally it is not.
The Gemara deflects the objection by stating that the baraita refers to an individual offering, not a communal one.

items.text: Objection from the Tzitz (frontplate) atonement
items.text_en: Objection from the Tzitz (frontplate) atonement
items.desc_en: A baraita says the Tzitz atones for impure blood, flesh, and fat, even in communal offerings. This challenges the idea that impurity is permitted. Rav Nachman answers that the baraita refers to individual offerings, or to those without a fixed time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that the Tzitz (frontplate) atones for impure blood, flesh, and fat in all cases, including communal offerings, challenging the idea that impurity is permitted in communal offerings.
The Gemara argues: if impurity were permitted in communal offerings, why would atonement from the Tzitz be needed?
Rav Nachman answers that the baraita about the Tzitz atoning refers only to individual offerings, not communal ones.
Alternatively, the Stam suggests that even if the baraita refers to communal offerings, it applies only to those without a fixed time, where impurity is not permitted.

items.text: Objection from the verse about the Tzitz bearing iniquity
items.text_en: Objection from the verse about the Tzitz bearing iniquity
items.desc_en: A baraita questions what iniquity the Tzitz bears, excluding piggul and notar which are already excluded. This further probes the scope of the Tzitz's atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that asks what iniquity the Tzitz (ציץ) bears, noting that piggul (פיגול) and notar (נותר) are already excluded by other verses, thereby challenging the scope of the Tzitz's atonement.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the earlier statement (that the ציץ only bears the sin of impurity that was permitted in the public domain) contradicts Rav Sheshet's view, and resolves that the issue is a Tannaitic dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the earlier statement (that the ציץ only bears the sin of impurity that was permitted in the public domain) contradicts Rav Sheshet's view.
The Gemara resolves that the issue is a Tannaitic dispute, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon holds that the ציץ effects atonement whether or not it is on the forehead.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Shimon vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Shimon vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Shimon holds the ציץ always effects atonement whether on the forehead or not, while Rabbi Yehuda holds it only effects atonement when on the forehead. Rabbi Shimon brings a proof from the High Priest on Yom Kippur, and Rabbi Yehuda counters that impurity was permitted for the public on that day.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the ציץ (frontlet) effects atonement only while it is on the forehead, but not when it is off.
Rabbi Shimon objects, citing the High Priest on Yom Kippur who atones without the ציץ on his forehead.
Rabbi Yehuda rejects the proof, arguing that on Yom Kippur impurity was permitted for the public, so the case is exceptional.
The Gemara infers that Rabbi Shimon holds impurity is merely pushed aside (דחויה) for the public, not fully permitted.

items.text: Abaye's distinction: broken vs. hanging ציץ
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction: broken vs. hanging ציץ
items.desc_en: Abaye clarifies that all agree a broken ציץ does not effect atonement; the dispute is only when the ציץ is hanging on a peg. Rabbi Yehuda requires it to be on the forehead based on the verse "על מצח... ונשא", while Rabbi Shimon derives from "תמיד לרצון" that it always effects atonement. The Gemara then explains that "תמיד" cannot mean always on the forehead, but rather always effects atonement.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that when the ציץ (frontlet) is broken, all agree it does not effect atonement, and the dispute is only when it is hanging on a peg.
Rabbi Yehuda requires the ציץ to be on the forehead based on the verse 'על מצח... ונשא' (on the forehead... and he shall bear).
Rabbi Shimon derives from 'תמיד לרצון לפני ה׳' (always for acceptance before the Lord) that the ציץ always effects atonement.
The Gemara questions what 'תמיד' (always) means, arguing it cannot mean the ציץ is always on the forehead since the priest must enter the bathroom and sleep.
The Gemara concludes that 'תמיד' (always) means the ציץ always effects atonement, rather than always being on the forehead.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's interpretation of "תמיד"
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's interpretation of "תמיד"
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda interprets the word "תמיד" and answers that it means one must not divert his attention from the ציץ, citing Rabbah bar Rav Huna's analogy to phylacteries.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Yehuda too, the verse says 'תמיד' — how does he interpret it?

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda interprets 'תמיד' as a requirement not to divert one's attention from the ציץ, citing Rabba bar Rav Huna's teaching that one must touch their תפילין (phylacteries) constantly, derived a קל וחומר (a fortiori) from the ציץ.

Rabbah bar Rav Huna supports this interpretation with a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: just as one must touch his תפילין (phylacteries) constantly, so too must one not divert attention from the ציץ (frontplate).

items.text: Kal va-chomer from the ציץ to תפילין
items.text_en: Kal va-chomer from the ציץ to תפילין
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the Torah requires constant attention to the ציץ, which contains only one mention of God's name, then תפילין, which contain many mentions, certainly require constant attention.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues a kal va-chomer (a fortiori argument): if the Torah demands constant attention to the ציץ (frontplate), which contains only one mention of God's name, then תפילין (phylacteries), which contain many mentions, certainly require constant attention.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's view on 'תמיד מרצה' and the verse 'על מצחו ונשא'
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's view on 'תמיד מרצה' and the verse 'על מצחו ונשא'
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses Rabbi Shimon's position that 'תמיד' indicates the ציץ always effects atonement, and explains that the phrase 'על מצחו ונשא' comes to establish the place of the ציץ. It then clarifies that for Rabbi Shimon, 'על מצחו' also teaches the place, and 'על מצחו ונשא' teaches that only a fit ציץ atones, excluding a broken one. For Rabbi Yehuda, the exclusion of a broken ציץ is derived from the words 'מצח' and 'מצחו'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's view that 'תמיד' indicates the ציץ always atones, given the verse 'על מצחו ונשא' which seems to limit atonement.
The Gemara answers that the phrase 'על מצחו ונשא' comes to establish the place of the ציץ on the forehead, not to limit atonement.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda derives the place of the ציץ, since he does not use 'על מצחו ונשא' for that purpose.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda derives the place from the word 'על מצחו' alone.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Shimon does not also derive the place from 'על מצחו' alone.
The Gemara answers that indeed Rabbi Shimon could derive the place from 'על מצחו' alone.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon does with the phrase 'על מצחו ונשא' if the place is already derived from 'על מצחו'.
Rabbi Shimon explains that 'על מצחו ונשא' teaches that only a ציץ fit for the forehead atones, excluding a broken one.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda derives the exclusion of a broken ציץ.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda derives the exclusion from the words 'מצח' and 'מצחו'.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon does not derive anything from the words 'מצח' and 'מצחו'.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute about sprinkling on the High Priest during his seven days
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute about sprinkling on the High Priest during his seven days
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir says that both the priest who burns the red heifer and the High Priest on Yom Kippur are sprinkled upon all seven days from all the sin-offerings available. Rabbi Yosei says only on the third and seventh days. Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim distinguishes: the priest who burns the heifer is sprinkled all seven days, but the High Priest on Yom Kippur only on the third and seventh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Tannaim in the baraita align with earlier Tannaitic positions regarding impurity in the public domain.

The baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir requires sprinkling all seven days for both the red heifer priest and the High Priest on Yom Kippur; Rabbi Yosei limits it to the third and seventh; Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim distinguishes between the two.

items.text: Initial assumption: Dispute about טומאה דחויה vs. היתר
items.text_en: Initial assumption: Dispute about טומאה דחויה vs. היתר
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the dispute is about whether טומאה is דחויה (pushed aside) or היתר (permitted) in public offerings. Rabbi Meir holds it is דחויה, requiring full purification, while Rabbi Yosei holds it is היתר, requiring only minimal sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei is about whether טומאה (ritual impurity) is דחויה (pushed aside) or היתר (permitted) in public offerings.

items.text: Rejection of initial assumption and new explanation: טבילה בזמנה מצוה
items.text_en: Rejection of initial assumption and new explanation: טבילה בזמנה מצוה
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the initial assumption, arguing that if Rabbi Yosei held טומאה is היתר, sprinkling would be unnecessary. Instead, all agree טומאה is דחויה. The real dispute is whether טבילה בזמנה מצוה (timely immersion is a mitzvah). Rabbi Meir holds it is, so he requires sprinkling all seven days to enable timely immersion; Rabbi Yosei holds it is not, so only third and seventh suffice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Yosei held that טומאה (impurity) is היתר (permitted) for the community, why would sprinkling be needed at all?
The Gemara resolves: all these Tannaim agree that טומאה (impurity) is דחויה (pushed aside) for the community, not permitted.

The Gemara explains the real dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that טבילה בזמנה מצוה (timely immersion is a mitzvah), so he requires sprinkling all seven days to enable timely immersion; Rabbi Yosei holds it is not, so only third and seventh suffice.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about טבילה בזמנה מצוה
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about טבילה בזמנה מצוה
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the new explanation by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei appears to hold that טבילה בזמנה מצוה (he allows immersion even when God's name is written on his skin). The Gemara resolves that in that baraita, the Tanna Kamma holds it is not a mitzvah, while Rabbi Yosei holds it is. So all the tannaim in our baraita agree that טבילה בזמנה מצוה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier claim that Rabbi Yosei holds that טבילה בזמנה אינה מצוה (immersion at its proper time is not a mitzvah), citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei permits immersion even when God's name is written on his skin.

The Gemara resolves that in the cited baraita, the Tanna Kamma holds that טבילה בזמנה אינה מצוה (immersion at its proper time is not a mitzvah), while Rabbi Yosei holds that it is a mitzvah; thus all the tannaim in our original baraita agree that טבילה בזמנה מצוה (immersion at its proper time is a mitzvah).

items.text: Final explanation: Dispute about comparing הזאה to טבילה
items.text_en: Final explanation: Dispute about comparing הזאה to טבילה
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the real dispute is whether we compare הזאה (sprinkling) to טבילה (immersion). Rabbi Meir holds we do, so sprinkling is required all seven days to parallel the seven-day immersion schedule. Rabbi Yosei holds we do not, so only third and seventh are needed. Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim holds we do not compare, but the priest who burns the heifer requires sprinkling all seven days as a special מעלה (stringency).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds we compare הזאה (sprinkling) to טבילה (immersion), requiring sprinkling all seven days; Rabbi Yosei holds we do not compare, so only third and seventh are needed.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim's position is inconsistent: if we compare, the High Priest on Yom Kippur should also require sprinkling all seven days; if we do not compare, the priest who burns the heifer should not require it either.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina holds we do not compare, but the priest who burns the heifer requires sprinkling all seven days as a special מעלה (stringency).

items.text: Transition to a baraita listing differences
items.text_en: Transition to a baraita listing differences
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a baraita that enumerates the differences between the priest who burns the red heifer and the High Priest on Yom Kippur, starting with the phrase 'אין בין... אלא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to whom does the rabbis' baraita go: 'There is no difference between the priest who burns the red heifer and the High Priest on Yom Kippur except...'

items.text: Distinction between separations for sanctity and purity
items.text_en: Distinction between separations for sanctity and purity
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between the High Priest's separation for sanctity (where other priests touch him) and for purity (where they do not). It attributes this distinction to either Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yosei, excluding Rabbi Chanina.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between the High Priest's separation for sanctity (where other priests touch him) and for purity (where they do not).
The Gemara asks which Tanna holds this view, suggesting either Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara excludes Rabbi Chanina, noting that his view would also include a third separation.

items.text: Objection about the fourth day's sprinkling
items.text_en: Objection about the fourth day's sprinkling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina objects: for days 1-3 and 5-7 there is a possible doubt (e.g., third day might be the actual third), but the fourth day has no possible doubt—it cannot be the third or seventh. The Gemara counters that sprinkling is not done on Shabbat, so the seven days exclude Shabbat; similarly, here the seven days exclude the fourth.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina objects that for days 1-3 and 5-7 there is a possible doubt (e.g., third day might be the actual third), but the fourth day has no possible doubt—it cannot be the third or seventh.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina asks: why is there any sprinkling on the fourth day at all, since it cannot be mistaken for either the third or seventh day?
The Gemara counters that sprinkling is not done on Shabbat, so the seven days exclude Shabbat; similarly, here the seven days exclude the fourth day.

items.text: Rava's ruling on separation timing
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on separation timing
items.desc_en: Rava rules: for the High Priest on Yom Kippur, separation depends on the fixed calendar (on the third of Tishrei). For the priest burning the red heifer, separation is on Thursday so that his fourth day falls on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that for the High Priest on Yom Kippur, whose separation depends on the fixed calendar, he must separate on the third of Tishrei.
Rava adds that for the priest burning the red heifer, whose timing is in our hands, we separate him on Thursday so that his fourth day falls on Shabbat.

items.text: The chamber Parhedrin and its name
items.text_en: The chamber Parhedrin and its name
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda questioning the name 'Parhedrin chamber', saying it was actually the 'Balvoti chamber'. The Gemara explains: originally called Balvoti, but because they gave money to the priesthood and changed it every twelve months like provincial governors (parhedrin), it was renamed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda questions the name 'Parhedrin chamber', asserting it was actually called the 'Balvoti chamber'.

The Gemara explains that originally it was called Balvoti, but because they paid the priesthood and replaced the high priest every twelve months like provincial governors (פַּרְהֶדְרִין), it was renamed Parhedrin.

items.text: Introduction to bakers' obligation
items.text_en: Introduction to bakers' obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: the Sages obligated bakers to separate only terumat ma'aser and challah. It explains that terumah gedolah is not required, as taught in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that the Sages obligated bakers to separate only תרומת מעשר (terumat maaser) and חלה (challah).
The Gemara explains that תרומה גדולה (terumah gedolah) is not required, as taught in a baraita.

items.text: Question about tithes in the second Temple period
items.text_en: Question about tithes in the second Temple period
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why only terumah gedolah was separated, but not first tithe or poor tithe, given the rule that the burden of proof is on the claimant. It then asks why second tithe was not separated and brought to Jerusalem to be eaten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the king saw only תרומה גדולה (the great priestly portion) being separated, and questions why first tithe and poor tithe were not separated.
The Gemara answers that regarding first tithe and poor tithe, the rule of המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה (the burden of proof is on the claimant) applies, so the king could not enforce separation.
The Gemara asks why second tithe was not separated and brought to Jerusalem to be eaten, since it is a positive commandment.

items.text: Ulla's answer about the parhedrin
items.text_en: Ulla's answer about the parhedrin
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that because the parhedrin (royal officers) would beat the people for twelve months, pressuring them to sell cheaply, the rabbis did not trouble them to separate tithes.

sub.desc_en: Ulla answers that because the royal officials (פרהדרין) pressured the people to sell their produce cheaply throughout the year, the rabbis did not impose the additional burden of bringing second tithe to Jerusalem.
The Gemara clarifies that the term פרהדרין means פורסי (Persian officials).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of a verse about the Temples
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of a verse about the Temples
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan interpreting a verse: 'Fear of the Lord adds days' refers to the first Temple which stood 410 years with only 18 high priests, while 'the years of the wicked are shortened' refers to the second Temple which stood 420 years but had over 300 high priests, showing that many served short terms due to corruption.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan interpreting the verse 'יראת ה' תוסיף ימים' (fear of the Lord adds days) as referring to the First Temple, which stood 410 years with only 18 high priests.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'ושנות רשעים תקצורנה' (years of the wicked will be cut short) as the Second Temple, which stood 420 years but had over 300 high priests, most serving less than a year.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta on the destruction of Shiloh
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta on the destruction of Shiloh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta states that Shiloh was destroyed because of two sins: forbidden sexual relations and disrespect for sacred offerings. He cites the verse about Eli's sons lying with the women at the Tent of Meeting, though Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in Rabbi Yochanan's name says that one who claims Eli's sons sinned is mistaken.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta asks why Shiloh was destroyed, and answers that it was due to two sins: גילוי עריות (forbidden sexual relations) and בזיון קדשים (disrespect for sacred offerings).
The Gemara cites the verse about Eli's sons lying with the women at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting as evidence for the sin of forbidden relations.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan's objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani cites Rabbi Yochanan who objects that anyone who says Eli's sons sinned is merely mistaken.
The gemara begins a digression with the word 'מִתּוֹךְ' (from within), likely introducing an explanation or continuation that is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening: The sin of delaying offerings and the disgrace of the sanctuary
