items.text_en: Opening: The sin of delaying offerings and the disgrace of the sanctuary
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a verse about the sons of Eli who disgraced the offerings, showing that delaying offerings is considered as if they had lain with the women. This introduces the theme of sin leading to destruction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the sin of Eli's sons who delayed the offerings, and the verse that equates this delay with lying with the women, introducing the theme of sin leading to destruction.

items.text: Why the First Temple was destroyed: Three cardinal sins
items.text_en: Why the First Temple was destroyed: Three cardinal sins
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the First Temple was destroyed because of idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed. It cites verses and interpretations: Rabbi Yonatan on the cramped bed, Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani on the narrow covering, and Rabbi Yitzchak on the seductive behavior of the daughters of Zion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the First Temple was destroyed.
The Gemara answers that it was due to idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed.
The Gemara cites a verse to support the charge of idolatry.
Rabbi Yonatan interprets the cramped bed as a metaphor for idolatry.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani interprets the narrow covering as a sign of divine displeasure.
The Gemara cites a verse to support the charge of sexual immorality.
Rabbi Yitzchak interprets the seductive behavior of the daughters of Zion.
The Gemara cites a verse to support the charge of bloodshed.

items.text: Why the Second Temple was destroyed: Baseless hatred
items.text_en: Why the Second Temple was destroyed: Baseless hatred
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts the Second Temple, where people engaged in Torah, mitzvot, and acts of kindness, yet it was destroyed because of baseless hatred. This teaches that baseless hatred is equivalent to the three cardinal sins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Second Temple was destroyed because of baseless hatred, despite the people's engagement in Torah, commandments, and acts of kindness, teaching that baseless hatred is equivalent to the three cardinal sins.

items.text: The wickedness of the First Temple generation and a question about baseless hatred
items.text_en: The wickedness of the First Temple generation and a question about baseless hatred
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the First Temple generation were wicked but trusted in God, so God brought three punishments. It then questions whether there was baseless hatred in the First Temple, citing a verse about people stabbing each other with their tongues, but limits this to the princes of Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the First Temple generation were wicked but trusted in God, so God brought three punishments corresponding to their three sins.
The Gemara questions whether there was indeed no baseless hatred in the First Temple, citing a verse about people stabbing each other with their tongues, as taught by Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara answers that the verse about tongue-stabbing applies only to the princes of Israel, not to the entire generation.

items.text: Debate: Were the earlier or later generations greater?
items.text_en: Debate: Were the earlier or later generations greater?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar state that the earlier generation's sin was revealed, so their end was revealed, while the later generation's sin was hidden. Rabbi Yochanan says the earlier generation's fingernail is better than the later generation's belly, but Resh Lakish argues the later generation is greater because they engaged in Torah despite subjugation. Rabbi Elazar is asked and points to the Temple as evidence.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar state that the earlier generation's sin was revealed, so their end was revealed, while the later generation's sin was hidden, so their end was not revealed.
Rabbi Yochanan asserts that the earlier generation's fingernail is better than the later generation's belly.
Resh Lakish objects, arguing that the later generation is greater because they engaged in Torah despite subjugation.
Rabbi Yochanan rejects Resh Lakish's argument, pointing to the Temple as evidence that the earlier generation was greater.
The gemara reports that Rabbi Elazar was asked whether the earlier or later generations were greater.
Rabbi Elazar answers by pointing to the Temple as evidence that the earlier generation was greater.

items.text: Resh Lakish's parable and the status of the Second Temple
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's parable and the status of the Second Temple
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish tells Rabba bar bar Chana that if they had all ascended like a wall in Ezra's time, they would be like silver, but now they are like doors. The Gemara questions how Resh Lakish could speak with Rabba bar bar Chana, given his stature, and Rav Papa resolves it. Rabbi Yochanan concludes that even if all had ascended, the Shekhinah would not have dwelt in the Second Temple, citing the verse about Yefet and Shem.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish tells Rabba bar bar Chana a parable: if they had all ascended like a wall in Ezra's time, they would be like silver, but now they are like doors.

The Gemara explains that 'cedar' refers to a 'sasmagor' (a type of wood), which Rabbi Abba identifies as a 'בת קול' (heavenly echo), citing a baraita that after the last prophets died, the Holy Spirit ceased but a בת קול remained.
The Gemara questions how Resh Lakish could speak with Rabba bar bar Chana, given that Resh Lakish would not even speak with Rabbi Eliezer, a leading sage, in the market.

Rav Papa resolves that a third person was between them (either Resh Lakish and Ze'iri, or Rabba bar bar Chana and Rabbi Elazar), and Rabbi Yochanan concludes that even if all had ascended, the Shekhinah would not have dwelt in the Second Temple, citing the verse about Yefet and Shem.

items.text: Shekhinah dwells only in tents of Shem
items.text_en: Shekhinah dwells only in tents of Shem
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that even though Yefet was blessed with beauty, the Divine Presence rests only in the tents of Shem, i.e., Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that despite Yefet's blessing of beauty, the Divine Presence (שכינה) dwells only in the tents of Shem.

items.text: Identifying the descendants of Yefet and other nations
items.text_en: Identifying the descendants of Yefet and other nations
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the nations descended from Yefet, including Persia, and then identifies other biblical places and giants. It cites traditions from Rav Yosef and others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the Persians (פרס) descend from Yefet, and cites the verse listing Yefet's sons.

The Gemara identifies each son of Yefet with a nation: Gomer is Germamia, Magog is Kandi, Madai is Macedonia, Yavan is as it sounds, Tubal is Beth Unayki, Meshekh is Musya, and Tiras is disputed between Rabbi Simai and the Rabbis.
Rav Yosef teaches that Tiras is Persia, resolving the dispute.
Rav Yosef identifies the places Sabta, Raamah, and Sabtecha as inner and outer Sakistan, with a hundred parasangs between them and a circumference of a thousand parasangs.
The Gemara identifies the cities in Nimrod's kingdom: Babel as itself, Erech as Orikhut, Akkad as Bashkar, and Calneh as Nofar Ninpi.
Rav Yosef identifies Ashur as Silak, and the cities Nineveh, Rehovot Ir, Kalach, and Resen as Perat d'Meishan, Perat d'Borsif, and Aktispon respectively.
The Gemara resolves a doubt: from the verse 'Nineveh was a great city of three days' walk', it is clear that Nineveh is the great city, not Resen.

A Tanna explains the names of the giants: Achiman means the most skilled among brothers, Sheshai makes the earth like pits, Talmai makes the earth like furrows; alternatively, they built cities; and 'y'lidei ha'anak' means they wear the sun as a necklace due to their height.

items.text: Rome will fall to Persia
items.text_en: Rome will fall to Persia
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi quotes Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) that Rome will fall to Persia, citing a verse about Edom.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Rabbi states that Rome will fall to Persia, citing a verse from Jeremiah.

items.text: Objection and resolution: 'young of the flock' refers to Persia
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: 'young of the flock' refers to Persia
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla objects that 'young of the flock' might refer to Greece. Rav Chaviva bar Sormaki reports a sage's answer: 'young of the flock' means the youngest brother, and Rav Yosef taught that Tiras is Persia.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla objects that 'young of the flock' (צעירי הצאן) could refer to Greece, not Persia, citing a verse about a goat (צפיר) as king of Greece.

sub.text: Rav Chaviva bar Sormaki's report of a sage's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Chaviva bar Sormaki's report of a sage's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Chaviva bar Sormaki reports a sage who explains that 'young of the flock' means the youngest brother (Tiras), and Rav Yosef taught that Tiras is Persia, thus resolving the objection.

items.text: A fortiori argument: Rome will fall to Persia
items.text_en: A fortiori argument: Rome will fall to Persia
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai that Rome will fall to Persia, using a kal vachomer from the First Temple.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan supports the prediction with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if the First Temple builders (Shem's descendants) fell to Persia, then the Second Temple builders (Persians) will cause Rome to fall.

items.text: Rav's counter: Persia will fall to Rome
items.text_en: Rav's counter: Persia will fall to Rome
items.desc_en: Rav states that Persia will fall to Rome. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object: builders fall to destroyers? Rav answers it is a royal decree. A baraisa supports this, citing that Persians destroyed synagogues, and quoting Rav Yehuda that the son of David will not come until Rome rules the world for nine months.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that Persia will fall to Rome.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object: builders (Persia, who built the Second Temple) fall to destroyers (Rome)?
Rav answers that it is a royal decree from God.
An alternative version says Rav added that the Persians themselves destroy synagogues, so they are not purely builders.
A baraita supports Rav: Persia will fall to Rome because they destroyed synagogues, and it is a royal decree that builders fall to destroyers.
Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that the son of David will not come until the wicked Roman kingdom rules the entire world for nine months, citing a verse.

items.text: Which chambers require a mezuzah?
items.text_en: Which chambers require a mezuzah?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that only the Parhedrin chamber had a mezuzah. Rabbi Yehuda objects that many chambers had dwelling space. The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: a house must be fit for summer and winter. Abaye challenges this with verses about summer and winter houses, and with the sukka, where Rabbi Yehuda requires a mezuzah. The Gemara questions whether the obligation is rabbinic or biblical regarding maaser.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that all chambers in the Temple lacked a mezuzah except the Parhedrin chamber, which had dwelling space for the High Priest.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that many chambers had dwelling space yet lacked a mezuzah, so the Parhedrin chamber's mezuzah was merely a rabbinic decree.
Rava explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: a house not fit for both summer and winter is not considered a permanent dwelling for the biblical obligation of mezuzah.
Abaye objects by citing the verse 'I will strike the winter house with the summer house,' but Rava responds that those are called 'winter house' and 'summer house,' not simply 'house.'
Abaye objects further from the sukka: Rabbi Yehuda obligates it in עירוב (eruv), mezuzah, and מעשר (tithe), even though a sukka is only used for seven days.
The Gemara questions whether the obligation of מעשר (tithe) in the sukka could be rabbinic, since eruv and mezuzah can be rabbinic, but מעשר (tithe) is biblically mandated.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: perhaps one might mistakenly exempt a liable dwelling and obligate an exempt one, leading to confusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that one might mistakenly exempt a liable dwelling and obligate an exempt one, leading to confusion.

items.text: Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that all agree the sukka is obligated during the seven days of Sukkot; the dispute is about the rest of the year, where the Rabbis decree due to the festival days, while Rabbi Yehuda does not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the objection by distinguishing the seven days of the festival from the rest of the year: all agree the sukkah is liable during the festival, and the dispute is only about the rest of the year, where the Rabbis decree a גזירה (precautionary extension) and Rabbi Yehuda does not.
Abaye explains that the dispute concerns the rest of the year: the Rabbis decree a prohibition due to the festival days, while Rabbi Yehuda does not.

items.text: Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rava objects: the mishna explicitly teaches about the sukka of the festival during the festival, implying the dispute applies even then.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah explicitly discusses the sukkah of the festival during the festival, contradicting Abaye's claim that the dispute is only about the rest of the year.

items.text: Rava's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rava's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rava proposes that all agree the sukka is exempt during the rest of the year; the dispute is only about the seven days of Sukkot. The sukka and the chamber have separate rationales.

sub.desc_en: Rava offers an alternative resolution: all agree the sukkah is exempt during the rest of the year, and the dispute is only about the seven days of the festival, but the sukkah and the chamber have separate rationales.

Rava explains that the sukka dispute follows each side's existing position: Rabbi Yehuda requires a permanent dwelling (דירת קבע) and thus obligates a mezuzah, while the Rabbis require a temporary dwelling (דירת עראי) and exempt it.

Rava explains that the chamber dispute follows a different rationale: the Rabbis consider coerced residence a valid dwelling (דירה), while Rabbi Yehuda does not, and the chamber's obligation is only rabbinic to avoid the appearance of the High Priest being imprisoned.

items.text: Rationale for the sukka
items.text_en: Rationale for the sukka
items.desc_en: The sukka's rationale: Rabbi Yehuda holds a sukka requires a permanent dwelling and is obligated in mezuzah; the Rabbis hold it is a temporary dwelling and exempt.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the sukkah's rationale
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the sukkah's rationale
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the sukkah's separate rationale is that Rabbi Yehuda holds a sukkah requires a permanent dwelling (דירת קבע) and is liable for a mezuzah, while the Rabbis hold it requires a temporary dwelling (דירת עראי) and is exempt.

items.text: Rationale for the chamber
items.text_en: Rationale for the chamber
items.desc_en: The chamber's rationale: the Rabbis consider a dwelling against one's will still a dwelling; Rabbi Yehuda does not, and the chamber was only instituted by rabbinic decree to prevent people from saying the High Priest is imprisoned.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the chamber's rationale
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the chamber's rationale
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the chamber's separate rationale is that the Rabbis hold a dwelling against one's will is still called a dwelling, while Rabbi Yehuda holds it is not called a dwelling, and the chamber's obligation is only rabbinic to prevent people from saying the High Priest is imprisoned.
The Rabbis hold that a dwelling against one's will (דירה בעל כרחה) is still considered a dwelling, so the chamber is a proper dwelling for the High Priest.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that a dwelling against one's will is not considered a dwelling, so the chamber is not a proper dwelling by Torah law.
The chamber was only instituted by rabbinic decree (מדרבנן) to prevent people from saying that the High Priest is imprisoned.

items.text: Transition to a new teaching
items.text_en: Transition to a new teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: who is the tanna of the teaching that the Rabbis taught?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita that the Rabbis taught regarding the chamber's obligation.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Exemption of gates except Nikanor
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Exemption of gates except Nikanor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all gates in the Temple lacked a mezuzah except for the Gate of Nikanor, which led to the Chamber of Parhedrin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all gates in the Temple lacked a mezuzah except for the Gate of Nikanor, which led to the Chamber of Parhedrin.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is this only Rabbanan?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is this only Rabbanan?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah aligns only with the Rabbis and not with Rabbi Yehuda, who might consider the gate itself a decree, but concludes that even according to Rabbi Yehuda it is one unified decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah reflects the view of the Rabbis and not Rabbi Yehuda, since Rabbi Yehuda might consider the gate itself a decree, and one does not make a decree upon a decree.
The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the entire matter is one single decree, so the Mishnah could align with his view.

items.text: Baraita: All gates require a mezuzah
items.text_en: Baraita: All gates require a mezuzah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that all gates—of houses, courtyards, provinces, and cities—have a mitzvah obligation for a mezuzah, based on the verse 'and you shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.'

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ' (in your gates) includes all types of gates — houses, courtyards, provinces, and towns — in the obligation of mezuzah.

items.text: Abaye's question about the gates of Mahoza
items.text_en: Abaye's question about the gates of Mahoza
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Safra why the Sages did not affix mezuzot on the gates of Mahoza. Rav Safra answers that they are only for strengthening the city gates. Abaye objects that even the city gate itself should require a mezuzah because it has a dwelling for the guard, as a synagogue with a dwelling for the caretaker is obligated. Abaye then answers that the reason is danger, citing a baraita that a public mezuzah is checked only once in a jubilee.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Safra why the Sages did not affix mezuzot on the gates of Mahoza.
Rav Safra answers that the gates are only for strengthening the city gates, not for dwelling.
Abaye objects that the city gate itself should require a mezuzah because it has a dwelling for the guard, citing a baraita about a synagogue with a caretaker's dwelling.
Abaye answers that the reason is danger, citing a baraita that a public mezuzah is checked only once in a jubilee.

items.text: Story of the mezuzah inspector and the danger
items.text_en: Story of the mezuzah inspector and the danger
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda relates a story of an inspector who checked mezuzot in Tzippori and was fined 1000 zuz by a Roman officer. The Gemara questions how this aligns with the principle that messengers of a mitzvah are not harmed, and answers that where danger is common, it is different, citing Samuel's fear of Saul.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda relates a story about a certain inspector who checked mezuzot in the upper market of Tzippori and was fined 1000 zuz by a Roman officer, illustrating the danger.
The Gemara questions the story, citing Rabbi Elazar's principle that those on a mission to perform a מצוה (commandment) are not harmed.
The Gemara answers that where danger is constant, the principle does not apply, citing the verse where Samuel feared Saul and God instructed him to take a calf as a pretext.

items.text: Rav Kahana's baraita and the dispute over 'ne'otot'
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's baraita and the dispute over 'ne'otot'
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana taught before Rav Yehuda that a barn, cattle shed, wood shed, and storehouse are exempt from mezuzah because women 'ne'otot' (bathe) there. Rav Yehuda objects that if the reason is bathing, then a standard one would be obligated, contradicting a baraita that a cattle shed is exempt. Rav Kahana then reinterprets 'ne'otot' as adorning, but a baraita says that a cattle shed where women adorn is obligated. The Gemara concludes that the dispute is between Tanna'im, citing a baraita with differing opinions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana teaches before Rav Yehuda that a barn, cattle shed, wood shed, and storehouse are exempt from mezuzah because women 'ne'otot' (bathe) there, explaining 'ne'otot' as washing.
Rav Yehuda objects that if the exemption is due to women bathing, then a standard cattle shed would be obligated, contradicting a baraita that a cattle shed is exempt from mezuzah.
Rav Kahana reinterprets 'ne'otot' as adorning, and states that even where women adorn, these buildings are exempt.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's objection to his own answer
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's objection to his own answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects that if 'ne'otot' means adorning, a baraita explicitly says a cattle shed where women adorn is obligated in mezuzah, contradicting his own statement.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute over 'ne'otot' is actually a dispute between Tanna'im, citing a baraita where some exempt and some obligate these buildings.

items.text: Baraita: Exemptions for bathhouses and similar
items.text_en: Baraita: Exemptions for bathhouses and similar
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a toilet, tannery, bathhouse, and mikveh, and places where women 'ne'otot' are exempt from mezuzah. The Gemara notes that Rav Kahana and Rav Yehuda each reconcile this with their own interpretations.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that a toilet, tannery, bathhouse, and immersion house, and places where women 'נְאוֹתוֹת' (bathe or adorn), are exempt from mezuzah.
The Gemara notes that Rav Kahana and Rav Yehuda each reconcile the baraita according to their own understanding.

items.text: Rav Kahana's reconciliation: 'ne'otot' as bathing
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's reconciliation: 'ne'otot' as bathing
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana reconciles the baraita with his view: the first baraita exempts standard barns etc., while the second baraita exempts bathhouses where women bathe. The Gemara questions why a bathhouse is mentioned separately, and explains that it teaches both a public and private bathhouse are exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reconciles the baraitot according to his view: the first baraita exempts standard barns etc., while the second baraita exempts bathhouses where women bathe (רוחצות).
The Gemara questions why a bathhouse is mentioned separately, since it is already included in the list of exempt structures.

The Gemara explains that the separate mention teaches both a public bathhouse (מרחץ דרבים) and a private bathhouse (מרחץ דיחיד) are exempt, countering the assumption that a private bathhouse might be obligated.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's reconciliation: 'ne'otot' as adorning
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's reconciliation: 'ne'otot' as adorning
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reconciles the baraita with his view: the first baraita exempts standard barns even if women adorn, while the second baraita exempts bathhouses even if women adorn, due to their foul odor.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reconciles by interpreting the baraita: 'בֵּיתֶךָ' exempts hay sheds etc. even if women adorn themselves, and the 'נְאוֹתוֹת' refers to adornment, but those places are exempt due to their filth.

items.text: Objection to Rav Yehuda from another baraita
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Yehuda from another baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Yehuda's claim that all agree standard barns are exempt, citing a baraita that includes barns, coops, straw sheds, and oil and wine storehouses as obligated for mezuzah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rav Yehuda's view that by default all agree they are exempt, citing a baraita that includes cattle sheds, chicken coops, hay sheds, and wine and oil storehouses as obligated in mezuzah.

items.text: Exclusions from mezuzah based on 'bayit'
items.text_en: Exclusions from mezuzah based on 'bayit'
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the word 'bayit' that only a house designated for dwelling is obligated in mezuzah, excluding gatehouses, porticos, and porches. It further excludes bathhouses, outhouses, and tanneries as not made for honor, and finally excludes the Temple Mount, chambers, and courtyards as sacred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by deriving from the word 'bayit' that only a house designated for dwelling is obligated in mezuzah, excluding gatehouses, porticos, and porches.

items.text: Baraita listing six gates exempt from mezuzah
items.text_en: Baraita listing six gates exempt from mezuzah
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda teaches a baraita listing six structures exempt from mezuzah: a straw house, cattle house, wood house, storehouse, the Median gate, a gate without a roof, and a gate less than ten handbreadths high. Rava objects that the baraita lists seven items, not six.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Yehuda teaches before Rava that six gates are exempt from mezuzah: straw barn, cattle barn, wood shed, storehouse, Median gate, uncovered gate, and gate under ten handbreadths.
Rava questions the count: you opened with six but ended with seven!
Rava answers that the Median gate is a tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Meir obligates a cupola in mezuzah, but Sages exempt; they agree that if it has ten handbreadths in its leg, it is obligated.
Abaye comments: universally, if it is ten high but lacks three in its leg, it is nothing; or if it has three in its leg but is not ten high, it is nothing.
The dispute is only when it is ten high, has three in its leg, but lacks four in its width, and has space to complete to four. Rabbi Meir holds one may carve to complete; Sages hold one may not.

items.text: Resolution: Median gate is a dispute
items.text_en: Resolution: Median gate is a dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda explains that the Median gate is subject to a tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding a gate with a curved top (kipa) that is ten handbreadths high but less than four wide. Rabbi Meir holds that we can carve out the sides to complete the width, obligating it in mezuzah, while the Sages disagree.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's answer to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's answer to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Median gate is subject to a tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding a gate with a curved top (kipa) that is ten handbreadths high but less than four wide, where Rabbi Meir holds we can carve out the sides to complete the width, obligating it in mezuzah, while the Sages disagree.

items.text: Synagogue, woman's house, and partners' house obligated in mezuzah
items.text_en: Synagogue, woman's house, and partners' house obligated in mezuzah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a synagogue, a woman's house, and a partners' house are obligated in mezuzah. The Gemara initially questions why this is not obvious, but explains that one might have thought 'your house' (ביתיך) excludes a woman's house and partners' houses. The Gemara rejects this, arguing that they also need life. Rava explains that 'your house' teaches that the mezuzah is placed on the right side upon entry, as a person first steps with the right foot.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that a synagogue, a woman's house, and a partners' house are obligated in mezuzah.
The Gemara questions why this ruling is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought 'your house' (בֵּיתֶךָ) excludes a woman's house and partners' houses, so the baraita teaches that they are included.
The Gemara objects that the exclusion could indeed be valid.

The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that the verse 'לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ יְמֵיכֶם' (so that your days may be multiplied) implies that all who need life are included, and women and partners also need life.
Rava explains that 'בֵּיתֶךָ' (your house) teaches that the mezuzah is placed on the right side upon entry, as a person first steps with the right foot.

items.text: Synagogue, partners' house, and woman's house susceptible to negaim
items.text_en: Synagogue, partners' house, and woman's house susceptible to negaim
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that a synagogue, partners' house, and woman's house are susceptible to biblical leprosy (negaim). The Gemara questions this, as one might have thought 'to whom the house belongs' (אשר לו הבית) excludes a woman and partners. The Gemara answers that the verse 'in a house of the land of your possession' includes them, and the word 'לו' teaches that one who hoards his house will be exposed when his house is emptied.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that a synagogue, partners' house, and woman's house are susceptible to negaim (biblical leprosy), and the Gemara notes that this is obvious but for the exclusion of 'לו' (to him).
The Gemara objects: perhaps the verse 'אשר לו הבית' (to whom the house belongs) indeed excludes a woman and partners.

The Gemara answers that the verse 'בבית ארץ אחזתכם' (in a house of the land of your possession) includes them, and the word 'לו' teaches that one who hoards his house will be exposed when his house is emptied, excluding one who lends his vessels to others.

items.text: Contradiction regarding synagogue's susceptibility to negaim resolved
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding synagogue's susceptibility to negaim resolved
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: a baraita says synagogues are not susceptible to negaim because they are not designated for an individual. The Gemara resolves this by attributing the conflicting views to Rabbi Meir and the Sages, or by distinguishing between a synagogue with a dwelling for the caretaker (obligated) and one without (exempt).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita explicitly states that synagogues are not susceptible to נגעים (leprosy of houses) because they are not designated for an individual.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the conflicting views to a tannaitic dispute: the baraita that obligates a synagogue in מזוזה (and thus in נגעים) follows Rabbi Meir, while the one that exempts it follows the Sages.

Alternatively, the Gemara resolves the contradiction even according to the Sages: the baraita that says a synagogue is susceptible to נגעים refers to a synagogue that has a residence for the caretaker, while the one that exempts it refers to a synagogue without such a residence.
A third resolution: both baraitot refer to a synagogue without a residence, yet they disagree about whether a synagogue itself is considered a dwelling for the purpose of נגעים.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between cities and villages regarding the High Priest's residence, asking why cities are excluded from leprosy laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between cities and villages regarding the High Priest's residence, asking why cities are excluded from leprosy laws.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and Rabbi Yehuda's qualification
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and Rabbi Yehuda's qualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that cities should be impure from leprosy based on a baraita, and cites Rabbi Yehuda who limits the exemption to the Temple Mount only, implying synagogues and study halls are susceptible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier distinction by asking whether synagogues in large cities are indeed not susceptible to leprosy impurity, citing a baraita that Jerusalem is exempt.
Rabbi Yehuda qualifies the exemption, stating he only heard that the Temple site is exempt, implying synagogues and study halls are susceptible.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that synagogues and study halls are susceptible even in large cities, contradicting the earlier distinction.
The Gemara emends Rabbi Yehuda's statement to say 'sacred site' (מקום מקודש) instead of 'Temple site' (מקום מקדש), thereby including synagogues and study halls in the exemption.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute: Tanna Kamma holds Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, while Rabbi Yehuda holds it was divided.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With regard to what principle do the first tanna and Rabbi Yehuda disagree?
The Gemara explains that the first tanna holds that Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that Jerusalem was divided among the tribes.

items.text: Supporting baraita on tribal portions
items.text_en: Supporting baraita on tribal portions
items.desc_en: A baraita details the portions of Judah and Benjamin in Jerusalem, including the altar on a strip from Judah's portion, and Benjamin's merit as host for the Divine Presence.

sub.desc_en: Introduces a baraita that supports the dispute about whether Jerusalem was divided among the tribes, by detailing the tribal portions of Judah and Benjamin.

The baraita specifies that the Temple Mount, chambers, and courtyards were in Judah's portion, while the Entrance Hall, Sanctuary, and Holy of Holies were in Benjamin's, with the altar built on a strip from Judah's portion.

The baraita concludes that Benjamin's distress over the strip led to his merit of hosting the Divine Presence, as alluded to in the verse 'וּבֵין כְּתֵפָיו שָׁכֵן' (and between his shoulders He rests).

items.text: Another baraita supporting no division and Abaye's inference
items.text_en: Another baraita supporting no division and Abaye's inference
items.desc_en: A baraita states houses in Jerusalem cannot be rented because they are not owned by individuals, supporting that Jerusalem was not divided; Abaye infers a custom of leaving a flask and hide for one's host.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that supports the view that Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, as houses there cannot be rented because they are not owned by individuals.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok adds that even beds were not rented in Jerusalem, further demonstrating that the city was not privately owned.
The baraita explains that because the hosts did not own the houses, they would take the hides of consecrated animals by force, as they were not legally entitled to them.
Abaye infers from this baraita that it is proper etiquette for a guest to leave his empty wine jug and hides for his host.

items.text: Challenge regarding villages and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge regarding villages and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that villages should also be exempt from leprosy based on a verse requiring conquest and division; it resolves that the Mishnah refers to a village suburb (מחוורתא) as previously taught.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that village synagogues should also be exempt from leprosy impurity, citing a baraita that requires conquest and division for the land to be subject to leprosy.
The Gemara resolves that the verse excludes houses not individually owned, and clarifies that the Mishnah's case refers to a village suburb (מחוורתא) as previously taught.

items.text: Question on inaugurating a substitute High Priest
items.text_en: Question on inaugurating a substitute High Priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a disqualification occurs after the morning tamid, with what service is the substitute High Priest inaugurated?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a disqualification occurs after the morning tamid, with what service is the substitute High Priest inaugurated?

items.text: Debate on the inauguration method
items.text_en: Debate on the inauguration method
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava suggests inauguration with the sash, but this depends on a dispute about the High Priest's sash; Abaye proposes wearing eight garments and performing a service with a fire pan, citing Rav Huna; Rav Pappa offers another view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava proposes that the replacement priest is inaugurated by wearing the belt (אבנט).

The Gemara notes that this works only for the view that the High Priest's belt is identical to the common priest's, but for the view that they differ, the belt cannot serve as a distinguishing inauguration.
Abaye suggests that the replacement dons the eight garments and performs a service with a fire pan, in accordance with Rav Huna.
Rav Huna states that a non-priest who turns over a limb on the altar with a fork is liable to death, indicating that this act constitutes Temple service.
Rav Pappa begins to offer an alternative view, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the baraita about service consecrating vessels
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the baraita about service consecrating vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as service consecrates vessels, so too the service of a priest consecrates him for his role, supporting the earlier point about the deputy high priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as service consecrates vessels, so too the service of a priest consecrates him for his role, supporting the earlier point about the deputy high priest.

items.text: Dispute over the material of the ordinary priest's belt
items.text_en: Dispute over the material of the ordinary priest's belt
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports a dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon: one says the ordinary priest's belt is of kilayim (wool and linen), the other says of butz (linen). The Gemara attempts to identify who said what, citing a baraita that distinguishes between the high priest and ordinary priest only by the belt, and clarifies that the dispute applies specifically to Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports a dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon over whether the ordinary priest's belt is of kilayim (wool and linen) or of butz (linen).

The Gemara attempts to conclude that Rabbi is the one who said the belt is of kilayim, citing a baraita that distinguishes between the high priest and ordinary priest only by the belt according to Rabbi.
The Gemara objects: if the baraita refers to ordinary days, there are many differences between the high priest and ordinary priest, not just the belt.
The Gemara answers that the baraita must refer to Yom Kippur, when the high priest wears only four garments like an ordinary priest.
Some reject this, saying the baraita refers to ordinary days but only to garments that are common to both priests.

items.text: Ravin's resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Ravin's resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Ravin clarifies that all agree the high priest's belt on Yom Kippur is of butz, and on other days of kilayim; the dispute is only about the ordinary priest's belt, whether on Yom Kippur or other days.

sub.desc_en: Ravin resolves the dispute by clarifying that all agree the high priest's belt on Yom Kippur is of butz and on other days of kilayim, while the dispute is only about the ordinary priest's belt on either occasion.

items.text: Derivation of the belt and headplate for ash removal
items.text_en: Derivation of the belt and headplate for ash removal
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'yilbash' that the belt and headplate are needed for ash removal. Rabbi Dosa says it includes the high priest's garments for Yom Kippur for an ordinary priest. Rabbi rejects both, arguing that the high priest's belt is not the same as the ordinary priest's, and that one cannot use garments from a higher sanctity for a lower one; instead, 'yilbash' includes the worn-out garments.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak introduces a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'יִלְבַּשׁ' that the belt and headplate are needed for ash removal.
Rabbi Dosa argues that 'יִלְבַּשׁ' includes the high priest's Yom Kippur garments, which are fit for an ordinary priest.
Rabbi raises the first objection: the high priest's Yom Kippur belt is not the same as the ordinary priest's belt.
Rabbi raises the second objection: garments used for a higher sanctity cannot be used for a lower sanctity.
Rabbi resolves that 'יִלְבַּשׁ' actually includes the worn-out garments (שחקין).

items.text: Rabbi Dosa's consistent view on garment storage
items.text_en: Rabbi Dosa's consistent view on garment storage
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Dosa follows his own reasoning, as he holds that garments used on Yom Kippur must be stored and not reused the next year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Dosa follows his own consistent reasoning, citing a baraita where he holds that Yom Kippur garments must be stored and not reused the next year.

items.text: Dispute about the deputy high priest's status
items.text_en: Dispute about the deputy high priest's status
items.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir says the first high priest returns to service and the deputy assumes all high priestly duties; Rabbi Yossi says the deputy is unfit for either high or ordinary priesthood. Rabbi Yossi cites a precedent with Yosef ben Ilem, and the reasons are enmity and the principle of ascending in sanctity. The Gemara begins to cite Rabbi Yochanan's statement.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Meir's position: if the high priest becomes disqualified and a deputy is appointed, the first returns to service and the deputy assumes all high priestly duties.
Rabbi Yossi states his dissenting view: the first high priest returns, but the deputy is unfit for either high or ordinary priesthood.

Rabbi Yossi cites a precedent with Yosef ben Ilem in Tzippori, where the sages ruled the deputy unfit for either role due to enmity (אֵיבָה) and the principle of ascending in sanctity (מעלין בקודש ולא מורידין).

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a statement by Rabbi Yochanan, transmitted by Rabbah bar bar Chanah, which will continue the discussion.

items.text: Rav's ruling on Rabbi Yosei's opinion
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on Rabbi Yosei's opinion
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav stating the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, who agrees that if the first wife dies, the second wife may serve. The Gemara questions the obviousness of this ruling and explains it precludes the assumption that the second wife is a rival to the living first wife.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav stating the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, who agrees that if the first wife dies, the second wife may serve.
The Gemara questions the obviousness of Rav's ruling.
The Gemara explains that Rav's statement precludes the assumption that the second wife is a rival (צָרָה) to the living first wife.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's position and the Rabbis' objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's position and the Rabbis' objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda requires preparing a second wife for the High Priest, while the Rabbis argue that impurity is common but death is not. The Gemara notes that the Rabbis' objection is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that a second wife must be prepared for the High Priest in case his first wife dies.
The Rabbis object that while טומאה (ritual impurity) is common, death is not, so preparing a second wife is unnecessary.
The Gemara affirms that the Rabbis' objection to Rabbi Yehuda is valid.

items.text: The Rabbis' argument and Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.text_en: The Rabbis' argument and Rabbi Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that if they prepare a second wife for every possible death, there is no end. Rabbi Yehuda responds that they only fear one death, not two. The Gemara questions why the Rabbis don't fear two deaths.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis object to Rabbi Yehuda that if they prepare a second wife for every possible death, there is no end to the preparations.
The Gemara notes that the Rabbis' objection is valid, then explains Rabbi Yehuda's response: they only fear one death, not two.
The Gemara questions the Rabbis: if there is reason to fear, why not fear even two deaths?

items.text: The Rabbis' self-justification and the Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: The Rabbis' self-justification and the Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Rabbis don't apply their own logic to themselves. They respond that the High Priest is vigilant, but the Gemara counters that if so, why prepare another priest at all? The Rabbis explain that the preparation itself makes him even more vigilant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Rabbis do not apply their own logic to themselves regarding the need for a substitute wife.
The Rabbis respond that the High Priest is vigilant (זריז) and therefore does not need a substitute wife.
The Gemara objects that if the High Priest is vigilant, why do they prepare another priest at all?
The Rabbis explain that the very preparation of a substitute makes the High Priest even more vigilant.

items.text: The problem of two wives from the Torah
items.text_en: The problem of two wives from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: the Torah says 'his house' (בֵּיתוֹ), implying one wife, not two. Even if he betroths the second wife, she is not his house until he marries her, leading to two houses, which contradicts the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the arrangement of a second wife is feasible, since the Torah says 'his house' (בֵּיתוֹ) implying one wife, and if he marries the second, he would have two houses, contradicting the verse.

items.text: Attempted solution: conditional divorce
items.text_en: Attempted solution: conditional divorce
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests he divorces the second wife, but the problem returns. It then proposes a conditional divorce: 'This is your get on condition that you die.' But if she doesn't die, he has two houses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if he divorces the second wife, the original problem of having no wife returns.
The Gemara proposes a conditional divorce: 'This is your get on condition that you die.'
The Gemara objects that if she does not die, he will have two houses, violating the verse.

items.text: Alternative condition: 'on condition that you do not die'
items.text_en: Alternative condition: 'on condition that you do not die'
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a condition that she not die. If she doesn't die, she is divorced; if she dies, the first wife remains. But if the second wife doesn't die and the first dies, he is left without a wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative condition: the husband gives the get (bill of divorce) on condition that the second wife does not die.
The Gemara objects that if the second wife does not die and the first wife dies, the husband is left without a wife, defeating the purpose of the arrangement.

items.text: Condition: 'on condition that one of you dies'
items.text_en: Condition: 'on condition that one of you dies'
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a condition that one of them dies, ensuring one wife remains. But if neither dies, he still has two houses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a conditional divorce where the condition is that one of the wives dies, but objects that if neither dies, the high priest still ends up with two houses.

items.text: Rava's principle on conditional divorce
items.text_en: Rava's principle on conditional divorce
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether such a conditional divorce is valid, citing Rava's ruling that a condition tied to the husband's lifetime is not a valid divorce (כְּרִיתוּת). However, a condition tied to another person's lifetime is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether such a conditional divorce is valid at all.
The Gemara cites Rava's principle that a condition tied to the husband's lifetime is not a valid divorce (כְּרִיתוּת).
Rava distinguishes that a condition tied to another person's lifetime is a valid divorce (כְּרִיתוּת).

items.text: Final condition: 'on condition that your friend does not die'
items.text_en: Final condition: 'on condition that your friend does not die'
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a condition that the other wife does not die. If the friend doesn't die, she is divorced; if the friend dies, the first wife remains. But if the friend dies mid-service, the situation is revealed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a conditional divorce: the husband says 'this is your get on condition that you do not die,' so if the wife does not die she is divorced, and if she dies the first wife remains.
The Gemara objects: if the second wife does not die but the first wife dies, the high priest is left without a wife at all, which is problematic.
The Gemara proposes a different condition: 'on condition that one of you dies,' so that whichever wife dies, the other remains.
The Gemara objects: if neither wife dies, the high priest ends up with two wives, violating the verse 'and he shall atone for himself and for his house' — not for two houses.

sub.text: Gemara's objection based on Rava's principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection based on Rava's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects further: such a conditional get is invalid because it lacks complete severance (כריתות), citing Rava's ruling that a condition dependent on the husband's lifetime is not a valid divorce.

The Gemara resolves: the husband says 'this is your get on condition that your friend does not die,' so if the friend does not die she is divorced; if the friend dies mid-service, the situation is revealed and the first wife remains.

items.text: First attempt to avoid serving in two houses
items.text_en: First attempt to avoid serving in two houses
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a conditional divorce that would prevent the High Priest from serving in two houses, but the condition could fail if the co-wife dies, leaving him without a house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if the divorce is retroactive, the condition could fail if the co-wife dies, leaving the High Priest without a house.

items.text: Second attempt with two conditions
items.text_en: Second attempt with two conditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes divorcing both wives with conditions that could both be fulfilled, but if both conditions are met, both divorces take effect and he is left without a house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes divorcing both wives with two conditions that could both be fulfilled, leaving him without a house.

items.text: Third attempt with opposite conditions
items.text_en: Third attempt with opposite conditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes conditions that ensure only one divorce takes effect at a time, but raises the concern that the co-wife might die mid-service, causing retroactive service in two houses. The solution is for the priest to enter the synagogue preemptively.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the concern that if the co-wife dies mid-service, the priest might retroactively perform service in two houses.
The Gemara answers that the priest can preemptively enter the synagogue to make the divorce retroactively effective before the co-wife's death.

items.text: Rav Asi's objection from yevamot
items.text_en: Rav Asi's objection from yevamot
items.desc_en: Rav Asi (or Rav Avira) objects: if we are concerned about serving in two houses, then two yevamot from one house should not be able to undergo yibbum, but the Torah includes them via the repetition of 'yevimto'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi (or Rav Avira) objects: if the concern about serving in two houses applies, then two yevamot from one house should not undergo yibbum, but the Torah includes them via the repetition of 'yevimto'.

items.text: Ravina's objection from an arusah
items.text_en: Ravina's objection from an arusah
items.desc_en: Ravina (or Rav Sherevya) objects: if we are concerned, then an arusah (betrothed woman) should not undergo yibbum, but the Torah includes her via the word 'hachutzah'.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects: if we are concerned about the possibility of the wife's death, then an arusah (betrothed woman) should not undergo yibbum, but the Torah includes her via the word 'hachutzah'.

items.text: Baraita on the High Priest as an onen
items.text_en: Baraita on the High Priest as an onen
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a High Priest may sacrifice while an onen but may not eat. Rabbi Yehuda says 'all day'. Rava explains this means he may be brought from his house to the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: a High Priest may sacrifice while an onen but may not eat; Rabbi Yehuda adds 'all day'.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda means by 'all day'.
Rava explains that Rabbi Yehuda's statement only permits bringing the High Priest from his house to the Temple on the day of his relative's death.

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: according to Rabbi Yehuda, if the priest is already at the altar and hears of a death, he must leave immediately, so how can we bring him from his house?

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rava's explanation: according to Rabbi Yehuda, if the priest is already at the altar and hears of a death, he must leave immediately, so how can Rava say we bring him from his house?

items.text: Rava's revised explanation
items.text_en: Rava's revised explanation
items.desc_en: Rava reinterprets 'all day' to mean something else, likely that the High Priest may sacrifice all day long even while an onen, not that he is brought from his house.

sub.desc_en: Rava reinterprets the phrase 'כל היום' (all day) in Rabbi Yehuda's statement, rejecting his earlier explanation that it refers to bringing the High Priest from his house.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's decree and the response
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's decree and the response
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges Rava: Rabbi Yehuda decrees a replacement wife lest the High Priest's wife die, but does not fear he will eat on Yom Kippur, so why here does he fear he will eat? Rava distinguishes: on Yom Kippur everyone fasts, so he won't eat, but here everyone eats, so he might. The Gemara then questions whether the High Priest would be distracted by mourning if his wife dies, concluding that even if the formal status of aninut does not apply, he would still be distracted.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's challenge to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's challenge to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges Rava: Rabbi Yehuda decrees a replacement wife lest the High Priest's wife die, but does not fear he will eat on Yom Kippur, so why here does he fear he will eat?
Rava distinguishes: on Yom Kippur everyone fasts, so he won't eat, but here everyone eats, so he might.
The Gemara questions whether the formal status of אנינות (mourning) would apply to the High Priest if his wife dies, given that she is divorced.
The Gemara concludes that even if the formal status of אנינות does not apply, the High Priest would still be distracted by mourning.

items.text: Mishnah: The High Priest's service during the seven days
items.text_en: Mishnah: The High Priest's service during the seven days
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that during the seven days before Yom Kippur, the High Priest performs the daily temple services—sprinkling blood, burning incense, trimming lamps, and offering the head and leg. On other days, he may offer if he wishes, as he takes a portion first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the High Priest's daily service during the seven days before Yom Kippur and his privilege to offer first on other days.

items.text: Gemara identifies the Tanna as not Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara identifies the Tanna as not Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a pure person upon whom sprinkling water falls becomes impure, thus the High Priest could not perform service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah.
Rav Chisda answers that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a pure person upon whom sprinkling water falls becomes impure, so the High Priest could not perform service.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages
items.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'and the pure one shall sprinkle upon the impure'—Rabbi Akiva expounds that sprinkling makes the pure impure and the impure pure, while the Sages say this applies only to items susceptible to impurity.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'וְהִזָּה הַטָּהוֹר עַל הַטָּמֵא' (and the pure one shall sprinkle upon the impure) — Rabbi Akiva expounds that sprinkling makes the pure impure and the impure pure, while the Sages say this applies only to items susceptible to impurity.

items.text: Supporting Mishnah for the Sages' view
items.text_en: Supporting Mishnah for the Sages' view
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: if one intended to sprinkle on an animal but sprinkled on a person, if there is enough hyssop, he repeats; if he intended for a person but sprinkled on an animal, he does not repeat—this aligns with the Sages' distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that distinguishes between sprinkling on an animal versus a person, supporting the Sages' view that the verse applies only to things that can receive טומאה (ritual impurity).

items.text: Scriptural basis for Rabbi Akiva and the Sages' rebuttal
items.text_en: Scriptural basis for Rabbi Akiva and the Sages' rebuttal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva derives his view from the extra phrase 'upon the impure,' implying that sprinkling affects the pure. The Sages counter that the verse teaches about items susceptible to impurity, and a kal vachomer would make the pure impure. Rabbi Akiva responds with Solomon's saying about wisdom being distant. The Sages then explain the verse teaches that the sprinkler and the one sprinkled upon are pure, but one who touches them is impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what scriptural basis leads Rabbi Akiva to his position, and explains that the extra phrase 'עַל הַטָּמֵא' (upon the impure) implies that sprinkling on the impure purifies, while sprinkling on the pure defiles.
The Sages counter that the verse teaches about items susceptible to impurity, and a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) would make the pure impure.
Rabbi Akiva responds by citing Solomon's saying that wisdom is distant, implying that the kal vachomer is not applicable here.
The Sages explain that the verse teaches that the sprinkler and the one sprinkled upon are pure, but one who touches them is impure.

items.text: Clarification of 'the sprinkler' in the verse
items.text_en: Clarification of 'the sprinkler' in the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the sprinkler can be pure, citing a verse that says 'the sprinkler of the water of impurity shall wash his garments.' It resolves that 'sprinkler' here means 'carrier,' and the term 'sprinkler' teaches that sprinkling requires a minimum measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the sprinkler can be pure, citing the verse 'וּמַזֵּה מֵי הַנִּדָּה יְכַבֵּס בְּגָדָיו' (the sprinkler of the water of impurity shall wash his garments), and rejects the interpretation that 'sprinkler' means 'one who touches.'
The Gemara resolves that 'מַזֶּה' (sprinkler) here means 'carrier,' and the term 'מַזֶּה' teaches that sprinkling requires a minimum measure (שִׁיעוּר הַזָּאָה).

items.text: Discussion on the required measure for sprinkling
items.text_en: Discussion on the required measure for sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the view that sprinkling requires a measure: for one who holds it does not, the Gemara explains that this applies to sprinkling on a person, but in a vessel a measure is needed, as per a Mishnah stating the water must be sufficient for dipping the hyssop.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: the verse's use of 'מזה' (sprinkler) to teach the measure requirement works only for one who holds that sprinkling requires a measure; for one who holds it does not, what can be said?

The Gemara answers: even for one who holds that sprinkling does not require a measure, that applies only to sprinkling on a person (אגבא דגברא), but for sprinkling from a vessel (במנא) a measure is needed, as per the Mishnah that the water must be sufficient for dipping the hyssop.

items.text: Abaye's resolution of the Mishnah with Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution of the Mishnah with Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that even according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds the High Priest performs all services on Yom Kippur, the Mishnah's order (incense before lamp-trimming) is possible because he immerses at the end of the day and then offers incense and trims lamps.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the Mishnah's order by explaining that even Rabbi Akiva, who holds the High Priest performs all services on Yom Kippur, can accommodate the sequence because the priest immerses at day's end and then offers incense and trims lamps.

items.text: Gemara's question from a baraita on the order
items.text_en: Gemara's question from a baraita on the order
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah implies incense precedes lamp-trimming, but a baraita lists the order as: one who wins the inner altar's ash removal, then the lamp, then the incense — contradicting the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah implies incense precedes lamp-trimming, but a baraita lists the order as inner altar ash removal, then lamp, then incense.

items.text: Rav Huna's attribution and its refutation
items.text_en: Rav Huna's attribution and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna suggests the Mishnah is taught by Rabbi Shimon of the Mitspah, but a baraita shows Rabbi Shimon reverses the order of the daily offering's blood application, contradicting the Mishnah's order, so this attribution fails.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna proposes that the Mishnah's order of the daily offering (תמיד) is taught by Rabbi Shimon of the Mitspah.
The gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon is known to reverse the order of blood application in the daily offering, contradicting the Mishnah's order.
A baraita confirms that Rabbi Shimon reverses the order of the daily offering's blood application, proving he cannot be the Mishnah's author.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative attribution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative attribution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan attributes the Mishnah (Seder Yoma) to Rabbi Shimon of the Mitspah, but then the Gemara raises a contradiction between this Mishnah and another Mishnah about the order of the daily lottery.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by attributing the entire Mishnah of Seder Yoma to Rabbi Shimon of the Mitspah.

items.text: Contradiction between two Mishnayot on the order
items.text_en: Contradiction between two Mishnayot on the order
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where the second lottery includes ash removal from the inner altar and lamp, while the third lottery is for incense — implying lamp precedes incense, contradicting Seder Yoma.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara juxtaposes two Mishnayot on the daily service order: the second lottery includes inner altar ash removal and lamp, and the third lottery is for incense – implying lamp precedes incense, contradicting the established 'Seder Yoma' order.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: two lamps vs. five lamps
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: two lamps vs. five lamps
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the trimming of two lamps (which occurs before incense) and the trimming of five lamps (which occurs after incense).

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the trimming of two lamps (which occurs before incense) and the trimming of five lamps (which occurs after incense).

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution: Abba Shaul vs. Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution: Abba Shaul vs. Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Abaye elsewhere says the daily offering's blood interrupts the lamp-trimming, not incense. It resolves that the dispute is between Abba Shaul (who holds lamp-trimming precedes incense) and the Rabbis (who hold incense precedes lamp-trimming), citing a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Abaye elsewhere states that the blood of the daily offering (דם התמיד) interrupts the lamp-trimming, not the incense (קטורת).
The Gemara answers that the contradiction is resolved by attributing the two positions to different Tannaim: Abba Shaul (אבא שאול) and the Rabbis (רבנן).
A baraita is cited: one should not trim the lamps before offering incense; Abba Shaul says one trims first and then offers incense.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of Abba Shaul's position.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'בַּבֹּקֶר בַּבֹּקֶר בְּהֵיטִיבוֹ אֶת הַנֵּרוֹת' (Exodus 30:7) places lamp-trimming before incense, supporting Abba Shaul.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of the Rabbis' position that incense precedes lamp-trimming.

items.text: Gemara's question on the order of ketoret and lamp trimming
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the order of ketoret and lamp trimming
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's implication that the ketoret is offered during the trimming of the lamps. It draws an analogy to the evening service where the ketoret is offered after lighting the lamps, citing a baraita that the lamps must burn all night. It concludes that the Torah requires the ketoret to be offered at the time of lighting, not trimming.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's implication that the ketoret is offered during the trimming of the lamps, drawing an analogy to the evening service where the ketoret is offered after lighting the lamps.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the lamps must burn all night, indicating that lighting the candelabrum is the final daily Temple service.
The Gemara concludes that the Torah requires the ketoret to be offered at the time of lighting, not trimming, resolving the analogy.

items.text: Abba Shaul's distinction
items.text_en: Abba Shaul's distinction
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul responds that the case is different because the verse says 'oto' (it), implying a unique rule for the evening ketoret.

sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul responds that the case of the afternoon incense is different because the verse includes the exclusionary term 'אותו' (it), implying a unique rule for that time.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution: mishnah as Rabbanan, lottery as Abba Shaul
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution: mishnah as Rabbanan, lottery as Abba Shaul
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by attributing the mishnah's first part to the Rabbanan and the lottery to Abba Shaul. He then notes that the mishnah's end (bringing the tamid) follows the Rabbanan, creating a mixed mishnah, which he accepts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by attributing the mishnah's first part to the Rabbanan and the lottery to Abba Shaul.
The Gemara objects that the end of the mishnah (bringing the tamid) follows the Rabbanan, creating a mixed mishnah.
Rav Pappa accepts that the mishnah is mixed: the beginning and end follow the Rabbanan, while the middle follows Abba Shaul.

items.text: Abaye's alternative explanation and Rav Pappa's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative explanation and Rav Pappa's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye rejects Rav Pappa's mixed mishnah and explains that the mishnah merely teaches the order of the service, not a dispute. Rav Pappa counters that the mishnah explicitly lists trimming two lamps first, then five, which implies a sequence that Abaye dismisses as mere instruction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Abaye does not accept Rav Pappa's position because he would not posit a mixed mishnah with different authorities in its sections.
The Gemara asks why Rav Pappa does not adopt Abaye's explanation instead.
Rav Pappa objects that the mishnah explicitly teaches trimming two lamps first and then five, implying a sequence that Abaye's explanation would dismiss.
Abaye responds that the mishnah is merely instructing the order of the service, and it repeats the sequence for teaching purposes.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah's practice
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah who changes the order of blood placement on the altar for the tamid, giving the western horn before the southern one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah's practice of changing the order of blood placement on the tamid altar, giving the western horn before the southern one, and then asks for the reason.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation via the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation via the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Shimon's practice based on a verse that treats the tamid's accompanying goat as a chatat, requiring a mixture of olah and chatat procedures. The Gemara questions why not give four applications, and answers that blood cannot atone twice, and that the verse forces the analogy.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing the school of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing the school of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Shimon's practice by citing a verse that treats the goat accompanying the tamid as a chatat, requiring the priest to perform the blood application with a mixture of olah and chatat procedures.

The Gemara questions why Rabbi Shimon's practice involves only two applications that count as two each, rather than four applications that count as four each, to fully satisfy both the olah and chatat requirements.

The Gemara answers that blood cannot atone twice (so four applications are impossible), and that the verse forces the analogy between the goat and the chatat, so the practice is accepted as a divine decree.

items.text: Further objections and resolution
items.text_en: Further objections and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the blood could be placed partly above and partly below, citing examples of such sprinkling. Rav Yehuda explains the 'like a whip' method, and another baraita about seven sprinklings on the altar's top is raised. Ravah bar Sheila rejects the comparison, concluding the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the blood could be placed partly below and partly above, citing the principle of פיסוק מתנות (discrete sprinklings).
The Gemara objects that we do not find blood half above and half below, but then cites a baraita that does exactly that.
Rav Yehuda explains that the sprinkling is done like a whip (כמצליף), meaning a single stroke that covers both above and below.
The Gemara objects further, citing a baraita about seven sprinklings on the top of the altar, suggesting a different method.
Ravah bar Sheila rejects the comparison, concluding the discussion.

items.text: Opening citation: the altar's side
items.text_en: Opening citation: the altar's side
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse describing the altar's appearance, comparing it to the clear sky, to introduce the discussion about the placement of blood on the altar corners.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse describing the altar's appearance, comparing it to the clear sky, to introduce the discussion about the placement of blood on the altar corners.

items.text: Why burnt-offering before sin-offering
items.text_en: Why burnt-offering before sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the burnt-offering is placed on the altar before the sin-offering, and answers that since the burnt-offering is entirely consumed, it takes precedence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the burnt-offering is placed on the altar before the sin-offering, suggesting the reverse order.
The Gemara answers that since the burnt-offering is entirely consumed, it takes precedence and is placed first.

items.text: Why northeast before southwest
items.text_en: Why northeast before southwest
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the northeast corner is used before the southwest, and explains that the southwest corner lacks a foundation, so the burnt-offering, which requires a foundation, cannot be placed there first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the northeast corner is sprinkled before the southwest, suggesting an alternative order.
The Gemara answers that the burnt-offering requires a foundation, and the southeast corner lacks one, so the northeast corner is used first.

items.text: Why not start with southwest
items.text_en: Why not start with southwest
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the southwest corner is not taken first, and answers that since one always turns to the right when going east, the first corner encountered is the northeast.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the southwest corner is not taken first, and answers that since one always turns to the right when going east, the first corner encountered is the northeast.
The Gemara answers that since one always turns to the right when going east, the first corner encountered is the northeast.

items.text: Proof that the Torah applies sin-offering rites to burnt-offering
items.text_en: Proof that the Torah applies sin-offering rites to burnt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the possibility that the Torah might apply burnt-offering rites to the sin-offering instead, but rejects this based on the verse 'עַל עוֹלַת הַתָּמִיד יֵעָשֶׂה', which indicates that sin-offering rites are applied to the burnt-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the assumption that the Torah applies sin-offering rites to the burnt-offering, suggesting the opposite might be true.
The Gemara rejects the alternative interpretation, citing the verse 'עַל עוֹלַת הַתָּמִיד יֵעָשֶׂה' to prove that sin-offering rites are applied to the burnt-offering.

items.text: Mishnah: the chamber of lambs
items.text_en: Mishnah: the chamber of lambs
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about the appointed one instructing to bring a lamb from the chamber of lambs, and describes the location of that chamber in the northwest corner, along with three other chambers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah about the appointed one instructing to bring a lamb from the Chamber of the Lambs, and describes the location of that chamber in the northwest corner, along with three other chambers.

items.text: Contradiction: four chambers of the fire-place
items.text_en: Contradiction: four chambers of the fire-place
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from another source that describes four chambers in the fire-place house, with two in the sacred area and two in the non-sacred, and identifies the southwest chamber as the chamber of lambs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that describes four chambers in the Hall of the Hearth, with the southwest chamber serving as the Chamber of the Sacrificial Lambs, conflicting with the mishna's location.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rav Huna's identification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rav Huna's identification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes four chambers in the corners of the Women's Courtyard. Rav Huna states that the author of Midos is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the four chambers in the corners of the Women's Courtyard and their functions.
Rav Huna identifies the author of the Mishnah of Midos as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

items.text: Supporting baraita from Midos
items.text_en: Supporting baraita from Midos
items.desc_en: A baraita from Midos is cited, detailing the four chambers in the Women's Courtyard and their functions, including the Nazirites' chamber, the wood chamber, the lepers' chamber, and the chamber for wine and oil. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov forgets the function of the fourth chamber, and Abba Shaul identifies it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes the Women's Courtyard and the first two chambers: the Nazirites' chamber and the wood chamber.
The baraita continues with the lepers' chamber and the fourth chamber, which Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov forgets and Abba Shaul identifies as the chamber for wine and oil.

items.text: Proof from architectural measurements
items.text_en: Proof from architectural measurements
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the Mishnah in Midos must be Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's because it records that all walls were high except the eastern one, allowing the priest burning the red heifer to see the entrance of the Heichal. Other measurements about gates, the sorag, the cheil, and the steps are cited, culminating in Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's unique statement about a step and a platform.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the Mishnah in Midos must be Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's because it records that all walls were high except the eastern one, allowing the priest burning the red heifer to see the entrance of the Heichal.
The Gemara cites additional measurements from the Mishnah in Midos about gates, the sorag, the cheil, and the steps.
The Gemara cites further measurements about the fifteen steps from the Israelite courtyard to the Women's courtyard and the space between the Ulam and the altar.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's unique statement about a step and a platform with three steps of half a half-cubit each.

items.text: Proof from the eastern wall's height
items.text_en: Proof from the eastern wall's height
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, the eastern wall was low enough to see the Heichal entrance, but according to the Rabbis, a half-amah of the entrance would be visible, which is inconsistent with the Mishnah's statement that the priest could see the entrance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, it makes sense that the eastern wall's low height would obscure the Heichal entrance from view.
