The Gemara objects that according to the Rabbis, half an amah of the Heichal entrance would still be visible, contradicting the Mishnah's claim that the priest could see the entrance.

items.text: Alternative attribution to Rabbi Yehudah
items.text_en: Alternative attribution to Rabbi Yehudah
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah suggests that the Mishnah might be Rabbi Yehudah's, who holds that the altar is centered in the courtyard, and provides a measurement of thirty-two amos.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's alternative attribution
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's alternative attribution
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah proposes that the Mishnah might be Rabbi Yehudah's, who holds that the altar is centered in the courtyard, with a measurement of thirty-two amos.

items.text: Mishnah's statement on altar placement
items.text_en: Mishnah's statement on altar placement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the altar was ten cubits opposite the Heichal entrance, eleven cubits to the north, and eleven to the south, making it aligned with the Heichal and its walls.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the altar's placement: ten cubits opposite the Heichal entrance, eleven cubits to the north, and eleven to the south, making it aligned with the Heichal and its walls.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: If Rabbi Yehuda, altar not centered
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: If Rabbi Yehuda, altar not centered
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, the altar would not be found in the center of the courtyard. It then cites a baraita detailing the courtyard's dimensions, showing the altar's position relative to other features.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, the altar would not be found in the center of the courtyard.
The Gemara cites a baraita detailing the courtyard's dimensions, showing the altar's position relative to other features.

items.text: Conclusion: Altar is in the south
items.text_en: Conclusion: Altar is in the south
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: if the Mishnah were Rabbi Yehuda's, the altar would not be in the center, since most of the altar stands in the south.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if the Mishnah were according to Rabbi Yehuda, the altar would not be in the center, since most of the altar stands in the south.

items.text: Conclusion that the mishnah is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Conclusion that the mishnah is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the mishnah must be according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, as inferred from the previous discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the mishnah must be according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, based on the inference from the previous discussion.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Rav Yitzchak's explanation of the chamber's location
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Yitzchak's explanation of the chamber's location
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Yitzchak explains that the chamber was set apart, appearing to those coming from the north as if in the south and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Yitzchak explains that the chamber was set apart, appearing to those coming from the north as if in the south and vice versa.

items.text: Resolution of the showbread contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the showbread contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara determines that the chamber was in the southwestern corner, based on a contradiction about the showbread tables. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua resolves the contradiction by noting that one Sage counts via the right path and the other via the left.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the chamber was in the southwestern corner, based on a contradiction between two sources about the showbread tables.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua resolves the contradiction by explaining that one Sage counts via the right path and the other via the left.

items.text: Resolution of the Table's orientation
items.text_en: Resolution of the Table's orientation
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Table was placed along the western side of the Sanctuary but oriented north-south, based on the resolution of the showbread arrangement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Chamber of the Lambs was in the southwest, resolving the contradiction about the showbread path.

items.text: Distinction between service and calculation
items.text_en: Distinction between service and calculation
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction: all turns should be to the right (eastward), but here the turn is to the left. It answers that this rule applies only to service, not to mere calculation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Master said all turns must be to the right, contradicting the leftward path.
The Gemara answers that the right-turn rule applies only to the service, but here it is a mere reckoning.

items.text: Baraita on the High Priest's portion
items.text_en: Baraita on the High Priest's portion
items.desc_en: A baraita explains how the High Priest offers a portion first and takes a portion first: he declares his offering verbally, and takes a portion of the showbread. Rabbi argues he always takes five loaves, based on the verse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita explains how the High Priest sacrifices and takes portions first, including the dispute about the showbread loaves.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi argues that the High Priest always takes five loaves, deriving from the verse that half goes to Aaron and half to his sons.

The Gemara points out the internal contradiction in the baraita: the first clause follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the middle clause follows the Rabbis, and the last clause follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi again.

Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the first and middle clauses are both the Rabbis, and they concede that a broken loaf is not given to the High Priest, so the first clause refers to a whole loaf.

items.text: Contradiction in the baraita's attribution
items.text_en: Contradiction in the baraita's attribution
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction: the first clause (one loaf from two) follows Rabbi, the middle clause (four or five) follows the Rabbis, and the last clause (always five) follows Rabbi again. This is inconsistent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out the internal contradiction in the baraita regarding the High Priest's portion.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: Rabbis agree on a broken loaf
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: Rabbis agree on a broken loaf
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction: the first and middle clauses are both the Rabbis, and they concede that a broken loaf is not given to the High Priest, so the first clause refers to a whole loaf, which they allow.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Rabbis concede about the piece of the loaf.

items.text: Calculation of wages for Rabbanan and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Calculation of wages for Rabbanan and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's numbers: according to the Rabbis, the deputy takes six entering and six exiting, totaling twelve, but without payment for closing doors, so they divide by two, and if one is missing from the half, he takes five. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the deputy takes seven entering (including two for closing doors) and five exiting, totaling ten, so they divide by two, and if one is missing from the half, he takes four.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's terms 'four or five' refer to and explains the calculation according to the Rabbis: the High Priest takes five loaves from a division of twelve.
According to Rabbi Yehuda, the High Priest takes four loaves from a division of ten.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda's view with a distinction
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda's view with a distinction
items.desc_en: Rava says the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda's view, but the difference between four and five depends on whether there is a deputy who stays overnight. If there is such a deputy, they divide from eight, so he takes four; if not, they divide from ten, so he takes five.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view, which aligns with Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara objects: If the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's, why would the High Priest take only four loaves? He should take five.
The Gemara resolves: There is no difficulty; the Mishnah refers to a case where a watch is detained, whereas the other case (five loaves) refers to when no watch is detained.
The Gemara clarifies: With a detained watch, the loaves are divided from eight, so the High Priest takes four; without a detained watch, they are divided from ten, so he takes five.

items.text: Challenge to Rava from the Mishnah's statement
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava from the Mishnah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava: if so, what does the Mishnah mean when it says 'Rabbi says: always five'? This is a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Rava: if the mishna is explained as referring to a detained watch, why does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi say the High Priest always takes five loaves, contradicting the four-loaf scenario?

items.text: Mishnah: Preparations for the High Priest on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Mishnah: Preparations for the High Priest on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that elders from the court read the order of the day before the High Priest, and they tell him to read aloud lest he forgot or never learned. On the eve of Yom Kippur, they stand him at the eastern gate and parade animals before him so he becomes familiar. For seven days they do not withhold food, but on the eve of Yom Kippur at nightfall they prevent him from eating much, as food brings sleep.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the elders reading the order of the day to the High Priest, parading animals before him for familiarity, and restricting his food on Yom Kippur eve to prevent sleep.

items.text: Gemara's question on appointing an ignorant High Priest
items.text_en: Gemara's question on appointing an ignorant High Priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how they could say 'lest he never learned' — would they appoint such a person? It cites a baraita that the High Priest must be greater in strength, beauty, wisdom, and wealth, and others say if he lacks, the priests make him great. Rav Yosef resolves: the Mishnah refers to the Second Temple, when wealth was a factor, as illustrated by the story of Martha bat Boethus paying King Yannai to appoint Yehoshua ben Gamla.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah could consider that the High Priest 'perhaps never learned', since only a wise man should be appointed High Priest.
The Gemara cites a baraita deriving from the verse that the High Priest must be greater in strength, beauty, wisdom, and wealth; Aḥerim add that if he lacks wealth, the priests make him great.

Rav Yosef resolves that the Mishnah refers to the Second Temple, when wealth could override wisdom, as illustrated by Rav Assi's story of Marta bat Baitos bribing King Yannai to appoint Yehoshua ben Gamla.

items.text: Why goats are not paraded before the High Priest
items.text_en: Why goats are not paraded before the High Priest
items.desc_en: A baraita includes goats in the parade, but our Mishnah omitted them because they come for sin and would weaken his spirit. The Gemara asks: the bull also comes for sin! It answers: the bull is for the High Priest and his fellow priests, and if any priest has a sin, he knows and can repent, but for all of Israel he does not know. Ravina cites a folk saying about not confronting a relative's debtor in the market.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that even goats were paraded before the High Priest.
The Gemara asks why our Mishnah's Tanna did not include goats among the paraded animals.
The Gemara answers that since goats come for sin, they would weaken the High Priest's spirit.
The Gemara objects: the bull also comes for sin, so why was it not omitted?
The Gemara resolves that the bull atones for the High Priest and his fellow priests, whose sins he knows and can correct, unlike the goats for all of Israel.
Ravina cites a folk saying about not confronting a relative's debtor in the market, illustrating that one should avoid those who know one's sins.

items.text: Dietary restrictions for the High Priest and others
items.text_en: Dietary restrictions for the High Priest and others
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Yehuda ben Nakosa's opinion to feed him fine flour and eggs to weaken him, but the Sages say that would cause overheating. Another baraita from Somkos in the name of Rabbi Meir lists foods to avoid: not אתרוג, eggs, old wine, etc. A further baraita discusses a zav, listing foods like milk, cheese, eggs, and wine that cause impurity, and adds five things that bring impurity, including garlic.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda ben Nakosa
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda ben Nakosa
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Nakosa says they feed him fine flour and eggs to weaken him, but the Sages object that this causes overheating.

sub.text: Baraita of Sumakhos in name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Baraita of Sumakhos in name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Sumakhos lists foods to avoid: not etrog, eggs, old wine; also fatty meat and white wine, because white wine causes impurity.

sub.text: Baraita of Elazar ben Pinchas in name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.text_en: Baraita of Elazar ben Pinchas in name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.desc_en: The Sages taught about a zav: one attributes emission to food; Elazar ben Pinchas adds not to feed milk, cheese, eggs, wine, bean soup, fatty meat, or pickled fish.
The Gemara asks what the category includes and answers it comes to include the five things that bring impurity, beginning with garlic.

items.text: Identification of 'orot' and the properties of gargir
items.text_en: Identification of 'orot' and the properties of gargir
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the 'orot' mentioned in the Mishnah as gargir (a type of vegetable), citing Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yochanan explains the name 'orot' because they illuminate the eyes. Rav Huna and Rav Pappa discuss the use of gargir for eye health.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the vegetables and other items that a nazirite may eat, including cress, purslane, eggs, and arugula (gargir).
The Gemara cites the verse from II Kings about collecting 'orot' to connect it to the Mishnah's gargir.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir identifies the 'orot' in the verse as gargir (arugula).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the name 'orot' is because they enlighten the eyes.
Rav Huna rules that one who finds gargir should eat it if possible, otherwise pass it over his eyes for benefit.
Rav Pappa specifies that gargir is most effective when it grows on the border of the field.

items.text: Conduct of a guest and announcements for Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Conduct of a guest and announcements for Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel quoting Rav states that a guest should not eat eggs or sleep in the host's cloak. The Gemara then relates that Rav and Rav Nachman would announce who would serve as the High Priest for Yom Kippur when they arrived in certain places.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav states that a guest should not eat eggs nor sleep in the host's garment due to concerns of seminal emission.
The Gemara relates that Rav would announce when arriving in Darshish: Who will be married to me for the day?
Similarly, Rav Naḥman would announce in Shekhantziv: Who will be married to me for the day?

items.text: Prohibition against marrying in two different locations
items.text_en: Prohibition against marrying in two different locations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that a person should not marry a woman in one city and then marry another in a different city, to avoid unknowingly causing siblings to marry, which would fill the world with mamzerut. The Gemara notes that the Rabbis have a reputation (kala) that prevents this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov forbids marrying in one state and then another, due to the risk of incest among unknowing children.
The Sages respond that the Sages generate publicity, so their children's identities are known, avoiding such errors.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction regarding the Rabbis' knowledge
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction regarding the Rabbis' knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from Rava's ruling that a woman who agrees to marry must wait seven clean days. Two answers are given: either the Rabbis would inform the families beforehand, or they would designate the women, as having bread in one's basket is different from not having it.

items.text: Mishnah: The elders' oath and preparation of the High Priest
items.text_en: Mishnah: The elders' oath and preparation of the High Priest
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how the elders of the court hand the High Priest over to the elders of the priesthood, bring him to the Chamber of Avtinas, administer an oath, and then depart. The High Priest weeps and they weep. If he is wise, he expounds; if not, the scholars expound before him. They read from Job, Ezra, and Chronicles, and Zecharya ben Kevutal adds Daniel.

items.text: Introduction of the two chambers and the Mishnah's description of the Temple chambers
items.text_en: Introduction of the two chambers and the Mishnah's description of the Temple chambers
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the High Priest had two chambers: the Parhedrin chamber and the Avtinas chamber, one in the north and one in the south. The Gemara then cites the Mishnah describing the six chambers in the Temple courtyard, three in the north and three in the south, detailing their functions.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches that the purpose of the chamber was to teach the High Priest the procedure of the handful (חפינה).
Rav Pappa states that the High Priest had two chambers, one in the north and one in the south.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah listing the six chambers in the Temple courtyard, three in the north and three in the south, detailing their functions.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Abba Shaul's statements
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and Abba Shaul's statements
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the three northern chambers: the Wood Chamber, the Chamber of the Exile, and the Chamber of Hewn Stone, with Abba Shaul adding that the High Priest's chamber was behind them.
The Mishnah details the functions of the Chamber of the Exile (water supply) and the Chamber of Hewn Stone (Sanhedrin judging priests).

items.text: Description of the seven gates of the courtyard
items.text_en: Description of the seven gates of the courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues with the Mishnah's description of the seven gates of the Temple courtyard, three in the north, three in the south, and one in the east, detailing each gate and its associated chambers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah listing the seven gates of the Temple courtyard, with three on the north, three on the south, and one on the east, detailing the names of the southern gates and the eastern gate with its two chambers.

items.text: The five immersions of the High Priest on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: The five immersions of the High Priest on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that the High Priest performs five immersions and ten sanctifications on Yom Kippur, all in the sacred area on the roof of the Parvah chamber, except for one immersion that was in the secular area by the Water Gate, near his chamber.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that the High Priest performs five immersions and ten sanctifications on Yom Kippur, all in the sacred area on the roof of the Parvah chamber, except for one immersion that was in the secular area by the Water Gate, near his chamber.

items.text: Determining the location of the chambers: north or south?
items.text_en: Determining the location of the chambers: north or south?
items.desc_en: The Gemara is uncertain whether the Parhedrin chamber was in the north and the Avtinas chamber in the south, or vice versa. It reasons that the Parhedrin chamber was likely in the south, based on the sequence of the High Priest's activities: he would first go to the south to immerse, then to the north for the חפינה (handful of incense), then to the Temple for the service, and finally return to the south to rest. If the Parhedrin chamber were in the north, he would have to travel back and forth excessively.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an uncertainty about which of the two chambers, Parhedrin and Avtinas, was located in the north and which in the south.

The Gemara reasons that the Parhedrin chamber was in the south, based on the logical sequence of the High Priest's activities: he would start in the south for immersion, go north for the חפינה (handful of incense), serve in the Temple all day, and finally return south to rest.
The Gemara objects that if the Parhedrin chamber were in the north, the High Priest would have to travel excessively back and forth at the end of the day, which is unreasonable.

items.text: Reasons for the extra travel: to distance Sadducees and to prevent arrogance
items.text_en: Reasons for the extra travel: to distance Sadducees and to prevent arrogance
items.desc_en: The Gemara responds that even if the Parhedrin chamber were in the north, the extra travel is justified: either to cause a Sadducee High Priest to withdraw (since he might reject the tradition of the חפינה), or to prevent him from becoming arrogant. Otherwise, why not have both chambers together or suffice with one?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the extra travel is imposed so that if the High Priest is a Sadducee, he will withdraw rather than violate the tradition of the חפינה.
The Gemara offers an alternative reason: to prevent the High Priest from becoming arrogant, for otherwise the two chambers could be combined or a single one would suffice.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Huna's view that priests are agents of God
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Huna's view that priests are agents of God
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the statement from the Mishnah that the elders said to the High Priest: 'My master, High Priest,' and questions whether this refutes Rav Huna bar Yehoshua, who said that priests are agents of God (and thus should not be addressed with such deference).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement that the elders addressed the High Priest as 'my master, High Priest,' and asks whether this refutes Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's view.
The Gemara cites Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's position that priests are שלוחי דרחמנא (agents of God), not agents of Israel, which would make the Mishnah's deferential address problematic.

items.text: The oath administered to the High Priest and its rationale
items.text_en: The oath administered to the High Priest and its rationale
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the content of the oath: 'We impose an oath upon you according to our opinion and the opinion of the court.' The High Priest then departs weeping, and the others weep as well. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that one who suspects the innocent is physically afflicted. The reason for all this is to prevent the High Priest from preparing incense outside and bringing it in, as the Sadducees do.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there is anything the sages cannot do that their agents can.
The Gemara explains that the oath is administered according to the opinion of the sages and the court.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's principle that one who suspects the innocent is physically afflicted, explaining the weeping.
The Gemara concludes that all this is done to prevent the High Priest from preparing incense outside and bringing it in, as the Sadducees do.

items.text: Story of a Sadducee who violated the procedure
items.text_en: Story of a Sadducee who violated the procedure
items.desc_en: The Sages taught about a Sadducee who prepared incense outside and brought it in. Upon exiting, he rejoiced greatly. His father warned him that even Sadducees fear the Pharisees. The son justified his action by citing the verse about appearing in a cloud. The Sages said he died shortly thereafter and was thrown into the garbage, with worms coming from his nose. Alternatively, he was struck upon exiting, as Rabbi Chiya taught that a sound was heard and an angel struck his face. The other priests found a mark like the sole of a calf's foot between his shoulders.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts a Sadducee who prepared incense outside and brought it in, and his father's warning and the son's defiant response.
The baraita concludes with the Sadducee's punishment: he died and was cast into the garbage, or was struck by an angel, leaving a calf's foot mark on his shoulder.
An alternative account states that upon exiting he was struck by an angel, and the priests found a mark like the sole of a calf's foot between his shoulders.

items.text: The correct pronunciation of Rabbi Zecharya ben Kevutal's name and the permissibility of gestures during Shema
items.text_en: The correct pronunciation of Rabbi Zecharya ben Kevutal's name and the permissibility of gestures during Shema
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava taught before Rav the name as 'ben Kefutal', but Rav gestured with his hand to correct it to 'Kevutal'. The Gemara questions why Rav did not simply speak, and explains that he was reciting Shema. This leads to a discussion: is it permitted to gesture during Shema? Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta states that one who recites Shema should not gesture with eyes, lips, or fingers. Rabbi Elazar Chasama adds that doing so violates a verse. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first chapter of Shema permits gestures, the second does not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, introducing Rabbi Zecharya ben Kevutal's statement.
Rav Chanan bar Rava taught before Rav the name as 'ben Kefutal', and Rav gestured with his hand to correct it to 'Kevutal'.
The Gemara asks why Rav did not simply speak the correction instead of gesturing.
The Gemara explains that Rav was reciting Shema and therefore could not speak.
The Gemara objects: is gesturing even permitted during Shema?

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta states that one who recites Shema should not gesture with eyes, lips, or fingers.
A baraita adds that Rabbi Elazar Chasama says one who gestures during Shema violates the verse 'And Me you have not called, O Jacob'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first chapter of Shema permits gestures, the second does not.

items.text: The prohibition of idle talk and the requirement to make Torah study permanent
items.text_en: The prohibition of idle talk and the requirement to make Torah study permanent
items.desc_en: The Sages taught from the verse 'And you shall speak of them' that one may speak only of Torah matters, not of other things. Rabbi Acha says to make Torah study fixed and not occasional. Rava states that engaging in idle conversation violates a positive commandment. Rav Acha bar Yaakov says it violates a negative commandment.

sub.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'and you shall speak of them' that one may speak only of Torah matters, not other things.
Rabbi Acha interprets the verse to mean that Torah study should be a fixed practice, not occasional.
Rava rules that engaging in idle conversation violates a positive commandment from the verse.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov argues that idle conversation violates a negative commandment from the verse 'All things are wearisome; a man cannot utter them.'

items.text: Keeping the High Priest awake: the finger and the activities
items.text_en: Keeping the High Priest awake: the finger and the activities
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that if the High Priest began to doze, young priests would snap their middle finger before him and say, 'My lord High Priest, stand and cool yourself once on the floor.' They would occupy him until the time of slaughter. The Gemara explains that 'tzarada' refers to the thumb. Rav Huna demonstrated that it makes a sound throughout the study hall. Rabbi Yitzchak explains that 'hafeig achat' means to bow once.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the High Priest began to doze, young priests would snap their middle finger before him and occupy him until the time of slaughter.
The Gemara asks what 'tzarada' means, and Rav Yehuda answers that it refers to the thumb.
Rav Huna demonstrated that snapping the thumb makes a sound throughout the study hall.
The Gemara asks what 'hafeig achat' means.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that 'hafeig achat' means to bow once.

items.text: Activities to keep the High Priest awake and the story of Nehardea
items.text_en: Activities to keep the High Priest awake and the story of Nehardea
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught that they occupied him not with musical instruments but with vocal recitation, saying 'If the Lord does not build a house, in vain do its builders labor.' The dignitaries of Jerusalem would not sleep all night so that the High Priest would hear noise and not fall asleep. Abba Shaul says this was also done in the outlying areas as a memorial to the Temple, but they would sin. Abaye or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak interprets this as referring to Nehardea, where Elijah told Rav Yehuda that on Yom Kippur many virgins were violated, and the Holy One, blessed be He, said something in response.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught that they occupied the High Priest not with musical instruments but with vocal recitation, specifically the verse 'If the Lord does not build a house, in vain do its builders labor.'
The dignitaries of Jerusalem would not sleep all night so that the High Priest would hear noise and not fall asleep.
Abba Shaul says that this practice was also done in the outlying areas as a memorial to the Temple, but they would sin.

sub.text: Abaye or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's interpretation
sub.text_en: Abaye or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's interpretation
sub.desc_en: Abaye or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak interprets the sin as referring to Nehardea, where Elijah told Rav Yehuda that on Yom Kippur many virgins were violated, and the Holy One, blessed be He, said something in response.

items.text: Satan's power on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Satan's power on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Satan cannot accuse on Yom Kippur: the gematria of 'השטן' equals 364, so he has power 364 days a year but not on Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'sin crouches at the door' refers to regarding Satan.
Rami bar Chama answers that Satan has no power to accuse on Yom Kippur.
Rami bar Chama proves from the gematria of 'השטן' (364) that Satan has power 364 days but not on Yom Kippur.

items.text: Mishnah: Time for clearing the altar
items.text_en: Mishnah: Time for clearing the altar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that on ordinary days the altar is cleared at cockcrow or near it, on Yom Kippur from midnight, and on festivals from the first watch. The courtyard was already full of Israelites by cockcrow.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the times for clearing the altar: on ordinary days at cockcrow or near it, on Yom Kippur from midnight, on festivals from the first watch, and the courtyard was already full of Israelites by cockcrow.

items.text: Tosefta on limbs that fell off
items.text_en: Tosefta on limbs that fell off
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: limbs that fell from the altar before midnight must be returned and have me'ilah; after midnight they are not returned and have no me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from elsewhere: limbs that fell from the altar before midnight must be returned and have מעילה (misappropriation liability); after midnight they are not returned and have no מעילה.

items.text: Rav's derivation from verses
items.text_en: Rav's derivation from verses
items.desc_en: Rav derives the division of the night: one verse says 'all night... burn' and another says 'all night... remove', so the night is split — half for burning, half for removal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the division of the night into two halves) derived?
Rav answers: one verse says 'all night... burn' and another says 'all night... remove', so the night is split — half for burning, half for removal.

items.text: Rav Kahana's objection from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's objection from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects by citing the Mishnah that on ordinary days the altar is cleared at cockcrow, which is before midnight, contradicting Rav's division of the night into halves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects by citing the Mishnah that on ordinary days the altar is cleared at cockcrow, which is before midnight, contradicting Rav's division of the night into halves.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the timing of the altar's removal
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the timing of the altar's removal
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idea that midnight is the Torah-mandated time for the removal of ashes, as that would not allow for earlier or later times. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse 'until morning' teaches that the morning is given to the night, so the removal is done at cockcrow or near it. On Yom Kippur, due to the High Priest's weakness, it is done from midnight; on festivals, due to many people and offerings, it is done from the first watch.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one could advance or delay the removal of ashes if midnight were the Torah-mandated time.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse 'until morning' teaches that the morning is given to the night, so the removal is done at cockcrow or near it.
The Gemara concludes that on ordinary days the removal is at cockcrow, on Yom Kippur from midnight due to the High Priest's weakness, and on festivals from the first watch due to the large crowd.

items.text: Dispute over the meaning of 'קריאת הגבר'
items.text_en: Dispute over the meaning of 'קריאת הגבר'
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Sheila dispute the meaning of 'קריאת הגבר': Rav says it means 'the call of a man' (a human herald), while Rabbi Sheila says it means 'the call of a rooster'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'קריאת הגבר' (cockcrow) means.
Rav interprets 'קריאת הגבר' as 'the call of a man' (a human herald).
Rabbi Sheila interprets 'קריאת הגבר' as 'the call of a rooster'.

items.text: Story of Rav and Rabbi Sheila, and Rav's encounter with Rabbi Chiyya
items.text_en: Story of Rav and Rabbi Sheila, and Rav's encounter with Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: Rav visits Rabbi Sheila's place and, acting as the expositor, explains 'קריאת הגבר' as 'the call of a man'. Rabbi Sheila questions why he didn't say 'the call of a rooster', and Rav responds with a proverb. Rav then recounts that when he served as expositor for Rabbi Chiyya, he said the same and was not corrected, but now Rabbi Sheila tells him to say 'rooster'. Rabbi Sheila realizes Rav's identity and apologizes, citing the principle of 'ascending in holiness, not descending'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that Rav visited Rabbi Sheila's place and, since there was no expositor, Rav stood up to serve as the expositor.
Rav explains that 'קריאת הגבר' means 'the call of a man'.
Rabbi Sheila questions Rav, asking why he did not say 'the call of a rooster'.
Rav responds with a proverb: 'A pipe for reeds — a musician plays; for gardeners — they do not accept it from him.'
Rav recounts that when he served as expositor for Rabbi Chiyya and gave the same explanation, Rabbi Chiyya did not correct him.
Rabbi Sheila realizes Rav's identity, apologizes, and cites the principle of 'ascending in holiness, not descending'.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav's interpretation
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav's interpretation
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rav's view: Gvini the herald would call out for the priests, Levites, and Israelites to prepare for service, and his voice was heard three parasangs away.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav's interpretation by describing the herald Gevini who would call out for the priests, Levites, and Israelites to take their positions, and his voice was heard three parasangs away.

items.text: The High Priest's voice and the sound of the sun's sphere
items.text_en: The High Priest's voice and the sound of the sun's sphere
items.desc_en: A story about King Agrippas hearing Gvini's voice from three parasangs away is followed by a statement that the High Priest's voice was even louder, as his recitation of 'Ana Hashem' was heard in Jericho, ten parasangs away. Rabbi Levi explains that daytime sounds are less audible because the sun's sphere saws through the sky like a carpenter, and this noise is called 'חירגא דיומא'. Nebuchadnezzar's verse is cited in support.

sub.desc_en: A story about King Agrippas hearing Gvini's voice from three parasangs away, demonstrating the great volume of the herald's voice.
Mar states that the High Priest's voice was even louder, as his recitation of 'Ana Hashem' was heard in Jericho, ten parasangs away, citing Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.
The gemara notes a difficulty: the High Priest's voice was heard despite his weakness, while Gvini was healthy; and it was daytime, while Gvini's voice was heard at night.

Rabbi Levi explains that daytime sounds are less audible because the sun's sphere saws through the sky like a carpenter, and this noise is called 'חירגא דיומא', citing Nebuchadnezzar's verse in support.

items.text: Three sounds that travel the world
items.text_en: Three sounds that travel the world
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught that three sounds travel from one end of the world to the other: the sound of the sun's sphere, the sound of Rome's multitude, and the sound of the soul departing the body. Some add the sound of childbirth.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if not for the sun's sphere, the sound of Rome's multitude would be heard, and vice versa, and lists three sounds that travel from one end of the world to the other: the sun's sphere, Rome's multitude, and the soul's departure from the body, with some adding childbirth.
Some add the sound of childbirth to the list of three sounds.

items.text: Opening baraita on the rooster's crow
items.text_en: Opening baraita on the rooster's crow
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Sheila's view about the danger of traveling before the rooster crows, with opinions on when exactly that is. It specifies that the rooster in question is an average one.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one who travels before קריאת הגבר (the rooster's crow) is responsible for his own blood, supporting Rabbi Sheila's position.
Rabbi Yoshiya gives his opinion that the danger lasts until the rooster crows a second time.
Another anonymous group (יש אומרים) holds that the danger continues until the rooster crows a third time.
The baraita specifies that the rooster referred to in all these opinions is an average, medium-sized rooster.

items.text: The miracle of standing crowded and bowing spacious
items.text_en: The miracle of standing crowded and bowing spacious
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav describes how Israelites would stand crowded but bow with space, one of the ten Temple miracles. The Mishnah lists these ten miracles, including that no woman miscarried from the sacred meat, no meat spoiled, no fly in the slaughterhouse, etc.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav describes that when Israelites ascend for the pilgrimage festival, they stand crowded but bow with space, extending eleven cubits behind the Holy of Holies, and this is one of the ten Temple miracles.

The Gemara cites the Mishnah that lists the ten Temple miracles: no woman miscarried from sacred meat scent, no meat spoiled, no fly in the slaughterhouse, no impurity for High Priest on Yom Kippur, no disqualification in omer/two loaves/shewbread, standing crowded but bowing spacious, no snake/scorpion harmed in Jerusalem, and no one complained about lack of space in Jerusalem.

items.text: Gemara's question: Mishnah begins with Temple and ends with Jerusalem
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Mishnah begins with Temple and ends with Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's list starts with Temple miracles but ends with Jerusalem miracles, implying two additional Temple miracles are missing. A baraita supplies them: rain never extinguished the altar fire, and wind never moved the smoke from the woodpile.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's list opens with Temple miracles but ends with Jerusalem miracles, implying two additional Temple miracles are missing.
The Gemara supplies a baraita providing two additional Temple miracles: rain never extinguished the altar fire, and wind never moved the smoke from the woodpile.

items.text: Objection: Are there more miracles?
items.text_en: Objection: Are there more miracles?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that there are additional miracles not listed, such as the swallowing of broken pottery, and Abaye adds that the murah, feathers, and ashes of the inner altar and menorah were also swallowed in place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there are additional miracles not listed in the mishna, citing Rav Shmaya's baraita about swallowed pottery shards and Abaye's addition of the crop, feathers, and ashes being swallowed in place.

items.text: Resolution: Counting and substitution
items.text_en: Resolution: Counting and substitution
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the three swallowing miracles were counted as one, and two were substituted for the two added from the baraita. However, this leaves a deficit, so Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds another miracle: the bread of the Presence was as hot when removed as when set out.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The disqualifications were three (omer, two loaves, shewbread) — were they counted as one? It explains: they counted them as one, removed two from the baraita and added two to complete ten.
The Gemara objects: If so, the swallowings (shards, crop and feathers, etc.) are also two miracles counted as one — this leaves a deficit in the required total of ten.

The Gemara resolves the deficit by citing another miracle: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi taught that a great miracle occurred with the shewbread — it was as hot upon removal as at arrangement, as the verse says 'to put hot bread on the day it was taken away'.

items.text: Further objection: More miracles from tradition
items.text_en: Further objection: More miracles from tradition
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects again, citing Rabbi Levi's tradition that the place of the Ark was not within the measured space, and Ravnai quoting Shmuel that the cherubim stood miraculously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether more miracles occurred in the Temple, citing Rabbi Levi's tradition that the Ark's place was not within the measured space.
Rabbi Levi states that it is a tradition from the ancestors that the place of the Ark (ארון) is not part of the measured space.
Ravnai quotes Shmuel that the cherubim (כרובים) stood miraculously, providing additional evidence of a miracle in the Temple.

items.text: Distinction: External vs. internal miracles
items.text_en: Distinction: External vs. internal miracles
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah counts only external miracles, not internal ones like the Ark and cherubim. It then questions why the bread of the Presence is included, and Resh Lakish explains it is external because the table was pure even when impure, implying a miracle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah counts only 외부 (external) miracles, not 내부 (internal) ones.
The Gemara questions why the bread of the Presence (לחם הפנים) is counted, as it too is an internal miracle.
Resh Lakish explains that the shewbread is an external miracle because the verse emphasizes that the table was pure, implying it could be impure and thus the miracle was visible.

items.text: Explanation of the wooden vessel used for the showbread
items.text_en: Explanation of the wooden vessel used for the showbread
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the wooden vessel used for the showbread is considered a vessel made for resting, which does not become impure and serves as a barrier against impurity. It was lifted up for the pilgrims to show them God's love, as the bread remained hot even when removed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the wooden vessel used for the showbread is a vessel made for resting, which does not become impure and serves as a barrier against impurity. It was lifted up for the pilgrims to show them God's love, as the bread remained hot even when removed.

items.text: Question about additional miracles and the response
items.text_en: Question about additional miracles and the response
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there were more miracles, citing Rav Oshaya's statement about golden trees planted by Solomon that bore fruit. The Gemara responds that these were constant miracles and thus not counted, and similarly the Ark and cherubs were constant miracles.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya describes the golden trees, their fruit falling when the wind blew, and their withering when the nations entered the Temple.
Rav Oshaya adds that the Holy One will restore the trees, citing the verse about Lebanon's glory.

items.text: Discussion about the smoke of the arrangement
items.text_en: Discussion about the smoke of the arrangement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mention of smoke from the arrangement, citing a baraita that the fire of the arrangement had five properties, including that it did not produce smoke. The Gemara resolves that the smoke referred to is from the common (non-sacred) fire brought by people, as commanded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing five properties of the fire of the arrangement, including that it did not produce smoke, contradicting the assumption that there was smoke.

items.text: Contradiction about the fire's appearance and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction about the fire's appearance and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one source says the fire was crouched like a lion, while Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim says he saw it crouched like a dog. The resolution is that the lion-like appearance was in the First Temple, and the dog-like in the Second. The Gemara then questions whether there was fire in the Second Temple, citing a verse listing five things missing, but concludes that the fire existed but did not assist.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the First Temple, where the fire was like a lion, and the Second Temple, where it was like a dog.
Rav Shmuel bar Inya explains that the verse 'ואכבד' (and I will be glorified) is written missing a heh, alluding to five things absent from the Second Temple, including fire.
The Sages respond that fire did exist in the Second Temple, but it did not assist in burning the offerings; it was merely visible above the wood.

items.text: Six types of fire enumerated
items.text_en: Six types of fire enumerated
items.desc_en: The Sages taught a baraita listing six types of fire: one that eats but does not drink, one that drinks but does not eat, one that eats and drinks, one that eats moist as dry, one that pushes fire, and one that eats fire. The Gemara explains each: the first is ordinary fire, the second is fire of illness, the third is Elijah's fire, the fourth is the arrangement's fire, the fifth is Gabriel's fire, and the sixth is the fire of the Divine Presence.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists six kinds of fire: one that consumes solids but not liquids, one that consumes liquids but not solids, one that consumes both, one that consumes wet like dry, one that repels other fire, and one that consumes other fire; the Gemara elaborates on each type.

items.text: Question about the smoke's immobility and its movement
items.text_en: Question about the smoke's immobility and its movement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the smoke of the arrangement was immovable, citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi's statement that people would observe the smoke's direction after the holiday to predict rain. The smoke would tilt north, south, east, or west, but it would not scatter.

items.text: Contradiction about wind directions and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction about wind directions and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the statement that east wind is always good and west wind always bad, and another baraita that describes different effects of winds on crops. Rav Yosef or Mar Zutra provides a mnemonic based on the table in the north and menorah in the south. The Gemara resolves that the first statement applies to us (in Babylonia) and the second to them (in Israel).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The original practice and the institution of the lottery
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The original practice and the institution of the lottery
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that initially anyone could volunteer to remove ash from the altar; if many came, they would run up the ramp, and the one who preceded his fellow by four cubits would win. If tied, the appointed officer would tell them to extend fingers. A story recounts that two were tied, one pushed the other, causing injury, leading the court to institute a lottery for this task, which was the first of four lotteries.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Why wasn't a lottery instituted initially?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Why wasn't a lottery instituted initially?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages did not originally institute a lottery for the ash removal. It answers that initially they thought it was a night service and people would not come, but when they saw that people did come and danger ensued, they instituted a lottery.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages did not institute a lottery from the outset for the removal of ashes.

The Gemara answers that initially they thought that since it is a nighttime service, it would not be important to the priests, so they would not come; when they saw that they did come and were in danger, they instituted a lottery.

items.text: Objection from limbs and fats, and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from limbs and fats, and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that limbs and fats (eivarim u'pedarim) are also a night service, yet a lottery was instituted for them. It answers that this is the end of the day service. The Gemara then notes that the ash removal is the beginning of the day service, citing Rabbi Yochanan that sanctifying hands for terumat hadeshen suffices for the next day since it is the beginning of the service. A textual correction is offered.

items.text: Alternative version: Reason of sleep coercion
items.text_en: Alternative version: Reason of sleep coercion
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is given: initially they thought that due to the coercion of sleep, people would not come, but when they saw they came and danger ensued, they instituted a lottery. The Gemara objects regarding limbs and fats, and answers that sleeping (mignei) is different from waking (meikam).

sub.desc_en: An alternative explanation is presented: initially they thought that due to sleepiness at night, priests would not come; when they saw they did come and were in danger, they instituted a lottery.
The Gemara objects: but the burning of limbs and fats also has the same sleepiness issue, yet a lottery was instituted for it from the outset.
The Gemara answers that lying down to sleep late is different from rising in the middle of the night; it is harder to wake up early than to stay up late.

items.text: Was the lottery a remedy for that side? Rav Ashi's two enactments
items.text_en: Was the lottery a remedy for that side? Rav Ashi's two enactments
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the lottery was a remedy for that side (the danger) or this side (the competition). A baraita states that the one who wins the ash removal also wins the arrangement of the wood pile and the two logs. Rav Ashi explains there were two enactments: initially they instituted a lottery, but then people stopped coming, so they added the additional tasks to incentivize participation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the mishna's account, asking whether the lottery was really enacted only to address the danger, or whether it was enacted for the other side — namely, to ensure participation in the lottery.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the one who wins the ash removal also wins the arrangement of the wood pile and the two logs, indicating that the lottery was tied to additional important tasks.

Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by explaining that there were two separate enactments: first a lottery was instituted to address the danger, but then priests stopped coming, so a second enactment added the wood arrangement and the two logs to the lottery to incentivize participation.

items.text: Rav Pappa's analysis of the four cubits rule
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's analysis of the four cubits rule
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that the four cubits mentioned in the Mishnah refer to the space on the ramp, not the ground, and that the rule applies only near the altar. He raises a question about whether the four cubits include the cubit of the base (yesod) and the cubit of the surrounding ledge (sovev).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that it is obvious to him that the four cubits are not measured on the ground, since the mishna says they run and ascend on the ramp, and he raises a dilemma whether the four cubits include the cubit of the base and the cubit of the surrounding ledge.

items.text: Unresolved question about the dimensions of the altar
items.text_en: Unresolved question about the dimensions of the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt whether the phrase 'bar me'ama yesod ve'ama sovev' refers to a specific measurement, and concludes with 'teiku' (let it stand unresolved).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved issue whether the measurement excludes the cubit of the base and the cubit of the ledge, concluding with 'teiku'.

items.text: Prohibition of counting Israelites
items.text_en: Prohibition of counting Israelites
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the appointed officer tells the priests to raise their fingers for counting, supporting Rabbi Yitzchak's view that counting Israelites is forbidden even for a mitzvah. Rav Ashi challenges the proof from the verse 'vayifkedeim beBezek', suggesting 'Bezek' might be a place name, and instead cites a different verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a tanna explained 'hatzbiu' as 'put out your fingers for a count,' supporting Rabbi Yitzchak's ruling that counting Israelites is forbidden even for a mitzvah, as derived from the verse 'vayifkedeim beBezek'.
Rav Ashi objects that the word 'Bezek' in the verse might be a place name rather than a term meaning 'shards,' citing the verse that mentions Adoni-bezek in Bezek.
The Gemara resolves the objection by citing a different verse, 'vayishma Shaul et ha'am vayifkedeim batela'im,' as the true proof that Saul counted via intermediaries, not directly.

items.text: Two prohibitions against counting
items.text_en: Two prohibitions against counting
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that counting Israelites violates a negative commandment, while Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that it violates two negative commandments based on the verse 'lo yimad ve'lo yisafeir'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that counting Israelites violates one negative commandment.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that counting Israelites violates two negative commandments.

items.text: Reconciling contradictory verses about Israel's countability
items.text_en: Reconciling contradictory verses about Israel's countability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports that Rabbi Yonatan resolves the contradiction between the verse that says Israel will be countable and the one that says they will not: one refers to when they do God's will, the other to when they do not. Rabbi offers an alternative resolution: one refers to counting by human hands, the other by heaven.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports that Rabbi Yonatan raises a contradiction between the verse stating Israel will be countable and the one saying it will not be counted.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that one verse refers to when Israel does God's will (innumerable) and the other to when they do not (countable like sand).

sub.text: Rabbi in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dostai
sub.text_en: Rabbi in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dostai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi offers an alternative resolution: one verse refers to counting by human hands (countable) and the other to counting by heaven (innumerable).

items.text: A leader becomes wealthy
items.text_en: A leader becomes wealthy
items.desc_en: Rav Nehila'i bar Idi quoting Shmuel teaches that once a person is appointed a leader over the community, he becomes wealthy, as seen from Saul's census: initially with pebbles (Bezek) and later with lambs (Tela'im). The Gemara questions whether the lambs were his own, but concludes that the point is the increase in wealth.

sub.text: Rav Nehila'i bar Idi citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nehila'i bar Idi citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nehila'i bar Idi cites Shmuel stating that a newly appointed community leader becomes wealthy, evidenced by Saul's census shifting from pebbles to lambs.

items.text: Saul's mercy and the bat kol
items.text_en: Saul's mercy and the bat kol
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani explains that Saul argued with God about destroying Amalek, citing the law of the heifer whose neck is broken for one life, and a bat kol told him not to be overly righteous. Later, when Saul ordered Doeg to kill the priests, a bat kol told him not to be overly wicked.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Mani interprets the verse 'וירב בנחל' (he strove in the valley) as Saul arguing with God about destroying Amalek, reasoning that if one life requires a heifer whose neck is broken, how much more so for many lives.
Saul further argues: if men sin, what did animals sin; if adults sin, what did children sin? A bat kol (Divine Voice) responds: 'Do not be overly righteous' (Ecclesiastes 7:16).
When Saul later orders Doeg to kill the priests, a bat kol says: 'Do not be overly wicked' (Ecclesiastes 7:17).

items.text: Saul's one sin vs. David's two sins
items.text_en: Saul's one sin vs. David's two sins
items.desc_en: Rav Huna contrasts Saul, who sinned once (with Agag) and was punished, with David, who sinned twice (with Uriah and inciting the census) and was not punished. The Gemara challenges that Saul also sinned at Nov, but that was forgiven. For David, the Gemara notes he was punished for the Bathsheba affair with four deaths, and for the census with a plague, but argues that David was punished in his body through leprosy and separation from the Sanhedrin and the Shechinah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna contrasts Saul, who sinned once and was punished, with David, who sinned twice and was not.
The Gemara identifies Saul's sin as the Agag incident but objects that he also sinned at Nob.
The Gemara answers that God regretted making Saul king already after the Agag incident, before Nob.
The Gemara identifies David's two sins: the Uriah incident and the incitement to conduct a census.
The Gemara objects that David also sinned with Bathsheba, and answers that he was already punished fourfold for that.
The Gemara objects that David was also punished for the census with a plague.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that David was not punished in his own body for the census.
The Gemara objects that David was not punished in his own body for the Bathsheba affair either.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav answers that David was punished in his body with leprosy for six months, and the Sanhedrin and Shechinah withdrew from him.

items.text: David's acceptance of lashon hara
items.text_en: David's acceptance of lashon hara
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a dispute: Rav says David accepted lashon hara (about Mephibosheth), while Shmuel says he did not. Even according to Rav, David was punished for this, as a bat kol decreed that the kingdom would be divided between Rehoboam and Jeroboam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Did Rav not say that David accepted lashon hara (slander), contradicting the claim that David's sins were limited to two? It then cites Shmuel's opposing view.
Rav Yehuda amends that even according to Rav's position, David was punished for this sin, as a bat kol (Divine Voice) decreed that Rehoboam and Jeroboam would divide the kingdom.

items.text: Saul as a one-year-old in sinlessness
items.text_en: Saul as a one-year-old in sinlessness
items.desc_en: Rav Huna interprets 'ben shanah Shaul bemolcho' as meaning he was like a one-year-old who never tasted sin. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that it could mean he was soiled with mud and filth, but a dream vision confirms the positive interpretation, with the bones of Saul ben Kish declaring their agreement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna interprets the verse about Saul's age as meaning he was like a one-year-old who never tasted sin.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that the phrase 'like a one-year-old' could alternatively mean he was filthy with mud and excrement.
A dream vision confirms the positive interpretation as Saul's bones declare their agreement after being properly honored.

items.text: Why Saul's dynasty did not continue
items.text_en: Why Saul's dynasty did not continue
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel explains that Saul's kingship did not continue because he had no flaw, and Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak states that a leader must have a 'box of reptiles' behind him to humble him if he becomes haughty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel states that Saul's kingship did not continue because he had no blemish in his lineage.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak states that a leader must have a 'box of reptiles' behind him, i.e., some questionable ancestry, to keep him humble.
The principle is explained: the flaw behind him serves as a reminder so that if he becomes haughty, one can tell him to turn back and see his roots.

items.text: Saul punished for forgiving his honor
items.text_en: Saul punished for forgiving his honor
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav explains that Saul was punished because he forgave the insult from the base people who did not bring him gifts, as this led to the Ammonite attack.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that Saul was punished because he forgave the insult from the base men who mocked him, which led to the Ammonite attack.

items.text: A Torah scholar's humility
items.text_en: A Torah scholar's humility
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak states that a Torah scholar must have a 'box of reptiles' behind him, as a safeguard against arrogance.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak that any Torah scholar must have humility, as symbolized by a box of reptiles behind him.

items.text: Definition of revenge and bearing a grudge
items.text_en: Definition of revenge and bearing a grudge
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the biblical prohibition of revenge and bearing a grudge applies only to monetary matters, not to personal insults. It provides examples of revenge (refusing to lend after being refused) and bearing a grudge (lending but reminding the other of their past refusal).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a Torah scholar who does not avenge himself and bear a grudge like a snake is not a proper scholar.
The Gemara questions how this can be, given the biblical prohibition against revenge and bearing a grudge.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition applies only to monetary matters, not to personal insults.
A baraita is cited that defines revenge and bearing a grudge with examples from borrowing and lending, confirming the monetary context.

items.text: The virtue of being insulted without retaliating
items.text_en: The virtue of being insulted without retaliating
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether personal suffering is exempt from the prohibition, citing a baraita that praises those who are insulted but do not insult, who hear their disgrace but do not respond. Rava adds that one who overlooks his attributes has his sins forgiven, but this applies only when they appease him and he is appeased.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the prohibition against vengeance applies to personal suffering, citing a baraita that praises those who are insulted but do not retaliate.
The Gemara answers that the scholar may keep resentment in his heart, but Rava adds that one who forgives his attributes has his sins forgiven, provided the offender appeases him.

items.text: The number of trumpets sounded for the daily offering
items.text_en: The number of trumpets sounded for the daily offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the priests would sound one or two trumpets. The Gemara questions why two are needed if one suffices. Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: for a healthy person, only one trumpet is sounded; for a sick person, two are sounded. A baraita supports this distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishna's statement that two fingers are taken out, asking if one is even necessary.
Rav Chisda answers that the mishna's statement applies to a healthy person, but for a sick person, even two fingers are taken out.
A baraita is cited to support Rav Chisda's distinction between a healthy and a sick person.

items.text: The rule about counting fingers and the meaning of 'pekia'
items.text_en: The rule about counting fingers and the meaning of 'pekia'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita that prohibits sounding with the third or thumb finger due to fraud, and if one did, he is counted only once. Abaye explains that he initially thought 'pekia' meant a wick, but after hearing that the appointee strikes with it, he concluded it means a whip. Rav and Rav Pappa define the whip as a leather strap with a split end.

items.text: The tragic incident of two priests racing up the ramp
items.text_en: The tragic incident of two priests racing up the ramp
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that two priests were running up the ramp, and one stabbed the other in the heart. Rabbi Tzadok stood on the steps and questioned who should bring the eglah arufah. The father of the dying boy declared his son an atonement, noting that the knife was not defiled, teaching that they valued purity of vessels more than bloodshed.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna recounts the incident of two priests running up the ramp, one reaching within four cubits of the other and stabbing him in the heart.
Rabbi Tzadok stood on the steps of the Entrance Hall and questioned who should bring the עגלה ערופה (heifer whose neck is broken), causing the people to weep.
The father of the dying boy declared his son an atonement, noted the knife was not defiled, teaching that they valued purity of vessels more than bloodshed, as in the verse about Manasseh.

items.text: Chronology of the incident and the institution of the lottery
items.text_en: Chronology of the incident and the institution of the lottery
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether the stabbing incident preceded or followed the case of the broken leg. It concludes that the stabbing came first, but initially they thought it was a fluke; when they saw that even accidental events led to danger, they instituted the lottery. The four cubits rule remained for cases of equal standing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions which incident came first, the broken leg or the murder, and concludes that the broken leg came first and led to the establishment of the lottery.
The Gemara answers that the broken leg incident came first, and the lottery was established in response to it.

items.text: Jerusalem's exemption from eglah arufah
items.text_en: Jerusalem's exemption from eglah arufah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Tzadok's statement about bringing the eglah arufah, noting that Jerusalem is not subject to that law, as one of the ten special rules about Jerusalem is that it does not bring the eglah arufah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Jerusalem is subject to the heifer whose neck is broken, citing a baraita about Jerusalem's unique status.

items.text: Question about bloodshed vs. purity of vessels
items.text_en: Question about bloodshed vs. purity of vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the story of the child's father indicates that bloodshed is less severe than purity of vessels, or vice versa. It resolves the question by citing the verse about Menashe, showing that bloodshed is considered less severe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a city whose murderer is unknown does not bring the עגלה ערופה (beheaded heifer), citing the verse 'לא נודע מי הכהו' (it is not known who struck him) — but here it IS known, so the verse is superfluous; rather, it comes to increase weeping.

The Gemara recounts the story of a father who finds his child dying and declares the child a כפרה (atonement) for the priests, teaching that the purity of vessels (טהרת כלים) is more severe than bloodshed (שפיכות דמים).

The Gemara resolves the question by citing the verse 'וגם דם נקי שפך מנשה' (and also innocent blood he shed, Menashe), concluding that bloodshed is less severe because it is 'flowing', while purity of vessels is severe because it is 'standing'.

The Gemara raises a question: Is bloodshed (שפיכות דמים) less severe because it is 'flowing' (זל), while purity of vessels (טהרת כלים) is severe because it is 'standing' (קיימא)? Or perhaps bloodshed is severe because it is 'standing', and purity of vessels is severe because it is more stringent?

items.text: Derivation of garments for removing ashes
items.text_en: Derivation of garments for removing ashes
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the verse 'He shall remove his garments and put on other garments' teaches that the garments for removing ashes are also sacred, though inferior. Rabbi Eliezer adds that this includes blemished priests.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse and raising the possibility that the priest removes ashes in ordinary clothes, like on Yom Kippur.
The baraita answers by citing the verse's phrase 'other garments' and using a היקש (verbal analogy) to teach that the garments for removing ashes are also sacred.
The baraita explains that 'other' means the second set of garments are of lower quality than the first.
Rabbi Eliezer offers a different interpretation: the juxtaposition of 'other' and 'carry out' teaches that blemished priests are eligible to carry out the ashes.

items.text: Explanation of 'inferior' garments
items.text_en: Explanation of 'inferior' garments
items.desc_en: Mar explains that 'other' means inferior, as taught by the school of Rabbi Yishmael: garments used for cooking should not be used for serving wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the first tanna's view: the word 'other' teaches that the second set of garments is of lower quality, as taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael — a servant who cooks for his master should not wear the same clothes when pouring a cup.
Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: The dispute is only about carrying out, but regarding lifting (הרמה), all agree it is a bona fide service (עבודה).

items.text: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on removal of ashes
items.text_en: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on removal of ashes
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish argues that the dispute about removal (hotza'ah) applies also to lifting (haramah), while Rabbi Yochanan holds that lifting is universally considered service. The Gemara explains Resh Lakish's reasoning: no service is performed with two vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning behind Resh Lakish's opinion.
The Gemara explains Resh Lakish's reasoning: if removal of ashes were a bona fide service, it would be anomalous to have a service performed with only two garments.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Torah revealed the tunic and trousers as examples, and the same applies to the mitre and belt, so all four garments are required.

items.text: Explanation of the verses for Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Explanation of the verses for Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rabbi Yochanan specifies the tunic and trousers, deriving from 'middo' and the requirement that nothing precede the trousers. Resh Lakish derives these from the same verses differently.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about including other garments
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about including other garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa about which garments are included for lifting. Rabbi rejects both views, arguing that garments used for a higher sanctity cannot be used for a lower one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish may be parallel to a tannaitic dispute, citing Rabbi Yehuda's view that the extra expression 'יִלְבַּשׁ' (shall he put on) includes the mitre and belt for the removal of the ashes.
Rabbi Dosa offers an alternative interpretation: the extra expression comes to include the High Priest's Yom Kippur garments, teaching that they are acceptable for use by a common priest.

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi raises two objections to Rabbi Dosa's view: first, the High Priest's belt differs from the common priest's belt; second, garments used for a higher sanctity cannot be used for a lower one, and he leaves the meaning of 'יִלְבַּשׁ' (shall he put on) unresolved.

items.text: Opening dispute on the ashes and their disposal
items.text_en: Opening dispute on the ashes and their disposal
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets the verse 'והניחם שם' to teach that the ashes require burial. Rabbi Dosa argues that the ashes are fit for a common priest, and the verse only prohibits using them for another Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The baraita interprets the verse 'והניחם שם' to teach that the ashes require burial, while Rabbi Dosa argues they are fit for a common priest and the verse only prohibits reuse on another Yom Kippur.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests the dispute is whether removing the ashes is a service (עבודה). It then rejects this, concluding that all agree it is a service, but disagree on whether a verse is needed to include it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute is whether removing the ashes is a service (עבודה).
The Gemara rejects the initial suggestion, concluding that all agree it is a service, but disagree on whether a verse is needed to include it.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's question on the measure of the ash removal
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's question on the measure of the ash removal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin asks whether the measure for removing the ashes (תרומת הדשן) is derived from the measure of terumat ma'aser or from the measure of the terumah of Midian. Rabbi Chiyya's tradition resolves it: a verbal analogy on 'והרים' teaches it is a handful (קומץ).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin asks whether the measure for removing the ashes (תרומת הדשן) is derived from the measure of תרומת מעשר (the priestly portion of tithe) or from the measure of the תרומה (portion) of Midian.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Chiyya's tradition that a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'והרים' (and he lifted) teaches that the measure is a handful (קומץ), just as in the meal-offering.

items.text: Rav and Levi dispute which services a non-priest is liable for death
items.text_en: Rav and Levi dispute which services a non-priest is liable for death
items.desc_en: Rav lists four services for which a non-priest (זר) is liable for death: sprinkling, burning, water libation, and wine libation. Levi adds the removal of the ashes (תרומת הדשן), and his baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: Rav lists four services for which a non-priest (זר) is liable for death: sprinkling, burning, water libation, and wine libation.
Levi adds the removal of the ashes (תרומת הדשן) to Rav's list, and his baraita supports this.

items.text: Gemara explains the scriptural bases for Rav and Levi
items.text_en: Gemara explains the scriptural bases for Rav and Levi
items.desc_en: Rav derives his list from the verse 'עבודת מתנה' (service of giving) and 'עבודה תמה' (complete service), excluding removal (סילוק). Levi derives the inclusion of ash removal from 'לכל דבר המזבח'. The Gemara explains how each handles the extra terms.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rav's scriptural basis is, and explains that he derives from the verse 'עבודת מתנה' (service of giving) and 'עבודה תמה' (complete service) to exclude removal (סילוק) and any service followed by another service.

The Gemara explains that Levi derives the inclusion of ash removal from the phrase 'לכל דבר המזבח' (for every matter of the altar), while Rav uses that phrase to include the seven sprinklings inside and for the leper.
The Gemara concludes that Levi derives the inclusion from the extra terms 'דבר' and 'כל דבר', while Rav does not expound those terms.

items.text: Objection from a general-particular principle
items.text_en: Objection from a general-particular principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if 'לכל דבר המזבח' is a general term and 'עבודת מתנה' is a particular, then by the rule of כלל ופרט only the particular (giving service) is included, excluding removal. The Gemara begins to answer with 'אמר קרא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if 'לכל דבר המזבח' is a general term and 'עבודת מתנה' is a particular, then by the rule of כלל ופרט (general and particular) only giving service is included, excluding removal service.
The Gemara begins to answer the objection by citing a verse that will expand the scope.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the verse 'ולמבית לפרוכת'
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the verse 'ולמבית לפרוכת'
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse to distinguish between service inside the curtain (placing blood) and removal service, and then questions whether the same applies to complete service versus service followed by another service. It resolves by noting that the verse 'ועבדתם' is paired with the context.
