The Gemara further objects that even the small amount of plaster should be considered, but resolves that since it was less than a cubit, it was not counted.

items.text: Reason for the linen sheet
items.text_en: Reason for the linen sheet
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a linen sheet was spread between the High Priest and the people: so he would recognize that the day's service is performed in linen garments, as taught by Rav Kahana.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a linen sheet (סדין של בוץ) specifically was used to screen the High Priest from the people.
Rav Kahana answers that the linen sheet was used so that the people would recognize that the Yom Kippur service is performed in linen garments (בגדי בוץ).

items.text: Mishnah: Procedure after immersion
items.text_en: Mishnah: Procedure after immersion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest's actions after immersion: he dries, puts on golden garments, washes hands and feet, slaughters the daily offering, receives the blood, and sprinkles it. It then lists the morning incense, lamp trimming, and other offerings, noting the order of the morning incense between blood and limbs, and the afternoon incense between limbs and libations. For an elderly or fastidious priest, hot water is mixed with cold to temper it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest's sequence: he removes his garments, immerses, dries, dons golden garments, sanctifies his hands and feet, and offers the daily sacrifice; it also notes that if he was elderly or sensitive, they would warm water to temper the cold.

The Mishnah lists the subsequent services: morning incense, lamp trimming, offering the head, limbs, חביתין (pancake offering), and wine, noting the order of incense between blood and limbs in the morning and between limbs and libations in the afternoon.
The Mishnah adds that for an elderly or fastidious High Priest, hot water is mixed with cold to temper its chill.

items.text: Rabbis' claim before Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Rabbis' claim before Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: The Rabbis assert before Rav Pappa that the Mishnah's single washing after immersion does not follow Rabbi Meir, who requires two washings upon changing garments.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis object before Rav Pappa that the Mishnah's single sanctification after donning golden garments does not align with Rabbi Meir's view, who requires two sanctifications upon donning.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that both Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis agree there is one washing for removing sacred garments and one for putting them on. Their dispute is over the verse 'And he shall take off and wash and put on': Rabbi Meir compares undressing to dressing—just as one washes after dressing, so one washes after undressing; the Rabbis compare undressing to dressing—just as one washes while dressed, so one washes while dressed (i.e., before undressing).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the dispute by stating that both sides agree there is one washing for undressing and one for dressing, and their disagreement is over the verse 'וּפָשַׁט וְרָחַץ וְלָבַשׁ' (and he shall take off and wash and put on): Rabbi Meir compares undressing to dressing, so just as one washes after dressing, one washes after undressing; the Rabbis compare undressing to dressing, so just as one washes while dressed, one washes while dressed (before undressing).

sub.text: Rav Pappa's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the Rabbis also compare undressing to dressing, but they derive that just as one washes while dressed (i.e., after putting on the garments), so one washes while dressed (i.e., before undressing).

items.text: Rabbis' objection with a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbis' objection with a baraita
items.desc_en: The Rabbis object to Rav Pappa, citing a baraita that explicitly states Rabbi Meir's position: he undresses, washes, immerses, dries, puts on golden garments, and then washes. Rav Pappa responds that if it is taught, it is taught (i.e., he accepts the baraita).

sub.desc_en: The rabbis object to Rav Pappa by citing a baraita that explicitly shows Rabbi Meir's order: he removes, sanctifies, immerses, dries, dons golden garments, and sanctifies again — contradicting Rav Pappa's interpretation.
Rav Pappa concedes, saying 'If it is taught, it is taught' (אי תניא תניא), accepting the baraita as authoritative.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Meir's view
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Meir's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze Rabbi Meir's position, noting that according to him, one can find two washings in the process.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze the baraita, noting that according to Rabbi Meir, one can find a consistent explanation for the sequence.

items.text: Gemara's question on the number of sanctifications
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the number of sanctifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Rabbis' count of ten sanctifications, noting that according to them there should only be nine, and explains that the final sanctification is performed when changing from sacred to profane garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Rabbis' count of ten sanctifications, noting that according to their position there should only be nine.
The Rabbis answer that the final sanctification is performed when changing from sacred to profane garments.

items.text: The placement of the pasuk about entering the Tent of Meeting
items.text_en: The placement of the pasuk about entering the Tent of Meeting
items.desc_en: The baraita states that the verse 'And Aaron shall come into the Tent of Meeting' is out of order, and Rav Chisda explains that without this placement, only three immersions and six sanctifications would be found.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the verse 'And Aaron shall come into the Tent of Meeting' is out of order in the Torah, and asks for the reason.
Rav Chisda explains that without this placement, only three immersions and six sanctifications would be found, rather than the required five and ten.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda derives the five immersions and ten sanctifications from the verse that mentions changing garments, teaching that any change from one service to another requires immersion.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda asks for the scriptural source for the five immersions and ten sanctifications.
Rabbi Yehuda cites the verse to derive that every change from one service to another requires immersion.
The baraita concludes that one learns from this that anyone who changes from one service to another requires immersion.

items.text: Rabbi's derivation and listing of the five services
items.text_en: Rabbi's derivation and listing of the five services
items.desc_en: Rabbi derives the five immersions and ten sanctifications from a different verse, and lists the five services that require changes of garments: the morning tamid, the Yom Kippur service, the ram of the people, the pan and shovel, and the afternoon tamid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi opens with a derivation from a verse (Vayikra 16:4) that every change of garments requires immersion, establishing the principle of five immersions and ten sanctifications.

Rabbi lists the five services that require garment changes: the morning tamid in gold garments, the Yom Kippur service in white, the ram of the people in gold, the pan and shovel in white, and the afternoon tamid in gold.

items.text: Derivation that each immersion requires two sanctifications
items.text_en: Derivation that each immersion requires two sanctifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that each immersion requires two sanctifications, one for removing the garments and one for putting on the new ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that each immersion requires two sanctifications.
The Gemara answers by citing the verses 'he shall remove and wash' and 'he shall wash and put on' to derive two sanctifications per immersion.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's kal vachomer and the response
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's kal vachomer and the response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon uses a kal vachomer to argue that where immersion is required, sanctification is certainly required. The Gemara then asks why not just one sanctification, and answers with a gezeirah shavah comparing removal to donning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon opens with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if where immersion is not required, sanctification is required, then where immersion is required, sanctification is certainly required.
The Gemara objects: if we compare to the case of donning, which requires only one sanctification, then here too only one sanctification should be required.

The Gemara resolves with a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy): the superfluous phrase 'אֲשֶׁר לָבַשׁ' (which he wore) teaches that removal is compared to donning — just as donning requires sanctification, so too removal requires sanctification.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's second derivation and the question about changing from gold to white
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's second derivation and the question about changing from gold to white
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda derives the five immersions from another verse, and the Gemara asks: we have found the source for changing from white to gold, but from gold to white, where do we derive it?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda again asks for the scriptural source for the five immersions and ten sanctifications.
Rabbi Yehuda cites a verse to derive that any change from one service to another requires immersion.
The Gemara asks for the source that a change from golden garments to white garments also requires immersion.

items.text: First kal vachomer for immersion when changing from gold to white garments
items.text_en: First kal vachomer for immersion when changing from gold to white garments
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael argues via a fortiori reasoning: if gold garments, which are not worn in the Holy of Holies, require immersion, then white garments, which are worn in the Holy of Holies, certainly require immersion. The Gemara raises a refutation: gold garments have greater atonement, so the kal vachomer is not valid.

sub.text: School of Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer
sub.text_en: School of Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael argues via a kal vachomer (a fortiori reasoning): if gold garments, which are not worn in the Holy of Holies, require immersion, then white garments, which are worn there, certainly require immersion.
The Gemara raises a refutation: gold garments have greater atonement (כפרה מרובה), so the kal vachomer is not valid.
The Gemara concludes that the requirement for immersion when changing garments is derived from Rabbi's teaching, not from the kal vachomer.

items.text: Rabbi's derivation of five immersions and ten sanctifications
items.text_en: Rabbi's derivation of five immersions and ten sanctifications
items.desc_en: Rabbi derives from the verse 'He shall put on the holy linen tunic' that any change from one service to another requires immersion. The Gemara asks: we have the derivation for changing from gold to white, but from white to gold, where do we derive it?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi derives from the verse 'He shall put on the holy linen tunic' that any change from one service to another requires immersion.
The Gemara asks: we have the derivation for changing from gold to white, but from white to gold, where do we derive it?

items.text: Second kal vachomer for immersion when changing from white to gold
items.text_en: Second kal vachomer for immersion when changing from white to gold
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael offers a second kal vachomer: if white garments, which have lesser atonement, require immersion, then gold garments, which have greater atonement, certainly require immersion. The Gemara refutes this: white garments are worn in the Holy of Holies, so the kal vachomer is not valid. The Gemara then cites the verse that teaches immersion for both directions.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael proposes a second kal vachomer: if white garments, which have lesser atonement, require immersion, then gold garments, which have greater atonement, certainly require immersion.
The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer: white garments are worn in the Holy of Holies, so the analogy is invalid.

The Gemara cites the verse 'בִּגְדֵי קוֹדֶשׁ הֵם וְרָחַץ אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ בַּמַּיִם וּלְבֵשָׁם' (They are holy garments, and he shall wash his flesh in water and put them on) as the source that teaches immersion for both directions of change.

items.text: Enumeration of the five services
items.text_en: Enumeration of the five services
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the five services that require a change of garments: the morning daily offering in gold, the service of the day in white, the ram of the High Priest and the ram of the people in gold, the spoon and fire-pan in white, and the afternoon daily offering in gold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates the five services that require a change of garments, listing each service and its corresponding garment type.

items.text: Derivation that each immersion requires two sanctifications
items.text_en: Derivation that each immersion requires two sanctifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verses 'He shall remove... and wash' and 'He shall wash... and put on' that each immersion requires two sanctifications. Since the immersion itself is already derived from the verse 'They are holy garments', these verses are applied to sanctification. The Gemara explains that this also teaches that immersion must be in a holy place, just as sanctification is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where is it derived that each immersion requires two sanctifications?
The Gemara answers: The verse teaches this through the juxtaposition of 'He shall remove... and wash' and 'He shall wash... and put on'.
The Gemara objects: But these verses are written regarding immersion itself, not sanctification!
The Gemara resolves: Since the requirement for immersion is already derived from 'They are holy garments', apply these verses to sanctification instead.
The Gemara asks: Why did the Torah write these verses in the language of immersion rather than explicitly in the language of sanctification?
The Gemara answers: This teaches that immersion is like sanctification — just as sanctification is performed in a holy place, so too immersion must be in a holy place.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's source for sanctification
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's source for sanctification
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda derives the requirement for sanctification from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where does Rabbi Yehuda derive the requirement for sanctification (קידוש)?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yehuda derives it from the teaching of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Rav Chisda's analysis of Rabbi's position vs. Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's analysis of Rabbi's position vs. Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that Rabbi's position differs from both the Rabbis and Rabbi Meir: the Rabbis say he sanctifies while dressed, Rabbi says while removing; Rabbi Meir says the second sanctification is while dressed, Rabbi says while removing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that Rabbi's position differs from both the Rabbis and Rabbi Meir: the Rabbis say he sanctifies while dressed, Rabbi says while removing; Rabbi Meir says the second sanctification is while dressed, Rabbi says while removing.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's ruling on the second sanctification
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's ruling on the second sanctification
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov states that everyone agrees regarding the second sanctification that he dresses first and then sanctifies, because the verse 'when they approach the altar' excludes one who still needs to dress.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov resolves the dispute by stating that everyone agrees regarding the second sanctification that he dresses first and then sanctifies, because the verse 'when they approach the altar' excludes one who still needs to dress.

items.text: Reconciliation of Rav Chisda and Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.text_en: Reconciliation of Rav Chisda and Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.desc_en: Rav Acha the son of Rava says to Rav Ashi that Rav Chisda and Rav Acha bar Yaakov disagree, because if both were accepted, Rabbi would have fifteen sanctifications instead of ten.

sub.text: Rav Acha the son of Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha the son of Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha the son of Rava tells Rav Ashi that Rav Chisda and Rav Acha bar Yaakov disagree, because if both were accepted, Rabbi would have fifteen sanctifications instead of ten.

items.text: Definition of 'קרצו' and the number of fingers for pinching
items.text_en: Definition of 'קרצו' and the number of fingers for pinching
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'קרצו' means cutting the trachea and esophagus, as per Ulla. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse to support this. Ulla then states that the pinching is done with the majority of two fingers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'קרצו' (he pinched it) means in the Mishnah.
Ulla explains that 'קרצו' is a term for killing, i.e., cutting the trachea and esophagus.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a verse (Jeremiah 46:20) and Rav Yosef's Aramaic translation to prove that 'קרץ' means killing.
The Gemara asks with how many fingers the pinching is performed.
Ulla states that the pinching is done with the majority of two fingers.

items.text: Support for the majority of two fingers from Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Support for the majority of two fingers from Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish agree that the pinching is with the majority of two fingers. Resh Lakish explains why the Mishnah teaches 'majority of one for a bird and majority of two for an animal' — because if the kohen did not pinch, the service might be invalid rabbinically.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the pinching (קריצה) is performed with the majority of two fingers.

Resh Lakish agrees with the majority of two fingers and explains why the Mishnah teaches 'majority of one for a bird and majority of two for an animal' — to prevent the service from being invalidated rabbinically if the kohen did not pinch.
The Gemara objects: if the service were invalid without the pinching, it would constitute a service performed by another person, which is impossible on Yom Kippur.
The Gemara resolves: the concern is that the service would be invalid only rabbinically (מדרבנן), not biblically.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule about the majority of one bird or two animals, then questions why the mitzvah of 'maruk' (wiping) is needed if there is no disqualification even rabbinically. The answer is that it is a mitzvah to wipe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule about the majority of one bird or two animals.
The Gemara questions why the mitzvah of 'maruk' (wiping) is needed if there is no disqualification even rabbinically.
The Gemara answers that it is a mitzvah to wipe.

items.text: Abaye's order of the Temple service
items.text_en: Abaye's order of the Temple service
items.desc_en: Abaye, citing the Gemara in the name of Abba Shaul, lists the entire sequence of the daily Temple service: the large arrangement precedes the second arrangement for incense, which precedes the two logs, then the inner altar's ash removal, the five lamps, the blood of the tamid, the two lamps, the incense, the limbs, the meal-offering, the griddle-cakes, the libations, the additional offerings, the showbread, and finally the afternoon tamid, based on the verse 'and he shall burn upon it the fat of the peace-offerings'.

sub.text: Abaye citing the Gemara in the name of Abba Shaul
sub.text_en: Abaye citing the Gemara in the name of Abba Shaul
sub.desc_en: Abaye begins listing the order of the Temple service, starting with the large arrangement preceding the second arrangement for incense, which precedes the two logs, which precedes the inner altar's ash removal.

Abaye continues the sequence: the five lamps precede the blood of the tamid, which precedes the two lamps, which precedes the incense, which precedes the limbs, the meal-offering, the griddle-cakes, and the libations.

Abaye concludes the sequence: the libations precede the additional offerings, which precede the showbread, which precedes the afternoon tamid, citing the verse 'and he shall burn upon it the fat of the peace-offerings' to indicate that all offerings are completed upon the altar.

items.text: Source and reasoning for the large arrangement preceding the second arrangement
items.text_en: Source and reasoning for the large arrangement preceding the second arrangement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that the large arrangement precedes the second arrangement for incense, citing a baraita from the verse 'it is the burnt-offering upon the hearth on the altar all night' for the large arrangement and 'and the fire of the altar shall be burning on it' for the second arrangement. It then considers reversing the order but concludes that the large arrangement is preferable because its atonement is greater, and alternatively, if there are no woods for the second arrangement, one can take from the large arrangement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that the large arrangement precedes the second arrangement for incense.
A baraita is cited, deriving the large arrangement from the verse 'it is the burnt-offering upon the hearth' and the second arrangement from 'and the fire of the altar shall be burning on it'.
The Gemara considers reversing the order but concludes that the large arrangement is preferable because its atonement is greater.
The Gemara objects that the second arrangement is preferable because it brings incense inside, but rejects this, affirming that greater atonement is decisive.
An alternative resolution is offered: if no wood is found for the second arrangement, one can take from the large arrangement, showing its priority.

items.text: Source for the second arrangement preceding the two logs
items.text_en: Source for the second arrangement preceding the two logs
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'and the priest shall burn wood on it in the morning, in the morning' that 'on it' means on the large arrangement, not on its companion, implying the second arrangement already exists. It then addresses a potential objection that the verse is needed for its own context, noting that two instances of 'on it' are written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the second arrangement precedes the arrangement of the two logs, and derives it from the verse 'וּבִעֵר עָלֶיהָ הַכֹּהֵן עֵצִים' — 'עָלֶיהָ' implies on the large arrangement, not on its companion, proving the companion already exists.
An objection is raised that the word 'עָלֶיהָ' is needed for its own context, and the Gemara responds that two instances of 'עָלֶיהָ' are written in the verse.

items.text: The two logs precede the inner altar's ash removal, with debate on the nature of the logs
items.text_en: The two logs precede the inner altar's ash removal, with debate on the nature of the logs
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the two logs precede the inner altar's ash removal, despite both having 'in the morning' written, because preparation (hakhsharah) is preferable. It then questions what the preparation is, noting that the two logs go to the large arrangement. Rabbi Yirmeya says they are for the scent of the wood, Ravina says since he began the arrangement he finishes, and Rav Ashi says if there are no woods for the second arrangement, one can take from the large arrangement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the arrangement of the two logs precedes the removal of ash from the inner altar, despite both having 'in the morning' written, because preparation (הכשר) is preferable.
The Gemara questions what the preparation is, noting that the two logs go to the large arrangement, so they are not a separate preparation for the inner altar.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the two logs are for the scent of the wood (שום עצים), a separate purpose from the large arrangement.
Ravina answers that since the priest began the arrangement of the large arrangement, he finishes it, and the two logs are part of that completion.
Rav Ashi answers that if there are no woods for the second arrangement, one can take from the large arrangement, so the two logs are a preparation for the second arrangement.

items.text: Inner altar's ash removal precedes the five lamps, with a principle from Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Inner altar's ash removal precedes the five lamps, with a principle from Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the inner altar's ash removal precedes the five lamps. Abaye says he has a tradition but no logical reason, while Rava cites Resh Lakish's principle that one does not pass over mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the ash removal from the inner altar precedes the kindling of the five lamps.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this priority.
Abaye says he has a tradition (גמרא) for this order but no logical reason (סברא).
Rava explains the priority by citing Resh Lakish's principle that one does not pass over מצוות (commandments).

items.text: Placement of the golden altar
items.text_en: Placement of the golden altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when entering the Sanctuary, one first encounters the golden altar because it is positioned slightly outward, as the table and menorah are set back two and a half cubits from the walls, while the altar is centered and slightly forward. This arrangement ensures the table and menorah face each other, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that upon entering the Sanctuary, one first encounters the golden altar because it is positioned slightly outward, while the table and menorah are set back two and a half cubits from the walls, as per the baraita, and they must face each other.

items.text: Rava's inference about arm to head tefillin
items.text_en: Rava's inference about arm to head tefillin
items.desc_en: Rava infers from Reish Lakish's statement that it is forbidden to pass the arm tefillin over the head tefillin, as the altar is not passed over the table and menorah.

sub.desc_en: Rava infers from Resh Lakish's position that passing the arm strap over the head-tefillin is forbidden, and explains how to properly don them.

items.text: Priority of five-lamp trimming over blood, and blood over two-lamp trimming
items.text_en: Priority of five-lamp trimming over blood, and blood over two-lamp trimming
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the extra 'in the morning' phrases from the wood-offering verses are applied here: one gives priority to the five-lamp trimming over the blood of the daily offering (since three verses vs. two), and the other gives priority to the blood over the two-lamp trimming (since atonement is superior, even though both have two verses).

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the priority: trimming five lamps precedes the blood of the daily offering, and the blood precedes trimming two lamps.
The gemara asks for the reason behind this priority.

Abaye explains that the extra 'בַּבֹּקֶר בַּבֹּקֶר' (morning, morning) from the wood-offering verses are applied: one gives priority to trimming five lamps over the blood, and the other gives priority to the blood over trimming two lamps.
The gemara elaborates that one extra phrase is assigned to trimming five lamps because there are three verses for it versus two for the blood.
The gemara explains that the other extra phrase is assigned to the blood over trimming two lamps because atonement (כפרה) is superior, even though both have two verses.

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge to Abaye
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge to Abaye
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa questions Abaye: why not apply one extra phrase to the removal of ashes from the inner altar to precede the blood (three vs. two), and the other to the blood to precede the five-lamp trimming (atonement is superior)? The Gemara responds that this would break the sequence of the service.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Abaye, suggesting an alternative allocation: one extra 'בַּבֹּקֶר' should prioritize the inner altar's removal over the blood, and the other should prioritize the blood over trimming five lamps, since atonement is superior.
Abaye rejects the objection, arguing that if so, how would one divide the two extra occurrences between the three items (inner altar removal, blood, trimming five lamps)?

items.text: Reish Lakish vs. Rabbi Yochanan on the extra phrases
items.text_en: Reish Lakish vs. Rabbi Yochanan on the extra phrases
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this explanation works for Reish Lakish, who says the repeated trimming is to alert the entire courtyard. But for Rabbi Yochanan, who says 'in the morning, in the morning' divides the service into two mornings, what can be said?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the explanation of the extra phrases works well for Reish Lakish, who says the repeated trimming is to alert the entire courtyard.
The Gemara asks: but for Rabbi Yochanan, who says 'בַּבֹּקֶר בַּבֹּקֶר' divides the service into two mornings, what can be said?

items.text: Ravina's question about the wood-offering verse
items.text_en: Ravina's question about the wood-offering verse
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: isn't the extra 'in the morning' from the wood-offering needed for its own context, to teach that the wood precedes the second arrangement of incense? Rav Ashi replies that the verse 'upon it' already implies there is another arrangement, so the extra phrase is indeed superfluous.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: is the extra 'בַּבֹּקֶר בַּבֹּקֶר' of the wood-offering truly superfluous? It is needed to teach that the wood-offering precedes the second arrangement of incense!
Rav Ashi answers: haven't we established that 'עָלֶיהָ' (upon it) implies 'and not upon its companion', indicating that there is a second arrangement?

items.text: Why five lamps first, not two or six
items.text_en: Why five lamps first, not two or six
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the five-lamp trimming is done first rather than the two-lamp trimming, and answers that once one begins, one does the majority. It then asks why not six lamps, and answers that the verse 'when he trims the lamps he shall burn it' implies no fewer than two lamps.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why does one trim five lamps first? Because once he starts, he performs the majority.
The Gemara asks: why not trim six? The verse says 'בְּהֵיטִיבוֹ אֶת הַנֵּרוֹת יַקְטִירֶנָּה' (when he trims the lamps, he shall burn incense), and there are no fewer than two lamps.
The Gemara asks why not trim six lamps instead of five.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'when he trims the lamps he shall burn it' implies no fewer than two lamps remain lit, so only five are trimmed.

items.text: Order of the remaining services
items.text_en: Order of the remaining services
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that the two-lamp trimming precedes the incense (from the verse), the incense precedes the limbs (since it has 'in the morning, in the morning'), the limbs precede the meal-offering (from a baraita), and nothing precedes the morning daily offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that trimming the two lamps precedes the incense, citing the verse 'בהטיבו את הנרות יַקְטִירֶנָּה' (when he trims the lamps he shall burn the incense).
The Gemara cites a baraita that the incense precedes the limbs, because the verse says 'בבקר בבקר' (morning, morning) for the incense, while the limbs only have one 'בקר'.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the limbs precede the meal-offering, and that nothing precedes the morning daily offering.

items.text: Establishing the order of the morning service
items.text_en: Establishing the order of the morning service
items.desc_en: Rava derives from the verse 'and he shall arrange the burnt offering upon it' that the burnt offering is the first offering. The Gemara then lists the sequence: the meal-offering for the griddle-cakes, the burnt offering and its meal-offering, the griddle-cakes for the libations, and the libations for the additional offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'וְעָרַךְ עָלֶיהָ הָעוֹלָה' (and he shall arrange the burnt offering upon it) that the burnt offering is the first offering.
Rava explicitly states that the term 'הָעוֹלָה' (the burnt offering) indicates it is the first offering.
The Gemara lists the sequence: the meal-offering for the griddle-cakes, the burnt offering and its meal-offering, and the griddle-cakes for the libations.
The Gemara continues the sequence: the libations for the additional offerings, and the additional offerings for the showbread pans.

items.text: Dispute about additional offerings and showbread
items.text_en: Dispute about additional offerings and showbread
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the list says additional offerings precede the showbread, but a baraita states showbread precedes additional offerings. It resolves that this is a dispute between Tanna'im.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the list says additional offerings (מוספין) precede the showbread bowls (בזיכין), but a baraita states that the bowls precede the additional offerings.
The Gemara resolves that the contradiction reflects a dispute between Tanna'im (תנאים), not a single authoritative tradition.

items.text: Abaye's reasoning and the derivation for showbread
items.text_en: Abaye's reasoning and the derivation for showbread
items.desc_en: Abaye supports the view that additional offerings precede showbread by analogy to the morning service: just as 'in the morning' indicates precedence, 'by day' indicates delay. The opposing view derives from a gezerah shavah of 'chukkah' from the griddle-cakes, but the Gemara limits this derivation using the phrase 'by day' to indicate delay.

sub.desc_en: Abaye supports the view that additional offerings (מוספין) precede the showbread bowls (בזיכין) by analogy: just as 'in the morning' indicates precedence, so 'by day' indicates delay.
The Gemara asks: what is the reasoning of the one who says the bowls precede the additional offerings? It answers: he derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'חוקה' from the griddle-cakes (חביתין).

The Gemara limits the verbal analogy: if he derived everything from there, he would learn the entire matter; therefore the phrase 'by day' (ביום) serves to delay the bowls after the additional offerings.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna for the morning incense order
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna for the morning incense order
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the morning incense was offered between the blood and the limbs. The Gemara questions which Tanna holds this view: if the Rabbis, it should be between blood and the lamps; if Abba Shaul, between lamps and limbs. It concludes it is the Rabbis, but the Mishnah does not list the full order.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the morning incense was offered between the blood and the limbs.
The Gemara asks which Tanna holds this view, noting that if it is the Rabbis, the incense should be between blood and lamps, and if Abba Shaul, between lamps and limbs.
The Gemara answers that it is indeed the Rabbis, but the Mishnah does not list the full order.

items.text: Source for the afternoon incense order
items.text_en: Source for the afternoon incense order
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the afternoon incense was offered between the limbs and the libations. Rabbi Yochanan derives this from the verse 'like the morning meal-offering and its libation you shall make', teaching that just as in the morning incense precedes libations, so too in the afternoon. The Gemara rejects an analogy to limbs because the verse says 'like the morning meal-offering', not 'like the morning limbs'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the afternoon incense was offered between the limbs and the libations.
The Gemara asks: from where are these matters derived?
Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse 'like the morning meal-offering and its libation you shall make' that just as in the morning incense precedes libations, so too in the afternoon.
The Gemara objects: just as in the morning incense precedes limbs, so too here incense should precede limbs.
The Gemara rejects the analogy: the verse says 'like the morning meal-offering', not 'like the morning limbs', so only the order relative to libations is derived, not relative to limbs.

items.text: Derivation of the libation measure
items.text_en: Derivation of the libation measure
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that from the verse 'and its libation a quarter of a hin' we learn that the morning service's libation is derived from the afternoon service's libation.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְנִסְכּוֹ רְבִיעִית הַהִין' (and its libation a quarter of a hin) to derive that the measure for the morning libation is learned from the afternoon libation.

items.text: Source for Rabbi's view on tamid funds
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi's view on tamid funds
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi's reasoning that the evening tamid comes from the morning's funds, given the verse 'between the evenings'. Rabba bar Ulla derives it from the word 'one' in the verse, indicating the unique morning tamid. The Rabbis interpret 'one' as the choicest of the flock, and Rabbi derives that from another verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi's view that the evening tamid offering is funded from the morning's allocation.
The Gemara notes that the Rabbis' position is straightforward from the verse 'between the evenings', but asks what is Rabbi's scriptural basis.
Rabba bar Ulla derives Rabbi's view from the verse 'to the one lamb', interpreting 'one' as referring uniquely to the morning tamid.
The Rabbis interpret 'one' as meaning the choicest of the flock, not a reference to the morning tamid.
Rabbi counters that the requirement for the choicest animal is already derived from the verse 'and the choice of your vows'.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis need both verses: one for obligatory offerings and one for voluntary offerings, and both are necessary.

items.text: Heating water for the High Priest
items.text_en: Heating water for the High Priest
items.desc_en: A baraita describes that iron pans were heated on Yom Kippur eve and placed into cold water to cool it. The Gemara objects that this process might constitute צירוף (forging). Rav Bibi answers that the heat did not reach the level of forging, and Abaye adds that even if it did, it is a case of דבר שאין מתכוין which is permitted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Yehuda describes that iron pans were heated on Yom Kippur eve and placed into cold water to cool it.
The Gemara objects that this process might constitute צירוף (forging), which is prohibited on Shabbat or Yom Tov.
Rav Bibi answers that the heat did not reach the level of forging, so the prohibition does not apply.
Abaye adds that even if the heat reached the level of forging, it is a case of דבר שאין מתכוין (an unintended action), which is permitted.

items.text: Contradiction from Abaye's other statement
items.text_en: Contradiction from Abaye's other statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's lenient view by citing a baraita where Abaye himself stated that Rabbi Yehuda considers דבר שאין מתכוין forbidden. Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Torah law and rabbinic law: the prohibition of צירוף here is only rabbinic, so even Rabbi Yehuda would permit it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's lenient position by citing a baraita where Abaye himself stated that Rabbi Yehuda considers דבר שאין מתכוין (an unintentional act) forbidden.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Torah law and rabbinic law: the prohibition of צירוף (forging metal) here is only rabbinic, so even Rabbi Yehuda would permit it.

items.text: Mishnah: The High Priest's preparations and vestments
items.text_en: Mishnah: The High Priest's preparations and vestments
items.desc_en: The mishnah describes the High Priest being brought to the Parvah chamber, where a linen sheet is spread between him and the people. He sanctifies his hands and feet, undresses, immerses, dries, and puts on white garments. The Gemara then records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about the value of the garments worn in the morning and evening.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest's procedure: he is brought to the Parvah chamber, a linen sheet is spread, he sanctifies hands and feet, undresses, immerses, dries, and dons white garments.
Rabbi Meir states that the order is reversed: he undresses first, then sanctifies hands and feet.
Rabbi Meir specifies that in the morning he wore Pelusin garments worth twelve maneh, and in the evening Hindevi garments worth eight hundred zuz.
The Sages say that in the morning he wore garments worth eighteen maneh, and in the evening twelve maneh, totaling thirty maneh.
The Mishnah concludes that these garments are from communal funds, but if the High Priest wishes to add, he may add from his own.

items.text: Explanation of 'Parvah'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'Parvah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Parvah' means, and Rav Yosef answers that it is a Persian magus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the name 'Parvah' means.
Rav Yosef answers that 'Parvah' means a Persian magus.

items.text: Reason for linen garments
items.text_en: Reason for linen garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why specifically linen (בוץ) is used, and Rav Kahana answers that it is to make the service of the day recognizable as being in linen garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why specifically linen (בוץ) is used for the sheet.
Rav Kahana answers that the linen sheet is used so that the day's service is recognizable as being performed in linen garments.

items.text: Purpose of the number of garments
items.text_en: Purpose of the number of garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tanna specifies the number of garments, and explains that it teaches that one should not use fewer than these, but if one uses more, there is no issue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tanna specifies the number of garments, since the number seems incidental.
The Gemara answers that the number teaches that one should not use fewer garments, but using more is unproblematic.

items.text: Source for superiority of morning garments
items.text_en: Source for superiority of morning garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that morning garments are superior, and Rav Huna bar Rav Illai answers that the repetition of 'bad' four times indicates that the finest of linen is chosen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the morning garments are superior.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Illai's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Illai's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Illai answers that the fourfold repetition of 'בד' (linen) in the verse indicates that the finest linen is chosen for the morning service.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding 'other garments'
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding 'other garments'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the interpretation of 'other garments' (בגדים אחרים) from the verse, suggesting it might mean more important garments. It resolves that 'other' means inferior garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the interpretation of 'other garments' (בגדים אחרים), suggesting it might mean more important garments.
The Gemara resolves that 'other' means inferior garments, not more important ones.

items.text: Baraita on a priest wearing a garment made by his mother
items.text_en: Baraita on a priest wearing a garment made by his mother
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda teaches that after communal service, a priest may wear a garment made by his mother for individual service, provided he gives it to the community. The Gemara cites stories of Rabbi Yishmael ben Piabi and Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom, and explains why the latter's garment was not worn.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda (or Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda)
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda (or Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda)
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda teaches that after communal service, a priest may wear a garment made by his mother for individual service, provided he gives it to the community.
The Gemara asks whether this ruling is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches that we do not suspect the priest might fail to properly give the garment to the community.

sub.text: Supporting story about Rabbi Yishmael ben Piabi
sub.text_en: Supporting story about Rabbi Yishmael ben Piabi
sub.desc_en: A story is told that Rabbi Yishmael ben Piabi's mother made him a valuable garment, which he wore for individual service and then gave to the community.

sub.text: Supporting story about Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom
sub.text_en: Supporting story about Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom
sub.desc_en: A story is told that Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom's mother made him an extremely expensive garment, but the other priests prevented him from wearing it because it appeared transparent.
The Gemara questions how the garment could appear transparent, given the requirement for thick fabric.
Abaye explains that the garment appeared transparent like wine in a glass, meaning the fabric was fine enough to reveal the body underneath despite being thick.

items.text: The poor person's excuse and Hillel's example
items.text_en: The poor person's excuse and Hillel's example
items.desc_en: The baraita states that a poor person who neglected Torah study cannot claim poverty as an excuse, citing Hillel the Elder who worked daily, paid half to enter the study hall, and once nearly froze on the roof to hear Torah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a poor person who neglected Torah study cannot excuse himself by poverty, and is asked whether he was poorer than Hillel.
The baraita recounts that Hillel the Elder worked daily, paid half his wages to enter the study hall, and once climbed onto the roof to hear Torah from Shmaya and Avtalyon.
The baraita concludes that it was a snowy Friday in Tevet, Hillel was found covered in three cubits of snow, and they declared him worthy of desecrating Shabbat to save him.

items.text: The rich person's excuse and Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom's example
items.text_en: The rich person's excuse and Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom's example
items.desc_en: The baraita continues: a rich person cannot claim wealth as an excuse, citing Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom who inherited vast wealth but traveled to study Torah, and once his own servants did not recognize him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a rich person who claims wealth as an excuse for not studying Torah is countered with the example of Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom.
The baraita describes Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom's vast inherited wealth and his daily practice of traveling to study Torah despite his riches.
The baraita recounts that Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom's servants once seized him, but he begged to be released to study Torah, and he never recognized them, dedicating himself entirely to Torah study.

items.text: The wicked person's excuse and Joseph's example
items.text_en: The wicked person's excuse and Joseph's example
items.desc_en: The baraita concludes: a wicked person cannot claim beauty as an excuse, citing Joseph the Righteous who resisted Potiphar's wife daily. The Gemara explains the verses and concludes that Hillel, Rabbi Elazar, and Joseph obligate the poor, rich, and wicked respectively.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a wicked person is asked why he did not study Torah, and if he claims beauty as an excuse, he is countered with Joseph's example.
The baraita recounts how Potiphar's wife daily attempted to seduce Joseph, changing her clothes constantly.
The narrative details Joseph's repeated refusals and his responses to Potiphar's wife's threats, culminating in her offering a thousand silver talents to no avail.
The Gemara concludes that Hillel obligates the poor, Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom obligates the rich, and Joseph obligates the wicked.

items.text: Mishnah: The High Priest's confession over the bull
items.text_en: Mishnah: The High Priest's confession over the bull
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest approaching his bull, standing between the Ulam and the altar, placing his hands on it, and reciting the confession for himself and his household, to which the people respond with 'Baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest approaching his bull, which stands between the Ulam and the altar, with the priest positioned to the east facing west.
The Mishnah states that the High Priest places both hands on the bull and recites the confession.
The Mishnah quotes the full text of the High Priest's confession, including the formula 'אנא השם' (Please, God) and the request for atonement for sins, transgressions, and iniquities.
The Mishnah concludes that the people respond after the High Priest's confession with 'ברוך שם כבוד מלכותו לעולם ועד' (Blessed be the Name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever).

items.text: Identifying the anonymous mishnah as Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Identifying the anonymous mishnah as Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds that the area between the Entrance Hall and the altar is considered north (for slaughter). It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda defines the north, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon adds the area between the Entrance Hall and the altar, and Rabbi adds the place where priests and Israelites tread. All agree that from the Hall of Hewn Stones inward is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds that the area between the Entrance Hall and the altar is considered north for slaughter.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah is Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position.

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda defines the north, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon adds the area between the Entrance Hall and the altar, Rabbi adds the place where priests and Israelites tread, and all agree that from the Hall of Hewn Stones inward is invalid.

items.text: Rejecting Rabbi as the author and resolving the difficulty
items.text_en: Rejecting Rabbi as the author and resolving the difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests the mishnah could be Rabbi, but objects that Rabbi adds to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda but not to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon. It then reframes: if it were Rabbi, he would have placed the slaughter anywhere in the entire courtyard. The Gemara concludes that the mishnah is indeed Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, but even so, why not place it between the altar and the wall? The answer is due to the High Priest's weakness, and the same applies to Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mishnah is Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and not Rabbi, then objects that if it were Rabbi, he would have added to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda but not to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara reframes: if it were Rabbi, he would have placed the slaughter anywhere in the entire courtyard, so the mishnah must be Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara objects: even if it is Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, why not place the slaughter between the altar and the wall?
The Gemara resolves: the slaughter is placed between the Ulam and the altar due to the High Priest's weakness, and the same applies to Rabbi.

items.text: Explaining the head placement and the concern for feces
items.text_en: Explaining the head placement and the concern for feces
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the animal's head can be to the south and its face to the west. Rav answers that one bends its head. The Gemara asks why not place it straightforwardly; Abaye explains it is a decree lest the animal defecate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the animal's head can be to the south and its face to the west simultaneously.
Rav answers that one bends the animal's head to achieve the described orientation.
The Gemara asks why not place the animal straightforwardly without bending its head.
Abaye explains that it is a decree lest the animal defecate, which would cause disrespect.

items.text: Baraita on semikhah and the dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Baraita on semikhah and the dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the procedure for semikhah: the owner stands in the north facing west, the one performing semikhah stands in the east facing west, places both hands between the horns, and confesses. For a sin-offering he confesses the sin of a sin-offering, for a guilt-offering the sin of a guilt-offering, and for a burnt-offering the sin of gleanings, forgotten sheaves, pe'ah, and the poor man's tithe — according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili. Rabbi Akiva says a burnt-offering only comes for a positive commandment or a prohibition that is remedied by a positive commandment. The Gemara asks what they disagree about, and Rabbi Yirmeya begins to explain.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes the procedure for semikhah (placing hands on the sacrifice) and the confessions for different offerings according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
Rabbi Akiva states that a burnt-offering (עולה) only comes for a positive commandment or a prohibition that is remedied by a positive commandment.
The Gemara asks what is the point of dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yirmeya begins to explain.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili about the prohibition of neveilah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili about the prohibition of neveilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially explains that Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili argue about whether the prohibition of neveilah is a 'superior' prohibition or not. Abaye then reinterprets the dispute, stating that everyone agrees the prohibition of neveilah is a 'superior' prohibition, and the real argument is about the interpretation of the word 'תעזוב' (abandon) in the context of a lost animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili concerns the prohibition of neveilah.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds the prohibition of neveilah is a 'superior' prohibition (לאו מעליא), while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds it is not a 'superior' prohibition.

Abaye rejects the initial explanation and states that everyone agrees the prohibition of neveilah is a 'superior' prohibition; the real dispute is about the interpretation of the word 'תעזוב' (abandon).
Abaye explains that Rabbi Akiva holds 'תעזוב' means 'abandon from the outset' (מעיקרא משמע), while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds it means 'abandon now' (השתא משמע).

items.text: The proper order of confession and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: The proper order of confession and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches the order of confession: 'I have committed iniquity, transgression, and sin.' Rabbi Meir derives this from the verse about the scapegoat and from Moses' prayer, while the Sages argue that 'iniquities' are intentional sins, 'transgressions' are rebellious acts, and 'sins' are unintentional sins. The Gemara questions why one would confess unintentional sins after intentional ones, and resolves that the confession should be in a different order. It then explains that Moses' prayer was that God treat intentional sins as unintentional when Israel repents.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: the Sages taught the order of confession, and Rabbi Meir derives the sequence from verses, including Moses' statement 'נושא עון ופשע וחטאה'.
The Sages argue that 'עונות' refers to intentional sins (זדונות), citing a verse, and 'פשעים' refers to rebellious sins (מרדים), citing verses about Moab and Libnah.

The Sages explain that 'לכל חטאתם' refers to unintentional sins (שגגות), and then raise an objection: after confessing intentional and rebellious sins, why would one repeat confession for unintentional sins?

The baraita resolves the objection by explaining the actual confession formula, citing David, Solomon, and Daniel, and concludes that Moses' verse means that when Israel repents, God treats intentional sins as unintentional.

items.text: Rabbah bar Shmuel rules in accordance with the Sages
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Shmuel rules in accordance with the Sages
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Shmuel states in the name of Rav that the halakha follows the Sages. The Gemara notes that this is obvious, as the majority opinion prevails, but suggests that Rav's statement is necessary to counter the possibility that Rabbi Meir's view is supported by the verse from Moses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Shmuel reports in Rav's name that the halacha follows the Sages; the Gemara notes this is obvious (since the majority rules), but Rav teaches that one might have thought Rabbi Meir's view is supported by Moses' verse, so the ruling is necessary.
The Gemara questions why Rav's ruling is necessary, since the principle is that the majority opinion prevails.
The Gemara explains that Rav's statement is needed to counter the assumption that Rabbi Meir's view is supported by the verse from Moses.

items.text: Story of a prayer leader who followed Rabbi Meir's practice
items.text_en: Story of a prayer leader who followed Rabbi Meir's practice
items.desc_en: A prayer leader who led the service before Rabbah followed Rabbi Meir's order of confession. Rabbah rebuked him for abandoning the Sages, but the leader defended himself by citing the verse from Moses' Torah.

sub.desc_en: A story is told: a certain person who led the prayer before Rabbah followed Rabbi Meir's opinion; Rabbah rebuked him, but the person defended himself by citing the verse in Moses' Torah.
Rabbah rebukes the prayer leader for abandoning the Sages and following Rabbi Meir's practice.
The prayer leader defends himself by stating that he follows Rabbi Meir because it is written in Moses' Torah.

items.text: Derivation that the High Priest's confession for himself is verbal, not through blood
items.text_en: Derivation that the High Priest's confession for himself is verbal, not through blood
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the word 'וְכִפֶּר' (and he shall atone) in the context of the bull refers to verbal atonement (confession), not blood atonement. The Gemara supports this by comparing the 'kaparah' mentioned here to that of the scapegoat, which is verbal. It then addresses a potential objection that one might learn from the inner goat, whose atonement is through blood, and concludes that the verse 'וְכִפֶּר' is stated before the bull is slaughtered, proving it refers to confession.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the word 'וְכִפֶּר' (and he shall atone) in the context of the bull refers to verbal atonement (confession), not blood atonement.
The Gemara supports the baraita by drawing a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the 'kaparah' stated here for the bull and that stated for the scapegoat, which is verbal.
The Gemara provides a second proof: the verse 'וְכִפֶּר' is stated before the bull is slaughtered, proving it refers to confession, not blood.
The Gemara clarifies the need for the second proof: one might object by learning from the inner goat, whose atonement is through blood, so the verse 'וְכִפֶּר' before slaughter shows it is verbal.

items.text: Derivation of the confession formula and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Derivation of the confession formula and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the confession must include both 'Ana' and 'HaShem' through verbal analogies (gezerah shavah) from the sin of the golden calf (Chorev) and the heifer whose neck is broken (eglah arufah). Abaye raises a difficulty: if the heifer's confession is derived from Chorev, why does the Mishnah in Sotah only mention 'Kafer le'amecha Yisrael' without 'Ana'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the confession formula including 'אנא' and 'השם', and derives both through גזירה שווה (verbal analogies) from the sin of the golden calf (חורב) and the heifer whose neck is broken (עגלה ערופה).
Abaye raises a difficulty: if the heifer's confession is derived from Chorev, why does the Mishnah in Sotah only mention 'כפר לעמך ישראל' without 'אנא'?

items.text: The congregation's response to the High Priest's blessing
items.text_en: The congregation's response to the High Priest's blessing
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi and Chananyah ben Achbi Rabbi Yehoshua, who explain that when the High Priest pronounces the Tetragrammaton, the people respond by blessing God, as derived from verses about Moses and the prophet.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi and Chananyah ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua each explain that when the leader mentions God's name, the people respond with praise, based on verses.
Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi cites a verse to show that the people bless God when the High Priest pronounces the Tetragrammaton.
Chananyah ben Achbi Rabbi Yehoshua cites a different verse to derive the same practice of blessing God in response.

items.text: Mishnah: The lottery and Temple improvements
items.text_en: Mishnah: The lottery and Temple improvements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest's arrival at the east of the courtyard, the placement of the segan and the head of the father's house, the two goats and the lottery box, and lists various improvements made by Ben Gamla, Ben Katin, Monbaz, Heleni, and Nikanor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest's arrival at the east of the courtyard with the segan and the head of the father's house, the two goats and the lottery box, and lists various Temple improvements made by Ben Gamla, Ben Katin, Monbaz, Heleni, and Nikanor.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's statement 'to the north of the altar' implies the altar is not in the north, which aligns with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view. It resolves an apparent contradiction by explaining that the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and the earlier clause refers to the area between the Entrance Hall and the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that the altar is not in the north, and identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion that the entire north must be clear.

The Gemara objects that the beginning of the Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon, and resolves that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's, with the clause about 'between the Entrance Hall and the Altar' being taught separately.
The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and the earlier clause refers to the area between the Entrance Hall and the altar.

items.text: The segan on the right and the head of the father's house on the left
items.text_en: The segan on the right and the head of the father's house on the left
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah states that walking to the right of one's teacher is boorish, which seems to contradict the Mishnah. The Gemara resolves this with Rav Shmuel bar Pappa's explanation that the segan walks slightly behind the High Priest to cover him, and a baraita is cited to clarify the proper position relative to one's teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rav Yehudah says walking to the right of one's teacher is boorish, but the Mishnah places the deputy (סגן) to the right of the High Priest.
A baraita is cited: when three walk, the teacher is in the middle, the greater student on the right, the lesser on the left, as exemplified by the three angels visiting Abraham.
Rav Shmuel bar Pappa resolves the contradiction before Rav Adda: the deputy stands to the right but slightly behind (מצדד אצדודי), so he is not truly to the right of his teacher.
Rav Shmuel bar Pappa explains that the segan walks slightly behind the High Priest (מצדד אצדודי, sidling) so as to cover him, not directly to his right, resolving the contradiction.

items.text: The lottery: two lots of any material
items.text_en: The lottery: two lots of any material
items.desc_en: The Sages derive from the verse 'and Aaron shall place lots upon the two goats' that the lots can be made of any material. The Gemara explains the necessity of this teaching, as one might have thought they must be gold like the tzitz, so the Torah repeats 'lot' to include lots of olive wood, nut wood, or boxwood.

sub.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'ונתן אהרן על שני השעירים גורלות' to teach that the lots can be made of any material, but must be identical in size and value, not one gold and one silver.

The Gemara asks why the baraita's statement that lots can be of any material is obvious, and answers that it is needed to counter a possible inference from the ציץ (frontplate) that the lots must be gold; the repetition of 'גורל' teaches they can be of olive, nut, or boxwood.
The baraita explains that without the repetition, one might think the lots must be gold like the ציץ, so the verse teaches they can be of any material.

The Gemara explains that the teaching is necessary because one might have thought the lots must be gold like the ציץ (frontplate), so the Torah repeats 'גּוֹרָל' to include lots of olive wood, nut wood, or boxwood.

items.text: Ben Katin's twelve spouts and the mukhni
items.text_en: Ben Katin's twelve spouts and the mukhni
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that Ben Katin made twelve spouts for the laver so that the twelve priests involved in the daily offering could sanctify their hands and feet simultaneously. Another baraita describes the morning and evening procedures for sanctification. Abaye explains that the mukhni was a wheel that lowered the laver into a well to prevent the water from being invalidated by remaining overnight.

sub.desc_en: A baraita explains that Ben Katin made twelve spouts for the laver so that the twelve priests involved in the daily offering could sanctify simultaneously, and another baraita describes the morning and evening sanctification procedures.
Abaye answers that the mukhni was a wheel that lowered the laver into a well to prevent the water from being invalidated by remaining overnight.

items.text: Monbaz's gold handles and a question
items.text_en: Monbaz's gold handles and a question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that King Monbaz made all the handles of the Yom Kippur vessels of gold. The Gemara asks: why not make the vessels themselves of gold?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Monbaz made only the handles of gold rather than the vessels themselves, implying that making the entire vessels of gold would be more straightforward.
The Gemara asks: why not make the vessels themselves of gold?

items.text: Abaye's interpretation of the golden handles
items.text_en: Abaye's interpretation of the golden handles
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the 'handles of knives' (ידות סכינין) mentioned in the Mishnah refer to the handles of axes and picks, not knives themselves. A baraita supports this by listing various golden implements made for Yom Kippur, including handles of knives, and Abaye clarifies that these are for tools like axes and picks.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the 'handles of knives' (ידות סכינין) in the Mishnah refer to handles of axes and picks.
The Gemara raises an objection by citing a baraita that lists golden handles of knives among the implements made for Yom Kippur, implying they are literal knife handles.
Abaye resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita refers to handles of axes and picks, not knives.

items.text: Helene's golden candelabrum and the time for Shema
items.text_en: Helene's golden candelabrum and the time for Shema
items.desc_en: A baraita describes that when the sun shone on Helene's golden candelabrum, sparks would emerge, signaling the time for the morning Shema. An objection is raised from another baraita stating that those who read Shema with the early-rising watchmen do not fulfill their obligation, as the watchmen rise early. Abaye resolves this by saying the candelabrum was for the general public of Jerusalem, not for the watchmen.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes that when the sun shone on Helene's golden candelabrum, sparks emerged, signaling the time for the morning Shema (קריאת שמע).
An objection is raised from a baraita stating that those who read Shema with the early-rising watchmen (אנשי משמר) do not fulfill their obligation, contradicting the candelabrum's signal.
Abaye resolves that the candelabrum was for the general public of Jerusalem (שאר עמא דירושלם), not for the watchmen, so the objection is irrelevant.

items.text: The tablet for teaching a child and Resh Lakish's ruling
items.text_en: The tablet for teaching a child and Resh Lakish's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Helene also made a tablet (טבלא) for the Sotah ritual. From this, it is inferred that one may write a scroll for a child to learn from. Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai clarifies that this is only permitted if the writing is in the order of the alphabet (אלף בית), not the actual Sotah text.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Helene also made a tablet (טבלא) for the Sotah ritual.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that one may write a scroll for a child to learn from.

sub.text: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish clarifies that this is only permitted if the writing is in the order of the alphabet (אלף בית), not the actual Sotah text.

items.text: Objections regarding copying from the tablet
items.text_en: Objections regarding copying from the tablet
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita that when writing, one sees and writes exactly what is written on the tablet, implying the actual Sotah text. The Gemara emends this to 'sees and writes like what is written on the tablet' (i.e., in the same script). A further objection cites the specific verses written on the tablet (e.g., 'If a man lies with you'), but the Gemara deflects this by noting that the discussion there is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that when writing, one sees and writes exactly what is written on the tablet, implying the actual Sotah text.
The Gemara emends the baraita to 'sees and writes like what is written on the tablet' (i.e., in the same script), not the exact text.
A further objection cites the specific verses written on the tablet (e.g., 'If a man lies with you'), challenging the emendation.
The Gemara deflects the objection by noting that the discussion there is different.

items.text: Conclusion of Nikanor's gates and the Mishnah's transition
items.text_en: Conclusion of Nikanor's gates and the Mishnah's transition
items.desc_en: The Gemara completes the story of Nikanor's gates, including the miracle of the lost gate's return and the verse applied to it. It then records the Mishnah that lists the families whose refusal to teach their crafts is considered disgraceful, contrasting them with the righteous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara transitions from the previous discussion to recount the miracles of Nikanor's gates.
The Gemara asks what specific miracles occurred with Nikanor's gates.

The baraita recounts the miracle: a wave threatened to sink the ship, one gate was thrown overboard, the sea calmed only when Nikanor insisted on being thrown with the second gate, and later the first gate emerged from the sea.

The Gemara applies the verse from Song of Songs to the gate, interprets 'ברותים' as 'ברית ים' (covenant of the sea), and notes that Nikanor's gates were left as copper due to the miracle, with a dispute about the copper's quality.
The Mishnah introduces the list of families whose refusal to teach their crafts is considered disgraceful, beginning with the house of Garmu and the house of Avtinas.
The Mishnah continues listing other individuals who refused to teach, and contrasts the righteous (who are remembered for blessing) with these disgraceful ones (whose name rots).

items.text: Gemara on the house of Garmu
items.text_en: Gemara on the house of Garmu
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the house of Garmu, who refused to teach the art of the showbread. Sages brought Alexandrian craftsmen who could bake but not remove the bread properly. The house of Garmu was reinstated with doubled wages, and they explained their refusal was to prevent misuse of the knowledge. They are praised for their integrity.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the house of Garmu, who were expert in baking the showbread but refused to teach; the sages brought Alexandrian craftsmen who could bake but not remove the bread properly, and the house of Garmu's bread did not mold.
The sages acknowledge that the skill is divinely given, reinstate the house of Garmu with doubled wages, and Rabbi Yehuda gives a different wage figure.

The sages ask why they refused to teach, and the house of Garmu explains they feared misuse of the knowledge for idolatry after the Temple's destruction; they are praised for never having clean bread in their homes, to avoid suspicion.

items.text: Gemara on the house of Avtinas
items.text_en: Gemara on the house of Avtinas
items.desc_en: The Gemara similarly discusses the house of Avtinas, who refused to teach the incense compounding. Alexandrian craftsmen could compound but not produce the straight smoke column. The house of Avtinas was reinstated with doubled wages, and they gave the same reason of preventing idolatry. They are praised for ensuring no one suspected them of using the incense for personal benefit.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the house of Avtinas, who refused to teach the incense compounding, and recounts that the sages brought Alexandrian craftsmen who could compound but not produce the straight smoke column.
The sages acknowledge the skill as created for God's honor, reinstate the house of Avtinas with doubled wages, and Rabbi Yehuda gives a higher wage figure.
The house of Avtinas explains they feared misuse of the incense knowledge for idolatry, and they are praised for ensuring no one suspected them of personal benefit from the incense.

items.text: Testimonies about the house of Avtinas and conclusion
items.text_en: Testimonies about the house of Avtinas and conclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael recounts meeting a descendant of the house of Avtinas who explained their intent to honor God. Rabbi Akiva relates a story of Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga who saw a descendant both cry and laugh, hinting at the future restoration of the incense knowledge. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri obtains the scroll of ingredients from a descendant, leading Ben Azzai to conclude that one should not speak disparagingly of these families.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael recounts meeting a descendant of the house of Avtinas and rebuking him for his ancestors' attempt to diminish God's honor.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva citing Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva citing Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva relates a story from Rabbi Yishmael ben Loga about a descendant who cried and laughed, explaining the future restoration of the incense knowledge.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri obtains the scroll of incense ingredients from a descendant, leading Rabbi Akiva to rule that it is forbidden to speak disparagingly of these families.
Ben Azzai concludes with a maxim that one's reputation and place are determined by one's actions, implying that the families' honor is restored.

items.text: Opening principle: no one touches what is prepared for another
items.text_en: Opening principle: no one touches what is prepared for another
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a general principle that a person does not touch what is prepared for their fellow, and no kingdom encroaches on another even by a hair's breadth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general principle that a person does not touch what is prepared for their fellow, and no kingdom encroaches on another even by a hair's breadth.

items.text: The skill of Hugras ben Levi
items.text_en: The skill of Hugras ben Levi
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how Hugras ben Levi would produce a pleasant sound by placing his thumb in his mouth and his finger between the strings, causing his fellow priests to recoil.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes how Hugras ben Levi would produce a pleasant sound by placing his thumb in his mouth and his finger between the strings, causing his fellow priests to recoil.

items.text: Ben Kamtzar's refusal to teach the art of writing
items.text_en: Ben Kamtzar's refusal to teach the art of writing
items.desc_en: The Sages relate that Ben Kamtzar refused to teach the art of writing, being able to write four quills at once. He could not justify his refusal, and the verse 'the name of the wicked shall rot' applies to him.

sub.desc_en: The Sages relate that Ben Kamtzar refused to teach the art of writing, being able to write four quills at once.
The Sages ask Ben Kamtzar why he refused to teach his skill.
The Sages conclude that Ben Kamtzar could not justify his refusal, and the verse 'the name of the wicked shall rot' applies to him.

items.text: Explanation of 'the name of the wicked shall rot' and a story of Doeg
items.text_en: Explanation of 'the name of the wicked shall rot' and a story of Doeg
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that 'rot' means decay of their names, as we do not mention them. Ravina challenges with the story of Doeg ben Yosef, whose mother weighed him in gold for the Temple, and Jeremiah lamented her fate, but the Holy Spirit responded with a verse showing his end.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'the name of the wicked shall rot' means.
Rabbi Elazar explains that 'rot' means decay of their names, as we do not mention them.
Ravina challenges with the story of Doeg ben Yosef, whose mother weighed him in gold for the Temple, and the enemy slaughtered and ate him.
Jeremiah lamented her fate, but the Holy Spirit responded with a verse showing his end.

items.text: The righteous are blessed through themselves, the wicked through others
items.text_en: The righteous are blessed through themselves, the wicked through others
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that the righteous are blessed through themselves, as it says 'the memory of the righteous is a blessing', and the wicked are cursed through their fellow, as it says 'the name of the wicked shall rot'.
