sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that the righteous are blessed through themselves, as it says 'the memory of the righteous is a blessing', and the wicked are cursed through their fellow, as it says 'the name of the wicked shall rot'.

items.text: Scriptural sources for the principles about righteous and wicked
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for the principles about righteous and wicked
items.desc_en: Ravina asks a Sage for the scriptural source for the principle that the memory of the righteous is a blessing, and the Sage cites verses about Abraham. Similarly, for the wicked, he cites Lot's dwelling in Sodom.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks a Sage who arranges aggadah before him for the scriptural source of the rabbinic principle that the memory of the righteous is a blessing.
The Sage initially answers by citing the verse itself, but Ravina presses for a Torah source.
The Sage provides the Torah source: God's blessing of Abraham before destroying Sodom, showing that the righteous are remembered with blessing.
Ravina asks for the Torah source of the principle that the name of the wicked rots.

sub.text: The Sage's answer for the wicked
sub.text_en: The Sage's answer for the wicked
sub.desc_en: The Sage cites the verse itself and then the Torah source: Lot's dwelling in Sodom, where the people are described as wicked, showing that the wicked are remembered with rot.

items.text: Righteous among wicked and wicked among righteous
items.text_en: Righteous among wicked and wicked among righteous
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that a righteous person living among two wicked people does not learn from their deeds (e.g., Obadiah), and a wicked person living among two righteous people does not learn from their deeds (e.g., Esau).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that a righteous person among two wicked people does not learn from their deeds (e.g., Obadiah), and a wicked person among two righteous people does not learn from their deeds (e.g., Esau).

items.text: Learning blessing from curse and vice versa
items.text_en: Learning blessing from curse and vice versa
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that from the blessing of the righteous you learn the curse of the wicked (e.g., Abraham's blessing leads to Sodom's punishment), and from the curse of the wicked you learn the blessing of the righteous (e.g., Sodom's evil leads to Abraham's blessing). He adds that the world was created even for one righteous person.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that from the blessing of the righteous you learn the curse of the wicked, citing the example of Abraham's blessing leading to the punishment of Sodom.

Rabbi Elazar adds that from the curse of the wicked you learn the blessing of the righteous, citing the evil of Sodom leading to Abraham's blessing, and concludes that the world was created even for one righteous person.

items.text: Punishment for forgetting Torah study
items.text_en: Punishment for forgetting Torah study
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says that one who forgets Torah study causes exile for his children, citing a verse. Rabbi Abahu says such a person is removed from greatness, citing another verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that one who forgets Torah study causes exile for his children, citing the verse 'ותשכח תורת אלהיך אשכח בניך גם אני'.
Rabbi Abahu adds that such a person is removed from greatness, citing the verse 'כי אתה הדעת מאסת ואמאסך מכהן לי'.

items.text: A righteous person is not taken until another is created like him
items.text_en: A righteous person is not taken until another is created like him
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says that a righteous person does not die until another righteous person like him is created, citing the verse about the sun setting and rising. He also says that God planted righteous people in every generation because they are few.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that a righteous person does not die until another righteous person like him is created, citing the verse 'וְזָרַח הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וּבָא הַשָּׁמֶשׁ' (the sun rises and sets) and the example of Eli and Samuel.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds that God saw that righteous people are few and planted them in every generation, citing the verse 'כִּי לַה' מְצוּקֵי אֶרֶץ וַיָּשֶׁת עֲלֵיהֶם תֵּבֵל' (for the pillars of the earth are the Lord's, and He set the world upon them).

items.text: The world endures even for one righteous person
items.text_en: The world endures even for one righteous person
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says the world endures even for one righteous person, citing 'the righteous is the foundation of the world'. Rabbi Chiyya himself derives it from 'He guards the feet of His pious ones', and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes it is written 'His pious one' (singular).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that the world endures even for one righteous person, citing the verse 'the righteous is the foundation of the world'.
Rabbi Chiyya himself derives the same principle from the verse 'He guards the feet of His pious ones', noting that the plural 'pious ones' implies many.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the difficulty by noting that the verse actually reads 'His pious one' (singular), supporting the idea that the world endures even for one righteous person.

items.text: One who has not sinned in most of his years will not sin again
items.text_en: One who has not sinned in most of his years will not sin again
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says that once most of a person's years have passed without sin, he will not sin again, citing 'He guards the feet of His pious ones'. The school of Rabbi Sheila says that if a person faces temptation twice and does not sin, he will not sin again.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that once most of a person's years have passed without sin, he will not sin again, citing the verse 'He guards the feet of His pious ones'.
The school of Rabbi Sheila adds an alternative criterion: if a person faces temptation twice and does not sin, he will not sin again, citing the same verse.

items.text: Opening for impurity, assistance for purity
items.text_en: Opening for impurity, assistance for purity
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse: one who comes to defile himself is given an opening, but one who comes to purify himself is assisted. The school of Rabbi Yishmael gives a parable of a seller of oil and balsam.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse: one who comes to defile himself is given an opening, but one who comes to purify himself is assisted.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael gives a parable of a seller of oil and balsam to illustrate the principle.

items.text: Opening baraitot on the effects of sin and sanctification
items.text_en: Opening baraitot on the effects of sin and sanctification
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites baraitot that interpret verses about impurity and sanctification, teaching that a person who defiles himself a little is defiled much, and one who sanctifies himself a little is sanctified much, both in this world and the next.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a parable: one who comes to measure oil is told to measure himself, but one who comes to measure balsam is asked to wait so both can be perfumed.
The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that sin clogs (מטמטם) a person's heart, citing the verse 'וְלֹא תִטַּמְּאוּ בָּהֶם וְנִטְמֵתֶם בָּם' and reading it as 'וְנִטַּמְטֵם' (clogged).
The Sages teach from the same verse that one who defiles himself a little is defiled much, from below is defiled from above, and in this world is defiled in the World to Come.

The Sages teach from the verse 'וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם וִהְיִיתֶם קְדוֹשִׁים' that one who sanctifies himself a little is sanctified much, from below is sanctified from above, and in this world is sanctified in the World to Come.

items.text: Mishnah: The lottery procedure for the two goats
items.text_en: Mishnah: The lottery procedure for the two goats
items.desc_en: The mishnah describes the lottery process: the appointed one shakes the urn, brings up two lots, and places them on the goats. The high priest declares 'to God a sin-offering,' and the people respond with 'Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever.'

sub.desc_en: The mishnah begins the lottery procedure with the appointed one addressing the high priest.
The mishnah describes how the appointed one shakes the urn, brings up two lots, and the deputy or head of the father's house directs the high priest to raise the appropriate hand.

sub.text: Mishnah's conclusion with Rabbi Yishmael's opinion
sub.text_en: Mishnah's conclusion with Rabbi Yishmael's opinion
sub.desc_en: The mishnah concludes with the high priest placing the lots on the goats and declaring 'to God a sin-offering,' with Rabbi Yishmael's dissenting view that only 'to God' is needed, and the people respond with the blessing.

items.text: Gemara: The purpose and material of the lottery urn
items.text_en: Gemara: The purpose and material of the lottery urn
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the urn was shaken to prevent intentional selection. Rava describes the urn as made of wood and containing sand, holding only two hands. Ravina objects that a wooden vessel cannot be used for sacred service, but the Gemara explains that the Torah spares Israel's money, so expensive materials are avoided.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the lottery urn was shaken, and answers that it was to prevent intentional selection.
Rava describes the urn as made of wood, containing sand, and holding only two hands.
Ravina objects that a wooden vessel cannot be used for sacred service, questioning the sand content.
The Gemara resolves that expensive materials like silver or gold are avoided because the Torah spares Israel's money.

items.text: Dispute about the lottery procedure: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Dispute about the lottery procedure: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda's version where the deputy and high priest both put their hands in the urn. The Gemara explains the dispute: one holds the deputy's right is superior to the high priest's left, the other holds they are equal. Rabbi Chanina, the deputy, explains that the deputy stands at the high priest's right to replace him if disqualified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the mishnah does not align with the baraita of Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Eliezer.

Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Eliezer describes a procedure where the deputy and high priest both insert their hands into the urn, and the deputy or head of the father's house instructs the high priest accordingly.
The Gemara questions why the deputy himself does not speak to the high priest when the lot comes up in the deputy's right hand.
The Gemara answers that since the lot did not come up in the deputy's own hand, his spirits would be low and he would not speak.
The Gemara asks what is the underlying dispute between the mishnah and Rabbi Yehuda's baraita.
The Gemara explains that one authority holds the deputy's right is superior to the high priest's left, while the other holds they are equal.

The Gemara identifies the Tanna who disputes Rabbi Yehuda as Rabbi Chanina, the deputy of the priests, who explains that the deputy stands at the high priest's right so that if the high priest becomes disqualified, the deputy can enter and serve in his place.

items.text: Baraita: Miraculous signs during Shimon HaTzaddik's tenure and their decline
items.text_en: Baraita: Miraculous signs during Shimon HaTzaddik's tenure and their decline
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that during Shimon HaTzaddik's forty years of service, the lot always came up in the right hand, the crimson thread turned white, the western lamp burned continuously, the altar fire was strong, and the offerings were blessed. Afterward, these signs became inconsistent, and a curse fell upon the offerings.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that during Shimon HaTzaddik's forty years of service, the lot always came up in the right hand, but afterward it sometimes came up in the left.

The baraita continues with additional miraculous signs: the crimson thread turned white and the western lamp burned continuously during Shimon HaTzaddik's tenure, but afterward these became inconsistent.
The baraita adds that the altar fire was strong and required minimal wood during Shimon HaTzaddik's time, but afterward it weakened and required constant wood.
The baraita concludes with the blessing on the offerings during Shimon HaTzaddik's tenure, the subsequent curse, and a story of a greedy priest who took his friend's portion.

items.text: Etymology of 'chamtzan' from Scripture
items.text_en: Etymology of 'chamtzan' from Scripture
items.desc_en: Two Amoraim derive the meaning of 'chamtzan' (oppressor) from biblical verses: Rabbah bar bar Sheila from Psalms, and Rava from Isaiah, focusing on the word play of 'ashru chamotz'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the term 'chamtzan' (oppressor) from the Mishnah.
Rabbah bar bar Sheila derives 'chamtzan' from Psalms, where 'chometz' means oppressor.
Rava derives 'chamtzan' from Isaiah, interpreting 'ashru chamotz' as 'do not call the oppressor fortunate'.

items.text: Omen of Shimon HaTzaddik's death
items.text_en: Omen of Shimon HaTzaddik's death
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that in the year Shimon HaTzaddik died, he told the Sages he would die that year because on Yom Kippur he was accompanied by an elder dressed in white, but this time the elder was dressed in black and did not exit with him. After the festival he fell ill and died, and thereafter the priests refrained from pronouncing the Tetragrammaton in the blessing.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by recounting that in the year Shimon HaTzaddik died, he told the Sages he would die that year.
The Sages ask Shimon HaTzaddik how he knows he will die that year.
Shimon HaTzaddik explains that on every Yom Kippur an elder dressed in white accompanied him in and out, but this time the elder was dressed in black and did not exit with him.
After the festival Shimon HaTzaddik fell ill and died, and thereafter the priests refrained from pronouncing the Tetragrammaton in the blessing.

items.text: Portents of the Temple's destruction and expositions on Lebanon
items.text_en: Portents of the Temple's destruction and expositions on Lebanon
items.desc_en: A baraita lists four signs that ceased forty years before the Temple's destruction: the lot did not come up in the right hand, the crimson thread did not whiten, the western lamp did not burn, and the Temple gates opened by themselves. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuked the gates citing Zechariah's prophecy. Rabbi Yitzchak and Rav Zutra explain the name 'Lebanon' as whitening sins and as a forest (ya'ar), with Rav Hoshaya describing golden trees planted by Solomon that bore fruit for the priests, which dried up when gentiles entered, and will be restored in the future.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three portents that ceased forty years before the Temple's destruction: the lot did not come up in the right hand, the crimson thread did not whiten, and the western lamp did not burn.

sub.text: Baraita (continued) with Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's rebuke
sub.text_en: Baraita (continued) with Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's rebuke
sub.desc_en: The baraita adds that the Temple gates opened by themselves, and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuked them, citing Zechariah's prophecy that Lebanon's doors will be consumed by fire.
Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tablai explains that the name 'Lebanon' (לבנון) alludes to its function of whitening (מלבין) the sins of Israel.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah citing Rav Hoshaya
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah citing Rav Hoshaya
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah explains that the Temple is called 'ya'ar' (forest) because it flourished like a forest, and Rav Hoshaya describes golden trees planted by Solomon that bore fruit for the priests' sustenance.
The stam concludes that when gentiles entered the Temple the trees dried up, but the Holy One will restore them in the future, as prophesied.

items.text: Ten mentions of the Name on Yom Kippur and its audibility
items.text_en: Ten mentions of the Name on Yom Kippur and its audibility
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the High Priest uttered the Tetragrammaton ten times on Yom Kippur. Rabbah bar bar Chanah notes that the distance from Jerusalem to Jericho is ten parasangs, implying the Name was heard even there.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the High Priest uttered the Tetragrammaton ten times on Yom Kippur: three times in each of the two confessions, three times over the scapegoat, and once for the lots.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah notes that the distance from Jerusalem to Jericho is ten parasangs, implying the Name was heard even at that distance.

items.text: Miraculous effects of the incense
items.text_en: Miraculous effects of the incense
items.desc_en: The sound of the Temple door hinges was heard far away. Goats in Jericho would sneeze from the incense aroma, women and brides in Jerusalem did not need perfume. Rabbi Yose ben Dulgai and Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin report personal traditions of goats sneezing and the scent lingering even at Shiloh.

sub.desc_en: The baraita reports that the sound of the Temple door hinges was heard far away, and that goats in Jericho sneezed from the incense aroma while women and brides did not need perfume.
רבי יוסי בן דולגאי (Rabbi Yose ben Dulgai) testifies that his father's goats in the hills of Mikhmar would sneeze from the incense aroma.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah
sub.desc_en: רבי חייא בר אבין (Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin) reports in the name of רבי יהושע בן קרחה (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah) that an elder told him he smelled the incense scent from between the walls of Shiloh.

items.text: Debate: is the lottery an essential requirement?
items.text_en: Debate: is the lottery an essential requirement?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai holds that drawing the lot from the box is essential (me'akevet) but placing it is not; Rabbi Yochanan says even drawing is not essential. Two versions of the debate are presented, each aligning the positions with Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Nechemya. An objection is raised from a baraita stating that the lottery is a mitzvah but not essential, and the Gemara resolves this for the second version.

sub.desc_en: רבי ינאי (Rabbi Yannai) states that drawing the lot from the box is essential but placing it on the goat is not.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) counters that even drawing the lot is not essential.

The Gemara explains the first version: according to רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda), all agree drawing is not essential; the dispute is according to רבי נחמיה (Rabbi Nechemya), where one side holds it is essential and the other argues that drawing is not a service.
The Gemara introduces a second version of the dispute.

The second version: according to רבי נחמיה (Rabbi Nechemya), all agree drawing is essential; the dispute is according to רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda), where one side says it is not essential and the other argues that the repeated phrase 'אשר עלה' (which came up) makes it essential.
An objection is raised from a ברייתא (baraita) that states the lottery is a מצוה (commandment) but if not performed, the service is still valid.
The Gemara resolves the objection: according to the second version, the ברייתא (baraita) aligns with רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda), who holds that drawing is not essential.

items.text: Analysis of the first version: who holds that lottery is not essential?
items.text_en: Analysis of the first version: who holds that lottery is not essential?
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the first version of the dispute, where one opinion holds that lottery does not impede. It identifies that opinion as Rabbi Yehuda's. For the opinion that lottery does impede, the Gemara cites a baraita that says 'it is a mitzvah to place' (the lots), implying it is not essential.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the first version of the dispute, for the opinion that lottery does not impede, whose view is it? It answers: it is Rabbi Yehuda's.
The Gemara asks: for the opinion that lottery does impede, whose view is it? It answers by citing a baraita that says 'it is a mitzvah to place' (the lots), implying it is not essential.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about lottery and confession
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about lottery and confession
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: 'It is a mitzvah to cast lots and to confess. If he did not cast lots or confess, it is valid.' The Gemara initially tries to interpret 'cast lots' as 'place the lots', but the continuation (Rabbi Shimon says: if he did not cast lots it is valid, but if he did not confess it is invalid) forces a reinterpretation. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon's statement means: if you mean actual lottery, I disagree on one count; if you mean placement, I disagree on two counts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that lottery and confession are a מצוה (commandment), but if omitted the service is valid, except Rabbi Shimon holds confession invalidates.
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'did not cast lots' in the baraita, and rejects the interpretation of 'did not place' because Rabbi Shimon elsewhere holds that lottery is not essential.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon misunderstood the Rabbis: if they meant actual lottery he disagrees on one count, if they meant placement he disagrees on two counts.

items.text: Proof from the order of the bull and goat
items.text_en: Proof from the order of the bull and goat
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: 'The bull impedes the goat, but the goat does not impede the bull in the inner sprinklings.' The Gemara explains that the bull impedes the goat if the goat's sprinklings precede the bull's. But what does 'the goat does not impede the bull' mean? If it means the order of sprinklings in the Sanctuary vs. the Holy of Holies, that is a fixed law (חוקה). Rather, it must mean that the bull's inner sprinklings can precede the lottery. Since the order does not impede, the lottery itself does not impede.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that the bull impedes the goat, but the goat does not impede the bull in the inner sprinklings.
The Gemara explains that the bull impedes the goat if the goat's sprinklings precede the bull's, then asks what 'the goat does not impede the bull' means.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that it refers to the order of sprinklings in the Sanctuary vs. the Holy of Holies, since a חוקה (fixed law) is written about them.
The Gemara concludes that it must mean the bull's inner sprinklings precede the lottery, and since the order does not impede, the lottery itself does not impede.

items.text: Rejection: the case is about the outer altar and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rejection: the case is about the outer altar and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: perhaps the case is where the bull's sprinklings on the outer altar preceded the goat's sprinklings in the Sanctuary, and it follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that outer services in white garments do not impede.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting the case involves the bull's sprinklings on the outer altar preceding the goat's sprinklings in the Sanctuary, following Rabbi Yehuda who holds that outer services in white garments do not impede.

items.text: Objection: the Mishnah says 'inner sprinklings'
items.text_en: Objection: the Mishnah says 'inner sprinklings'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the Mishnah explicitly says 'inner sprinklings', not outer. Therefore, the case must be about inner sprinklings, and the opinion must be Rabbi Shimon, who holds that lottery does not impede.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'inner sprinklings', so the case must be about inner sprinklings, and the opinion must be Rabbi Shimon, who holds that lottery does not impede.

items.text: Alternative answer: it is Rabbi Yehuda, but lottery still impedes
items.text_en: Alternative answer: it is Rabbi Yehuda, but lottery still impedes
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: it could still be Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that while the order does not impede, the lottery itself does impede. This aligns with their respective positions, as taught in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the mishnah could still be Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that while the order does not impede, the lottery itself does impede.
The Gemara introduces a baraita that will demonstrate that Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages follow their respective positions on whether the lottery impedes.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on the duration of the scapegoat's standing
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on the duration of the scapegoat's standing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the scapegoat must stand alive until the moment of its fellow's blood offering (Rabbi Yehuda) or until the confession (Rabbi Shimon). The Gemara explains their dispute: Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse 'lekhapper' that it refers to blood atonement, while Rabbi Shimon holds it refers to verbal confession.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says the scapegoat must stand alive until the blood offering of its fellow, Rabbi Shimon says until the verbal confession.
The Gemara asks: On what basis do they disagree?
A baraita explains Rabbi Yehuda's position: the verse 'לְכַפֵּר' (to atone) refers to blood atonement, as derived from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) with the verse 'וְכִלָּה מִכַּפֵּר אֶת הַקֹּדֶשׁ'.
Rabbi Shimon holds that the verse 'לְכַפֵּר עָלָיו' (to atone for him) speaks of verbal atonement (confession), not blood.

items.text: Question about the lottery falling on the left side
items.text_en: Question about the lottery falling on the left side
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story where Rabbi Akiva's students asked if the goat that came up on the left can be returned to the right. Rabbi Akiva said not to give place to heretics. The Gemara questions this: if the lottery is essential, how can it be returned? Rava explains they meant whether the goat and its fellow can be returned to the right side.

sub.desc_en: The students of Rabbi Akiva ask: if the lot for God came up on the left hand, may the High Priest return it to the right hand?
Rabbi Akiva answers: do not give the heretics an opportunity to dominate.
The Gemara objects: if not for the concern about heretics, would we return it? But if the lottery is indispensable, once the left hand designated it, how could we return it?
Rava resolves: the students meant whether the lot and its goat can be returned to the right side, not changing the designation; Rabbi Akiva's answer remains the same.

items.text: Derivation that placement of the goat is not essential
items.text_en: Derivation that placement of the goat is not essential
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if the verse said 'the goat which upon him', one might think it must remain on him, but the verse says 'which came up', indicating once it is on him, no further need. The Gemara initially assumes this refers to essentiality, but Rava explains it refers to the duration until slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that if the verse said 'the goat which upon him', one might think the lot must remain on the goat, but the verse says 'which came up', indicating once it is on him, no further need.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita refers to a mitzva or indispensability, and concludes that the drawing of the lots is indispensable but the placement is not.
Rava explains that the baraita means the lot need not remain on the goat until slaughter, not that placement is non-essential.

items.text: Proof that the lottery designates the goat, not the name
items.text_en: Proof that the lottery designates the goat, not the name
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a verse: 'and he shall make it a sin-offering' — the lottery makes it a sin-offering, not the name. A logical argument might suggest otherwise, but the verse concludes that the lottery alone designates.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְעָשָׂהוּ חַטָּאת' (and he shall make it a sin-offering) to prove that the lottery designates the goat as a sin-offering, not the verbal naming.

The baraita raises a possible a fortiori argument: if in a place where the lottery does not consecrate, the name does consecrate, then in a place where the lottery does consecrate, the name should certainly consecrate.
The baraita concludes with the verse 'וְעָשָׂהוּ חַטָּאת' (and he shall make it a sin-offering) to teach that the lottery alone makes it a sin-offering, not the verbal designation.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Chisda from the Sifra
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Chisda from the Sifra
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Sifra that states the lottery designates the goat as a sin-offering, not the name. This implies that the lottery is indispensable, contradicting Rav Chisda's view that designation occurs only at purchase or priestly action. The Gemara declares this a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Sifra (attributed to Rabbi Yehuda) which states that the lottery designates the goat as a sin-offering, not the name, implying the lottery is indispensable, and declares this a refutation of Rav Chisda's view.

items.text: Rav Chisda's principle and its scriptural basis
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's principle and its scriptural basis
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that bird-offerings are designated only at the time of purchase or at the time of the priest's action. Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains the scriptural basis: the verses use 'and she shall take' and 'and he shall make', indicating designation occurs at either of these times.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that bird-offerings (קינין) are designated only at the time of the owner's purchase or at the time of the priest's action.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains Rav Chisda's scriptural basis: the verses use 'וְלָקְחָה' (and she shall take) and 'וְעָשָׂה' (and he shall make), indicating designation at either purchase or action.

items.text: First objection from the baraita on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: First objection from the baraita on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that teaches that the lottery designates the goat as a sin-offering, not the name. This seems to show that designation occurs at the time of the lottery, which is neither purchase nor priestly action, contradicting Rav Chisda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that teaches that the lottery designates the goat as a sin-offering, not the name, challenging Rav Chisda's ruling.
The baraita presents a logical a fortiori argument that if verbal designation works where the lottery does not, it should work where the lottery does.
The baraita concludes with a verse that the lottery alone designates, not verbal designation.
The Gemara points out that the lottery occurs at neither purchase nor priestly action, yet the baraita implies designation is possible, contradicting Rav Chisda.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the baraita refers to purchase and action times
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the baraita refers to purchase and action times
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the baraita's argument is that even where the lottery does not sanctify (at purchase or action), the name sanctifies at those times. The verse teaches that the lottery sanctifies only at its own time, not the name. Thus, the baraita does not contradict Rav Chisda, as it discusses the same times.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the baraita's a fortiori argument is that even where the lottery does not sanctify (at purchase or action), the name sanctifies at those times; so where the lottery does sanctify (not at those times), the name should sanctify at those times.
Rava concludes that the verse teaches that the lottery sanctifies only at its own time, not the name, so the baraita does not contradict Rav Chisda.

items.text: Second objection from the case of a poor person who became rich
items.text_en: Second objection from the case of a poor person who became rich
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection: a poor person who designated money for a sin-offering and a burnt-offering, then became rich, can add to the sin-offering money but not to the burnt-offering money. This shows that designation occurred at the time of speech, not at purchase or action, contradicting Rav Chisda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: a poor person who designated money for a sin-offering and a burnt-offering, then became rich, can add to the sin-offering money but not to the burnt-offering money, showing that designation occurred at the time of speech.
The Gemara infers that since the designation occurred neither at the time of purchase nor at the time of action, yet the baraita rules that it is binding, this contradicts Rav Chisda's position.

Rav Sheshet rejects the objection by citing Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Hoshaya: a rich person who brought a poor person's offering has not fulfilled his obligation, so the designation cannot be binding.
Rav Sheshet resolves the baraita by explaining that the designation was already made at the time of the original separation when the person was poor, not at the later speech.

The Gemara notes an alternative view from Rabbi Chaggai citing Rabbi Yoshiya, who holds that a rich person who brought a poor person's offering has fulfilled his obligation, which would affect the analysis.

items.text: Rav Sheishet's resolution: the designation was at the time of separation
items.text_en: Rav Sheishet's resolution: the designation was at the time of separation
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet rejects the objection, citing Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Hoshaya that a rich person who brings a poor person's offering does not fulfill his obligation. Therefore, the designation must have been effective from the time of separation (when he was still poor), not at the later speech. Thus, it aligns with Rav Chisda's principle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet objects to the objection by citing Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Hoshaya that a rich person who brings a poor person's offering does not fulfill his obligation, questioning how the designation could take effect.

Rav Sheishet resolves that just as in the cited case the designation must have been made while he was still poor, here too the designation was effective from the time of separation (when he was still poor), not at the later speech.

sub.text: Alternative opinion of Rabbi Chagga quoting Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.text_en: Alternative opinion of Rabbi Chagga quoting Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.desc_en: The gemara notes an alternative opinion of Rabbi Chagga quoting Rabbi Yoshiya who holds that a rich person who brings a poor person's offering does fulfill his obligation, which would undermine Rav Sheishet's resolution.

items.text: Gemara's question about the order of purchasing and designating animals
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the order of purchasing and designating animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the correct order of actions when one purchases an animal for a sacrifice and then designates it. Rav Papa explains a case where one buys a single animal and then determines whether it is for a burnt offering or a sin offering, and the consequences for the remaining funds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the correct order of purchasing and designating an animal for a sacrifice, proposing that the phrase should be read as 'and afterward he purchased and said' rather than 'and afterward he said'.
The Gemara objects that if he purchased an animal, the concept of 'adding and bringing his obligation' is problematic because there is no redemption for a bird.

Rav Papa explains the case as one who purchased a single animal; if it was bought for a burnt offering, he adds and brings his obligation from the sin offering funds, and if for a sin offering, the sin offering goes to death.

items.text: Dispute about a rich person bringing a poor person's offering
items.text_en: Dispute about a rich person bringing a poor person's offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Chaggai dispute whether a rich person who brings a poor person's offering fulfills his obligation. The Gemara brings a baraita about a poor leper who brings a rich person's offering, and derives from the verses "זֹאת" and "תּוֹרַת" that the rich person does not fulfill his obligation, while the poor person does.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya that a rich person who brings a poor person's offering does not fulfill his obligation.
Rabbi Chaggai states in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya that the rich person does fulfill his obligation.

The Gemara cites a baraita that a poor leper who brings a rich person's offering fulfills his obligation, but a rich person who brings a poor person's offering does not, supporting Rabbi Elazar's position.
The Gemara distinguishes the case of the leper, because the verse 'זֹאת' (this) limits the law to the poor leper's specific context.

The Gemara objects that if the verse 'זֹאת' limits the rich person's case, then the first clause of the baraita (poor leper bringing a rich offering) should also be limited, but a baraita teaches that 'תּוֹרַת' (the law of) includes the poor leper, while 'זֹאת' excludes the rich person.
The Gemara resolves that one cannot derive the general law from the leper's case, because the verse 'וְאִם דַּל הוּא' (and if he is poor) explicitly limits the law to the poor person's offering.

items.text: Mishnah: Binding the crimson thread and the confession
items.text_en: Mishnah: Binding the crimson thread and the confession
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for the scapegoat and the goat that is slaughtered, including tying a crimson thread on the scapegoat's head and positioning it opposite the place of its dispatch. It then describes the High Priest's confession over the second bull, including the formula and the response of the people.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes tying a crimson thread on the scapegoat's head and positioning both goats opposite their respective places.
The Mishnah describes the High Priest's confession over the second bull and the people's response.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry about the phrase "וְלַנִּשְׁחָט"
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry about the phrase "וְלַנִּשְׁחָט"
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase "וְלַנִּשְׁחָט" in the Mishnah refers to tying the thread or positioning the goat. Rav Yosef's baraita clarifies that it refers to tying, to prevent mixing between the goats and with others. The Gemara concludes that it must refer to tying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's phrase 'וְלַנִּשְׁחָט' (and for the slaughtered goat) refers to tying the thread or positioning the goat.

sub.text: Supporting baraita cited by Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita cited by Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef's baraita is brought as evidence: the Mishnah describes tying the thread on the scapegoat and positioning both goats to prevent mixing.
The Gemara concludes that the phrase must refer to tying, because if it referred to positioning, the goats could still mix with others.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's tradition about two threads and the dispute about their size
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's tradition about two threads and the dispute about their size
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak heard that one of the threads (for the red heifer or the scapegoat) requires a minimum size and one does not. Rav Yosef deduces that the scapegoat's thread requires a size because it needs to be divided, while the red heifer's does not. Rami bar Chama objects that the red heifer's thread needs weight, and Rava says that weight is a dispute among Tannaim. Abaye challenges the idea that the red heifer's thread does not need division, citing a baraita that it is wrapped with the remaining thread, but the Gemara emends the text.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak reports a tradition that he heard about two threads (one for the red heifer and one for the scapegoat), one requiring a minimum size (שיעור) and one not, but he does not know which is which.

Rav Yosef deduces that the scapegoat's thread requires a minimum size because it needs to be divided (for the two goats), while the red heifer's thread does not require division and therefore does not need a minimum size.
Rami bar Chama objects that the red heifer's thread also requires a minimum weight (כובד) for the burning ceremony, so it too needs a size requirement.
Rava responds that the requirement of weight (כובד) for the red heifer's thread is a dispute among Tannaim, so it does not definitively prove that the thread needs a minimum size.

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's assumption that the red heifer's thread does not need division, citing a baraita that the thread is wrapped with the remaining thread (שיירי לשון), implying it is divided.
The Gemara emends the baraita: instead of 'שיירי לשון' (remaining thread), it should read 'בזנב לשון' (the tail of the thread), meaning the thread is not divided but simply tied to the tail.

items.text: Discussion about the cedar wood and crimson thread that caught fire
items.text_en: Discussion about the cedar wood and crimson thread that caught fire
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanin says that if the cedar wood and crimson thread were caught by a flame, they are still valid. An objection is raised from a baraita that if the thread became scorched, one must bring another thread and sanctify it. Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a flame that licks and one that chars. Rava then explains that the requirement of weight is a Tannaic dispute, citing the opinions of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanin in the name of Rav rules that cedar wood and crimson thread caught by a flame are still valid for the red heifer ceremony.
An objection is raised from a baraita that if the thread became scorched, one must bring another thread and sanctify it, contradicting Rav's leniency.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a flame that licks (קולחת) and one that chars (נכפפת).
Rava explains that the requirement of weight (כובד) for the thread is a Tannaic dispute, citing the opinions of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's tradition about three threads and their weights
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's tradition about three threads and their weights
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan heard about three threads: one for the red heifer, one for the scapegoat, and one for the leper, each with a specific weight (ten zuz, two selas, and one shekel), but he could not specify which weight corresponds to which. When Ravin came, he explained the tradition from Rabbi Yonatan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan heard about three threads (for the red heifer, scapegoat, and leper) each with a specific weight, but he could not specify which weight corresponds to which.
Ravin arrives and explains the tradition from Rabbi Yonatan, resolving which weight corresponds to which thread.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the required weights: the red heifer's wood weighs ten zuz, the scapegoat's coin weighs two selas, and the leper's offering weighs one shekel.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the required weights for the red heifer's wood, the scapegoat's coin, and the leper's offering.

items.text: Dispute about the red heifer and scapegoat
items.text_en: Dispute about the red heifer and scapegoat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports a dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta and the Rabbis about the red heifer's weight. Rabbi Yirmiyah from Difti challenges this, arguing the dispute is actually about the scapegoat, and notes that Rabbiya bar Kisi died that day, using his name as a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports a dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta and the Rabbis about the red heifer's weight, with one saying ten zuz and the other a shekel, and provides a mnemonic.
Rabbi Yirmiyah from Difti challenges Ravina, arguing the dispute is actually about the scapegoat, and notes that Rabbiya bar Kisi died that day, using his name as a mnemonic.

items.text: Two slaughter traditions for the red heifer and bull
items.text_en: Two slaughter traditions for the red heifer and bull
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states he heard two traditions about slaughter: one for the red heifer and one for the bull of the High Priest, but does not know which is valid for a non-priest. The Gemara then reports a dispute between Rav and Shmuel: one says the red heifer is invalid when slaughtered by a non-priest, the other says the bull is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states he heard two traditions about slaughter — one for the red heifer (פָּרָה) and one for the High Priest's bull (פָּרוֹ) — one valid for a non-priest (זָר) and one invalid, but he does not know which is which.

sub.text: Stam (report of dispute between Rav and Shmuel)
sub.text_en: Stam (report of dispute between Rav and Shmuel)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: one says the red heifer (פָּרָה) is invalid when slaughtered by a non-priest and the bull (פָּרוֹ) is valid; the other says the bull is invalid and the heifer is valid.

items.text: Rav's position and the Gemara's challenge
items.text_en: Rav's position and the Gemara's challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rav holds the red heifer is invalid, citing Rabbi Zeira and Rav's statement that the red heifer requires Elazar and a חוקה. The Gemara challenges: why distinguish the red heifer from the bull, which also has Aharon and a חוקה? The answer is that slaughter is not a service, but the red heifer is consecrated for Temple maintenance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rav holds the red heifer is invalid when slaughtered by a non-priest, citing Rabbi Zeira and Rav's statement that the red heifer requires Elazar and a חוקה (statute).
The Gemara challenges Rav: why distinguish the red heifer from the bull (פרו), which also has Aharon and a חוקה (statute) written for it?
The Gemara answers that slaughter is not a service (עבודה), but the red heifer is consecrated for Temple maintenance (קדשי בדק הבית), so it requires a priest even for non-service acts.

items.text: Objection and resolution
items.text_en: Objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the logic should apply equally to the bull. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi answers that the bull is like the appearances of leprosy, which is not a service but requires a priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the bull's slaughter is valid by a non-priest because slaughter is not a service, then the same logic should apply to the red heifer (פרה), which is also slaughtered by a non-priest.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi answers that the red heifer is like the appearances of leprosy (מראות נגעים), which is not a service but still requires a priest, so the objection fails.

items.text: Shmuel's position and the derivation
items.text_en: Shmuel's position and the derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Shmuel holds the bull is invalid. Shmuel answers that the verse says 'and he shall slaughter it before him,' meaning a non-priest slaughters while Elazar watches. Rav interprets this as preventing distraction. Shmuel derives the same for the heifer from 'and he shall burn the heifer before his eyes.' Rav distinguishes: one verse for slaughter, one for burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Shmuel why he holds the bull (פרו) is invalid, given that the cow (פרה) also has the terms 'Elazar' and 'chok'.
Shmuel answers that the bull is different because the verse says 'and he shall slaughter it before him,' meaning a non-priest slaughters while Elazar watches.
Rav interprets the same verse as preventing distraction, not as requiring a non-priest.
The Gemara asks where Shmuel derives the rule of not being distracted.
Shmuel derives the distraction rule from the verse 'and he shall burn the cow before his eyes.'
Rav distinguishes: one verse applies to slaughter, the other to burning.

items.text: Need for both verses
items.text_en: Need for both verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both verses are necessary: if only slaughter were written, one might think burning does not require a priest; if only burning, one might think slaughter does not. Therefore both are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both verses are necessary: if only slaughter were written, one might think burning does not require a priest; if only burning, one might think slaughter does not, so both are needed.

items.text: What is excluded?
items.text_en: What is excluded?
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to ask what is excluded from the requirement, considering whether it is the gathering of ashes or filling water for sanctification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is excluded from the requirement, considering whether it is the gathering of ashes or filling water for sanctification.

items.text: Exclusion of non-essential rites from the heifer's service
items.text_en: Exclusion of non-essential rites from the heifer's service
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the verse "למשמרת למי נדה" excludes the throwing of cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool, as they are not part of the heifer's body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'למשמרת למי נדה' (for a guard of sprinkling water) excludes the throwing of cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool because they are not part of the heifer's body.

items.text: Dispute on slaughter by a non-priest
items.text_en: Dispute on slaughter by a non-priest
items.desc_en: An explicit dispute is recorded: Rabbi Ami and Ulla rule the slaughter is valid, while Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha and some say Ulla rule it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute about the validity of a non-priest (זר) slaughtering the red heifer: Rabbi Ami and Ulla rule it valid, while Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha rules it invalid, with an alternate version reversing Ulla's position.

items.text: Attempted proof from the baraita of Rabbi Yehoshua bar Abba
items.text_en: Attempted proof from the baraita of Rabbi Yehoshua bar Abba
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Abba brings a baraita to support Rav: it derives from "תורה" that slaughter, blood reception, blood sprinkling, burning, and throwing of wood etc. are limited to daytime and invalid for women, while ash gathering, water filling, and sanctification are not. The Gemara questions whether this is a proof.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Abba cites a baraita that derives from the word 'תורה' that slaughter, blood reception, blood sprinkling, burning, and throwing of cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool are included in the daytime and male-only requirement, while ash gathering, water filling, and sanctification are excluded via 'זאת' because they are valid with women and at night.

The baraita derives from the word 'תורה' that slaughter, blood reception, sprinkling, burning, and throwing of wood etc. are included, while ash gathering, water filling, and sanctification are excluded by 'זאת'.
The baraita explains the logic: all included acts are learned from the sprinkling of water, which is invalid for women and only by day.
The baraita concludes that acts invalid for women are only valid by day, while acts valid for women are valid both day and night.

items.text: Refutation of the proof
items.text_en: Refutation of the proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: if the baraita meant that rites invalid for women are invalid for a non-priest, then the sprinkling of its waters (which is invalid for women but valid for a non-priest) would disprove the analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita does not prove the invalidity of a non-priest (זר) for slaughter, because the water sprinkling (הזאת מימיה) is invalid for women but valid for a non-priest, breaking the analogy.

items.text: Abaye's resolution of the proof
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution of the proof
items.desc_en: Abaye explains the proof: just as a woman is excluded by "אלעזר" (not a woman), so too a non-priest is excluded by "אלעזר" (not a non-priest).

sub.desc_en: Abaye clarifies the refutation: just as a woman is excluded from the service by the verse 'אלעזר' (Eleazar, not a woman), so too a non-priest (זר) is excluded by the same verse 'אלעזר' (Eleazar, not a non-priest).

items.text: Ulla's general principle
items.text_en: Ulla's general principle
items.desc_en: Ulla states that the entire passage implies exclusion from implication and inclusion from explicit statement.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that the entire passage (of the red heifer) derives its meaning from context, with one meaning emerging from another and some meaning being inherent.

items.text: The verse "ונתתם אותה אל אלעזר" and its application for generations
items.text_en: The verse "ונתתם אותה אל אלעזר" and its application for generations
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse: "אותה" to Eleazar, not for generations to Eleazar. There is a dispute whether for generations it is a High Priest or an ordinary priest. For the one who says an ordinary priest, it is straightforward; for the one who says a High Priest, it is derived from a gezerah shavah of "חוקה" from Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'ונתתם אותה אל אלעזר' (and you shall give it to Eleazar the priest) to mean that the red heifer is given to Eleazar specifically, not to future generations through Eleazar.
One opinion holds that for future generations the red heifer is performed by a High Priest (כהן גדול).
Another opinion holds that for future generations the red heifer is performed by an ordinary priest (כהן הדיוט).
The Gemara notes that for the one who says an ordinary priest, the matter is straightforward, as the verse's exclusion of Eleazar leaves the default of any priest.
The Gemara asks: for the one who says a High Priest, from where does he derive this requirement?
The Gemara answers that it is derived from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of the word 'חוקה' (statute) from the Yom Kippur service, where the High Priest performs the service.

items.text: The verse "והוציא אותה" and the dispute about a second heifer
items.text_en: The verse "והוציא אותה" and the dispute about a second heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that "אותה" means alone, as in the Mishnah: one does not take out a black or red heifer with it. Rabbi says the reason is the verse, while the Tanna Kamma (Rabbi Shimon) derives the reason from the verse but also gives a rationale. The Gemara asks what difference there is between them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the verse 'וְהוֹצִיא אוֹתָהּ' and cites the Mishnah that one does not take out a black or red heifer with the red heifer, to prevent false claims.
Rabbi argues that the prohibition is not due to appearance but because the verse says 'אותה' (alone).
The Gemara asks how the Tanna Kamma can ignore the verse 'אותה', and answers that the Tanna Kamma is Rabbi Shimon, who derives reasons from the verse.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbi and the Tanna Kamma (Rabbi Shimon).

items.text: Deriving the laws of the red heifer from the verses
items.text_en: Deriving the laws of the red heifer from the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets each phrase in the verses about the red heifer, deriving specific halakhot: that a donkey was taken with it, that only one heifer is slaughtered, that the priest must not divert his attention (according to Rav) or that a non-priest may slaughter while Elazar watches (according to Shmuel), and that the priest must be in his priesthood for the collection of blood and the burning of the cedar wood, hyssop, and crimson wool. The section concludes with the derivation that the priest who burns the heifer must be in his priesthood for future generations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that a donkey was taken together with the red heifer.

The Gemara derives from 'וְשָׁחַט אוֹתָהּ' that only one heifer is slaughtered, and from 'לְפָנָיו' that according to Rav the priest must not divert his attention, while according to Shmuel a non-priest may slaughter while Elazar watches.

The Gemara derives from 'וְלָקַח אֶלְעָזָר הַכֹּהֵן' that according to Shmuel it emphasizes Elazar's priesthood, while according to Rav it is a מיעוט אחר מיעוט (double limitation) to include even an ordinary priest.

The Gemara derives from 'וְלָקַח הַכֹּהֵן' that according to Shmuel even an ordinary priest may take the cedar wood, hyssop, and crimson wool, while according to Rav the verse is necessary to teach that a priest is required for these items.
The Gemara derives from 'וְכִבֶּס בְּגָדָיו הַכֹּהֵן' and 'וְטָמֵא הַכֹּהֵן' that the priest must be in his priesthood for future generations.

items.text: Question about the priesthood requirement for future generations
items.text_en: Question about the priesthood requirement for future generations
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: according to the opinion that future generations require a high priest, why does the verse need to specify 'the priest in his priesthood'? It answers that even though it could be derived by a fortiori argument, the Torah wrote it explicitly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that future generations require a high priest, why does the verse need to specify 'the priest in his priesthood'?
The Gemara answers: even though the requirement could be derived by a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument), the Torah wrote it explicitly.

items.text: Deriving qualifications for gathering the ash
items.text_en: Deriving qualifications for gathering the ash
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse about gathering the ash: 'a man' includes a non-priest, 'pure' includes a woman, and 'and he shall place' excludes a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor who lack understanding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'וְאָסַף אִישׁ טָהוֹר' to derive that 'איש' includes a non-priest, 'טהור' includes a woman, and 'והניח' excludes deaf-mutes, imbeciles, and minors who lack understanding.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis on sanctification
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis on sanctification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone is fit to sanctify the ash except a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, while Rabbi Yehuda validates a minor but disqualifies a woman and an androgynous. The Gemara explains the reasoning: the Rabbis derive from the verse 'and they shall take' that those disqualified for gathering are also disqualified for sanctification, and those qualified for gathering are qualified for sanctification. Rabbi Yehuda argues that the plural 'and they shall take' includes even a minor, and he disqualifies a woman from the singular 'and he shall give'. The Rabbis counter that the combination of singular and plural teaches that even if two take and one gives, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone is fit to sanctify the ash except a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, while Rabbi Yehuda validates a minor but disqualifies a woman and an androgynous.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive from the verse 'וְלָקְחוּ' that those disqualified for gathering are also disqualified for sanctification, and those qualified for gathering are qualified for sanctification.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that the plural 'וְלָקְחוּ' includes even a minor, who is disqualified for gathering but is fit for sanctification.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda's disqualification of a woman
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's disqualification of a woman
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda disqualifies a woman from the singular 'וְנָתַן' (and he shall give), implying a male, not a female.
The Rabbis counter that the combination of singular 'וְנָתַן' and plural 'וְלָקְחוּ' teaches that even if two take and one gives, it is valid, thereby including a woman in the giving role.

items.text: Dispute about sprinkling and a supporting baraita
items.text_en: Dispute about sprinkling and a supporting baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute regarding the verse about sprinkling: according to the Rabbis, 'a man' excludes a woman, and 'pure' includes a minor; according to Rabbi Yehuda, 'a man' excludes a minor, and 'pure' includes a woman. A baraita is then brought that supports the Rabbis' position: everyone is fit to sprinkle except a tumtum, an androgynous, and a woman, and a minor who has understanding may sprinkle with a woman assisting him.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the Rabbis, the verse 'אִישׁ טָהוֹר' (a pure man) teaches that 'אִישׁ' excludes a woman, and 'טָהוֹר' includes a minor.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, 'אִישׁ' excludes a minor, and 'טָהוֹר' includes a woman.

A baraita is cited that supports the Rabbis' position: everyone is fit to sprinkle except a tumtum, an androgynous, and a woman, and a minor who has understanding may sprinkle with a woman assisting him.

items.text: Abaye's resolution of Rabbi Yehuda's dispute
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution of Rabbi Yehuda's dispute
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that Rabbi Yehuda does dispute the earlier point, based on the principle that a statement can be derived from another statement or from context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda indeed disputes the earlier point.
Abaye resolves that Rabbi Yehuda does dispute, based on the principle that a statement can be derived from another statement or from context.

items.text: Derivation regarding the red heifer
items.text_en: Derivation regarding the red heifer
items.desc_en: A derivation from the verse 'the pure one shall sprinkle upon the impure' teaches that a טבול יום is valid for the red heifer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'וְהִזָּה הַטָּהוֹר עַל הַטָּמֵא' (the pure one shall sprinkle upon the impure) that a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) is valid for the red heifer, since the term 'טָהוֹר' (pure) implies he was previously impure.

items.text: Rabbi Asi's report on Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's report on Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports that Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish could not resolve the red heifer issue and instead relied on the principle of deriving meaning from context.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports that Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish could not resolve the red heifer issue and instead relied on the principle of deriving meaning from context.

items.text: Dispute over slaughter of the red heifer by a non-priest
items.text_en: Dispute over slaughter of the red heifer by a non-priest
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rabbi Yochanan that all slaughter is valid by a non-priest except the red heifer. Rabbi Yochanan rebuked him, citing a tradition from Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak that it is invalid, though he personally holds it is valid.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rabbi Yochanan that all slaughter is valid by a non-priest except the red heifer.
Rabbi Yochanan rebuked the Tanna, telling him to teach outside that we have never found slaughter by a non-priest to be invalid.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan's rebuke was not just for the Tanna but even for his teacher Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak, who held the red heifer's slaughter by a non-priest is invalid, while Rabbi Yochanan himself holds it is valid.

items.text: Reason for the difference between the two confessions
items.text_en: Reason for the difference between the two confessions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the high priest includes 'the sons of Aaron, Your holy people' in the second confession but not the first. The school of Rabbi Yishmael answers that it is fitting for the innocent to atone for the guilty, not the guilty for the guilty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the high priest omits 'the sons of Aaron, Your holy people' in the first confession but includes it in the second.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael answers that it is fitting for the innocent (the high priest alone) to atone for the guilty, not the guilty (the priests) for the guilty.

items.text: Mishnah: Yom Kippur deviations from the daily routine
items.text_en: Mishnah: Yom Kippur deviations from the daily routine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists numerous ways the Yom Kippur service differs from the daily service, including the handling of blood, coal scooping, incense, and the high priest's actions, with disputes among Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Menachem.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the Yom Kippur procedure for receiving the bull's blood and scooping coals from the outer altar.
The Mishnah contrasts the daily practice of using a silver coal-pan and pouring into a gold one with Yom Kippur's use of a single gold pan.
The Mishnah states that daily the coal-pan holds four kavs and is poured into a three-kav pan, but on Yom Kippur the three-kav pan is used directly, with Rabbi Yose disputing the daily measure.
Rabbi Menachem lists three physical differences of the coal-pan on Yom Kippur: lighter, longer handle, and red gold instead of green.
The Mishnah notes that daily incense is half a maneh each time, but on Yom Kippur a full handful is added, and the incense is ground extra fine.

The Mishnah states that daily priests ascend the ramp on the east and descend on the west, but on Yom Kippur the high priest ascends and descends in the middle; Rabbi Yehuda says this is always the high priest's practice.
The Mishnah notes that daily the high priest sanctifies from the laver, but on Yom Kippur from a golden pitcher; Rabbi Yehuda says this is always the high priest's practice.

sub.text: Mishnah's seventh deviation (Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Yehuda)
sub.text_en: Mishnah's seventh deviation (Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Yehuda)
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute about the number of wood arrangements on the altar: Rabbi Meir says four daily and five on Yom Kippur, Rabbi Yose says three and four, Rabbi Yehuda says two and three.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's location
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's location
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's mention of the fourth row in the Heichal, citing the verse that no man should be in the Tent of Meeting. Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah refers to the fourth row of the Heichal, and a Baraisa elaborates on the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's mention of the fourth row in the Heichal, citing the verse that no man should be in the Tent of Meeting.
Rav Yehuda answers that the Mishnah refers to the fourth row of the Heichal, not inside the Tent of Meeting.
A Baraisa elaborates on the verse, supporting the interpretation that the prohibition applies only inside the Tent of Meeting.

items.text: Derivation of the requirement for incense in the Holy of Holies
items.text_en: Derivation of the requirement for incense in the Holy of Holies
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that the incense offering must be performed specifically in the Holy of Holies, not just in the courtyard. It extends the requirement to the Tabernacle in the wilderness, Shiloh, and the Temple, and includes the time of blood application and the High Priest's exit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possibility that the incense could be offered in the courtyard, but rejects it with a verse requiring it in the Tent of Meeting, and extends the requirement to Shiloh and the Temple.
The Gemara extends the incense requirement to the time of blood application and the High Priest's exit, using additional verses.

items.text: Order of atonement: High Priest, his household, priests, Israel
items.text_en: Order of atonement: High Priest, his household, priests, Israel
items.desc_en: The verse establishes a hierarchy: the High Priest's atonement precedes that of his household, which precedes that of the priests, which precedes that of all Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma cites the verse to establish the hierarchy of atonement: the High Priest's atonement precedes that of his household, which precedes that of the priests, which precedes that of all Israel.

items.text: Gemara's question: What atonement is equal for all?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What atonement is equal for all?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which atonement is equal for the High Priest, his household, the priests, and all Israel. Rava, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi, and Rabbi Elazar answer that it is the incense offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the source that the atonement mentioned in the verse refers specifically to the time of incense offering?

sub.text: Rava, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi, and Rabbi Elazar's answer
sub.text_en: Rava, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi, and Rabbi Elazar's answer
sub.desc_en: Rava, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi, and Rabbi Elazar answer that the verse 'וְכִפֶּר בַּעֲדוֹ וּבְעַד בֵּיתוֹ וּבְעַד כָּל קְהַל יִשְׂרָאֵל' teaches that the atonement equal for all is the incense offering.

items.text: Proof that incense atones
items.text_en: Proof that incense atones
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that incense atones, citing Rabbi Chananya's teaching from the verse about Aaron, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael's explanation that it atones for gossip.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether incense (קטורת) atones.
The Gemara answers affirmatively, citing Rabbi Chananya's teaching that incense atones, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael's explanation that it atones for gossip (לשון הרע).

items.text: Mishnah: Withdrawing from between the Entrance Hall and the Altar
items.text_en: Mishnah: Withdrawing from between the Entrance Hall and the Altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah that people withdraw from between the Entrance Hall and the Altar during the incense offering. Rabbi Elazar limits this to the outer incense, not the inner incense.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah stating that people withdraw from between the Entrance Hall and the Altar during the incense offering.

Rabbi Elazar limits the mishnah's withdrawal rule to the outer incense offering in the Sanctuary (היכל), but for the inner incense offering in the Holy of Holies (לפני לפנים), people withdraw only from the Sanctuary itself, not from between the Entrance Hall and the Altar.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the scope of withdrawal
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the scope of withdrawal
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects with a baraita that includes other offerings, and the Gemara clarifies that the distinction is between the Heikhal and the area between the Entrance Hall and the Altar: in the Heikhal, people withdraw even without incense, but between the Entrance Hall and the Altar only during incense.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says that people withdraw from between the Entrance Hall and the Altar not only during incense but also during blood presentations of other offerings.

The baraita asks what higher standard applies to the Sanctuary relative to the area between the Entrance Hall and the Altar, and answers that in the Sanctuary people withdraw both during and not during incense, whereas between the Entrance Hall and the Altar they withdraw only during incense.
The Gemara infers that the baraita's rule about withdrawing during incense applies even to the incense of the innermost chamber, challenging Rabbi Elazar's opinion.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers only to the incense of the Sanctuary, not the innermost chamber.

The Gemara objects that if the baraita refers only to Sanctuary incense, it should have mentioned an additional higher standard: that in the Sanctuary people withdraw even during the innermost incense, whereas between the Entrance Hall and the Altar they withdraw only during Sanctuary incense.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita indeed teaches only one higher standard: in the Sanctuary people withdraw both during and not during incense, whereas between the Entrance Hall and the Altar they do not withdraw at all except during incense.

items.text: Clarification of the withdrawal rule
items.text_en: Clarification of the withdrawal rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why priests withdraw only during the incense offering from the area between the Porch and the Altar, but from the Heichal they withdraw during both the Heichal's and the Holy of Holies' service. Rava answers that the withdrawal is considered one unified act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why priests withdraw from the area between the Porch and the Altar only during the incense offering, while from the Heichal they withdraw during both the Heichal's and the Holy of Holies' service.
Rava answers that the withdrawal is considered one unified act, so the rule applies uniformly.

items.text: Source for the withdrawal rule for other offerings
items.text_en: Source for the withdrawal rule for other offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the same withdrawal rule applies to the bull of the anointed priest, the bull of the congregation for an unwitting sin, and the goats for idolatry. Rabbi Pedat derives it via a verbal analogy of 'kaparah' from Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the offerings during which priests withdraw: the bull of the anointed priest, the bull of the congregation's unwitting sin, and the goats of idolatry.
Rabbi Pedat derives the rule via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'כפרה' (atonement) used in the Yom Kippur service.

items.text: Proof that the withdrawal rules are Torah law
items.text_en: Proof that the withdrawal rules are Torah law
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Ahavah infers that the withdrawal rules are Torah law, not rabbinic. The Gemara explains that if they were rabbinic, there would be no distinction between the area between the Porch and the Altar and the rest of the Temple courtyard, since the concern of entering inadvertently applies everywhere.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Ahavah infers from the Mishnah's distinction that the withdrawal rules (מעלות) are of Torah origin (דאורייתא) and were transmitted as such.

The Gemara questions: if the withdrawal rules were only rabbinic (דרבנן), why would the Mishnah distinguish between the area between the Porch and the Altar and the rest of the courtyard? In both places there is a concern that one might inadvertently enter further.

The Gemara answers: the area between the Porch and the Altar has no partition, so the withdrawal is not noticeable; the rest of the courtyard has the outer Altar as a partition, making the withdrawal noticeable, hence the distinction is logical even for a rabbinic rule.

items.text: The sanctity of the Porch and the Heichal
items.text_en: The sanctity of the Porch and the Heichal
items.desc_en: Rava infers that the sanctity of the Porch and the Heichal is one, otherwise a rabbinic decree would be added to another decree. The Gemara clarifies that the Porch and the area between the Porch and the Altar share one sanctity, while the Heichal and the Porch have two distinct sanctities.

sub.desc_en: Rava infers from the previous discussion that the sanctity of the אולם (Porch) and the היכל (Sanctuary) is one, otherwise a rabbinic decree would be added to another decree.
The Gemara clarifies that the אולם (Porch) and the area between the Porch and the Altar share one sanctity, while the היכל (Sanctuary) and the אולם (Porch) have two distinct sanctities.

items.text: Reason for the material of the coal shovel
items.text_en: Reason for the material of the coal shovel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on a regular day the shovel was silver, but on Yom Kippur it was gold. The Gemara explains that the Torah is frugal with Israel's money on regular days, and on Yom Kippur the gold shovel is used due to the High Priest's weakness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why on a regular day the coal shovel is made of silver.
The Gemara answers that the Torah is frugal with Israel's money, so a cheaper silver shovel is used.
The Gemara asks why on Yom Kippur the shovel is made of gold.
The Gemara answers that the gold shovel is used due to the High Priest's weakness, to minimize his exertion.

items.text: Dispute about the size of the shovel
items.text_en: Dispute about the size of the shovel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on a regular day the shovel held four kav, but on Yom Kippur it held three kav. A baraita mentions that spilled coals were swept into the gutter. There is a dispute between a baraita that says one kav and another that says two kav. Rav Chisda identifies the latter as Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka. Rav Ashi suggests it could be Rabbi Yossi, interpreting the measures as desert se'ah and Jerusalem kav.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on a regular day the shovel held four kav, and on Yom Kippur it held three kav.
A baraita teaches that spilled coals were swept into the gutter.
The Gemara notes a dispute between two baraitot: one says one kav spilled, another says two kav, and questions who holds the two-kav position.
Rav Chisda identifies the two-kav baraita as Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's position.
Rav Ashi alternatively suggests it could be Rabbi Yossi, interpreting the measures as a desert se'ah poured into three Jerusalem kav.

items.text: Characteristics of the shovel and types of gold
items.text_en: Characteristics of the shovel and types of gold
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that on a regular day the shovel was heavy, thick, and short, but on Yom Kippur it was light, thin, and long to assist the High Priest.
