items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the layout of the two curtains (outer and inner) and the High Priest's path to the Ark, where he places the coal pan and offers incense, then exits and prays briefly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the outer curtain opened from the south and the inner from the north, and the High Priest's path between them to the Ark.
The Mishnah details the High Priest's actions upon reaching the Ark: placing the coal pan, offering incense, exiting, and praying briefly to avoid alarming Israel.

items.text: Gemara's question: First or Second Temple?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: First or Second Temple?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah refers to the First Temple (which had a curtain but no Ark?) or the Second Temple (which had an Ark? but no curtain?). It cites a baraita that the Ark was hidden by King Josiah along with other items, and Rabbi Elazar derives this from scriptural analogies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah refers to the First Temple (which had a curtain but no Ark?) or the Second Temple (which had an Ark? but no curtain?).
The Gemara cites a baraita that the Ark was hidden by King Josiah along with other items, and explains the scriptural basis for his action.
Rabbi Elazar derives the hiding of the Ark from scriptural analogies using the words 'שמה' (there), 'דורות' (generations), and 'משמרת' (charge).

items.text: Resolution: Second Temple, place of the Ark
items.text_en: Resolution: Second Temple, place of the Ark
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to the Second Temple, and 'reached the Ark' means the place where the Ark had been. The phrase 'between the two staves' is interpreted as 'like between the two staves'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to the Second Temple, 'reached the Ark' means the place where the Ark had been, and 'between the two staves' is interpreted as 'like between the two staves'.

items.text: Dispute about gathering the incense
items.text_en: Dispute about gathering the incense
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a dispute about how the High Priest gathers the incense: one baraita says he gathers it inward (toward himself), another says outward. Abaye explains these are different Tannaic views and prefers the one that says inward, citing a teaching that they instruct him to be careful.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the High Priest gathered the incense on the coals.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah follows the view that one gathers the incense (צוֹבְרָהּ).
One baraita teaches that he gathers it inward (toward himself), which is outward relative to the ark.
Another baraita teaches that he gathers it outward (away from himself), which is inward relative to the ark.
Abaye resolves that the two baraitot represent a dispute between different Tannaic views.
Abaye further rules that the preferable view is the one saying he gathers inward (toward himself), citing a teaching that they instruct him to be careful.

items.text: Refutation of the Sadducees' interpretation of the incense placement
items.text_en: Refutation of the Sadducees' interpretation of the incense placement
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a baraita that refutes the Sadducees, who claim the incense should be prepared outside and then brought in. The Sages argue from the verse 'and he shall put the incense upon the fire before the Lord' that it must be done inside. The verse 'for in a cloud I will appear' is interpreted to teach that one must create a column of smoke, and if one fails to do so or omits any ingredient, he is liable to death.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a warning not to begin the incense preparation outside, and then cites the verse 'וְנָתַן אֶת הַקְּטוֹרֶת עַל הָאֵשׁ לִפְנֵי ה׳' to refute the Sadducees who claim one should prepare it outside and bring it in.

The Gemara asks what verse the Sadducees derive their position from, and answers that they interpret 'כִּי בֶּעָנָן אֵרָאֶה עַל הַכַּפּוֹרֶת' to mean one should prepare the incense outside and bring it in.
The Sages object that the verse 'וְנָתַן אֶת הַקְּטוֹרֶת עַל הָאֵשׁ לִפְנֵי ה׳' already requires the incense to be placed inside, and ask what then the verse 'כִּי בֶּעָנָן אֵרָאֶה' teaches.
The baraita answers that the verse teaches one must create a column of smoke (מעלה עשן), and that if one fails to do so or omits any ingredient, he is liable to death.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about liability for entering empty-handed
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about liability for entering empty-handed
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the one who enters without the proper incense is liable for death, as he might be liable for entering empty-handed. Rav Sheshet answers that the case involves one who was negligent about entering but intentional about the incense offering. Rav Ashi offers an alternative: even if he was intentional about both, he might have brought two incense offerings, one complete and one deficient, so he is liable only for the deficient one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why is the one who enters without proper incense liable for death, since he might be liable for entering empty-handed (ביאה ריקנית)?
Rav Sheshet answers that the case involves one who was negligent (שוגג) about entering but intentional (מזיד) about the incense offering, so he is liable only for the incense.

Rav Ashi offers an alternative: even if he was intentional about both, he might have brought two incense offerings—one complete and one deficient—so he is liable only for the deficient one, not for entering empty-handed.

items.text: Deriving the requirement for the column of smoke from the verse 'and cover'
items.text_en: Deriving the requirement for the column of smoke from the verse 'and cover'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation of the smoke column from the verse 'and cover'. Rav Yosef explains that the verse teaches that one must create a rising smoke column. Abaye objects, citing a baraita that describes the smoke rising like a staff and then spreading. Abaye then reinterprets: the verse teaches the initial rising smoke, while the spreading is derived from another verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a second verse is needed to derive the requirement for a smoke-raiser, since it was already derived from another verse.
Rav Yosef explains that the first verse only teaches about the leaf of the smoke-raiser, while the second verse teaches about the root.
Abaye objects, citing a baraita that describes the root of the smoke-raiser as producing a column of smoke, implying the root is the primary ingredient, not the leaf.
Abaye reinterprets: the first verse teaches about the root of the smoke-raiser, and the second verse teaches about the leaf.

items.text: Alternative interpretations of the verse 'and cover'
items.text_en: Alternative interpretations of the verse 'and cover'
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet suggests the verse teaches that the law applies to the Tabernacle, Shiloh, and the Temple. This is rejected because it is derived elsewhere. He then says it teaches that the law applies to Yom Kippur and other days. Rav Ashi says one verse is for the mitzvah and one for preventing the offering. Rava says one is for punishment and one for warning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet suggests that the verse 'and cover' teaches that the law of including a smoke-raiser applies to the Tabernacle, Shiloh, and the Temple.
The Gemara objects that this law is already derived from the verse 'and so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting that dwells with them'.
Rav Sheshet revises his interpretation: the verse teaches that the law applies to Yom Kippur and to the rest of the year.
Rav Ashi says one verse teaches the mitzvah itself and one teaches that the requirement is indispensable.
Rava says one verse teaches the punishment and one serves as a warning.

items.text: The timing of the warning and punishment for Nadav and Avihu
items.text_en: The timing of the warning and punishment for Nadav and Avihu
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the verse 'and he shall not die' is the punishment, and 'for in a cloud I will appear' is the warning. The warning was given before the death of Nadav and Avihu, and the punishment after. Rava explains that the warning was given before the cloud appeared. The Gemara adds that Nadav and Avihu died for ruling in the presence of Moses, as they taught that fire should be brought from ordinary sources even though fire descended from heaven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the verse 'וְלֹא יָמוּת' (and he shall not die) is the punishment, and 'כִּי בֶּעָנָן אֵרָאֶה' (for in a cloud I will appear) is the warning.
The baraita deduces from the verses that the warning was given before the death of Nadav and Avihu, and the punishment after.
The Gemara asks what the scriptural derivation is, and Rava explains that the warning was given before the cloud appeared, then questions why they were punished if the warning was not yet in effect.
The Gemara answers with a baraita that Nadav and Avihu died for ruling in the presence of Moses, teaching that fire should be brought from ordinary sources even though fire descended from heaven.

items.text: The manner of exiting the Holy of Holies and departing from a teacher
items.text_en: The manner of exiting the Holy of Holies and departing from a teacher
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from Solomon's journey to Gibeon that one should exit facing the holy place, just as one enters facing it. This applies to priests, Levites, and Israelites when leaving the Temple service. Similarly, a student should not turn his back on his teacher when departing, but should walk sideways. Examples are given of Rabbi Elazar and Rava showing respect to their teachers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the halacha that one exits the Holy of Holies facing it, just as one enters facing it.

The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this practice, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan cites the verse about Solomon's journey to Gibeon, questioning why Gibeon is juxtaposed with Jerusalem.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani / Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani / Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: The answer explains that the verse equates Solomon's exit from Gibeon to his entry into Jerusalem, teaching that one must face the holy place when leaving as when entering.
A baraita applies the same rule to priests, Levites, and Israelites when departing from the Temple service: they do not turn their backs but walk sideways.
The Gemara extends the rule to a student departing from his teacher, citing the example of Rabbi Elazar who would remain bowed in place until Rabbi Yochanan was out of sight.
The Gemara provides further examples: Rabbi Elazar would walk backwards until out of Rabbi Yochanan's sight, and Rava would walk backwards until his feet struck the threshold of Rav Yosef's house.

items.text: Opening anecdote about Rava's practice
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about Rava's practice
items.desc_en: They told Rav Yosef that Rava acted in a certain way, and Rav Yosef expressed a wish that Rava's head be raised over all the city.

sub.desc_en: The narrator reports that people told Rav Yosef about Rava's practice.
Rav Yosef responds with a blessing that Rava's head be raised over the entire city.

items.text: The requirement to step back three steps after prayer
items.text_en: The requirement to step back three steps after prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one must step back three steps after prayer before giving peace. Rav Mordechai adds that one must stand there and not immediately return, like a student taking leave of his teacher. A baraita supports this and adds that one gives peace to the right and then to the left, citing verses. The Gemara explains the second verse as addressing a potential objection.

sub.text: Rabbi Alexandri citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who prays must take three steps backward and then give peace.
Rav Mordechai adds that after stepping back, one must stand there and not return immediately, comparing it to a student who leaves his teacher and returns like a dog to its vomit.
A baraita supports the requirement to step back three steps and adds that one gives peace to the right first, then to the left, citing verses.
The Gemara asks why a second verse is needed, suggesting it might be merely the usual manner to give with the right hand.

The Gemara answers that the second verse 'יִפּוֹל מִצִּדְּךָ אֶלֶף וּרְבָבָה מִימִינֶךָ' (A thousand may fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right side) shows the right side is more significant, addressing the potential objection.

items.text: Rava corrects Abaye on the direction of giving peace
items.text_en: Rava corrects Abaye on the direction of giving peace
items.desc_en: Rava saw Abaye giving peace first to his right and corrected him: the right referred to is God's right, which is the left of the person. Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna reports that Abaye and Rava would step back three steps in a single bow.

sub.desc_en: Rava corrects Abaye, explaining that the right side to bow to first is God's right, which corresponds to the person's left.
Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna reports that both Abaye and Rava would take the three steps backward in a single bow.

items.text: The content of the High Priest's short prayer in the outer sanctuary
items.text_en: The content of the High Priest's short prayer in the outer sanctuary
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the High Priest prays a short prayer in the outer sanctuary. Rava bar Rav Ada and Ravin bar Rav Ada in the name of Rav say the prayer is for a rainy and warm year. The Gemara questions the term 'warm' and corrects it. Rav Acha bar Rava in the name of Rav Yehuda adds additional requests: that the kingdom of the house of Judah not cease, that Israel not need sustenance from each other, and that the prayer of wayfarers not enter before God.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the High Priest prays a short prayer in the outer sanctuary.
The Gemara asks what the High Priest prays.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Ada and Ravin bar Rav Ada in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Ada and Ravin bar Rav Ada in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: They answer that the prayer is for a rainy and warm year.
The Gemara objects that a warm year is not a blessing.
The Gemara corrects the text to say: if the year is warm, let it be rainy.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava adds additional requests: that the kingdom of Judah not cease, that Israel not need sustenance from each other, and that the prayer of wayfarers not enter before God.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and the High Priest's prayer
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and the High Priest's prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa prayed for rain to stop and then to resume, demonstrating his power. Rav Yosef questions what the High Priest's prayer accomplishes compared to Rabbi Chanina. A baraita recounts a High Priest who prolonged his prayer, causing concern among the other priests; he explained he prayed for them and the Temple not to be destroyed, but they warned him not to be accustomed to doing so lest he frighten Israel.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa prays to stop the rain and then to resume it, demonstrating his power over nature.
Rav Yosef questions what the High Priest's prayer accomplishes compared to Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's power.
A baraita recounts a High Priest who prolonged his prayer, explaining he prayed for the priests and the Temple, but they warned him not to frighten Israel.

items.text: Mishnah: The procedure of the blood sprinklings on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Mishnah: The procedure of the blood sprinklings on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that after the Ark was taken, there was a foundation stone (Even HaShetiya) upon which the High Priest placed the fire-pan. He then took the blood from the one stirring it, entered the Holy of Holies, and sprinkled once upward and seven times downward, counting in a specific manner. He then did the same with the goat's blood, and later mixed the bloods and sprinkled on the curtain. Rabbi Yehuda argues there was only one stand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing that after the Ark was taken, there was a foundation stone (אבן השתיה) upon which the High Priest placed the fire-pan.
The Mishnah describes the High Priest taking the bull's blood, entering the Holy of Holies, and sprinkling once upward and seven times downward with a specific counting method.
The Mishnah states that after the sprinkling, the High Priest placed the blood bowl on a golden stand in the Heikhal.
The Mishnah describes the High Priest slaughtering the goat, sprinkling its blood in the same manner, and placing it on a second golden stand.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that there was only one stand, not two, and the High Priest would place the bull's blood and then the goat's blood on the same stand.
The Mishnah concludes by describing the High Priest mixing the bloods and sprinkling on the curtain, then pouring the full bowl into the empty one.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute over the fate of the Ark
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute over the fate of the Ark
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'after the Ark was taken' (not 'hidden'), supporting the view that the Ark was exiled to Babylon. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai both hold it was exiled, citing verses. Rabbi Yehuda (ben Lakish) argues it was hidden in its place, citing a verse about the poles. This disagrees with Ulla, who recounts that Rabbi Matya ben Charash asked Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in Rome about a second exile of the Ark, citing a verse from Lamentations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah uses the term 'ניטל' (taken) rather than 'נגנז' (hidden), implying the Ark was removed, not hidden in place.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah aligns with the view that the Ark was exiled to Babylon.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer holds that the Ark was exiled to Babylon, citing a verse from Chronicles.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai also holds that the Ark was exiled to Babylon, citing a verse from Jeremiah about the Ten Commandments.
Rabbi Yehuda (ben Lakish) argues that the Ark was hidden in its place, citing a verse from Kings about the poles of the Ark being visible.
Ulla recounts that Rabbi Matya ben Charash asked Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in Rome about a second exile of the Ark, citing a verse from Lamentations.

items.text: Opening dispute: meaning of 'כל הדרה'
items.text_en: Opening dispute: meaning of 'כל הדרה'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'כל הדרה' means, interpreting it as 'חדרה' (her chamber). It then presents a view that the Ark was hidden in its place, citing the verse about the staves being long.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'כל הדרה' means and interprets it as 'חדרה' (her chamber).
The Gemara presents the view that the Ark was hidden in its place, citing the verse about the staves being long.

items.text: Rabbah's challenge: 'עד היום הזה' not always eternal
items.text_en: Rabbah's challenge: 'עד היום הזה' not always eternal
items.desc_en: Rabbah questions Ulla: does 'עד היום הזה' always mean forever? He cites the verse about the Jebusites dwelling in Jerusalem 'עד היום הזה' to show it does not imply permanence.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah challenges Ulla by asking whether 'עד היום הזה' always implies permanence, citing the verse about the Jebusites dwelling in Jerusalem 'עד היום הזה' to show it does not.

items.text: Supporting traditions: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Supporting traditions: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: Rabbi Yehuda says no one passed through Judah for 52 years, and Rabbi Yosei says sulfur and salt endured for seven years. Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning via a verbal analogy on 'ברית'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Yehuda states that for 52 years no one passed through Judah, based on a gematria (numerical value) of the word 'בהמה' (animal) equaling 52.
A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Yosei states that sulfur and salt endured for seven years in the land of Israel.

Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'ברית' (covenant), linking the verse about a covenant for one week to the verse about abandoning the covenant of the Lord.

items.text: Ulla's answer and refutation: 'שם' indicates permanence
items.text_en: Ulla's answer and refutation: 'שם' indicates permanence
items.desc_en: Ulla answers that the word 'שם' (there) in the verse about the Ark indicates permanence, unlike the Jebusite verse. However, a challenge is raised from the verse about the Simeonites who dwelt 'שם עד היום הזה', but Sennacherib later mixed up all nations, proving it is not eternal.

sub.desc_en: Ulla answers that the word 'שָׁם' (there) in the verse about the Ark indicates permanence, unlike the Jebusite verse.
The Gemara raises an objection from the verse about the Simeonites who dwelt 'שָׁם' (there) until this day.
The Gemara refutes Ulla's answer by noting that Sennacherib later mixed up all nations, proving the Simeonites' dwelling there was not eternal.

items.text: Alternative view: Ark hidden in the Chamber of the Wood
items.text_en: Alternative view: Ark hidden in the Chamber of the Wood
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a tradition that the Ark was hidden in the Chamber of the Wood. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this with a story of a priest who saw a distinctive floor tile and died before revealing it, and another story of two blemished priests whose axe fell and was consumed by fire.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a baraita that the Sages say the Ark was hidden in the Chamber of the Wood.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this with a Mishnah story of a priest who saw a distinctive floor tile and died before revealing the Ark's hiding place.
The Gemara asks what the priest was doing when he saw the tile.
Rabbi Chelbo answers that the priest was occupied with his axe.
The Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael adds a supporting story of two blemished priests whose axe fell and was consumed by fire, confirming the Ark's location.

items.text: Contradiction in verses about the staves: visible yet not seen
items.text_en: Contradiction in verses about the staves: visible yet not seen
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda notes a contradiction: one verse says the staves were seen, another says they were not seen outside. The resolution: they pressed and bulged through the curtain, appearing like two breasts of a woman, as per the verse 'בין שדי ילין'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda raises a contradiction between two verses: one says the staves were seen, the other says they were not seen outside.
The gemara resolves that the staves were visible yet not seen: they pressed and bulged through the curtain, appearing like two breasts of a woman, as per the verse 'בין שדי ילין'.

items.text: Cherubim displayed to pilgrims; objections and resolution
items.text_en: Cherubim displayed to pilgrims; objections and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ketina says that during festivals, the curtain was rolled back to show the cherubim intertwined, demonstrating God's love for Israel. Rav Chisda objects with a verse about not seeing the holy vessels. Rav Nachman explains with a parable: a bride is modest in her father's house but not in her husband's. Rav Chana bar Rav Ketina objects with the story of the priest who died; Rav Nachman responds that the cherubim were like a divorced wife who returns to her first love.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ketina states that during the pilgrimage festivals, the curtain was rolled back to show the cherubim intertwined, demonstrating God's love for Israel.
Rav Chisda objects with a verse prohibiting seeing the holy vessels, citing Rav Yehuda's explanation that this applies when the vessels are being placed in their cases.
Rav Nachman answers with a parable: a bride is modest in her father's house but not in her husband's, explaining why the cherubim are shown only after the Temple is built.

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Rav Ketina's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Rav Ketina's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Rav Ketina objects with the story of the priest who died when he saw the hidden ark, implying that the cherubim should not be shown.
Rav Nachman resolves the objection by comparing the situation to a divorced wife who returns to her first love, explaining that the cherubim's display is appropriate after the Temple's destruction.

items.text: Clarifying the context: First or Second Temple?
items.text_en: Clarifying the context: First or Second Temple?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the discussion refers to the First or Second Temple. In the First Temple there was no curtain, and in the Second Temple there were no cherubim. Two answers: Rav Zeira says it refers to the First Temple with a curtain for the gates; Rav Acha bar Yaakov says it refers to the Second Temple with cherubim depicted on the walls, as per the verse 'כמער איש ולויות'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the discussion about the cherubim and the curtain refers to the First Temple (which had no curtain) or the Second Temple (which had no cherubim).
Rav Zeira answers that the discussion refers to the First Temple, and the 'curtain' mentioned is the curtain of the gates (פָּרוֹכֶת דְּבָבֵי), listing the thirteen curtains in the First Temple.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the discussion refers to the Second Temple, where cherubim were depicted on the walls, citing the verse about carved cherubim and palm trees.
Rabbah bar Rav Sheila begins to explain the verse 'כמער איש ולויות' (like the appearance of a man and his companions), which supports the depiction of cherubim on the walls.

items.text: The cherubim embracing and the Gentiles' reaction
items.text_en: The cherubim embracing and the Gentiles' reaction
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish recounts that when Gentiles entered the Temple, they saw the cherubim embracing and mocked Israel for engaging in such matters, leading to their disgrace as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a simile comparing the cherubim's embrace to a man embracing his companion.
Reish Lakish recounts that when Gentiles entered the Temple, they saw the cherubim embracing, mocked Israel, and thereby disgraced them, as the verse states.

items.text: The Even Shetiyah and the world's creation
items.text_en: The Even Shetiyah and the world's creation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the foundation stone was called 'Shetiyah' because from it the world was founded, supporting the view that the world was created from Zion, citing Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Foundation Stone
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Foundation Stone
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the stone in the Holy of Holies was called 'Shetiyah' (Foundation Stone).
A baraita explains that the stone is called Shetiyah because from it the world was founded (הושתח).
The Gemara notes that this baraita aligns with the opinion that the world was created from Zion, citing Rabbi Eliezer's view that the world was created from its center.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yitzchak's views on creation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yitzchak's views on creation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua argues the world was created from the sides, while Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha says God cast a stone into the sea from which the world was founded, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the world was created from the sides, citing a verse about snow and rain.
Rabbi Yitzchak (Nappacha) says that God cast a stone into the sea from which the world was founded, citing a verse about the foundation stone.

items.text: The Sages' view: creation from Zion
items.text_en: The Sages' view: creation from Zion
items.desc_en: The Sages assert that the world was created from Zion, citing Psalms that describe Zion as the perfection of beauty from which the world's beauty was derived.

sub.desc_en: The Sages state that the world was created from Zion, citing Psalms that describe God's beauty emanating from Zion.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol's interpretation of creation
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol's interpretation of creation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol interprets the verse 'These are the generations of the heavens and the earth' to mean that the heavens were created from heaven and the earth from earth.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol interprets the verse 'These are the generations of heaven and earth' to mean that heaven was created from heaven and earth from earth.

items.text: The Sages' rebuttal: both from Zion
items.text_en: The Sages' rebuttal: both from Zion
items.desc_en: The Sages counter that both heaven and earth were created from Zion, citing Psalms that God called the earth from the east and that Zion is the perfection of beauty.

sub.desc_en: The Sages assert that both heaven and earth were created from Zion, citing verses that describe God calling the earth from Zion.

items.text: The blood sprinkling motion explained
items.text_en: The blood sprinkling motion explained
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the meaning of 'like one who cracks a whip' and Rav Yehudah demonstrates the motion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the Mishnah about taking blood from the one stirring it and asks: What does 'like one who whips' mean?
Rav Yehuda demonstrates the motion of whipping to explain the Mishnah's term.

items.text: Opening baraita on sprinkling technique
items.text_en: Opening baraita on sprinkling technique
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how the High Priest sprinkles the blood: not directly on the ark cover but opposite its thickness, and he angles his hand downward when sprinkling upward and upward when sprinkling downward.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that when the High Priest sprinkles the blood, he does not sprinkle directly on the ark cover but opposite its thickness, angling his hand downward for upward sprinkling and upward for downward sprinkling.

items.text: Gemara's question and derivation of the technique
items.text_en: Gemara's question and derivation of the technique
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for this practice. Rav Acha bar Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Zeira derives it from the verse 'and he shall sprinkle it upon the ark cover and before the ark cover,' using a comparison between the goat and the bull. The Gemara then challenges this derivation, suggesting an alternative interpretation, and resolves it with a teaching from the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the practice of sprinkling the goat's blood below the ark cover.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Zeira derives the practice from the verse 'וְהִזָּה אוֹתוֹ עַל הַכַּפֹּרֶת וְלִפְנֵי הַכַּפֹּרֶת' (and he shall sprinkle it upon the ark cover and before the ark cover), arguing that the superfluous 'לְמַטָּה' (below) in the goat's sprinkling comes to equate 'עַל' (upon) with 'לִפְנֵי' (before), meaning not directly upon.
The Gemara objects that one could reverse the argument: the superfluous 'לְמַעְלָה' (above) in the bull's sprinkling could equate 'לִפְנֵי' to 'עַל', meaning directly upon the ark cover.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution with the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution with the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who taught that 'עַל פְּנֵי הַכַּפֹּרֶת קֵדְמָה' (upon the face of the ark cover eastward) establishes a general principle that 'פָּנִים' (face) always means east; thus the bull's 'לְמַעְלָה' is needed for that teaching, leaving the goat's 'לְמַטָּה' for the equation, whereas the reverse would leave the bull's 'לְמַעְלָה' without purpose.

items.text: Derivation of seven sprinklings below for the goat
items.text_en: Derivation of seven sprinklings below for the goat
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that we know the number of sprinklings above for the goat (one) but not below. A logical comparison is made: just as below for the bull is seven, so too below for the goat should be seven. An alternative comparison is rejected, and a verse is cited to establish that all sprinklings of the goat are equal to those of the bull, yielding seven below.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that from the verse we know the number of sprinklings above for the goat (one), but the number below is unknown.
A logical comparison is proposed: just as below for the bull is seven, so too below for the goat should be seven.
An alternative comparison is raised: just as above for the goat is one, so too below for the goat should be one.
The first comparison is preferred: we derive below from below, not below from above.
A counter-objection is raised: we should derive the goat's own law from itself (above) rather than from another animal (the bull).
A verse is cited to resolve the dispute: 'וְעָשָׂה אֶת דָּמוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה' teaches that all sprinklings of the goat are equal to those of the bull, yielding seven below.

items.text: Derivation of one sprinkling above for the bull
items.text_en: Derivation of one sprinkling above for the bull
items.desc_en: Similarly, we know the number below for the bull and goat (seven) but not above for the bull. A logical comparison is made: just as above for the goat is one, so too above for the bull should be one. An alternative comparison is rejected, and the same verse is used to establish that all sprinklings are equal, yielding one above for the bull.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that we already know the number of sprinklings below for the bull and goat (seven), but not above for the bull, and proposes a logical comparison: just as above for the goat is one, so too above for the bull should be one.
An alternative comparison is raised: just as below for the bull is seven, so too above for the bull should be seven.

The Gemara resolves by citing the verse 'וְעָשָׂה אֶת דָּמוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה' (and he shall do with its blood as he did), which teaches that all sprinklings are equal, yielding one above for the bull.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on counting method
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on counting method
items.desc_en: The Sages teach the counting method: one, one-and-one, one-and-two, etc. (Rabbi Meir) or one, one-and-one, two-and-one, etc. (Rabbi Yehuda). The Gemara explains they do not disagree but follow different local customs.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents Rabbi Meir's counting method for the sprinklings: one, one-and-one, one-and-two, up to one-and-seven.
Rabbi Yehuda presents an alternative counting method: one, one-and-one, two-and-one, three-and-one, up to seven-and-one.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda do not actually disagree; each follows the local custom of his region.

items.text: Reason for counting the first sprinkling with each one
items.text_en: Reason for counting the first sprinkling with each one
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first sprinkling must be counted with each subsequent one. Rabbi Elazar says it is to avoid error in the sprinklings. Rabbi Yochanan derives it from the verse 'and before the ark cover he shall sprinkle,' teaching that the first sprinkling requires counting with each one. The difference between them is a case where one did not count but also did not err.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the first sprinkling must be counted with each subsequent one.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the first sprinkling is counted with each one to prevent error in the sprinklings.
Rabbi Yochanan derives the requirement from the verse 'וְלִפְנֵי הַכַּפֹּרֶת יַזֶּה' (and before the ark cover he shall sprinkle), teaching that the first sprinkling needs counting with each one.
The Gemara identifies the practical difference between the two opinions: a case where one did not count but also did not err.

items.text: Transition to a related topic: mixing of offerings
items.text_en: Transition to a related topic: mixing of offerings
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that the High Priest went out and placed the blood on a golden stand in the Sanctuary. The Gemara connects this to a teaching about Rabbi Yehuda's concern for mixing of offerings, and discusses the reason for the mixing and a possible solution.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that the High Priest went out and placed the blood on a golden stand in the Sanctuary, and the Gemara connects this to a teaching about Rabbi Yehuda's concern for mixing of offerings.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that there were no collection horns for obligatory bird offerings (קינֵי חובה) because of the concern for mixing (תערובות).
The Gemara asks: what is the meaning of 'because of the mixing'?
Rav Yosef answers: because of the concern that an obligatory offering (חובה) might be mixed with a voluntary offering (נדבה).
Abaye objects: why not make two collection horns and write on them which is for obligatory offerings and which for voluntary offerings?

items.text: Gemara's initial question and Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda prohibits having two chests for the bull and goat, suggesting that writing on them would solve confusion. It concludes that Rabbi Yehuda does not allow writing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's position that only one chest was used for the bull and goat, suggesting that writing on two chests would prevent confusion.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehuda does not allow writing on the chests, which is why he prohibits having two.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of thirteen shofarot
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of thirteen shofarot
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing thirteen collection chests in the Temple, each with written labels, according to Rabbi Yehuda. This challenges the claim that Rabbi Yehuda rejects writing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing thirteen collection chests (שופרות) in the Temple, each with written labels, to challenge the claim that Rabbi Yehuda rejects writing.
The baraita explains the meaning of each label on the chests, concluding that all the offerings are עולות (burnt-offerings), according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: First answer: concern for a sin-offering whose owners died
items.text_en: First answer: concern for a sin-offering whose owners died
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports a Western explanation: the prohibition is a decree due to concern for a sin-offering whose owners died. The Gemara objects, citing a mishnah that assumes the owner is alive.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports a Western explanation that the prohibition is a decree due to concern for a sin-offering whose owners died.
The Gemara objects by citing a mishnah that assumes the owner is alive, showing we do not normally worry about the owner's death.

items.text: Second answer: concern for a definite sin-offering whose owners died
items.text_en: Second answer: concern for a definite sin-offering whose owners died
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises the concern to a definite case where the owner died. It then suggests selecting four zuz and throwing them into water to nullify the mixture, but notes that Rabbi Yehuda rejects the principle of bereira.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises the concern to a definite sin-offering whose owners died, then proposes selecting four zuz and throwing them into water to nullify the mixture.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda rejects the principle of bereira (retroactive selection), so the proposed solution fails.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Yehuda rejects bereira
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Yehuda rejects bereira
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks to prove that Rabbi Yehuda rejects bereira, citing a mishnah about a Jew buying wine from Cutheans on Shabbat eve, where he designates future terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that Rabbi Yehuda rejects bereira? It proposes to cite a mishnah.
The Gemara cites the mishnah about a Jew buying wine from Cutheans on Shabbat eve, who designates two future lugim as תרומה (priestly portion), implying that Rabbi Yehuda rejects bereira.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that ten blood applications are made: the first nine are from the bull and the tenth from the goat, and then the Kohen Gadol mixes the blood and sprinkles it. This is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that ten blood applications are made: the first nine from the bull and the tenth from the goat, and then the Kohen Gadol mixes the blood and drinks it immediately; this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Opening dispute on ברירה
items.text_en: Opening dispute on ברירה
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon prohibit, implying no ברירה. The Gemara questions this inference.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon prohibit, implying that there is no ברירה (retroactive selection).

items.text: Gemara's challenge and Rabbi Meir's response
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and Rabbi Meir's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the inference, suggesting the case is different due to the concern of the wineskin bursting. Rabbi Meir responds that designation is only retroactively invalid if it bursts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the inference that there is no retroactive designation (ברירה), suggesting the case of the wineskin is different because of the concern it might burst.
Rabbi Meir responds that the designation is only retroactively invalid if the wineskin actually bursts, not from the outset.

items.text: Proof from the baraita of Ayo and Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
items.text_en: Proof from the baraita of Ayo and Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda prohibits conditional eiruv on two directions simultaneously, proving he rejects ברירה. Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Yehuda permits conditional eiruv when the sage has already arrived, avoiding the need for retroactive designation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Ayo's baraita where Rabbi Yehuda prohibits conditional eiruv on two directions simultaneously, establishing that he rejects ברירה (retroactive designation).
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda prohibits conditional eiruv on two directions simultaneously, answering that it is because he rejects ברירה (retroactive designation).
The Gemara objects that even conditional eiruv on one direction should be invalid according to Rabbi Yehuda, since it also involves retroactive designation.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the objection by explaining that Rabbi Yehuda permits conditional eiruv when the sage has already arrived, so no retroactive designation is needed.

items.text: Application to Yom Kippur: writing two bulls
items.text_en: Application to Yom Kippur: writing two bulls
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not write two bulls for Yom Kippur, given Rabbi Yehuda's rejection of ברירה. It answers that due to the high priest's weakness, he cannot keep track; otherwise, size differences would suffice. The same reason applies to blood collection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since Rabbi Yehuda rejects ברירה (retroactive clarification) but accepts writing, why not place two pedestals on Yom Kippur and write on them which is for the bull and which for the goat?

The Gemara answers: due to the high priest's weakness from fasting, the writing would not be on his mind; otherwise, even without writing, the size difference between the bowls would suffice to avoid confusion.

The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the high priest does not collect all the bull's blood, making the bowls equal in size; but Rav Yehuda rules that the slaughterer must collect all the blood, as the verse states.

The Gemara rejects another objection: even if some blood spills, the colors differ (goat's blood is white, bull's is red), but the high priest's weakness prevents him from noticing; thus writing would also not help.

items.text: Rava's correction of a mishna reciter
items.text_en: Rava's correction of a mishna reciter
items.desc_en: A reciter describes the high priest placing the bull's blood and then taking the goat's blood. Rava corrects the order to match the mishna: place the goat's blood first, then take the bull's blood.

sub.desc_en: A reciter before Rava describes the high priest placing the bull's blood on the second pedestal and then taking the goat's blood.
Rava objects that the reciter's description mixes the opinions of the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda, and corrects the order to place the goat's blood first and then take the bull's blood.

items.text: Derivation of sprinkling in the Heikhal
items.text_en: Derivation of sprinkling in the Heikhal
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the sprinkling in the Heikhal parallels that in the Holy of Holies: one upward and seven downward for both bull and goat blood. It also notes that the Shekhinah dwells with Israel even when they are impure.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'וְכֵן יַעֲשֶׂה לְאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' and explains that the sprinkling in the Heikhal parallels that in the Holy of Holies.
The baraita specifies that just as in the Holy of Holies one sprinkles once upward and seven times downward from the bull's blood, so too in the Heikhal.
The baraita adds that the same pattern of one upward and seven downward applies to the goat's blood in the Heikhal.
The baraita concludes by citing the verse 'הַשּׁוֹכֵן אִתָּם בְּתוֹךְ טוּמְאֹתָם' to teach that the Shekhinah dwells with Israel even when they are impure.

items.text: Opening of a Sadducee challenge
items.text_en: Opening of a Sadducee challenge
items.desc_en: A Sadducee begins a question to Rabbi Chanina, setting up the next section.

sub.desc_en: A Sadducee begins a question to Rabbi Chanina, setting up the next section.

items.text: Gemara's opening: the Shekhina dwells among Israel even in impurity
items.text_en: Gemara's opening: the Shekhina dwells among Israel even in impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse to show that even when Israel is impure, the Divine Presence dwells among them, challenging a prior assumption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse to show that even when Israel is impure, the Divine Presence dwells among them, challenging a prior assumption.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about a hekesh (analogy)
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about a hekesh (analogy)
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a matter learned through a hekesh can teach another hekesh. It offers two answers: that this is a case of 'from it and something else' (not a hekesh), or that the places (the curtains) are learned from each other. A baraita is cited about the placement of blood opposite the parochet, not on it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a matter learned through a היקש (analogy) can itself teach another היקש.
The first answer argues that this is a case of הימנו ודבר אחר (from it and something else), which is not a true היקש.
The Gemara objects that this answer only works for the opinion that it is not a היקש, but what about the opinion that it is a היקש?
The second answer explains that the places (the curtains) are learned from each other, not through a היקש.
An alternative answer states that the rule of 'outside and inside' was learned in one instance, so no היקש is needed.
A ברייתא (baraita) is cited stating that the blood is sprinkled opposite the parochet, not on it, and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei testifies that he saw blood drops on the parochet in Rome.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's testimony about blood stains in Rome
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's testimony about blood stains in Rome
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi testifies that he saw blood stains on the parochet in Rome from the bull and goat of Yom Kippur. The Gemara questions whether they might be from other offerings, and he clarifies based on the order of the stains.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that when the High Priest sprinkles the blood on Yom Kippur, he does not sprinkle directly on the parochet (curtain) but opposite it.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi testifies that he saw the parochet in Rome with many drops of blood from the bull and goat of Yom Kippur.
The Gemara questions whether the blood might be from the bull of the anointed priest's unwitting sin (פר העלם דבר של ציבור) and the goats of idolatry (שעירי עבודה זרה), not Yom Kippur.

The Gemara answers that he saw the stains arranged in order (כסדרן), and cites a baraita that for the bull of unwitting sin the sprinkling does not touch the curtain, so the stains must be from Yom Kippur.

Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi clarifies that he also saw blood from the bull of unwitting sin and goats of idolatry, and those were arranged out of order (שלא כסדרן), confirming the Yom Kippur blood was in order.

items.text: Rava's ruling on mixed blood from different offerings
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on mixed blood from different offerings
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if blood from a bull and a goat (of Yom Kippur) became mixed, the priest may place one sprinkling above and seven below, and it counts for both.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if blood from a bull and a goat (of Yom Kippur) became mixed, the priest may place one sprinkling above and seven below, and it counts for both.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection and alternative ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection and alternative ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects to Rava's ruling, arguing that it violates the order of the Torah (first the bull, then the goat). He proposes instead that the priest should give one above and seven below for the bull, then repeat for the goat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects to Rava's ruling, arguing that it violates the Torah's order by giving the goat's upper sprinkling before the bull's lower sprinklings.
Rabbi Yirmeya proposes that the priest should give one above and seven below for the bull, then repeat for the goat, preserving the correct order.

items.text: Rav Pappa's proposal and Rava's rejection regarding later sprinklings
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's proposal and Rava's rejection regarding later sprinklings
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa suggests a procedure for mixed blood in the later sprinklings (on the altar), but Rava rejects it, noting that it would place the lower sprinkling of the goat before the upper sprinkling of the goat, violating the Torah's order.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa proposes that for mixed blood in the later sprinklings, the priest should give seven lower sprinklings for both the bull and goat, then one upper sprinkling for the goat.
Rava rejects Rav Pappa's proposal, arguing that it places the lower sprinkling of the goat before the upper sprinkling of the goat, violating the Torah's order of upper then lower.

items.text: Rava's ruling on mixing cups of blood
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on mixing cups of blood
items.desc_en: Rava states that if the cups of blood for the bull and goat are mixed, the priest gives seven applications below for the bull, then one above and seven below for the goat, repeating three times.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that when cups of blood are mixed, the priest gives seven applications below for the bull, then one above and seven below for the goat, repeating three times.

items.text: Question about partially mixed blood
items.text_en: Question about partially mixed blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if only some of the bloods are mixed, it is obvious that the priest gives from the unmixed bloods. But the question is whether the mixed bloods are considered leftover (שיריים) and poured onto the foundation, or rejected (דחויין) and poured into the channel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the obvious case: if only some bloods are mixed, the priest gives from the unmixed ones.
The Gemara raises the real question: are the mixed bloods considered leftover (שיריים) poured to the foundation, or rejected (דחויין) poured to the channel?

items.text: Rav Pappa's answer
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that even according to the one who says one cup makes its fellow leftover, that applies only when the priest could have given from it, but here he cannot, so it is not leftover.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that even according to the one who says one cup makes its fellow leftover, that applies only when the priest could have given from it, but here he cannot, so it is not leftover.

items.text: Rav Huna's objection
items.text_en: Rav Huna's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua objects to Rav Pappa, arguing that even according to the one who says one cup makes its fellow rejected, that applies only when the priest actively rejected it, but here he did not, so it is not rejected.

sub.text: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua objects to Rav Pappa, arguing that even according to the one who says one cup makes its fellow rejected (דחוי), that applies only when the priest actively rejected it, but here he did not, so it is not rejected.

items.text: Baraita on blood poured to the foundation
items.text_en: Baraita on blood poured to the foundation
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: from verses about the bull and goat, we derive that if blood was collected in four cups and one application was given from each, all are poured to the foundation. But if all four applications were from one cup, only that cup goes to the foundation, the others to the channel. Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon disagrees, saying all go to the foundation. Rav Ashi explains that the verse 'and its blood' excludes leftover blood on the animal's neck.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing two verses: one about the bull (וְאֶת דָּמוֹ יִשְׁפּוֹךְ) and one about the goat (וְאֶת כׇּל דָּמָהּ יִשְׁפּוֹךְ), establishing the scriptural basis for the laws of pouring leftover blood.
The Tanna Kamma derives from the verse 'וְאֶת כׇּל דָּמָהּ יִשְׁפּוֹךְ' that if blood was collected in four cups and one application was given from each, all four cups are poured to the foundation.

The Tanna Kamma then limits the rule: if all four applications were from one cup, only that cup goes to the foundation, while the other cups are poured into the channel, as derived from the verse 'וְאֶת דָּמוֹ יִשְׁפּוֹךְ'.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Shimon disagrees, arguing that even if all four applications were from one cup, all cups are poured to the foundation, based on the inclusive verse 'וְאֶת כׇּל דָּמָהּ יִשְׁפּוֹךְ'.

Rav Ashi resolves the apparent contradiction: the verse 'וְאֶת דָּמוֹ יִשְׁפּוֹךְ' is not needed for the cup case but rather excludes leftover blood on the animal's neck from being poured to the foundation.

items.text: Dispute about mixing bloods for the horns
items.text_en: Dispute about mixing bloods for the horns
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the blood of the bull is poured into the blood of the goat, implying they are mixed. This supports the view that one may mix bloods for the horns. The dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan is cited: one says mixing is allowed, the other says not. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yoshiya allows mixing, and a baraita explicitly states that the bloods must be mixed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the blood of the bull is poured into the blood of the goat, implying they are mixed.
The Gemara infers that the Mishnah supports the view that one may mix bloods for the horns.
The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan: one says mixing is allowed, the other says not.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yoshiya allows mixing, reasoning that even without the word 'together' it is as if it were written.
The Gemara considers that even Rabbi Yonatan might agree here because the verse uses the word 'one' (אחת), implying mixing.
A baraita explicitly states that the bloods must be mixed, according to Rabbi Yoshiya, contradicting the alternative explanation.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya on mixing blood
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya on mixing blood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan argues that the blood of the bull and goat are taken separately, while Rabbi Yoshiya objects citing the verse 'one'. Rabbi Yonatan responds that the verse teaches that only one application is made from each blood, not that they are mixed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan states that the blood of the bull and the goat are taken separately, each on its own.
Rabbi Yoshiya objects, citing the verse that says 'one', implying the bloods are mixed.

Rabbi Yonatan responds that the verse 'from the blood of the bull and from the blood of the goat' teaches that each blood is taken separately, and the word 'one' teaches that only one application is made from each blood, not two.

items.text: Baraita supporting mixing and siding with Rabbi Yoshiya
items.text_en: Baraita supporting mixing and siding with Rabbi Yoshiya
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'and he shall take from the blood of the bull and from the blood of the goat' implies they must be mixed together, and the word 'one' supports this. The baraita concludes that the anonymous opinion aligns with Rabbi Yoshiya.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that interprets the verse to require mixing the bloods, and concludes that the anonymous opinion follows Rabbi Yoshiya.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about placing a full vessel inside an empty one
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about placing a full vessel inside an empty one
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether placing a full vessel inside an empty one constitutes a valid mixing (חציצה). Rav Chisda initially suggests the Mishnah's phrase 'he placed the full into the empty' means inserting one vessel into another, but then clarifies it means pouring, as the earlier clause already discusses pouring.

sub.text: Rami bar Chama's question to Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question to Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda: if one placed a full bowl inside an empty bowl and received blood in the inner bowl, does the inner bowl act as a חוצץ (interposition) since it is the same material?

Rav Chisda answers by citing the Mishnah that says 'he poured the full into the empty', explaining that this refers to pouring from one bowl to another, not placing one inside the other, and the purpose is to mix the bloods well.
The Gemara rejects Rav Chisda's interpretation, clarifying that the Mishnah means pouring, not inserting.
The Gemara supports this by noting that the earlier clause already discusses pouring, so the later clause must also refer to pouring for proper mixing.

items.text: Proof from standing on a vessel or friend's foot
items.text_en: Proof from standing on a vessel or friend's foot
items.desc_en: A proof is brought: if one stands on a vessel or a friend's foot, the service is invalid. Rav Chisda distinguishes that a foot cannot be nullified, implying that a vessel might be different. An alternative version questions whether this is a valid mode of service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to bring a proof from a baraita that if a priest stood on a vessel or his friend's foot, the service is invalid, implying that an interposition invalidates.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing that a foot cannot be nullified, unlike a vessel which can be בטל (nullified).
An alternative version presents the inquiry differently: whether standing on a vessel constitutes a valid mode of service at all.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yishmael's school
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yishmael's school
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that teaches: two vessels and one service, implying that using two vessels for one service is invalid.

items.text: Alternative version and proof from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Alternative version and proof from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the question asks whether this is a valid mode of service. The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the verse 'all the service vessels' implies two vessels for one service, supporting that placing one vessel inside another is valid.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rami bar Chama's question
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rami bar Chama's question
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rami bar Chama asked whether placing a bowl inside another bowl is considered a valid mode of service (דרך שירות) or not.

sub.text: Proof from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Proof from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that the verse teaches 'two vessels and one service', implying that using two vessels in one service is valid.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about fiber in the vessel
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about fiber in the vessel
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether placing fiber inside the vessel to receive blood constitutes an interposition (חציצה). Rav Chisda initially cites a Mishnah about water seeping through a sponge, but distinguishes because water is thin. An alternative version states that for blood it is valid, but for a handful (קומץ) it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether placing fiber inside the vessel to receive blood constitutes an interposition (חציצה) since it is a different substance, or whether it does not interpose because it is porous.
Rav Chisda cites a Mishnah about water seeping through a sponge, but distinguishes because water is thin (קלישי) and therefore not comparable to blood.
An alternative version states that Rav Chisda resolved: for blood it is valid (כשר), but for a handful (קומץ) it is invalid (פסול).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Order of sprinkling on the inner altar
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Order of sprinkling on the inner altar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for sprinkling blood on the Golden Altar: the priest starts at the northeast corner and proceeds to northwest, southwest, southeast. Rabbi Eliezer says he stands in place and sprinkles. The Mishnah also details the placement of blood on the altar and the disposal of leftover blood.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by identifying the Golden Altar and describing the order of sprinkling from the northeast corner.
Rabbi Eliezer states an alternative view that the priest stands in place and sprinkles.
The Mishnah details the placement of blood on the altar and the disposal of leftover blood into the Kidron stream.

items.text: First baraita: Derivation that the priest stands inside the altar
items.text_en: First baraita: Derivation that the priest stands inside the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Nehemiah explains the verse "and he shall go out to the altar" teaches that the priest stands inside (before) the altar, unlike the bull for all commandments where he stands outside.

sub.desc_en: A baraita asks why the verse says 'and he shall go out to the altar,' and Rabbi Nehemiah suggests it might imply the priest stands outside the altar like with the bull for all commandments.
The baraita resolves that the verse teaches the priest was inside the altar, not outside.

items.text: Second baraita: Derivation that the priest stands outside the altar
items.text_en: Second baraita: Derivation that the priest stands outside the altar
items.desc_en: Another baraita from Rabbi Nehemiah explains the phrase "before the Lord" teaches that the priest stands outside the altar, unlike the bull and goat of Yom Kippur where he stands inside. The conclusion is that he stands outside the altar and sprinkles.

sub.desc_en: Another baraita asks why the verse says 'before the Lord,' and Rabbi Nehemiah suggests it might imply the priest stands inside the altar like on Yom Kippur.
The baraita resolves that the altar is before the Lord, not the priest, so the priest stands outside the altar and sprinkles.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yose HaGelili on starting corner
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yose HaGelili on starting corner
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Akiva says the priest starts at the southeast corner, then southwest, northwest, northeast. Rabbi Yose HaGelili says he starts at the northeast, then northwest, southwest, southeast. The baraita notes that where one starts, the other ends.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Akiva's order of sprinkling starting from the southeast corner and Rabbi Yose HaGelili's order starting from the northeast corner.
The Gemara notes that where Rabbi Yose HaGelili begins, Rabbi Akiva ends, and vice versa.

items.text: Reason for not starting at the first corner encountered
items.text_en: Reason for not starting at the first corner encountered
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that all agree the priest does not sprinkle on the first corner he encounters when entering. Shmuel says this is because the verse "and he shall go out to the altar" implies he must go out to the entire altar first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all agree that the priest does not sprinkle on the first corner he encounters.
Shmuel answers that the verse 'and he shall go out to the altar' requires the priest to go out completely from the altar before starting.

items.text: First explanation: Dispute over Rami bar Yechezkel's principle
items.text_en: First explanation: Dispute over Rami bar Yechezkel's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yose HaGelili might be about whether to follow Rami bar Yechezkel's rule that all turns should be to the right (eastward). One master accepts this rule, the other does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Akiva's order follows the right-hand rule, suggesting the dispute is about Rami bar Yechezkel's principle.
Rami bar Yechezkel's principle from Solomon's sea teaches that all turns should be to the right, and the Gemara suggests the dispute is whether one accepts this principle.

items.text: Second explanation: Dispute over deriving inner from outer
items.text_en: Second explanation: Dispute over deriving inner from outer
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the first explanation, stating that all accept Rami bar Yechezkel's principle. The real dispute is whether we derive the order for the inner altar from the outer altar. Rabbi Yose HaGelili derives it, Rabbi Akiva does not. Rabbi Akiva would prefer to start at the first corner due to the principle of not passing over mitzvot, but cannot because of the verse requiring going out to the entire altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous explanation, asserting that all parties accept Rami bar Yechezkel's principle.
The Gemara resolves that the real dispute is whether we derive the order for the inner altar (פנים) from the outer altar (חוץ).
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Akiva, who does not derive the inner from the outer, would not simply choose any starting corner at will.
Rabbi Akiva explains that he would prefer to start at the first corner he encounters due to the principle of אין מעבירין על המצות (not passing over mitzvot).

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva cannot start at the first corner because the verse 'וְיָצָא אֶל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ' requires going out to the entire altar, so after starting at one corner he must return to the corner he was obligated to start at.

items.text: Two alternative explanations for the dispute about encircling the altar
items.text_en: Two alternative explanations for the dispute about encircling the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative resolutions for the dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGlili and the Sages: either all agree that encircling is done by foot, and they argue about deriving the inner altar from the outer; or all agree it is by hand, and they argue about deriving hand from foot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers the first alternative: if encircling is done by foot, then all agree that the inner altar is derived from the outer, and the dispute is about whether encircling is by hand or foot.
The Gemara offers the second alternative: if all agree encircling is by hand, then the dispute is about whether we derive hand from foot.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yose HaGlili's position and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yose HaGlili's position and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yose HaGlili actually holds that encircling is by hand, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says he stands in place and sprinkles, implying the first Tanna disagrees. It resolves that the dispute is about encircling by hand vs. foot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yose HaGlili's position that encircling is by hand, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer's statement implies the first Tanna disagrees.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about encircling by hand vs. by foot, as originally stated.

items.text: Third alternative: dispute about the size of the inner altar
items.text_en: Third alternative: dispute about the size of the inner altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a third alternative: the dispute is about whether the inner altar's perimeter is like the outer altar's, or whether the entire inner altar stands in place of one horn of the outer altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a third alternative: the dispute is about whether the inner altar's perimeter is like the outer altar's.
The Gemara states the second position: the entire inner altar stands in place of one horn of the outer altar.

items.text: Baraita: Two High Priests dispute encircling method
items.text_en: Baraita: Two High Priests dispute encircling method
items.desc_en: A baraita records that two High Priests in the First Temple argued: one said he encircled by hand, the other by foot. Each gave a reason: one compared the inner altar's perimeter to the outer, the other said the entire inner altar is like one horn of the outer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael introduces a baraita about two High Priests from the First Temple who disputed the method of encircling the inner altar.
The first High Priest supports his claim by comparing the perimeter of the inner altar to that of the outer altar.
The second High Priest supports his claim by asserting that the entire inner altar is like one horn of the outer altar.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion and the tannaitic dispute about sprinkling order
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion and the tannaitic dispute about sprinkling order
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says the priest stands in place and sprinkles. The Gemara identifies the mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's version, contrasting with Rabbi Meir's version regarding whether the sprinkling is from top to bottom or bottom to top.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that the priest stands in place and sprinkles.
The Gemara identifies the mishnah as following Rabbi Yehuda's version.
A baraita cites Rabbi Meir's version of Rabbi Eliezer's opinion: he sprinkles from top to bottom except for the diagonal one, which is from bottom to top.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's version of Rabbi Eliezer's opinion: he sprinkles from bottom to top except for the one directly before him, which is from top to bottom to avoid soiling his garments.

items.text: Interpretation of 'taharo' of the altar
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'taharo' of the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the meaning of 'taharo' of the altar. Rabba bar Rav Sheila first suggests it means half of the altar, but an objection is raised. He then explains it means the exposed part of the altar, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'taharo' of the altar means.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Sheila's first answer
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Sheila's first answer
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Sheila answers that 'taharo' means half of the altar, citing a folk expression about midday.
An objection is raised from a baraita that the priest clears coals and ashes before sprinkling, implying the sprinkling is not on half the altar.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Sheila's revised answer
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Sheila's revised answer
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Sheila revises his answer: 'taharo' means the exposed part of the altar, citing the verse 'like the very heavens for brightness'.

items.text: Dispute about where the blood is placed on the altar
items.text_en: Dispute about where the blood is placed on the altar
items.desc_en: Chananya says the blood is placed on the north side, Rabbi Yose on the south side. They argue about where the entrance is. All agree that the blood is placed on the roof of the altar where the horn applications are, based on the verse 'v'tiharo v'kiddsho'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Chananya and Rabbi Yose disputing whether the blood is placed on the north or south side of the altar.
The gemara asks what underlies the dispute between Chananya and Rabbi Yose.
The gemara explains that they disagree about the location of the entrance to the sanctuary: one holds it is in the south, the other in the north.

The gemara concludes that all agree the blood is placed on the roof of the altar where the horn applications end, citing the verse 'וְטִהֲרוֹ וְקִדְּשׁוֹ' (and he shall purify it and sanctify it) to show that the place of sanctification is the place of purification.

items.text: Location for pouring leftover blood: outer altar's western or southern foundation
items.text_en: Location for pouring leftover blood: outer altar's western or southern foundation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states leftover blood is poured on the western foundation of the outer altar. The Gemara explains this is because when exiting the Sanctuary, one first encounters that foundation. For the outer altar's blood, it is poured on the southern foundation, derived by analogy from the priest's descent from the ramp.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that leftover blood is poured on the western foundation of the outer altar.
The Gemara explains that when exiting the Sanctuary, the priest first encounters the western foundation, as derived from the verse about pouring the bull's blood.
The Mishnah states that for the outer altar's blood, it is poured on the southern foundation.
A baraita is cited: the foundation of the altar is the southern one, with a question whether it might be the western one.
The Gemara resolves by analogy: just as exiting the Sanctuary leads to the nearby western foundation, descending the ramp leads to the nearby southern foundation.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai about the foundation
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai about the foundation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael says both foundations are western; Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says both are southern. The Gemara explains Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning: learn the unspecified from the explicit. For Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, Rav Ashi says he holds the entrance is in the south. A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael in the school of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states both are southern.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yishmael stating both foundations are western, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai stating both are southern.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning: he learns the unspecified (the inner altar's foundation) from the explicit (the outer altar's foundation).
The Gemara asks: what is Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's reasoning?
Rav Ashi answers: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai holds that the entrance to the Temple is in the south, so the priest exits southward and pours the blood on the southern foundation.

sub.text: Baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael in the school of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that both foundations are southern, with a mnemonic: 'the men drew the man to their side.'

items.text: Dispute about misuse of consecrated property with blood
items.text_en: Dispute about misuse of consecrated property with blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the leftover blood from both altars mixes in the channel and flows out. The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon say there is misuse of consecrated property with blood, while the Sages say there is not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the leftover blood from both altars mixes in the channel and flows out.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon rule that there is misuse of consecrated property (מעילה) with blood.
The Sages disagree and rule that there is no misuse of consecrated property with blood.

items.text: Introduction of the dispute's scope
items.text_en: Introduction of the dispute's scope
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier dispute about me'ilah in the blood before atonement is only rabbinic, but by Torah law there is no me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the earlier dispute about me'ilah in the blood before atonement applies only rabbinically, but by Torah law there is no me'ilah.

items.text: Source from Ulla and the school of Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Source from Ulla and the school of Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Ulla derives from the verse 'lachem' that the blood is for you, and the school of Rabbi Shimon derives from 'lechaper' that it is given for atonement, not for me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that there is no Torah-level me'ilah) derived?
Ulla derives from the verse 'לָכֶם' (for you) that the blood is given to you, and the school of Rabbi Shimon teaches from 'לְכַפֵּר' (to atone) that it is given for atonement, not for me'ilah.
The school of Rabbi Shimon teaches from the verse 'לְכַפֵּר' (to atone) that the blood is given for atonement (כפרה) and not for me'ilah.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation from 'hu'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation from 'hu'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from the word 'hu' that the blood before atonement is like after atonement: just as after atonement there is no me'ilah, so too before atonement there is no me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from the word 'הוּא' (it) that the blood before atonement is like after atonement: just as after atonement there is no me'ilah, so too before atonement there is no me'ilah.

items.text: Objection and resolution
items.text_en: Objection and resolution
