items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the analogy could be reversed, implying me'ilah after atonement, but answers that once a mitzvah is performed, there is no me'ilah. It then questions this principle with the example of terumat hadeshen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: One could reverse the analogy and say that after atonement should be like before atonement, so that there would be me'ilah after atonement as well.
The Gemara rejects the objection: There is no item whose mitzvah has been performed and yet me'ilah applies to it.
The Gemara objects: Is that so? But consider the removal of the ashes (תרומת הדשן), whose mitzvah is performed yet me'ilah applies.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya: two verses coming as one
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya: two verses coming as one
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the laws of Terumat HaDeshen and the priestly garments are two verses that come as one and therefore cannot teach other laws. It then questions this explanation according to Rabbi Dosa, who holds that the garments are usable by a regular priest, and answers that the same principle applies to Terumat HaDeshen and the Eglah Arufah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the laws of תרומת הדשן (removal of the ashes) and priestly garments are two verses that come as one, and therefore do not teach other cases.
The Gemara notes that this explanation works well for the רבנן (Rabbis), who hold that the garments require interment.
The Gemara questions what can be said according to רבי דוסא (Rabbi Dosa), who holds that the garments are fit for a common priest.

The Gemara answers that the same principle applies to תרומת הדשן (removal of the ashes) and עגלה ערופה (the heifer whose neck is broken), which are two verses that come as one and do not teach other cases.

items.text: Objection: What about those who say they do teach?
items.text_en: Objection: What about those who say they do teach?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that this reasoning only works for those who hold that two verses coming as one do not teach, but for those who hold that they do teach, a different answer is needed. It answers that there are two exclusions written: 'vesamo' and 'ha'arufah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous reasoning only works for those who hold that two verses coming as one do not teach, but for those who hold that they do teach, a different answer is needed.
The Gemara answers that there are two exclusions written: 'vesamo' and 'ha'arufah', which limit the halakha to those specific cases.

items.text: The three verses about blood: why are they needed?
items.text_en: The three verses about blood: why are they needed?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why three verses are needed regarding blood. It answers that one excludes notar, one excludes me'ilah, and one excludes tum'ah. However, no verse is needed to exclude piggul, because the Mishnah teaches that anything that has matirin is subject to piggul, and blood itself is a matir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why three verses are needed regarding blood.
The Gemara answers: one verse excludes notar, one excludes me'ilah, and one excludes tum'ah.
The Gemara explains that no verse is needed to exclude piggul, because the Mishnah teaches that anything with matirin is subject to piggul, and blood itself is a matir.

items.text: Mishnah: The order of Yom Kippur services
items.text_en: Mishnah: The order of Yom Kippur services
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all Yom Kippur services must be done in order; if one precedes another, it is invalid. It gives specific rules about the blood of the goat and the bull, and what to do if blood is spilled. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say that one continues from where he stopped.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all Yom Kippur services must be performed in order, and if one precedes another it is invalid.
The Mishnah gives a specific rule: if the blood of the goat was presented before the blood of the bull, one must go back and sprinkle from the goat's blood after the bull's blood.
The Mishnah rules that if the blood was spilled before completing the inner sprinklings, one brings other blood and starts the inner service from the beginning.
The Mishnah extends the same rule to the Sanctuary and the Golden Altar, since each is an independent atonement.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon state that one continues from where he stopped, rather than starting over.

items.text: Gemara: The debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya
items.text_en: Gemara: The debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Yehuda limits the rule of order to inner services in white garments, while outer services in white garments are valid if done out of order. Rabbi Nechemya extends this to all white garments, but excludes golden garments. Rabbi Yochanan says both derive from the same verse: 'VeHayta Zot Lachem LeChukat Olam Achat BaShanah'.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states that all Yom Kippur services must be performed on the seder (in prescribed order), otherwise they are invalid.
Rabbi Yehuda limits the invalidation to inner services performed in white garments; outer services in white garments are valid even if performed out of order.
Rabbi Nechemya extends the stringency to all services in white garments (both inner and outer), but excludes golden-garment services from the order requirement.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that both sages derive their positions from the same verse, 'וְהָיְתָה זֹּאת לָכֶם לְחוּקַּת עוֹלָם אַחַת בַּשָּׁנָה'.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Nechemya
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Nechemya
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yehuda holds that atonement is achieved in a specific place once a year, while Rabbi Nechemya holds that atonement is achieved through specific items once a year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that atonement is achieved in a specific place (the Holy of Holies) once a year, while Rabbi Nechemya holds that atonement is achieved through specific items (the incense and blood) once a year.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's position, noting that the verse does not mention 'place'. It then explains that both derive their views from the words 'zot' and 'achat' in the verse, with Rabbi Yehuda using them to exclude the outer garments and golden garments, and Rabbi Nechemya to exclude golden garments and the remaining blood (shrayim). The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yehuda holds that shrayim may or may not be essential.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's position by asking whether the verse actually mentions 'place'.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives his view from the words 'זֹאת' (this) and 'אַחַת' (one), using one to exclude the outer white garments and the other to exclude the golden garments.

items.text: Baraita on completion of atonement
items.text_en: Baraita on completion of atonement
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda debate the meaning of the verse 'and he shall finish atoning for the Sanctuary'. Rabbi Akiva says that if he atoned, he finished; if not, he did not finish. Rabbi Yehuda argues that the verse should be read as: if he finished, he atoned; if he did not finish, he did not atone, meaning that missing even one application invalidates the service.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse 'וְכִלָּה מִכַּפֵּר' to mean that if atonement was achieved, the service is complete; if not, it is not complete.

Rabbi Yehuda objects to Rabbi Akiva's interpretation, arguing that the verse should have been phrased 'if he completed, he atoned' to indicate that missing any sprinkling invalidates the entire service.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda. Two opinions are given: one says the difference is in the interpretation of the verse, and the other says it is whether the remaining blood (shrayim) is essential.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya, and introduces the opinions of Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

One opinion (Rabbi Yochanan) holds that the difference lies in how they interpret the verses' implications, while the other (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) holds that the difference is whether the remaining blood (שיריים) is indispensable.
The other Amora (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) says the difference is whether the remaining blood (שיריים) is essential (מעכב).

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's statements
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan previously said that Rabbi Nechemya holds like the one who says shrayim is essential, but here he seems to take a different position. This is a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's consistency, noting that elsewhere he stated that Rabbi Nechemya follows the opinion that the remaining blood is indispensable, which contradicts his own position here.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's ruling on the incense and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's ruling on the incense and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that if one scooped the incense before slaughtering the bull, it is invalid. The Gemara suggests this is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, but then resolves that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the need for the inner service is considered like the inner service itself. The Gemara then cites a mishnah that if blood was spilled before completing the inner sprinklings, one brings new blood and starts over from the beginning inside, implying that one does not need to re-scoop the incense, which contradicts the earlier logic.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that if one scooped the incense before slaughtering the bull, it is invalid.
The Gemara questions whether this ruling aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's position, suggesting it does not.
The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the 'חוקה' (statute) applies only to actions performed in white garments inside the Holy of Holies, not to the incense scooping before slaughter.
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the need for the inner service (צורך פנים) is considered like the inner service itself, so the ruling can align with Rabbi Yehuda.

The Gemara cites a mishnah that if blood was spilled before completing the inner sprinklings, one brings new blood and starts over from the beginning inside, implying that one does not need to re-scoop the incense.
The Gemara challenges that if the incense scooping were considered part of the inner service, the mishnah should require re-scooping the incense, which it does not.

items.text: Ulla's ruling on slaughter timing and the baraita's challenge
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on slaughter timing and the baraita's challenge
items.desc_en: Ulla states that if the goat was slaughtered before the bull's blood was presented, it is invalid. The Gemara challenges this from a mishnah that says if goat blood was presented before bull blood, one goes back and presents goat blood after bull blood—implying the slaughter was valid. Ulla resolves by limiting his ruling to the presentations in the Heikhal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous discussion does not deal with the incense.
Ulla rules that if the goat was slaughtered before the presentation of the bull's blood, the slaughter is entirely invalid.

The Gemara challenges Ulla from a mishnah that says if goat blood was presented before bull blood, one goes back and presents goat blood after bull blood—implying the slaughter was valid, so why not require re-slaughter?
Ulla resolves the challenge by limiting his ruling to the presentations in the Heikhal, not the inner sanctuary.
Rabbi Appas similarly limits the ruling to the presentations in the Heikhal.

items.text: Baraita on the atonement of the goat and bull
items.text_en: Baraita on the atonement of the goat and bull
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds verses to show that the bull's blood atones for the priests and the goat's blood for Israel regarding impurity of the Temple. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon debate the scope of atonement: the scapegoat covers other sins for all, while Rabbi Shimon draws parallels between the inner goat and the bull.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds verses to identify the areas atoned by the bull's blood: קודש הקדשים (Holy of Holies), אהל מועד (the Sanctuary), מזבח (the altar), and עזרות (the courtyards).
The baraita continues: the priests, Israel, and Levites are all atoned by the scapegoat for other sins, according to Rabbi Yehuda.

Rabbi Shimon argues that the inner goat's blood atones for Israel's Temple impurity, and the bull's blood for the priests' Temple impurity, while the scapegoat's confession atones for other sins of Israel and the bull's confession for other sins of the priests.

items.text: Baraita on restarting blood applications after spillage
items.text_en: Baraita on restarting blood applications after spillage
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if blood was spilled after partial applications in the Holy of Holies, Heikhal, or altar, one brings new blood and starts over. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon argue that one continues from where he stopped. The baraita details the rules for each location and concludes that after completing the altar applications, all agree the remaining blood does not impede.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'וְכִלָּה מִכַּפֵּר אֶת הַקּוֹדֶשׁ' and interpreting each term to refer to a different location (Holy of Holies, Heikhal, altar), teaching that each location requires its own separate atonement.
The baraita rules that if blood was spilled after partial applications in the Holy of Holies, one brings new blood and starts over from the beginning.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon argue that one continues from where he stopped, not from the beginning.
The baraita rules that if blood was spilled after completing all applications in the Holy of Holies, one brings new blood and starts over in the Heikhal.
The baraita rules that if blood was spilled after partial applications in the Heikhal, one brings new blood and starts over in the Heikhal.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon again argue that one continues from where he stopped.
The baraita rules that if blood was spilled after completing the Heikhal applications, one brings new blood and starts over at the altar.
The baraita rules that if blood was spilled after partial applications at the altar, one brings new blood and starts over at the altar.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon argue that one continues from where he stopped at the altar as well.
The baraita concludes that after completing all altar applications, all agree that the remaining blood does not impede the atonement.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of the dispute's scriptural basis
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of the dispute's scriptural basis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that both sides derive their positions from the verse 'from the blood of the sin-offering of atonements once a year.' Rabbi Meir holds that 'one sin-offering' means only one blood application is required, so restarting is necessary. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold that 'one atonement' means one act of atonement, so continuing is sufficient.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by stating that both sides derive their positions from the same verse: 'from the blood of the sin-offering of atonements once a year'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Meir's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Meir's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Meir holds the verse means 'one sin-offering' — only one blood application is required, so if interrupted one must restart.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold the verse means 'one atonement' — one act of atonement, so continuing from where one stopped is sufficient.

items.text: Rabbi's statement about Rabbi Yaakov's teaching on the log of oil
items.text_en: Rabbi's statement about Rabbi Yaakov's teaching on the log of oil
items.desc_en: Rabbi says Rabbi Yaakov taught him a distinction regarding the log of oil for the leper: if oil was spilled after partial applications, one restarts only in the Heikhal but continues from where he stopped on the fingers. The Gemara questions this, citing a baraita that seems to contradict, and resolves that Rabbi Yaakov taught the rule specifically for the log of oil.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi reports that Rabbi Yaakov taught him a distinction regarding the log of oil for the leper.
The Gemara questions Rabbi's statement by citing a baraita that seems to contradict it regarding the log of oil.

The baraita details the rules for the log of oil: if oil was spilled after partial applications, one restarts in the Heikhal but continues from where he stopped on the fingers, and the finger applications do not impede.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by clarifying that Rabbi Yaakov taught the rule specifically for the log of oil, not for blood.

items.text: Reason why head applications do not impede and a new statement by Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Reason why head applications do not impede and a new statement by Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the head applications of oil do not impede, suggesting a verse about leftover oil. It rejects a parallel to the meal-offering, distinguishing because the verse says 'from the remainder' and 'the leftover.' The daf ends with Rabbi Yochanan beginning a new statement.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that the head applications of oil do not impede the atonement process.

The Gemara asks for the reason, proposing that it might be derived from the verse 'והנותר מן השמן' (the leftover of the oil), and then challenges this by comparing to the meal-offering where a similar phrase would imply non-impediment.
The Gemara distinguishes the case of the meal-offering, noting that there the verse uses both 'מיתר' (from the remainder) and 'והנותר' (the leftover), implying a different rule.
Rabbi Yochanan begins a new statement, shifting the discussion to a new topic.

items.text: Initial dispute about the leper's guilt-offering
items.text_en: Initial dispute about the leper's guilt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon regarding an asham metzora slaughtered not for its own sake. Rabbi Meir holds that one brings another animal and starts from the beginning, while Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold that it has no remedy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of an asham metzora slaughtered not for its own sake and frames it within the dispute of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Meir holds that one must bring another animal and begin the slaughter from the start, applying his general principle to this case.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold that since the sacrifice was invalid from the start, there is no remedy and the animal cannot be replaced.

items.text: Rav Chisda's objection
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's view, citing the verse that says 'oto' (it), implying the same animal must be used, which would require a remedy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects by citing the verse that says 'אותו' (it), implying the asham metzora must be specifically that animal, making the dispute irrelevant.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yochanan and resolution of Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yochanan and resolution of Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's view that the offering requires another asham but is valid for the altar. Rav Chisda explains that 'needs' means it needs but has no remedy, citing a parallel from a Nazirite case where Beit Shammai say 'needs' but it has no remedy.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's view: a leper's guilt-offering slaughtered not for its sake or without blood on the thumbs is offered on the altar with libations, but requires another guilt-offering to make the leper fit.
Rav Chisda explains that 'needs' in the baraita means it needs but has no remedy, reconciling it with his earlier objection.
The Gemara questions whether a tanna would teach 'needs' when it has no remedy.
The Gemara answers yes, citing a parallel from a Nazirite case where Beit Shammai say 'needs' but it has no remedy, as explained by Rabbi Avina.

items.text: Rabbi Pedat's comparison
items.text_en: Rabbi Pedat's comparison
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pedat argues that Beit Shammai and Rabbi Elazar said the same thing: both hold that if a required element is missing, there is no remedy. He cites Rabbi Elazar's ruling about a leper lacking a thumb or big toe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Pedat disagrees with the previous interpretation.
רבי פדת (Rabbi Pedat) states that בית שמאי (Beit Shammai) and רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) said the same thing, referring to the previously mentioned case of the bald nazirite.
רבי פדת (Rabbi Pedat) cites a ברייתא (baraita) regarding רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar)'s ruling that a leper lacking a thumb or big toe has no permanent purification.
רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) says the priest puts the blood on the spot where the thumb was, and the leper fulfills his obligation.
רבי שמעון (Rabbi Shimon) says that if the priest put the blood on the left hand or foot, the leper has fulfilled his obligation.

items.text: Derivation of hand-reception for the leper's asham
items.text_en: Derivation of hand-reception for the leper's asham
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that the blood of the leper's guilt-offering must be received by the priest's hand, not a vessel, for application to the leper. However, for the altar, it is received in a vessel, requiring two priests.

sub.desc_en: The Sages derive from the verse that the taking of the blood is by the kohen's hand, not a vessel.
The Gemara concludes that for the altar, a vessel is required, so two kohanim receive the blood: one by hand for the metzora and one in a vessel for the altar.

items.text: Discussion on the scapegoat and Rava's question
items.text_en: Discussion on the scapegoat and Rava's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about the scapegoat and other goats that are burned, with a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon and the Sages. Rava asks Rav Nachman how many goats are sent, and Rav Nachman responds dismissively.

items.text: Gemara's objection to the previous sugya
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to the previous sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to a previous comparison, arguing that the case of a lost animal is different because there the word "oto" is not written, whereas here it is written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of a lost animal is not comparable because there the word 'אותו' (it) is not written, whereas here it is written.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Papi and Rav Shimi
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Papi and Rav Shimi
items.desc_en: Rav Papi says in the name of Rava that the first goat is sent, while Rav Shimi says in the name of Rava that the last goat is sent. The Gemara explains Rav Shimi's reasoning: since atonement was completed with it. It then suggests that Rav Papi holds like Rabbi Yosi, who says the mitzvah is in the first.

sub.desc_en: It was stated: Rav Pappi in the name of Rava says the first goat is sent, and Rav Shimi in the name of Rava says the last goat is sent.
The Gemara explains Rav Shimi's reasoning: he holds that the last goat is sent because atonement has already been completed with it.
The Gemara asks: what is Rav Pappi's reasoning?
The Gemara answers that Rav Pappi holds like Rabbi Yosei, who says the מצוה (commandment) is fulfilled with the first.

items.text: First possible source for Rabbi Yosi: the barrels
items.text_en: First possible source for Rabbi Yosi: the barrels
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether Rav Papi's view aligns with Rabbi Yosi's statement about the three barrels used for tithing the chamber, where Rabbi Yosi says the first is used first because the mitzvah is in the first. The Gemara rejects this, as that case might be different because the later barrels were not yet available when the first was used.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: which Rabbi Yosei is meant? It first suggests Rabbi Yosei of the baskets, who taught about three baskets for tithing the chamber.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei explains that the letters אב״ג were written to know which basket was tithed first, because the מצוה (commandment) is with the first.
The Gemara rejects this suggestion: perhaps there, when the first basket was available, the later one was not yet available, so it is not analogous.

items.text: Second possible source for Rabbi Yosi: the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Second possible source for Rabbi Yosi: the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Papi holds like Rabbi Yosi's view regarding a Paschal lamb that was lost and then found, where Rabbi Yosi says the mitzvah is in the first, unless the second is superior. This is accepted as the correct source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara instead identifies Rabbi Yosei of the Passover offering, who taught that when one set aside a Paschal lamb and it was lost, then set aside another, and the first was found, the מצוה (commandment) is with the first, but if the second is superior, one brings it.

items.text: Transition to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Transition to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the Mishnah with the phrase "We return to you" regarding the two goats of Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the Mishnah with the phrase 'הדרן עלך הוציאו לו' (we return to you, 'they brought out for him').

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of the two Yom Kippur goats
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of the two Yom Kippur goats
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the two goats must be equal in appearance, height, and value, and purchased together, though if not equal they are still valid. It then discusses the case where one goat dies before or after the lottery, and the procedure for replacing it. Rabbi Yehuda argues that the remaining goat must die.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the ideal requirement that the two Yom Kippur goats be equal in appearance, height, and value, and purchased together, but rules that even if they are not equal or were bought on different days, they are still valid.
The Mishnah states the rule for when one goat dies before the lottery: a new pair is obtained for the remaining goat; if after the lottery, a new pair is brought and the lottery is performed anew.

The Mishnah details the conditional declaration for the new goats and rules that the leftover goat is left to graze until blemished, sold, and its proceeds go to a free-will offering, because a communal sin-offering (חטאת צבור) does not die.
Rabbi Yehuda objects to the Tanna Kamma's ruling and asserts that the leftover goat must die.

items.text: Additional statement of Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Additional statement of Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda adds that if the blood of the goat is spilled, the sent goat must die; if the sent goat dies, the blood must be spilled.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda further states: if the blood was spilled, the sent-away goat dies; if the sent-away goat dies, the blood is spilled.

items.text: Derivation of equality and validity for Yom Kippur goats
items.text_en: Derivation of equality and validity for Yom Kippur goats
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from "שני" that the two goats must be equal, and from the repetition of "שעיר" that they are valid even if not equal. It then questions the source for disqualification if not equal, suggesting that without the repetition one might think they are invalid due to the three occurrences of "שני". The Gemara explains that the three "שני" are used for appearance, height, and value.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse that the two Yom Kippur goats must be equal, but the repetition of 'שָׂעִיר' teaches they are valid even if not equal.
The Gemara asks: without the repetition, from where would we derive that inequality disqualifies the goats (not just invalidates them)?
The Gemara answers: one might have thought the three occurrences of 'שְׁנֵי' teach disqualification.
The Gemara resolves: now that the repetition teaches validity, the three 'שְׁנֵי' are used for appearance, height, and value.

items.text: Parallel derivation for leper's lambs
items.text_en: Parallel derivation for leper's lambs
items.desc_en: A baraita applies the same logic to the two lambs of a leper: "שני" requires equality, and the repetition of "כֶּבֶשׂ" allows validity even if not equal. The Gemara questions the source for disqualification, suggesting that without the repetition one might think they are invalid due to the word "תִּהְיֶה". The word "תִּהְיֶה" is then used for the rest of the leper's process.

sub.desc_en: A baraita applies the same derivation to the leper's two lambs: the word 'כְּבָשִׂים' (lambs) limits to two, 'שְׁנֵי' (two) requires equality, and the repetition of 'כֶּבֶשׂ' (lamb) allows validity even if not equal.
The Gemara questions the source for disqualification if the lambs are not equal, absent the repetition of 'כֶּבֶשׂ'.
The Gemara answers that one might have thought the word 'תִּהְיֶה' (it shall be) implies disqualification if not equal.
Now that the repetition of 'כֶּבֶשׂ' teaches validity, the word 'תִּהְיֶה' is used for the rest of the leper's process.

items.text: Parallel derivation for leper's birds
items.text_en: Parallel derivation for leper's birds
items.desc_en: A baraita applies the same logic to the two birds of a leper: "שתי" requires equality, and the repetition of "ציפור" allows validity even if not equal. The Gemara again questions the source for disqualification, suggesting that without the repetition one might think they are invalid due to the word "תִּהְיֶה". The word "תִּהְיֶה" is then used for the rest of the leper's process.

sub.desc_en: A baraita applies the same logic to the two birds of a leper: the word 'שתי' requires equality, and the repetition of 'ציפור' allows validity even if not equal.
The Gemara questions the source for disqualification if the birds are not equal, suggesting that without the repetition one might think they are invalid due to the word 'תִּהְיֶה'.
The Gemara explains that without the repetition, one might think the word 'תִּהְיֶה' (it shall be) implies invalidity if the birds are not equal.
The Gemara resolves that since the repetition 'ציפור' 'ציפור' already teaches validity, the word 'תִּהְיֶה' is used for the rest of the leper's process (other requirements of his purification).

items.text: Application to daily offerings and resolution
items.text_en: Application to daily offerings and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the same derivation applies to the daily offerings (תמידין), requiring equality. It answers that the word "שניים" there is needed for a different teaching: that the two lambs correspond to the day (one in the morning and one in the afternoon), as derived from a baraita. The baraita explains that the verse "את הכבש אחד תעשה בבקר" already states the obligation of the day, so "שניים ליום" teaches that they are offered corresponding to the day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the same derivation requiring equality applies to the daily offerings (תמידין), and whether it is only a preferred standard (מצוה) or an absolute requirement.
The Gemara answers that the word 'שניים' in the daily offering context is needed for a different teaching, as cited in a baraita.
The baraita explains that the phrase 'שניים ליום' teaches that the two lambs correspond to the day (one in the morning and one in the afternoon), not that they are a single obligation of the day.

The baraita concludes by describing the practical placement of the daily offerings: the morning lamb is slaughtered on the northwest corner at the second ring, and the afternoon lamb on the northeast corner at the second ring.

items.text: Requirement for additional offerings on Shabbat
items.text_en: Requirement for additional offerings on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the additional offerings (מוספין) of Shabbat certainly need to be equal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the additional offerings (מוספין) of Shabbat certainly need to be equal.

items.text: Liability for slaughtering Yom Kippur goats outside the Temple
items.text_en: Liability for slaughtering Yom Kippur goats outside the Temple
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one slaughters the two Yom Kippur goats outside the Temple before the lottery, he is liable for both; after the lottery, he is liable only for the one designated for God and exempt for the scapegoat. Rav Chisda explains that before the lottery, they are fit for the goat offered outside (i.e., a sin-offering brought outside). The Gemara questions why the goat designated for inside is not fit due to lacking the lottery, and Rav Chisda holds that lack of time (מחוסר זמן) is not considered a disqualification within the day.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches the liability for slaughtering the two Yom Kippur goats outside the Temple: before the lottery, liable for both; after the lottery, liable only for the goat designated for God.
Rav Chisda explains that before the lottery, both goats are fit for the goat offered outside (a sin-offering brought outside the Temple).
The Gemara objects: why is the goat for inside not fit due to lacking the lottery, while the goat for outside is also not yet fit because it lacks the day's service?
Rav Chisda holds that lack of time (מחוסר זמן) is not considered a disqualification within the same day, so the goat for outside is fit despite the pending service.

items.text: Ravina's inference regarding Rav Chisda's principle
items.text_en: Ravina's inference regarding Rav Chisda's principle
items.desc_en: Ravina notes that since Rav Chisda considers lacking the lottery as lacking an action, this supports a statement by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: peace-offerings slaughtered before the Temple doors are opened are invalid, based on the verse "ושחטו פתח אהל מועד" — when it is open, not when it is locked.

sub.desc_en: Ravina infers from Rav Chisda's principle (that lacking the lottery counts as lacking an action) that it supports Rav Yehuda's ruling in the name of Shmuel: peace-offerings slaughtered before the Temple doors are opened are invalid, because Scripture says "ושחטו פתח אהל מועד" (and he shall slaughter it at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting) — when it is open, not when it is locked.

items.text: Opening statement: Slaughter before doors open
items.text_en: Opening statement: Slaughter before doors open
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one slaughters the goats (of Yom Kippur) outside before the Heichal doors are opened, he is exempt. The Gemara explains the reason: lacking the opening is considered lacking an action.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one slaughters the Yom Kippur goats outside before the Heichal doors are opened, he is exempt.
The Gemara explains the reason: lacking the opening is considered lacking an action.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Chisda's principle of 'ho'il'
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Chisda's principle of 'ho'il'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Chisda holds the principle of 'ho'il' (since it could have been offered for another purpose). It cites Rav Chisda's ruling that a Paschal lamb slaughtered outside during the rest of the year is exempt if done for its own sake but liable if not for its own sake, and challenges why the exempt case isn't liable based on 'ho'il'. The Gemara answers that the Paschal lamb requires 'akirah' (nullification of its designation), which is not needed here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Chisda holds the principle of 'ho'il' (since it could have been offered for another purpose).
The Gemara cites Rav Chisda's ruling that a Paschal lamb slaughtered outside during the rest of the year is exempt if done for its own sake but liable if not for its own sake.
The Gemara objects that the exempt case (slaughtered for its own sake) should be liable based on 'ho'il' (since it could have been offered for another purpose inside).
The Gemara answers that the Paschal lamb requires 'akirah' (nullification of its designation), which is not needed here.

items.text: Rabba bar Shimi's version and resolution
items.text_en: Rabba bar Shimi's version and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Shimi teaches the above in the name of Rabba, and finds a contradiction in Rabba's own statements. He resolves it as previously explained.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Shimi teaches the above tradition in the name of Rabba, and notes a contradiction between Rabba's own statements.
Rabba bar Shimi resolves the contradiction using the same distinction previously explained.

items.text: Rav Dimi's version: Rabbi Yochanan exempts both cases
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's version: Rabbi Yochanan exempts both cases
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that a Paschal lamb slaughtered outside during the rest of the year is exempt whether for its own sake or not. Rav Dimi questions the latter case, and Rabbi Yirmeya explains that 'akirat chutz' (nullification outside) is not considered a valid nullification.

sub.text: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that a Paschal lamb slaughtered outside during the rest of the year is exempt whether for its own sake or not.
Rav Dimi questions why the case of not for its own sake is exempt, since it is fit for that purpose inside.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that 'akirat chutz' (nullification outside) is not considered a valid nullification.

items.text: Ravin's version: Rabbi Yochanan holds liable in both cases
items.text_en: Ravin's version: Rabbi Yochanan holds liable in both cases
items.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that a Paschal lamb slaughtered outside during the rest of the year is liable whether for its own sake or not. The Gemara challenges this with a Mishnah about those lacking atonement who are exempt for their sin-offerings and guilt-offerings. Rav Chilkiah bar Tovi distinguishes: the Mishnah only exempts when done for its own sake, but for not its own sake it is liable. The Gemara then questions why the exempt case isn't liable based on 'ho'il', and answers that the Paschal lamb during the rest of the year is considered a peace-offering, which does not require 'akirah'.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that a Paschal lamb slaughtered outside during the rest of the year is liable whether for its own sake or not.

The Gemara objects: even for its own sake? But we learned in a Mishnah that those lacking atonement who offer their sin-offerings and guilt-offerings outside are exempt, while their burnt-offerings and peace-offerings are liable.
Rav Chilkiah bar Tovi distinguishes: the Mishnah's exemption applies only when done for its own sake, but for not its own sake one is liable.
The Gemara questions: why is the for-its-own-sake case exempt? Let us apply the principle of 'ho'il' (since it is fit for not-its-own-sake inside).

The Gemara rejects the question: there (in the Mishnah) the offering requires 'akirah' (formal designation change), but here the Paschal lamb during the rest of the year is considered a peace-offering and does not require 'akirah'.

items.text: Rav Ashi and Rav Yirmeya midifti's versions
items.text_en: Rav Ashi and Rav Yirmeya midifti's versions
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi teaches that the ruling is liable, as stated. Rav Yirmeya midifti teaches that it is exempt, reasoning that the Paschal lamb during the rest of the year requires 'akirah', and 'akirat chutz' is not valid. This disagrees with Rav Chilkiah bar Tovi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi teaches that the ruling is liable, as previously stated.

Rav Yirmeya midifti teaches that it is exempt, reasoning that the Paschal lamb during the rest of the year requires עקירה (a formal act of designation), and עקירת חוץ (designation performed outside the Temple) is not valid, disagreeing with Rav Chilkiah bar Tovi.

items.text: Baraita on liability for the goats of Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Baraita on liability for the goats of Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: from the time the lots are cast, one is liable for the goat designated for God but exempt for the goat designated for Azazel. The baraita then quotes the verse from Leviticus about slaughtering outside the camp.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that from the time the lots are cast, one is liable for slaughtering the goat designated for God outside the Temple, but exempt for the goat designated for Azazel.
The rabbis cite a baraita quoting the verse from Leviticus about slaughtering outside the camp, which serves as the scriptural basis for the liability.

items.text: Exclusion of kodshei bedek habayit and scapegoat
items.text_en: Exclusion of kodshei bedek habayit and scapegoat
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that only offerings fit for the Tent of Meeting are liable for slaughter outside; the scapegoat, though fit, is excluded by the word 'laHashem' as it is not uniquely dedicated to God.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that only offerings fit for the Tent of Meeting are liable for slaughter outside, excluding kodshei bedek habayit (consecrated property for Temple maintenance).
The Gemara excludes the scapegoat and the red heifer from liability for slaughter outside, because the word 'לה׳' (to God) requires that the offering be uniquely dedicated to God.

items.text: Contradiction from another verse
items.text_en: Contradiction from another verse
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: elsewhere 'laHashem' includes the scapegoat, not excludes it. The Gemara resolves by context: in the verse about 'isheh', 'laHashem' includes the scapegoat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'laHashem' is meant to exclude, citing a contradictory verse where 'laHashem' includes the scapegoat.
The Gemara resolves by showing that in the context of 'isheh', 'laHashem' includes the scapegoat.

items.text: Rava's resolution by context
items.text_en: Rava's resolution by context
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the same word 'laHashem' functions differently based on context: in the verse about 'el petach' it excludes, in the verse about 'isheh' it includes.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the word 'לה׳' functions differently based on context: in the verse about 'אל פתח' it excludes the scapegoat, while in the verse about 'אשה' it includes the scapegoat.

items.text: Implication for scapegoat's sanctity
items.text_en: Implication for scapegoat's sanctity
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that without Rabbi's derivation, one might think the scapegoat is sanctified even when blemished or time-deficient, but the lottery only determines for what is fit for God.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one could think the scapegoat is sanctified when time-deficient, given that the lottery only determines for what is fit for God.

items.text: Rav Yosef's identification with Chanan HaMitzri and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's identification with Chanan HaMitzri and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef first suggests the mishnah follows Chanan HaMitzri, who allows pairing a scapegoat with blood in a cup, but is rejected because Chanan does not reject the lottery. He then identifies it with Rabbi Shimon, who allows bringing a partner without lottery if one dies.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests the mishnah follows Chanan HaMitzri, who allows pairing a scapegoat with blood in a cup.
The gemara objects that Chanan HaMitzri may still require a lottery, which the mishnah does not.
Rav Yosef revises his identification, stating the mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who allows bringing a partner without lottery if one dies.

items.text: Ravina's alternative: blemish and redemption
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative: blemish and redemption
items.desc_en: Ravina suggests the case is where the scapegoat became blemished and was redeemed onto another animal.

sub.desc_en: Ravina proposes that the case is where the scapegoat became blemished and was redeemed onto another animal.

items.text: Proof that blemish disqualifies scapegoat and necessity of both verses
items.text_en: Proof that blemish disqualifies scapegoat and necessity of both verses
items.desc_en: A baraisa derives from 'isheh' and 'laHashem' that blemished parts and the scapegoat are included. The Gemara explains why both blemish and time-deficiency need to be written: each has a unique leniency the other lacks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we know that a blemish disqualifies the scapegoat?
A baraisa derives from the verse 'וְאִשֶּׁה לֹא תִתְּנוּ מֵהֶם' that blemished parts are excluded, and from 'לַה׳' that the scapegoat is included.
The Gemara explains why both blemish and time-deficiency need to be written: each has a unique leniency the other lacks, so both verses are necessary.

items.text: Rava's example of slaughtering a mother on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Rava's example of slaughtering a mother on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: Rava gives an example of a person who slaughters his mother on Yom Kippur to save a sick person, and the Gemara questions whether this is prohibited, citing the principle that slaughtering an animal in distress is considered valid slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Rava gives an example of a person who slaughters his mother on Yom Kippur to save a sick person.
The Gemara questions whether this case is actually prohibited, arguing that the Torah's prohibition 'לֹא תִשְׁחֲטוּ' (do not slaughter) does not apply because this is not considered valid slaughter.
The Gemara answers by citing the Western tradition that pushing an animal off a cliff is considered valid slaughter.

items.text: Mishnah citation: If the designated goat died
items.text_en: Mishnah citation: If the designated goat died
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that if the goat designated for Azazel died, the second goat in the pair is offered, and the one that ascended the mountain is left to graze.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that if the goat designated for Azazel died, the second goat in the pair is offered, and the one that ascended the mountain is left to graze.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan on the second goat
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan on the second goat
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan dispute which second goat is offered when the first is lost: Rav says the second of the first pair is offered, while Rabbi Yoḥanan says the second of the second pair is offered. The Gemara explains their disagreement is based on whether living animals are subject to rejection (nidḥin).

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the second goat of the first pair is offered, while the second of the second pair is left to graze.
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that the second goat of the first pair is left to graze, while the second of the second pair is offered.
The Gemara explains that the dispute hinges on whether living animals are subject to rejection (נידחין): Rav holds they are not, Rabbi Yoḥanan holds they are.

items.text: Rav's reasoning: analogy to a temporary blemish
items.text_en: Rav's reasoning: analogy to a temporary blemish
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests Rav learns from a time-deficient animal, but rejects it because that animal was never fit. Instead, Rav learns from a temporary blemish, which is derived from the verse 'כִּי מׇשְׁחָתָם בָּהֶם מוּם בָּם' — once the blemish passes, the animal is acceptable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rav's reasoning is, and initially suggests he learns from a time-deficient animal (מחוסר זמן).
The Gemara explains the analogy: just as a time-deficient animal, though currently unfit, becomes fit later, so too here the second animal is not permanently rejected.
The Gemara objects that the cases are not comparable: the time-deficient animal was never fit, whereas here the animal was fit and then rejected (נראה ונדחה).
The Gemara rejects the first analogy and instead says Rav learns from a temporary blemish (בעל מום עובר), which was once fit and then became unfit, yet later becomes fit again.
The Gemara cites the verse 'כִּי מׇשְׁחָתָם בָּהֶם מוּם בָּם' to prove that once the blemish passes, the animal is acceptable.

items.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan's reasoning and Rav's alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan's reasoning and Rav's alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan derives from the same verse that rejected animals remain rejected, while Rav interprets the verse to allow mixing of blemished and unblemished limbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yoḥanan interprets the verse, and answers that he reads 'בָּהֶם' (in them) as excluding all rejected animals, so once rejected they remain rejected.
The Gemara explains that Rav interprets 'בָּהֶם' to mean that blemished animals themselves are not accepted, but through mixtures they are accepted.

items.text: Supporting Mishnah and further analysis
items.text_en: Supporting Mishnah and further analysis
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about mixing perfect and blemished limbs, and discusses the derivation of the word 'בָּהֶם' and 'בָּם' for Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about mixing perfect and blemished limbs, with Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages disputing the procedure.
The Gemara asks how the other opinion (Rabbi Yoḥanan) derives the rule, and answers that he derives it from the words 'בָּם' and 'בָּהֶם', while the other (Rav) does not expound these words.

items.text: Rav's view and the principle of mitzvah in the first
items.text_en: Rav's view and the principle of mitzvah in the first
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav doesn't allow either goat to be offered, and Rava explains that Rav follows Rabbi Yosei's principle that the mitzvah is performed with the first. The Gemara considers two versions of Rabbi Yosei's ruling — from the collection boxes and from the Paschal lamb — and concludes with the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav: even if living animals are not rejected (אינן נדחין), why can't one offer either goat at will?
Rava answers that Rav follows Rabbi Yosei's principle that the mitzvah is performed with the first (מצוה בראשון).
The Gemara asks which specific ruling of Rabbi Yosei is being referenced.
The Gemara proposes Rabbi Yosei's ruling about the collection boxes (קופות), where the first box is used for the mitzvah.
The Gemara objects that the case of the collection boxes is different because the later boxes were not yet available when the first was taken.
The Gemara resolves that the reference is to Rabbi Yosei's ruling about the Paschal lamb (פסח), where both animals are present and Rabbi Yosei rules that the mitzvah is performed with the first.

items.text: Opening Mishnah clause
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah clause
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the second goat was more select than the first, one brings it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if the second goat is more select than the first, one brings it.

items.text: Rava's proof from Mishnah and baraita
items.text_en: Rava's proof from Mishnah and baraita
items.desc_en: Rava asserts that the Mishnah supports Rav (animals are not pushed aside) and the baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan (animals are pushed aside). He cites the Mishnah's ruling that if the goat designated for the Name dies, the one that received the lot for the Name is substituted, and the other remains as is. The baraita questions which 'second' is meant and derives from the verse 'he shall stand alive' that it does not refer to a case where its fellow has already died.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that the Mishnah supports Rav's position and the baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's position, citing the Mishnah's language about the designated goat being replaced.
The baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan by interpreting 'second' as the second in the first pair and deriving from 'יעמוד חי' (shall stand alive) that it must be alive, not already standing.

Rava cites the baraita that questions which 'second' is meant and derives from the verse 'יעמוד חי' (he shall stand alive) that it does not refer to a case where its fellow has already died, supporting Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that if the blood was spilled, the scapegoat must die, and if the scapegoat dies, the blood must be spilled. This is consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's view that animals can be pushed aside, but poses a difficulty for Rav who holds they cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's view that animals cannot be pushed aside (אֵינָן נִדְחִין) by citing Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that if the blood was spilled the scapegoat must die, which seems to require pushing aside.

items.text: Rav's response: limited to Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Rav's response: limited to Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: Rav responds that he was not speaking about Rabbi Yehuda's opinion; he only stated his view according to the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rav clarifies that his earlier statement was limited to the view of the Rabbis (רבנן), not that of Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Counter-challenge: what do Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis dispute according to Rabbi Yochanan?
items.text_en: Counter-challenge: what do Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis dispute according to Rabbi Yochanan?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rav, Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis dispute about the principle of animals being pushed aside. But according to Rabbi Yochanan, what is their dispute? Rava answers that the Mishnah already supports Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted that for Rav the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis is clear, but for Rabbi Yochanan, what is the dispute about?
Rava answers that we already said the Mishnah supports Rav, implying that Rabbi Yochanan's position is not reflected in the Mishnah.

items.text: Further challenge from the rule that a communal sin-offering does not die
items.text_en: Further challenge from the rule that a communal sin-offering does not die
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that a communal sin-offering does not die, implying that an individual's sin-offering in a similar case would die. This is consistent with Rabbi Yochanan's view as explained by Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that a communal sin-offering does not die, implying an individual's sin-offering in such a case does die.
The Gemara asks: granted for Rabbi Yochanan this follows Rabbi Abba's statement in the name of Rav, but what about Rav's own view?

items.text: Rav's position on the lost goat
items.text_en: Rav's position on the lost goat
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rav, the case of a lost goat is like one who sets aside two sin-offerings for liability, where one is offered and the other grazes. Rava clarifies that Rav follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that the mitzvah is performed with the first, so initially it is considered designated for loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that all agree: if atonement was achieved with the non-lost goat, the lost goat dies.
Rava explains that for Rav, the lost goat is like one who sets aside two sin-offerings for liability, where one is offered and the other grazes, as taught by Rabbi Oshaya.
Rava clarifies that Rav follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that the mitzvah is performed with the first, so initially it is considered designated for loss.

items.text: Reconciling Rabbi Yehuda with Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Reconciling Rabbi Yehuda with Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that the second goat dies fits with Rav's view that the second goat of the second pair grazes. It resolves that Rabbi Yehuda refers to the second goat of the first pair, not the second pair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that the second goat dies fits with Rabbi Yochanan's view that the second goat of the first pair grazes, and explains that for Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Yehuda's ruling applies to the second goat of the second pair.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty for Rav by clarifying that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling refers to the second goat of the first pair, not the second pair.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yehuda's additional statement
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yehuda's additional statement
items.desc_en: An alternative challenge is raised from Rabbi Yehuda's statement about the blood being spilled or the goat dying. For Rav, the first and second clauses address different cases, but for Rabbi Yochanan, the word 'further' is problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the challenge, citing Rabbi Yehuda's statement that if the blood is spilled the goat dies, and if the goat dies the blood is spilled.
The Gemara explains that for Rav the first and second clauses of Rabbi Yehuda's statement address different cases, but for Rabbi Yochanan the word 'further' (ועוד) is problematic.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on blood and goat
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on blood and goat
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if the blood is spilled, the goat must die because its mitzvah was not yet performed. But if the goat dies, why should the blood be spilled? The school of Rabbi Yannai answers with a verse: the goat must be alive until the blood of its counterpart is presented.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that if the blood is spilled, the goat sent to Azazel must die.
The Gemara questions why, if the goat dies, the blood should be spilled, since the goat's mitzvah was already performed.
The school of Rabbi Yannai answers with a verse that the goat must remain alive until the blood of its counterpart is presented.

items.text: Mishnah on lost shekels and Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.text_en: Mishnah on lost shekels and Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about townspeople whose shekels were lost; if the terumah was already taken, they swear to the treasurers; otherwise to the townspeople. Rabbi Yehuda says the found shekels count for the next year. Rava explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that obligations of one year can be offered in the next.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about townspeople whose shekels were lost or stolen, detailing the oath and replacement rules, and that found shekels do not count for the next year.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the found shekels do count for the next year, opposing the first anonymous view.
Rava explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: he holds that obligations (חובות) of one year can be offered in the next year.

items.text: Abaye's objection from Yom Kippur offerings
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from Yom Kippur offerings
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's explanation with a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda rules that lost Yom Kippur goats and idolatry goats all die, while Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon say they graze. This contradicts the idea that obligations can be fulfilled in the next year.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that lost Yom Kippur goats and idolatry goats all die, contradicting the idea that obligations can be fulfilled in the next year.
The baraita adds that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon rule that the lost animals graze, since a communal sin-offering never dies.
The gemara marks the end of Abaye's objection with a brief narrative transition indicating that Rava will respond.

items.text: First answer: communal offerings require new funds
items.text_en: First answer: communal offerings require new funds
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially answers that communal offerings must be brought from the new terumah of the year, citing Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya who derives this from the verse 'Zot olat chodesh be'chodsho'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the question concerns communal offerings.

The Gemara answers that communal offerings are different, citing Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya who derives from the verse 'זֹאת עוֹלַת חֹדֶשׁ בְּחׇדְשׁוֹ' that the Torah requires bringing a new offering from the new תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: Objection: the bull is not a communal offering
items.text_en: Objection: the bull is not a communal offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that this explanation works for the goat, but the bull is a personal offering of the High Priest, so a different reason is needed. It proposes a decree that the bull is prohibited because of the goat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous explanation works for the goat but not for the bull, which is a personal offering of the High Priest, and proposes a decree that the bull is prohibited because of the goat.

items.text: Rejection: decree cannot cause death, and the mitzvah is not absolute
items.text_en: Rejection: decree cannot cause death, and the mitzvah is not absolute
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the decree because it would cause the animals to die, which is too severe. Furthermore, the mitzvah to bring from the new is not absolute, as Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says one fulfills the obligation even with old offerings, merely lacking a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a mere decree cannot cause the animals to die.
The Gemara further objects that the mitzvah to bring from the new is not absolute, citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that one fulfills the obligation even with old offerings, merely lacking a mitzvah.

items.text: Second answer: the lot does not determine from year to year
items.text_en: Second answer: the lot does not determine from year to year
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira answers that the lot for the two goats does not determine which is for God and which for Azazel from one year to the next, so they must be purchased in the same year. The Gemara objects that they could simply cast lots, but a decree is made lest people think the lot carries over. The same objection about the bull arises, and the decree is again proposed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira answers that the lot does not determine which goat is for God and which for Azazel from one year to the next, so the goats must be purchased in the same year.
The Gemara objects that they could simply cast lots each year to determine the goats' designations.
The Gemara rejects the objection by decreeing that casting lots is forbidden lest people mistakenly think the lot carries over from year to year.
The Gemara objects that the decree applies only to the goat, but what about the bull, which has no lot?
The Gemara resolves that the decree is extended to the bull because of the goat, to prevent confusion.

items.text: Rejection of decree and third answer: decree due to sin-offering whose owners died
items.text_en: Rejection of decree and third answer: decree due to sin-offering whose owners died
items.desc_en: The Gemara again rejects the decree causing death. The Sages propose before Abaye that the decree is due to a sin-offering whose owners died. The Gemara objects that this works for the bull (which is a sin-offering) but not for the goat (which is not), so a decree is made for the goat because of the bull.

sub.desc_en: The Sages propose before Abaye that the decree causing death is due to a sin-offering whose owners died.
The Gemara objects that this explanation works for the bull (which is a sin-offering) but not for the goat (which is not).
The Sages respond that a decree is made for the goat because of the bull.

items.text: Rejection and fourth answer: decree due to sin-offering whose year passed
items.text_en: Rejection and fourth answer: decree due to sin-offering whose year passed
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the decree again, asking if it would cause death. It then offers a new answer: the decree is due to a sin-offering whose year has passed. The Gemara objects that this is itself the very sin-offering whose year passed, so the decree is circular.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the proposed decree (that the bull would die) is too severe, asking whether animals should die merely due to a decree.
The Gemara offers a new answer: the decree is due to a sin-offering whose year has passed (חטאת שעברה שנתה), which must be left to die.
The Gemara objects that this is circular: the bull itself is the very sin-offering whose year passed, so the decree is not a separate concern but the same issue.

items.text: Resolution: according to Rabbi's definition of a year
items.text_en: Resolution: according to Rabbi's definition of a year
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the circular objection by explaining that the decree applies according to Rabbi, who defines a 'complete year' as 365 days, so the sin-offering's year has not yet passed. The Sages disagree, counting twelve months from day to day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi's definition of a complete year as 365 days, so the sin-offering's year has not passed, while the Sages count twelve months from day to day.

items.text: Gemara's question on the ruling for a pregnant animal
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the ruling for a pregnant animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling that a pregnant animal goes to the seller, and asks about the case of a bull (par) versus a goat (sa'ir). It raises a difficulty: if the concern is a decree (gezeirah) that the bull might be confused with the goat, would that justify letting it die? It then cites Resh Lakish's ruling that a sin-offering that has passed its year is left to graze.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the ruling that a pregnant animal goes to the seller, asking what applies to a bull (par) versus a goat (sa'ir), and suggests a decree (גזירה) that the bull might be confused with the goat.
The Gemara objects that a decree (גזירה) cannot justify letting the animal die.
The Gemara cites Resh Lakish's ruling that a sin-offering (חטאת) that has passed its year is left to graze, not left to die.

items.text: Rava's explanation: a decree due to potential misuse (takalah)
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: a decree due to potential misuse (takalah)
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the concern is a decree due to potential misuse (takalah). He then cites a baraita that in the present time one should not consecrate, vow valuations, or devote property; if one does, the animal is to be 'uprooted' (by locking it in a pen to die), produce and garments are left to rot, and money and metal vessels are thrown into the Dead Sea.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the concern is a decree due to potential misuse (תקלה), and cites a baraita detailing that in the present time one should not consecrate, vow valuations, or devote property; if one does, the animal is to be 'uprooted' by locking it in a pen to die.

items.text: Clarifying the nature of the takalah
items.text_en: Clarifying the nature of the takalah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what kind of takalah is involved: if it is the takalah of offering the animal, then all animals that graze would be subject to the same concern; if it is the takalah of shearing or working the animal, again all grazing animals would be affected. The Gemara answers that the takalah is specifically about offering, and only an animal fit for sacrifice (like this one) causes concern, whereas other animals are not fit for sacrifice and thus not a concern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what kind of takalah (stumbling block) is involved, and objects that if it is the takalah of offering or of shearing/working, then all grazing animals would be subject to the same concern.
The Gemara answers that the takalah is specifically about offering, and only an animal fit for sacrifice causes concern, whereas other animals are not fit for sacrifice and thus not a concern.

items.text: The takalah itself is disputed by Tannaim
items.text_en: The takalah itself is disputed by Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the concern for takalah itself is a dispute among Tannaim, citing two baraitot about a Pesach offering that was not offered in its proper time: one says it may be offered later, the other says it may not. The Gemara initially suggests the dispute is about takalah, but then rejects that, explaining that all agree about takalah and the dispute is between Rabbi and the Rabbis. However, a later baraita about money forces the conclusion that the dispute is indeed about takalah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asserting that the concern for takalah (stumbling block) itself is a dispute among Tannaim.
The Gemara cites a baraita stating that a Pesach offering not brought on its first opportunity may be brought on the second, and if not on the second, it may be brought the following year.
The Gemara cites a second baraita that says the Pesach offering may not be brought later.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute between the two baraitot is about the concern for takalah (stumbling block).

The Gemara rejects the initial suggestion, explaining that all agree about takalah, and the dispute is actually between Rabbi and the Rabbis regarding the rule of a Pesach offering that was not offered in its proper time.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that mentions money as well, implying the dispute is about takalah.
The Gemara concludes that the dispute is indeed about takalah (stumbling block), as the baraita about money forces this conclusion.

items.text: Mishnah: The scapegoat ceremony
items.text_en: Mishnah: The scapegoat ceremony
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest coming to the scapegoat, laying his hands on it, and confessing the sins of the people. The people and priests in the courtyard would bow and say 'Baruch shem kevod malkhuto le'olam va'ed' upon hearing the explicit name of God. The goat is then handed to the one who leads it away; all are fit to lead it, but the priests made it a fixed practice and did not allow Israelites to do so. Rabbi Yose recounts a story where an Israelite named Arsala led it, and a ramp was made for him because Babylonians would pull out his hair.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest approaching the scapegoat, laying hands on it, and confessing the sins of the people, citing the verse from the Torah.

The Mishnah describes the people and priests bowing upon hearing the explicit name of God, and notes that while all are fit to lead the goat, the priests made it a fixed practice and excluded Israelites.
Rabbi Yose recounts a story where an Israelite named Arsala led the goat, and a ramp was made for him because Babylonians would pull out his hair and say 'take and go out'.

items.text: Gemara: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah?
items.text_en: Gemara: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the confession does not mention 'the sons of Aaron, your holy people,' and asks who the Tanna is. Rabbi Yirmeya says it is not Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yehuda holds that the priests have atonement through the scapegoat. Abaye counters that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the priests are included in 'your people Israel.' The Gemara then cites a baraita that expounds the word 'ish' to include a non-priest (zar) and 'itti' for the one who leads the goat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's confession omits 'the sons of Aaron, your holy people,' and asks who the Tanna is.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the Mishnah is not Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yehuda holds that the priests have atonement through the scapegoat.
Abaye objects that even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the priests are included in 'your people Israel.'
The Gemara cites a baraita that expounds the word 'איש' (a man) to include a non-priest (זר) and 'עִתִּי' (the appointed one) for the one who leads the goat.

items.text: Derashot on the verses for the scapegoat
items.text_en: Derashot on the verses for the scapegoat
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the words 'itti' and 'ish' from the verse to teach that the scapegoat can be sent even on Shabbat and even in impurity, and that a non-priest is qualified to send it.

items.text: Carrying a sick goat on Shabbat
items.text_en: Carrying a sick goat on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that 'itti' even on Shabbat means that if the goat is sick, one may carry it on his shoulder. The Gemara notes this disagrees with Rabbi Natan, who holds that a living being carries itself, but distinguishes sickness.

items.text: Rafram's inference about eiruv and hotza'ah
items.text_en: Rafram's inference about eiruv and hotza'ah
items.desc_en: Rafram deduces from the allowance to carry the goat on Shabbat that the laws of eiruv and carrying apply on Shabbat but not on Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: Rafram infers from the allowance to carry the goat on Shabbat that the laws of עירוב (eruv) and הוצאה (carrying out) apply on Shabbat but not on Yom Kippur.

items.text: Sending a defiled goat
items.text_en: Sending a defiled goat
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that 'itti' even in impurity means that if the goat becomes defiled, the sender may enter the Temple courtyard in impurity to send it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the word 'עתי' permits sending the goat even if it becomes defiled, allowing a defiled person to enter the Temple courtyard to send it.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's responses to halakhic questions
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's responses to halakhic questions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer is asked about carrying a sick goat, sending it via another, and killing it if it doesn't die from the push. He gives evasive answers, while the Sages provide direct rulings.

sub.desc_en: The Sages ask Rabbi Eliezer about carrying a sick goat, sending it via another, and killing it if it doesn't die; he responds enigmatically to each.
The Sages provide clear rulings: carry it if sick, send via another if defiled, and go down to kill it if it survives.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's policy of not speaking without tradition
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's policy of not speaking without tradition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer deflects questions about a person's share in the world to come, saving a shepherd or sheep from a lion, and a mamzer's inheritance, because he only says what he heard from his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Sages ask Rabbi Eliezer about a person's fate in the world to come, saving a sheep or shepherd from a lion, and a mamzer's inheritance; he deflects each question.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer's deflection was not mockery but because he never said anything he did not hear from his teacher.

items.text: The wise woman's question and the dispute about the golden calf
items.text_en: The wise woman's question and the dispute about the golden calf
items.desc_en: A wise woman asks Rabbi Eliezer why the punishment for the golden calf varied; he dismisses her. A dispute between Rav and Levi details the punishments for different levels of involvement.

sub.desc_en: A wise woman asks Rabbi Eliezer why the punishment for the Golden Calf was not uniform; he dismisses her with a verse about women's wisdom being in spinning.
One opinion (Rav or Levi) states that those who sacrificed and burned were killed by the sword, those who embraced and kissed died by plague, and those who rejoiced in heart died by dropsy.
The other opinion (Rav or Levi) states that punishment depended on witnesses and warning: with both, death by sword; with witnesses but no warning, death by plague; with neither, death by dropsy.

items.text: The tribe of Levi did not worship the golden calf
items.text_en: The tribe of Levi did not worship the golden calf
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that the tribe of Levi did not participate in the golden calf, citing the verse about Moses at the gate. Ravina's teaching is challenged by the sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba, who interpret the verse about Levi's loyalty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that the tribe of Levi did not worship the Golden Calf, citing the verse where Moses stood at the gate.

sub.text: Sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba's objection
sub.text_en: Sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba's objection
sub.desc_en: The sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba challenge Ravina's teaching by interpreting the verse 'האומר לאביו ולאמו לא ראיתיו' as referring to Levites who did not recognize their maternal grandfather or half-brothers from Israel.

items.text: The identity of the ramp builders and the scapegoat's lament
items.text_en: The identity of the ramp builders and the scapegoat's lament
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana and Rabbi Yehuda say the ramp builders were Alexandrians, not Babylonians. A baraita laments that the scapegoat bears the sins of the generation.

items.text: Mishnah: The escort and sukkot
items.text_en: Mishnah: The escort and sukkot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that dignitaries of Jerusalem would escort the scapegoat to the first sukkah, and there were ten sukkot from Jerusalem to the cliff.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the distinguished men of Jerusalem would accompany the scapegoat to the first booth, and there were ten booths from Jerusalem to the cliff.

items.text: Mishnah: The scapegoat's journey and the crimson thread
items.text_en: Mishnah: The scapegoat's journey and the crimson thread
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the ten sukkot spaced along the route, the provision of food and water, and the escort from sukkah to sukkah except the last. It then details how the crimson thread is split, tied to the rock and the goat's horns, and the goat is pushed backward, dismembering before reaching halfway down the mountain. The time of garment defilement is debated.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the ten sukkot spaced along the route, the provision of food and water, and the escort from sukkah to sukkah except the last.
The Mishnah details how the crimson thread is split, tied to the rock and the goat's horns, and the goat is pushed backward, dismembering before reaching halfway down the mountain.
The Mishnah records the debate about when the garments become defiled, with Rabbi Shimon's opinion that it is from the time of the goat's push off the cliff.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute on the number of sukkot and miles
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute on the number of sukkot and miles
