items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei regarding the number of sukkot and miles. Rabbi Yosei reports that his son Elazar said that with an eruv, even two sukkot and ten miles would suffice.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the Tanna Kamma's position that there were ten sukkot and twelve miles.
Rabbi Yehuda states that there were nine sukkot and ten miles.
Rabbi Yosei says that there were five sukkot and ten miles, all facilitated by an eruv.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei citing his son Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei citing his son Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei reports that his son Elazar said that with an eruv, even two sukkot and ten miles would suffice.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the authority of the Mishnah's last sukkah
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the authority of the Mishnah's last sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which authority holds that the last escort does not accompany the goat to the cliff, and answers that it aligns with Rabbi Meir's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which authority holds the baraita that the last escort does not accompany the goat to the cliff.
The Gemara answers that the baraita aligns with Rabbi Meir's opinion, who holds there were ten sukkot.

items.text: Gemara: The purpose of offering food and water
items.text_en: Gemara: The purpose of offering food and water
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that although no one ever needed the food and water, it was provided to ease the mind of the one who has bread in his basket versus one who does not.

sub.desc_en: A baraita explains that although no one ever needed the food and water, it was provided to ease the mind of the one who has bread in his basket versus one who does not.

items.text: Gemara: Why the thread is split between rock and goat
items.text_en: Gemara: Why the thread is split between rock and goat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the thread is not tied entirely to the rock or entirely between the goat's horns. It answers that if entirely on the rock, the goat might whiten early and cause complacency; if entirely on the horns, the goat might rub its head and forget.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the entire thread was not tied to the rock.
The Gemara answers that if the thread were entirely on the rock, the goat might whiten early and cause complacency.
The Gemara answers that if the thread were entirely between the goat's horns, the goat might rub its head and forget the thread.

items.text: Gemara: Evolution of the crimson thread practice
items.text_en: Gemara: Evolution of the crimson thread practice
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how the thread was initially tied outside the Temple, then inside, and finally split between the rock and the goat to avoid shame. Rabbi Nachum bar Pappa cites Rabbi Elazar HaKappar that the thread would whiten when the goat reached the wilderness, fulfilling the verse about sins becoming white as snow.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts the evolution of the crimson thread practice: initially tied outside the Temple, then inside, and finally split between the rock and the goat to avoid public shame.

sub.text: Rabbi Nachum bar Pappa citing Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Nachum bar Pappa citing Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nachum bar Pappa cites Rabbi Elazar HaKappar that the thread would whiten when the goat reached the wilderness, fulfilling the verse about sins becoming white as snow.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute on the status of the dismembered limbs
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute on the status of the dismembered limbs
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry about whether the limbs of the goat are permitted for benefit. Rav and Shmuel disagree: one permits, the other prohibits. The text begins the opinion of the one who permits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry about whether the dismembered limbs of the goat are permitted for benefit (הנאה), and introduces the dispute between Rav and Shmuel: one permits, the other prohibits.

sub.text: Rav's or Shmuel's position (the one who permits)
sub.text_en: Rav's or Shmuel's position (the one who permits)
sub.desc_en: The text begins to present the opinion of the one who permits the limbs for benefit, though the full reasoning is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Debate on the meaning of "midbar" and "gezeirah"
items.text_en: Debate on the meaning of "midbar" and "gezeirah"
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the dispute between those who interpret "midbar" (wilderness) as permitting the scapegoat to be sent anywhere in the wilderness and those who interpret "gezeirah" (precipice) as requiring a specific cliff. Each side explains how the other's verse is used for other teachings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting the two scriptural bases for the dispute: one side cites 'במדבר' (in the wilderness) and the other cites 'גזירה' (precipice).
The Gemara asks: for the one who says the goat is forbidden (and therefore requires a specific cliff), what does he do with the verse 'במדבר' (in the wilderness)?
The Gemara answers: he uses the verse to include the sanctuaries of Nov, Givon, Shiloh, and the eternal Temple, as taught in a baraita.
The Gemara asks: and the other side (who permits sending anywhere), what does he do with the verse 'גזירה' (precipice)?
The Gemara answers: he uses it for the teaching that 'גזירה' means a cut cliff, and alternatively that it means something that is cut off and falls.

The Gemara adds a third teaching: 'גזירה' teaches that one might think the scapegoat ritual is a meaningless act, but the verse 'אני ה׳' (I am the Lord) declares that God decreed it and one may not question it.

items.text: Rava's ruling on the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava rules in favor of the opinion that the scapegoat is permitted to be sent anywhere in the wilderness, reasoning that the Torah would not command sending the goat to a place that would cause it to fall and create a stumbling block.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the opinion permitting the goat to be sent anywhere in the wilderness is more reasonable, because the Torah would not command 'send' in a way that leads to stumbling.

items.text: Derivations of the name "Azazel"
items.text_en: Derivations of the name "Azazel"
items.desc_en: Two baraitot and a teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael explain the name "Azazel": one says it means a hard and rough place, another says it means the hardest of mountains, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael says it atones for the sin of the angels Uzza and Azael.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita derives the name 'Azazel' from 'עז' (strong) and 'קשה' (hard), and specifies it must be in a rough cliff (צוק) in the wilderness.
The second baraita interprets 'Azazel' as the hardest of mountains, citing a verse about 'אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ' (the mighty of the land).
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that 'Azazel' atones for the sin of the angels Uzza and Azael.

items.text: Distinction between mishpatim and chukkim
items.text_en: Distinction between mishpatim and chukkim
items.desc_en: A baraita distinguishes between mishpatim (rational laws) and chukkim (decrees). Mishpatim include idolatry, forbidden relations, murder, theft, and blasphemy — laws that would be logical even if not written. Chukkim include eating pork, wearing sha'atnez, yibbum chalitzah, purification of a leper, and the scapegoat — laws that the Satan challenges, but God decreed them and one may not question them.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches: 'את משפטי תעשו' (My judgments you shall do) refers to matters that, even if not written, would be logical to write: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, murder, theft, and blasphemy.

The baraita continues: 'את חקותי תשמרו' (My statutes you shall keep) refers to matters that the Satan challenges: eating pig, wearing sha'atnez, halitza of a yevama, purification of a metzora, and the scapegoat; one might think they are meaningless, but the verse 'אני ה׳' declares that God decreed them and one may not question.

items.text: When does the sender of the scapegoat become impure?
items.text_en: When does the sender of the scapegoat become impure?
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the one who sends the scapegoat becomes impure and requires laundering of his garments, but the one who sends the sender does not. Rabbi Yehuda says impurity begins when the goat leaves the wall of Jerusalem; Rabbi Yosei says when it reaches the cliff; Rabbi Shimon says the verse "the sender of the goat to Azazel shall wash his clothes" implies he becomes impure only when he throws it off the cliff.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the one who sends the scapegoat becomes impure and requires laundering, but the one who sends the sender does not.

The baraita raises a possible inference that impurity begins when the goat leaves the Temple courtyard, but rejects it with the verse 'the sender'; then considers that it might only begin when the goat reaches the cliff, but rejects that with the extra 'and the sender'.
Rabbi Yehuda resolves the contradiction: impurity begins when the goat leaves the wall of Jerusalem.
Rabbi Yosei derives from the verse 'עֲזָאזֵל וְכִבֶּס' that impurity begins only when the goat reaches the cliff.

Rabbi Shimon holds that impurity begins only when the goat is thrown off the cliff, as the verse 'וְהַמְשַׁלֵּחַ אֶת הַשָּׂעִיר לַעֲזָאזֵל יְכַבֵּס בְּגָדָיו' implies the act of sending is completed at the cliff.

items.text: Mishnah: Procedure for the bull and goat that are burned
items.text_en: Mishnah: Procedure for the bull and goat that are burned
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for the bull and goat whose blood is brought inside the Holy of Holies: the High Priest tears them open, removes the sacrificial portions, places them on a dish, and burns them on the altar. He then braids them in ropes and takes them to the place of burning. They become impure and require laundering of garments from the time they leave the Temple courtyard; Rabbi Shimon says from the time fire is kindled in the majority of them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes: he comes to the bull and goat that are burned, tears them open, removes their sacrificial portions, places them on a dish, and offers them on the altar.

The Mishnah continues: he plaits them and takes them to the place of burning; from when do they render garments impure? From when they leave the Temple courtyard; Rabbi Shimon says: from when the fire catches in the majority of them.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifications on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifications on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording "and he burned them" (past tense) and corrects it to "to burn them" (future tense). Rabbi Yochanan explains that "braided them in ropes" means like a braid. A baraita teaches that the High Priest did not cut the animals into pieces like a burnt offering, but left the skin on the flesh. Rabbi derives this from a verbal analogy between the word "skin, flesh, and dung" used here and in another context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's past-tense wording 'וְהִקְטִירָן' (and he burned them), noting it is impossible, and corrects it to the future-tense 'לְהַקְטִירָן' (to burn them).
The Gemara completes the correction, specifying that the burning is performed on the altar.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'קְלָעָן בְּמִקְלָעוֹת' (braided them in ropes) means like a braid.
A baraita teaches that the High Priest did not cut the animals into pieces like a burnt offering, but left the skin on the flesh.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this practice.
Rabbi derives the rule from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the words 'עוֹר וּבָשָׂר וָפֶרֶשׁ' (skin, flesh, and dung) used here and in another context.

items.text: Comparison of dismemberment and skinning between the bull and the red heifer
items.text_en: Comparison of dismemberment and skinning between the bull and the red heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as the bull of the High Priest is burned after dismemberment but not after skinning, so too the red heifer must be burned after dismemberment without skinning. It derives this from a verse about the bull, and Rav Pappa explains that the flesh remains with the skin, just as the dung remains in the intestines.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by comparing the bull of the High Priest to the red heifer, arguing that just as the bull is burned after dismemberment (ניתוח) and not after skinning (הפשט), so too the red heifer must be burned after dismemberment without skinning.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְקִרְבּוֹ וּפִרְשׁוֹ וְהוֹצִיא' (and its innards and its dung he shall take out) that the bull is first taken out whole, but then a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from 'ראשו וכרעיו' (its head and its legs) teaches that it is burned after dismemberment.

Rav Pappa resolves the potential objection that the bull might require skinning by explaining that the verse 'וְקִרְבּוֹ וּפִרְשׁוֹ' teaches that just as the dung remains inside the innards, so too the flesh remains with the skin, meaning no skinning is performed.

items.text: When do the garments become impure?
items.text_en: When do the garments become impure?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks from when the garments of those involved in the burning become impure. It cites a baraita that teaches that once the animal is taken outside one camp, it imparts impurity to garments, based on the verse 'outside the camp'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from when the garments of those involved in the burning become impure.
A baraita teaches that once the animal is taken outside one camp, it imparts impurity to garments, based on the verse 'outside the camp'.

items.text: Derivation of three camps for the bull
items.text_en: Derivation of three camps for the bull
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how we know that the bull of the High Priest is burned outside three camps. It cites a baraita that derives from the verse about the bull of the congregation and the verse about the ash that there are three camps: one outside the camp, a second camp, and a third camp.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the bull is burned outside three camps?
The baraita cites the verse 'וְהוֹצִיא אֶת כׇּל הַפָּר' to teach that the bull is taken outside three camps.
The Tanna Kamma derives the three camps from the extra verses about the bull of the congregation and the ash, giving a second and third camp.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's interpretation and the location of burning
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's interpretation and the location of burning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon uses the verse 'outside the camp' to teach that the burning is east of Jerusalem, just as the bull is burned east of Jerusalem. The Rabbis then ask where the red heifer is burned, citing a baraita that questions the location.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon does with the verse 'outside the camp' (מחוץ למחנה) that the Rabbis used for the three-camp derivation.
Rabbi Eliezer's baraita explains that Rabbi Shimon uses the verse for a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) to teach that the burning is east of Jerusalem, just as the bull is burned east of Jerusalem.
The Rabbis ask where the red heifer is burned, citing a baraita that questions the location.
The baraita is cited as the source for the Rabbis' question about the location of the burning.

items.text: Dispute over the burning place of the bull and goat
items.text_en: Dispute over the burning place of the bull and goat
items.desc_en: Rava identifies Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as the one who disagrees with Rabbi Yosei regarding the location of the burning. Abaye questions whether the dispute is only about the place being sloped.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the bull and goat are burned north of Jerusalem, outside three camps; Rabbi Yosei says they are burned at the ash-place.
Rava identifies Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov as the Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Yosei, citing a baraita that interprets the verse 'אֶל שֶׁפֶךְ הַדֶּשֶׁן' to require the place to be sloped.
Abaye objects that perhaps the dispute is only about whether the place must be sloped, not about the location of the burning.

items.text: Who is the 'burner' and when does impurity apply
items.text_en: Who is the 'burner' and when does impurity apply
items.desc_en: The baraita defines who is considered the 'burner' that imparts impurity to garments, and limits the impurity to the time before the flesh becomes ash. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon adds a distinction regarding the flesh being charred.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by defining the 'burner' (השורף) as the one who actively assists during the burning, not the one who kindles the fire or arranges the pyre, and this burner imparts impurity to garments.
The baraita limits the impurity to before the flesh becomes ash, deriving from the word 'אותם' (them) that only the burning process itself, not the ash, imparts impurity to garments.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon adds a distinction: the bull itself imparts impurity, but once the flesh is melted (ניתּך) it no longer imparts impurity to garments.
The gemara asks what practical difference exists between the Tanna Kamma's position and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position.
The gemara resolves that the difference lies in a case where the flesh has been charred (חרוכא) but not yet fully melted into ash.

items.text: Signs that the scapegoat reached the wilderness
items.text_en: Signs that the scapegoat reached the wilderness
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how they knew the scapegoat arrived at the wilderness: people stationed along the way waved cloths. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael offer alternative signs involving distance and a crimson tongue that turns white.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that they told the High Priest that the scapegoat had reached the wilderness, and describes the signal system of waving cloths along the route.
Rabbi Yehuda offers an alternative sign: the known distance of three mil between Jerusalem and Beit Ḥadudo, with the messenger's travel time indicating arrival.

Rabbi Yishmael offers another sign: a crimson tongue tied at the Temple entrance would turn white when the scapegoat reached the wilderness, citing the verse 'if your sins be as scarlet, they shall become white as snow.'

items.text: Abaye's inference from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Abaye's inference from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: Abaye deduces from Rabbi Yehuda's words that Beit Ḥadudo is in the wilderness and that once the goat reaches the wilderness, its mitzvah is fulfilled.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by inferring from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that Beit Ḥadudo is located in the wilderness.
Abaye resolves that Rabbi Yehuda holds that once the goat reaches the wilderness, its mitzvah is fulfilled.

items.text: The High Priest's Torah reading on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: The High Priest's Torah reading on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the High Priest reading from the Torah after the Yom Kippur service, including the order of passing the scroll, the passages read, and the eight blessings recited. It also notes that one cannot see both the reading and the burning of the bull and goat simultaneously due to distance.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the High Priest coming to read the Torah, optionally in his white linen garments or his own white cloak.
The Mishnah describes the chain of passing the Torah scroll from the synagogue attendant to the High Priest, and the passages he reads.
The Mishnah lists the eight blessings recited by the High Priest after the Torah reading.
The Mishnah notes that one cannot see both the High Priest reading and the burning of the bull and goat simultaneously due to distance, not prohibition.

items.text: Gemara: May priestly garments be used for non-service purposes?
items.text_en: Gemara: May priestly garments be used for non-service purposes?
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that reading is not a service, and that priestly garments may be used for benefit. It questions whether this applies to eating and walking, citing a baraita that priests eat the sin-offering for atonement, and concludes that walking might also be permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'in his own white cloak' that reading is not a service (עבודה).
The Gemara asks: from the Mishnah's statement that the High Priest may read in priestly garments, does this imply that priestly garments were permitted for benefit (הנאה)?
The Gemara deflects: perhaps reading is different because it is a need of the service (צורך עבודה).
The Gemara notes that the general question of whether priestly garments are permitted for benefit remains unresolved.
The Gemara brings a baraita: priests did not sleep in sacred garments, implying that eating (but not sleeping) was permitted.
The Gemara deflects again: eating is also a need of the service, as the verse teaches that priests eat the sin-offering and the owners achieve atonement (כפרה).
The Gemara asks: from the baraita, sleeping is forbidden, but walking (הליכה) might be permitted; however, it concludes that walking should also be forbidden.

items.text: Question on using priestly garments for bedding
items.text_en: Question on using priestly garments for bedding
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the mishnah's allowance to spread and fold priestly garments under one's head implies they may be used for benefit. Rav Pappa suggests the text should read 'opposite their heads' rather than 'under their heads', and Rav Mesharshiya infers that tefillin may be placed at the side.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the mishnah's allowance to spread and fold priestly garments under one's head implies they may be used for benefit.
Rav Pappa answers that the mishnah should be read as 'opposite their heads' rather than 'under their heads', avoiding the implication of benefit.
Rav Mesharshiya infers from this that tefillin may be placed at the side, not only on the head.

items.text: Proof that garments are placed opposite the head
items.text_en: Proof that garments are placed opposite the head
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if garments were under the head, one would benefit from kilayim in the belt. It addresses the dispute about the high priest's belt and the general prohibition of kilayim even under bedding, concluding that the garments must be opposite the head.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that it is reasonable that the garments were placed opposite the head, because if under the head, one would violate the prohibition of kilayim due to the high priest's belt (אבנט).

The Gemara objects that this argument works only for the opinion that the high priest's belt is the same as the ordinary priest's belt (containing kilayim), but for the opinion that they differ, what can be said?

The Gemara raises a further objection: one might argue that kilayim is only forbidden in wearing or raising, but spreading under oneself is permitted, yet the rabbis forbade it lest a thread wrap around the flesh.

The Gemara rejects the possibility of an intervening layer by citing Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi quoting the Holy community of Jerusalem that even ten mattresses with kilayim underneath are forbidden to sleep on, concluding that the garments must be opposite the head.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative answer: garments are stiff
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative answer: garments are stiff
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the garments may indeed be under the head, but since priestly garments are stiff, they do not provide the prohibited benefit of kilayim, similar to a hard felt blanket.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that the garments are indeed under their heads, but priestly garments are stiff and therefore do not provide the prohibited benefit of kilayim.

sub.text: Supporting statement of Rav Huna brei d'Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Supporting statement of Rav Huna brei d'Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rabbi Yehoshua supports Rav Ashi by citing that a hard felt blanket (נמטא גמדא דנרש) is permitted for use under one's head despite containing kilayim, because it is stiff.

items.text: Baraita permitting priestly garments in the Temple
items.text_en: Baraita permitting priestly garments in the Temple
items.desc_en: A baraita states that priestly garments are forbidden outside the Temple but permitted in the Temple at all times because they were given for benefit. This supports the earlier conclusion.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited to support the conclusion that priestly garments were given for benefit, stating they are forbidden outside the Temple but permitted inside at all times.

items.text: Story of Shimon HaTzaddik and the Samaritan threat
items.text_en: Story of Shimon HaTzaddik and the Samaritan threat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the prohibition of priestly garments outside the Temple by citing a story where Shimon HaTzaddik wore them to meet Alexander the Great. The Gemara resolves that either the garments were fitting for him or the principle of 'time to act for God' applied.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the ruling that priestly garments are forbidden outside the Temple by citing a baraita about the 25th of Tevet, the day of Mount Gerizim, when mourning is prohibited.

The baraita recounts the story of Shimon HaTzaddik who, to avert the Samaritan plot to destroy the Temple, wore priestly garments and went out to meet Alexander the Great, ultimately saving the Temple.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction with two alternative explanations: either Shimon HaTzaddik was fitting to wear the garments (like a High Priest), or the principle of 'עת לעשות לה׳ הפרו תורתך' (it is time to act for God, they have violated Your Torah) permitted the temporary violation.

items.text: Honor for the high priest in the synagogue
items.text_en: Honor for the high priest in the synagogue
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the synagogue attendant takes the Torah scroll, implying that students honor the rabbi in his presence. Abaye explains that all this is for the honor of the high priest, and the mishnah states that the high priest stands, implying he was sitting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah that the synagogue attendant takes the Torah scroll, implying that students honor the rabbi in his presence.
Abaye explains that all this is for the honor of the high priest.
The Gemara notes that the mishnah states the high priest stands, implying he was sitting.
The Gemara prepares to cite the mishnah that contradicts this implication.

items.text: Sitting in the Courtyard and the Location of Ezra's Reading
items.text_en: Sitting in the Courtyard and the Location of Ezra's Reading
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's rule that only Davidic kings may sit in the courtyard, citing Rav Chisda that David sat in the Women's Courtyard. A baraita is brought about where the Torah was read, with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov saying it was on the Temple Mount, and Rav Chisda again specifies the Women's Courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's rule that only Davidic kings may sit in the courtyard, citing Rav Chisda's explanation that David sat in the Women's Courtyard, and applies the same here.
A baraita is brought about where the Torah was read, with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov saying it was on the Temple Mount, and Rav Chisda again specifies the Women's Courtyard.

items.text: The Meaning of 'Great' in Ezra's Blessing
items.text_en: The Meaning of 'Great' in Ezra's Blessing
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav says 'great' means Ezra pronounced the ineffable Name. Rav Giddel says it refers to the blessing 'Blessed is the Lord... from eternity to eternity.' Abaye questions Rav Dimi, who responds that the ineffable Name is not recited outside the Temple. A contradiction is raised from another verse where Rav Giddel says Ezra used the ineffable Name, and it is resolved that it was a hora'at sha'ah (an emergency ruling).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'great' means in the verse describing Ezra's blessing.
Rav Yosef citing Rav says 'great' means Ezra magnified God by pronouncing the ineffable Name (שם המפורש).
Rav Giddel says 'great' refers to the blessing 'Blessed is the Lord God of Israel from eternity to eternity.'
Abaye questions Rav Dimi, suggesting that perhaps Ezra indeed magnified God with the ineffable Name.
Rav Dimi rejects the possibility, stating that the ineffable Name is not recited outside the Temple (בגבולים).
The Gemara objects by citing another verse where Rav Giddel himself said Ezra used the ineffable Name.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that Ezra's use of the ineffable Name was a הוראת שעה (an emergency ruling).

items.text: The Cry Against the Evil Inclination and the Seal of Truth
items.text_en: The Cry Against the Evil Inclination and the Seal of Truth
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what the people cried out when they gathered: they lamented that the evil inclination for idolatry destroyed the Temple and exiled Israel, and they rejected it. A note fell from heaven with the word 'Emet' (Truth). Rav Chanina deduces that God's seal is Truth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the people cried out when they gathered.
Rav (or Rabbi Yochanan) reports that the people lamented the evil inclination for idolatry destroyed the Temple and exiled Israel, and they rejected both it and its reward.
A note fell from heaven with the word 'Emet' (Truth) written on it.
Rav Chanina deduces from this that God's seal is Truth (אמת).

items.text: Capturing and Neutralizing the Evil Inclination for Idolatry
items.text_en: Capturing and Neutralizing the Evil Inclination for Idolatry
items.desc_en: The people fasted and the evil inclination emerged as a fiery lion cub from the Holy of Holies. A prophet identified it as the evil inclination for idolatry. They captured it, but a hair fell out and its roar was heard far away. They sealed it in a lead pot with lead cover to muffle its sound. They prayed to be given the evil inclination for sin, and it was handed over. They were warned that killing it would destroy the world. They imprisoned it for three days, causing a shortage of fresh eggs. They ultimately blinded it and released it, which prevented it from inciting close relatives.

sub.desc_en: The people fasted for three days and three nights, and the evil inclination for idolatry emerged from the Holy of Holies as a fiery lion cub, identified by a prophet.
When they captured it, a hair fell out and its roar was heard 400 parasangs away; the prophet instructed them to seal it in a lead pot with a lead cover to muffle the sound, citing a verse.
The sages, seeing it was a time of favor, prayed to be given the evil inclination for sin, and it was handed over to them.

The prophet warned that killing it would destroy the world; they imprisoned it for three days, causing a shortage of fresh eggs, then blinded it and released it, preventing it from inciting close relatives.

items.text: The Men of the Great Assembly Restoring the Crown of God's Attributes
items.text_en: The Men of the Great Assembly Restoring the Crown of God's Attributes
items.desc_en: In the West, Rav Giddel and Rav Mattana dispute the meaning of 'great'. Rav Mattana's view is linked to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who explains why the Men of the Great Assembly are so named: they restored the crown of God's attributes. Moses said 'great, mighty, and awesome'; Jeremiah omitted 'awesome' because nations destroyed the Temple; Daniel omitted 'mighty' because nations enslaved Israel. But the Men of the Assembly said: on the contrary, His might is in restraining His anger, and His awesomeness is that one nation survives among many. The Gemara asks how they could uproot Moses' enactment, and Rabbi Elazar answers that because they knew God is true, they did not lie about Him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that in the West they teach two interpretations of 'great' in the verse: Rav Giddel says Ezra magnified God with the explicit name, and Rav Mattana says it refers to the attributes 'the great, the mighty, and the awesome'.

The Gemara links Rav Mattana's view to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who explains why the Men of the Great Assembly are so named: they restored the crown of God's attributes, which Moses had originally stated as 'great, mighty, and awesome', but Jeremiah omitted 'awesome' and Daniel omitted 'mighty'.
The Men of the Great Assembly restored the attributes by reinterpreting God's might as His restraint of anger and His awesomeness as the survival of one nation among many.
The Gemara objects: how could the Men of the Great Assembly uproot an enactment established by Moses?
Rabbi Elazar resolves the objection: because the Men of the Great Assembly knew that God is true, they did not lie about Him, so their reinterpretation is valid.

items.text: Rules for Skipping Verses in Torah and Prophets Readings
items.text_en: Rules for Skipping Verses in Torah and Prophets Readings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the reader skips from 'Acharei Mot' to 'Ach Be'Asor'. A contradiction is raised: one may skip in the Prophets but not in the Torah. Abaye resolves that the Mishnah allows skipping only to allow the translator to pause, while the baraita prohibits skipping when the translator does not pause. Another baraita clarifies that one may skip within the same topic in the Torah, and within two topics in the Prophets, but not from one prophet to another, except in the Twelve Minor Prophets.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the reader skips from 'Acharei Mot' to 'Ach Be'Asor'.
The gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita permits skipping in the Prophets but not in the Torah.
The gemara resolves: the Mishnah allows skipping only when the translator pauses, while the baraita prohibits skipping when the translator does not pause.
The gemara objects: the baraita itself states that one may skip in the Prophets only as long as the translator does not pause, but in the Torah one may not skip at all.
Abaye resolves: the Mishnah allows skipping within the same topic, while the baraita prohibits skipping between two different topics.
A baraita supports Abaye: one may skip in the Torah within the same topic, in the Prophets within two topics, but not from one prophet to another except in the Twelve Minor Prophets.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The High Priest reads from the Torah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The High Priest reads from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the High Priest reads from the Torah on Yom Kippur, but he may not skip from the end of the book to the beginning. He rolls the Torah scroll to avoid disrespect.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that the High Priest may not skip from the end of the Torah scroll to the beginning, and he rolls the scroll to avoid casting aspersions on the Torah.

items.text: Gemara: Why read the passage from Numbers by heart?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why read the passage from Numbers by heart?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the passage from the book of Numbers is recited by heart rather than read from a scroll. Rav Sheshet explains it is because one does not roll a Torah scroll in public due to the honor of the congregation. Alternative reasons are given: the shame of the first scroll and an unnecessary blessing. The Gemara then addresses a challenge from a case where multiple scrolls are used.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the passage from the book of Numbers is recited by heart rather than read from a scroll.
Rav Sheshet answers that one does not roll a Torah scroll in public due to the honor of the congregation.
The Gemara objects that they could bring another scroll and read from it.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda answers that it is due to the shame of the first scroll.
Reish Lakish answers that it is due to an unnecessary blessing.
The Gemara objects that we do not worry about shame, citing Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's case where three Torah scrolls are brought on Rosh Chodesh Tevet that falls on Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves that three people reading from three scrolls has no shame, but one person reading from two scrolls does have shame.

items.text: The blessings recited by the High Priest
items.text_en: The blessings recited by the High Priest
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the eight blessings recited by the High Priest after the Torah reading: on the Torah, the service, the thanksgiving, the forgiveness of sin, the Temple, the priests, Israel, and the rest of the prayer. Another baraita details the content of the concluding prayer and notes that each person then brings a Torah scroll from home to show their strength in public.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the eight blessings the High Priest recites after the Torah reading: on the Torah, the service, the thanksgiving, the forgiveness of sin, the Temple, the priests, Israel, and the rest of the prayer.
Another baraita details the content of the concluding prayer and notes that each person then brings a Torah scroll from home to show their strength in public.

items.text: Why the High Priest reads first
items.text_en: Why the High Priest reads first
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the High Priest reads first not because he is not permitted to read later, but to avoid the principle of not passing over a mitzvah, as stated by Reish Lakish. The mitzvah here is the honor of the many.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's statement that the High Priest may read from the Torah is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that one may pass over a mitzvah, contrary to Reish Lakish's principle, because of the honor of the congregation.
The Gemara explains that the statement is necessary because one might have thought otherwise due to Reish Lakish's principle.
Reish Lakish states the principle that one does not pass over a mitzvah.
The Gemara identifies the mitzvah as the honor of the many, based on the verse 'בְּרׇב עָם הַדְרַת מֶלֶךְ' (in a multitude of people is the king's glory), and concludes that the mishnah teaches this.

items.text: Mishnah: The order of the High Priest's service and offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: The order of the High Priest's service and offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the sequence of the High Priest's service: he reads in linen garments, then changes, offers the ram of the High Priest and the ram of the people, and the seven lambs. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva disagree on when these offerings are brought relative to the daily offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins describing the High Priest's service: if he reads in linen garments, he sanctifies his hands and feet, removes, immerses, dries, dons gold garments, and sanctifies again.
Rabbi Eliezer states that the High Priest then goes out and offers his ram, the people's ram, and seven unblemished year-old lambs.
Rabbi Akiva says that these offerings were brought with the morning daily offering, while the bull for the burnt offering and the goat done outside were brought with the afternoon daily offering.
The Mishnah continues: he sanctifies his hands and feet, removes, immerses, ascends, and dries.
They bring him white garments, he dons them, sanctifies, enters to remove the ladle and fire-pan, then sanctifies again, removes, immerses, ascends, and dries.
They bring him gold garments, he dons them, sanctifies, enters to burn the afternoon incense and trim the lamps, then sanctifies again, removes, immerses, ascends, and dries.
They bring him his own garments, he dons them, and they escort him home; he would make a festive day for his friends when he left the sanctuary in peace.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the precise meaning of Rabbi Akiva's statement: whether all offerings are with the morning tamid or only some. It raises difficulties regarding the timing of the bull and the portions of the sin-offering. Rava resolves the issue by citing the baraita of the school of Shmuel for Rabbi Eliezer and the Tosefta for Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a query about the precise meaning of Rabbi Akiva's statement: whether the bull and the goat are both with the morning tamid or only the bull.
The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Eliezer, who left the bull for the afternoon, when is it actually offered?
The Gemara asks: according to both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva, when are the portions of the sin-offering (אימורי חטאת) offered?
Rava resolves the difficulties by stating that the only consistent explanation is either the baraita of the school of Shmuel for Rabbi Eliezer or the Tosefta for Rabbi Akiva.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The baraita of the school of Shmuel clarifies Rabbi Eliezer's position: the ram, the ram of the people, and the portions of the sin-offering are offered in the morning, while the bull, the seven lambs, and the goat are with the afternoon tamid.

The Tosefta clarifies Rabbi Akiva's position: the bull and the seven lambs are offered with the morning tamid, as the verse states 'apart from the morning burnt-offering,' and afterward the service of the day.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the order of offerings after the goat: the outer goat, then the ram of the people, then the fats of the sin-offering, then the afternoon tamid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the order of offerings after the goat: the outer goat, then the ram of the people, then the fats of the sin-offering, then the afternoon tamid.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: he follows the order of the Torah portions, doing the offerings from Torat Kohanim first, then those from Chumash HaPekudim. Rabbi Akiva, citing the verse 'besides the morning burnt-offering,' holds that the additional offerings are done with the morning tamid. The Gemara then asks what Rabbi Eliezer does with the verse 'besides the sin-offering of atonement,' and answers that it teaches that the outer goat atones for what the inner goat atones for.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning for his order of the additional offerings.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer follows the written order, performing the offerings from Torat Kohanim first and then those from Chumash HaPekudim.
The Gemara states that Rabbi Akiva, citing the verse 'besides the morning burnt-offering,' holds that the additional offerings are performed with the morning tamid.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer does with the verse 'besides the sin-offering of atonement.'
The Gemara answers that the verse teaches that the outer goat atones for what the inner goat atones for.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's opinions
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's opinions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says in Rabbi Eliezer's name that one lamb is offered with the morning tamid and six with the afternoon tamid. Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon says in his name that six are offered with the morning tamid and one with the afternoon tamid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states in Rabbi Eliezer's name that one lamb is offered with the morning tamid and six with the afternoon tamid.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon states in Rabbi Eliezer's name that six lambs are offered with the morning tamid and one with the afternoon tamid.

items.text: Reason for the Sages' dispute
items.text_en: Reason for the Sages' dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages derive from two verses: 'besides the morning burnt-offering' and 'and he shall go out and make his burnt-offering,' so they place some lambs here and some there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason of the Sages, and answers that they derive from two verses, placing some lambs here and some there.

items.text: Reason for the difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Reason for the difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda holds that one lamb is done first with the morning tamid, then the service of the day, lest the High Priest become weak. Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon holds that once he begins, he does six, lest he procrastinate, but regarding the service of the day he is diligent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the point of dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that one lamb is offered with the morning tamid first, then the service of the day, lest the High Priest become weak.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon holds that once he begins, he does six lambs with the morning tamid, lest he procrastinate, but regarding the service of the day he is diligent.

items.text: Dispute about the number of rams
items.text_en: Dispute about the number of rams
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that all agree there is one ram, following Rabbi's view that the ram mentioned here is the same as in Chumash HaPekudim. Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon holds there are two rams. The Gemara explains their scriptural proofs: Rabbi learns from 'one,' while Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon interprets 'one' as the choicest of the flock. Rabbi derives further from 'the choice of your vows,' and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between a vow and a freewill offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that all agree there is one ram, following Rabbi's view.
The baraita cites Rabbi's position that the ram mentioned here is the same as in Chumash HaPekudim, and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's position that there are two rams.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi's scriptural proof, and answers that he derives it from the word 'אחד' (one).
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon interprets 'אחד', and answers that he interprets it as the choicest of the flock.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi derives the choiceness requirement, and answers that he derives it from the verse 'מבחר נדריך' (the choice of your vows).
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between a vow and a freewill offering, and both interpretations are necessary.

items.text: Beginning of a new topic: sanctification of hands and feet
items.text_en: Beginning of a new topic: sanctification of hands and feet
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the High Priest sanctifies his hands and feet. The Gemara begins a baraita explaining the verse 'And Aaron shall come into the Tent of Meeting' — why does he come? To remove the ladle and the censer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the High Priest sanctifies his hands and feet, and the Gemara introduces a baraita explaining that Aaron enters the Tent of Meeting to remove the ladle and censer.

items.text: The anomaly of the verse's placement
items.text_en: The anomaly of the verse's placement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the entire passage is said in order except for one verse. Rav Chisda explains that there is a tradition of five immersions and ten sanctifications, and if the verse were in order, only three immersions and six sanctifications would be found.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the entire passage is said in order except for one verse.
Rav Chisda explains that there is a tradition of five immersions and ten sanctifications, and if the verse were in order, only three immersions and six sanctifications would be found.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that perhaps the High Priest interrupts the sequence with the scapegoat ceremony. Abaye answers that the verse 'and he shall go out and make his burnt offering' indicates that from the first exit he performs the ram and the ram of the people.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that perhaps the High Priest interrupts the sequence with the scapegoat ceremony performed outside.
Abaye answers that the verse 'וְיָצָא וְעָשָׂה אֶת עוֹלָתוֹ' (and he shall go out and make his burnt offering) indicates that from the first exit he performs his ram and the ram of the people.

items.text: Rava's alternative proof and Rabba bar Rav Sheila's objection
items.text_en: Rava's alternative proof and Rabba bar Rav Sheila's objection
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different proof from the verse 'and he shall remove the linen garments' which says 'which he had worn', implying he had already worn them. Rabba bar Rav Sheila objects that perhaps the scapegoat interrupts, but the verse 'and he shall go out and make' shows it does not.

sub.desc_en: Rava offers a different proof from the verse 'וּפָשַׁט אֶת בִּגְדֵי הַבָּד' (and he shall remove the linen garments), arguing that the superfluous phrase 'אֲשֶׁר לָבַשׁ' (which he had worn) implies he had already worn them, thus proving the sequence.
Rabba bar Rav Sheila objects that perhaps the scapegoat interrupts the sequence, but the verse 'וְיָצָא וְעָשָׂה' (and he shall go out and make) shows it does not.

items.text: A contradiction from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: A contradiction from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the verses mention burning the fat of the sin-offering before the bull and goat, but the Mishnah says one who sees the High Priest reading does not see the bull and goat being burned. The Gemara suggests the exception applies from this verse onward, and Abaye provides a proof from the verses about the sender and burner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the verses mention burning the fat of the sin-offering before the bull and goat, but the Mishnah says one who sees the High Priest reading does not see the bull and goat being burned.
The Gemara suggests that the exception applies from this verse onward, resolving the contradiction.
The Gemara objects: why reinterpret the verses rather than reinterpret the Mishnah?
Abaye provides a proof from the verses about the sender and burner, showing that the burning occurs at the outset.
The Gemara counters: one could argue the opposite — just as the burner acts now, so too the sender acts now.

Rava resolves the issue by citing the verse 'יעמוד חי' (he shall stand alive), indicating that the goat must stand alive only until the time of atonement, which is the blood application, and no further.

items.text: Debate on the order of the sender and burner
items.text_en: Debate on the order of the sender and burner
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that just as the sender is from the beginning, so too the burner is from the beginning. The Gemara objects that perhaps the opposite is true. Rava explains that the verse 'he shall stand alive' indicates the goat must be alive until the time of atonement, which is at the blood presentation.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues from the verse that just as the sender (משלח) is from the beginning, so too the burner (שורף) is from the beginning.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the opposite inference is correct: just as the burner is now (after the fact), so too the sender is now.
Rava resolves by citing the verse 'יעמוד חי' (he shall stand alive), teaching that the goat must be alive until the time of atonement, which is at the blood presentation, and no further.

items.text: The messenger's report and Rabba's farewell blessing
items.text_en: The messenger's report and Rabba's farewell blessing
items.desc_en: The messenger who sends the scapegoat meets the High Priest and reports that the mission was accomplished. Rabba relates that when the rabbis in Pumpedita parted, they would bless each other with a formula invoking the 'Life of lives'.

sub.desc_en: The messenger who sends the scapegoat meets the High Priest in the market or at home and reports that the mission was accomplished.
Rabba relates that when the rabbis in Pumpedita parted, they would bless each other with a formula invoking the 'Life of lives'.

items.text: Expositions on verses about life and Torah scholars
items.text_en: Expositions on verses about life and Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets 'I will walk before the Lord in the lands of the living' as referring to the marketplace. Rabbi Elazar explains that 'length of days and years of life' refers to years that change from bad to good. Rabbi Berechya identifies 'men' in Proverbs as Torah scholars who are like women but act with valor, and advises marrying a scholar's daughter to ensure Torah continuity.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets the verse 'I will walk before the Lord in the lands of the living' as referring to the marketplace.
The gemara questions the verse 'length of days and years of life', asking whether there are years of life and years that are not of life.
Rabbi Elazar explains that these are years that change for a person from bad to good.
Rabbi Berechya identifies 'men' in Proverbs as Torah scholars who are like women but act with valor.
Rabbi Berechya advises that one who wishes to pour wine on the altar should fill the throats of Torah scholars with wine, citing the verse.
Rabbi Berechya advises that if one sees Torah ceasing from his offspring, he should marry a Torah scholar's daughter, citing the verse.

items.text: Story of the High Priest and Shemayah and Avtalyon
items.text_en: Story of the High Priest and Shemayah and Avtalyon
items.desc_en: A story is told about a High Priest who left the Temple and was followed by the people until they saw Shemayah and Avtalyon, whom they then followed. The High Priest later greeted them sarcastically as 'children of nations,' and they responded that they are children of nations who do the work of Aaron, while he, a son of Aaron, does not.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that a High Priest left the Temple and the people followed him until they saw Shemayah and Avtalyon, whom they then followed instead.
The High Priest sarcastically greets Shemayah and Avtalyon as 'children of nations,' implying they are not of priestly lineage.
Shemayah and Avtalyon respond that they, though 'children of nations,' perform the deeds of Aaron, while the High Priest, a son of Aaron, does not.

items.text: Mishnah: Garments of the High Priest and Ordinary Priest
items.text_en: Mishnah: Garments of the High Priest and Ordinary Priest
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the High Priest serves in eight garments, while an ordinary priest serves in four: tunic, pants, turban, and sash. The High Priest adds the breastplate, ephod, robe, and forehead-plate. These are used for inquiry via the Urim and Thummim, which is only done for a king, the head of the court, or one whom the community needs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the eight garments of the High Priest and the four of an ordinary priest, and states that the Urim and Thummim are consulted only for a king, the head of the court, or one whom the community needs.

items.text: Baraita: Number of Threads in Garments
items.text_en: Baraita: Number of Threads in Garments
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that items made of 'shesh' have six-ply threads, 'mushzar' has eight, the robe has twelve, the curtain has twenty-four, and the breastplate and ephod have twenty-eight.

sub.desc_en: The baraita enumerates the number of threads for each garment: six for 'shesh', eight for 'mushzar', twelve for the robe, twenty-four for the curtain, and twenty-eight for the breastplate and ephod.

items.text: Derivation of Six-Ply Threads and Identification of Shesh as Linen
items.text_en: Derivation of Six-Ply Threads and Identification of Shesh as Linen
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that 'shesh' means six-ply from five verses. It then questions how we know 'shesh' is linen, with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina citing a verse using 'bad' (linen). Ravina brings a proof from Ezekiel. Rav Ashi challenges this, but the Gemara resolves that it is a tradition supported by Ezekiel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that each thread is six-ply, and explains that five verses teach five points: linen, six-ply, twisted, other garments, and indispensability.

The Gemara asks how we know that 'shesh' means linen; Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains from the word 'bad' (linen), and replies to a potential objection that flax also splinters, but only when beaten.
Ravina brings a proof from Ezekiel's verse that explicitly says 'פשתים' (linen) for the headdress and trousers.
Rav Ashi objects that before Ezekiel came, who said that 'shesh' means linen?

The Gemara resolves by citing Rav Chisda's principle that such traditions were received from Moses and Ezekiel merely anchored them in verses; the same applies here, so Ezekiel's use confirms a prior tradition.

items.text: Derivation of Eight-Ply for Mushzar and the Robe
items.text_en: Derivation of Eight-Ply for Mushzar and the Robe
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that 'mushzar' means eight-ply by comparing the robe's 'mushzar' to the curtain's 'mushzar' (twenty-four threads, so each of the three colors is eight). It rejects a derivation from the breastplate and ephod, and instead uses a logical argument from the sash. Rav Mari and Rav Ashi offer alternative derivations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that 'מׇשְׁזָר' (twisted) means eight-ply, and answers by deriving from the curtain (פָּרוֹכֶת) via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) that the robe's twenty-four threads yield eight per color.

The Gemara objects that one could derive from the breastplate and ephod (twenty-eight threads) instead, but counters that the robe is a garment without gold, unlike the breastplate and ephod which have gold, and the curtain is an tent, not a garment.
The Gemara resolves that we derive from the sash (אַבְנֵט), which is a garment without gold, and we do not derive from something without gold to something with gold.
Rav Mari offers an alternative derivation: the verse says 'תַּעֲשֶׂנּוּ' (you shall make it), implying that the robe's threads are made for it alone, not for another garment.
Rav Ashi offers another derivation: the verse 'וְעָשִׂיתָ' (and you shall make) teaches that all the robe's threads must be equal, leading to eight-ply per color.

items.text: Derivation of Twelve-Ply for the Robe
items.text_en: Derivation of Twelve-Ply for the Robe
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to derive that the robe has twelve-ply threads from a verse, but the segment is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that the robe (מעיל) has twelve-ply threads, citing the verse 'וְעָשִׂיתָ אֶת מְעִיל הָאֵפוֹד' as the beginning of the derivation.

items.text: Deriving the number of threads in the robe from the parochet
items.text_en: Deriving the number of threads in the robe from the parochet
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the robe (me'il) has six threads, like the parochet, via a verbal analogy on 'techelet'. It rejects a derivation from the ephod's bells and pomegranates (eight threads) because one derives a garment from a garment, not from an ornament. An alternative argument that one should derive the robe from itself (the ephod) is dismissed, as the robe is not included in the 'six' mentioned for other garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the robe (me'il) has six threads, like the parochet, via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'techelet'.
An objection proposes deriving the robe from its bells and pomegranates, which have eight threads.
The Gemara rejects the objection: one derives a garment from a garment, not from an ornament, and the robe is not included in the 'six' mentioned for other garments.

items.text: The parochet has 24 threads
items.text_en: The parochet has 24 threads
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the parochet has 24 threads, calculated as four times six (the six threads of each of the four colors). It dismisses this as obvious and not needing further discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the parochet has twenty-four threads (four of each of six colors), and this is a settled matter beyond dispute.

items.text: Deriving the 28 threads of the choshen and ephod
items.text_en: Deriving the 28 threads of the choshen and ephod
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the choshen and ephod have 28 threads: 24 from the four colors (six each) plus four for gold. It then questions whether gold also has six threads. Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers from the verse 'and he cut threads' that there are four gold threads. Rav Ashi answers from the verse 'to make within the techelet and within the argaman' that the gold threads are made of two threads each, but the total must be equal in all the work.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that the choshen and ephod have 28 threads, and calculates 24 from four colors (six each) plus four for gold.
The Gemara objects that perhaps gold also has six threads, like the other colors.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers from the verse 'וְקִצֵּץ פְּתִילִים' (and he cut threads) that the word 'פְּתִילִים' (threads) in the plural indicates four gold threads.

Rav Ashi answers from the verse 'לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּתוֹךְ הַתְּכֵלֶת וּבְתוֹךְ הָאַרְגָּמָן' (to make within the techelet and within the argaman) that the gold threads are made of two threads each, but the total must be equal in all the work, yielding four gold threads.

items.text: Prohibition against tearing priestly garments
items.text_en: Prohibition against tearing priestly garments
items.desc_en: Rachava quoting Rav Yehuda states that one who tears priestly garments is liable, based on the verse 'lo yikara' (it shall not be torn). Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that perhaps the verse means to make a hem so it won't tear, but the Gemara notes that the verse does not say 'shelo yikara' (so that it not be torn).

sub.desc_en: Rachba says in the name of Rav Yehuda that one who tears priestly garments is liable to lashes, as it is stated 'lo yikare'a' (it shall not be torn).
Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects: perhaps the verse merely instructs to make a hem so it won't tear, not to prohibit tearing; the verse does not say 'so that it not be torn'.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that the verse does not say 'שֶׁלֹּא יִקָּרֵעַ' (so that it not be torn), but rather 'לֹא יִקָּרֵעַ' (it shall not be torn), implying a prohibition.

items.text: Prohibition against removing the choshen and ark poles
items.text_en: Prohibition against removing the choshen and ark poles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that one who removes the choshen from the ephod or removes the ark's poles is liable, based on the verses 'lo yizach' and 'lo yasuru'. Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that perhaps the verses mean to secure them properly so they don't move, but the Gemara notes that the verses do not say 'shelo yizach' or 'shelo yasuru'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that one who removes the choshen from the ephod or removes the poles of the Ark is liable to lashes, based on the verses 'lo yizach' and 'lo yasuru'.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects: perhaps the verses merely instruct to secure them properly so they do not slip, not to prohibit removal; the verses do not say 'so that they not slip'.

The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the verses do not say 'שלא יזח' or 'שלא יסורו' (so that they do not move), but rather 'לֹא יִזַּח' and 'לָא יָסוּרוּ' (they shall not move), which implies a prohibition.

items.text: Reconciling verses about the ark's poles
items.text_en: Reconciling verses about the ark's poles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina notes a contradiction: one verse says the poles shall be in the rings and not removed, another says they shall be brought into the rings. He resolves that they can be loosened but not completely removed. A baraisa supports this, explaining that they are removable but not detachable.

sub.text: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.text_en: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.desc_en: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina) raises a contradiction between two verses: one says the poles shall be in the rings and not removed, another says they shall be brought into the rings.

sub.text: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.text_en: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.desc_en: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina) resolves the contradiction: the poles can be loosened but not completely removed.
A baraita supports this resolution, explaining through a hermeneutic process that the poles are removable but not detachable.

items.text: Interpretations of 'standing' acacia wood and the priestly garments
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'standing' acacia wood and the priestly garments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains the verse 'atzey shitim omedim' (acacia wood standing) in three ways: they grow upright, they support the gold overlay, and they endure forever. He then begins to discuss the verse about the 'bigdei hasrad' (service garments).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina opens by asking the meaning of the verse 'עֲצֵי שִׁטִּים עוֹמְדִים' (acacia wood standing) and gives the first interpretation: the boards stood in the direction of their growth.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina gives a second interpretation: 'standing' means the boards support their gold plating.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina gives a third interpretation: 'standing' teaches that the boards endure forever, allaying concern that their hope is lost.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina shifts to a new topic, asking the meaning of the verse 'אֶת בִּגְדֵי הַשְּׂרָד לְשָׁרֵת בַּקּוֹדֶשׁ' (the plaited garments for serving in the Sanctuary).

items.text: Priestly garments and the needlework exception
items.text_en: Priestly garments and the needlework exception
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a statement about the protective power of the priestly garments, then discusses the type of weaving used. A baraita states that priestly garments must be woven, not sewn with a needle, but Abaye clarifies that this applies only to the sleeves, which are woven separately and attached.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that without the priestly garments, no remnant of Israel's enemies would survive.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing the school of Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing the school of Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani cites a baraita from the school of Rabbi Shimon about garments that are scraped from their looms, and Reish Lakish identifies these as needlework.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that priestly garments must be made by weaving, not needlework.
Abaye resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita refers only to the sleeves, which are woven separately and attached.

items.text: The three arks made by Bezalel
items.text_en: The three arks made by Bezalel
items.desc_en: Rachbah quoting Rav Yehudah describes the three arks: an outer, middle, and inner one with specific measurements. A contradiction is raised from a baraita that gives a different measurement for the outer ark, resolved by a dispute about whether the ark had a handbreadth thickness, and the 'something extra' is identified as the crown.

sub.desc_en: Rachava cites Rav Yehuda that Bezalel made three arks: a middle wooden one of nine handbreadths, an inner gold one of eight, and an outer one of ten plus a little.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that states the outer ark was eleven handbreadths plus a little.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the two measures to different opinions about whether the ark's lid had a handbreadth thickness, and identifies the 'little' as the crown (זֵיר).

items.text: The three crowns: altar, ark, and table
items.text_en: The three crowns: altar, ark, and table
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan lists three crowns: for the altar (taken by Aaron), the table (taken by David), and the ark (still available for anyone who wants it). He then makes a wordplay on 'zer' (crown) and 'zar' (stranger), teaching that if one merits, it becomes a crown; if not, it remains alien.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan lists three crowns: of the altar (taken by Aaron), of the table (taken by David), and of the ark (still available for anyone who merits).
The Gemara supports that the ark's crown is not diminished by citing the verse 'By me kings reign' (Proverbs 8:15).

items.text: The Torah scholar and his community obligations
items.text_en: The Torah scholar and his community obligations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verses about the ark that a Torah scholar's townspeople are obligated to do his work. Rava then teaches that a Torah scholar whose inside is not like his outside is not a true scholar. Abaye or Rabbah bar Ulla adds that such a person is called 'abominable'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan contrasts the words 'זָר' (stranger) and 'זֵיר' (crown) to teach that Torah study can be a crown for the worthy or alien for the unworthy.
Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verses about the ark that townspeople are obligated to do the work of a Torah scholar.
Rava teaches from the verse about the ark's gold overlay that a Torah scholar whose inside is not like his outside is not a true scholar.

sub.text: Abaye or Rabbah bar Ulla's addition
sub.text_en: Abaye or Rabbah bar Ulla's addition
sub.desc_en: Abaye or Rabbah bar Ulla adds that such a person is called 'abominable', citing a verse from Job.

items.text: Woe to Torah scholars without fear of Heaven
items.text_en: Woe to Torah scholars without fear of Heaven
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan laments Torah scholars who study without fear of Heaven. Rabbi Yannai declares woe to one who has no courtyard but makes a gate for it. Rava warns the rabbis not to inherit two Gehinnoms, implying that Torah without fear leads to punishment.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan interprets a verse to lament Torah scholars who study Torah without יראת שמים (fear of Heaven).
Rabbi Yannai declares woe to one who has no courtyard (fear of Heaven) yet makes a gate (Torah study) for it, illustrating the same point.
Rava warns the rabbis not to inherit two Gehinnoms, implying that Torah without fear of Heaven leads to double punishment.

items.text: Torah as a potion of life or death
items.text_en: Torah as a potion of life or death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that Torah can be a potion of life or death depending on one's merit. Rava echoes this in Aramaic. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani adds that the verses 'Pikudei Hashem' and 'Imrat Hashem' imply that if one merits, Torah rejoices him; if not, it refines him. Reish Lakish says it refines him to life or death.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that Torah becomes a potion of life or death based on one's merit.
Rava restates the same idea in Aramaic: Torah is a potion of life for one who is expert in it, and a potion of death for one who is not.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan's contradiction
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan's contradiction
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports that Rabbi Yonatan raises a contradiction between the verses 'Pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev' and 'Imrat Hashem tzrufah'.
Rabbi Yonatan resolves the contradiction: if one merits, Torah rejoices him; if not, it refines him.
Reish Lakish derives from the same verse itself that Torah refines one to life if he merits, and to death if not.

items.text: Fear of Heaven and the crafts of the priestly garments
items.text_en: Fear of Heaven and the crafts of the priestly garments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains that 'fear of Heaven is pure' refers to one who studies Torah in purity, i.e., after marrying. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba says the testimony of Torah is faithful to its students. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Nechemya discuss the difference between 'rokem' (needlework) and 'choshev' (weaving), with the former having one face and the latter two.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina interprets 'fear of the Lord is pure' as referring to one who studies Torah in purity, which he explains means marrying a woman first and then studying Torah.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba explains that 'the testimony of the Lord is faithful' means it faithfully testifies on behalf of its students.
Rabbi Elazar explains the difference between 'ma'aseh rokem' (needlework) and 'ma'aseh choshev' (weaving): the former is embroidered where the design is planned.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Nechemya
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Nechemya
sub.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Nechemya clarifies: 'rokem' is needlework, producing only one face (design on one side), while 'choshev' is weaving, producing two faces (design on both sides).

items.text: Garments of the High Priest and the anointed for war
items.text_en: Garments of the High Priest and the anointed for war
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses that the garments of the High Priest can be used by the anointed for war, based on a verse. Rav Adda bar Ahavah raises an objection: can the son of the anointed for war serve in his place like the son of the High Priest? The section ends mid-objection.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi states that the garments in which the High Priest serves can also be used by the anointed for war (the priest anointed for battle), based on a verse.
Rav Adda bar Ahava raises an objection: could one think that the son of the anointed for war serves in his place like the son of the High Priest serves in his place?

items.text: Exclusion of the anointed for war from Temple service
items.text_en: Exclusion of the anointed for war from Temple service
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially questions whether the anointed for war, who is not permitted to enter the Tent of Meeting, can serve in the Temple. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the verse refers to one whose primary anointing is for the Tent of Meeting, excluding the anointed for war whose anointing is for battle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the anointed for war cannot serve in the Temple, citing the verse that limits service to those fit to enter the Tent of Meeting.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the verse refers to one whose primary anointing is for the Tent of Meeting, excluding the anointed for war whose anointing is for battle.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that the anointed for war does not serve in four garments like a common priest nor in eight like the High Priest. Abaye challenges that this would make him like a non-priest, and explains that he does not serve in eight due to enmity (איבה) and not in four due to the principle of ascending in holiness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that the anointed for war (משוח מלחמה) does not serve in four garments like a common priest nor in eight like the High Priest.
Abaye objects that if the anointed for war serves in neither four nor eight garments, he would be like a non-priest (זר), which is impossible.
Abaye resolves that he does not serve in eight garments due to enmity (איבה) and not in four due to the principle of ascending in holiness (מעלין בקודש ואין מורידין).

items.text: Discussion of enmity and the baraita of differences between priests
items.text_en: Discussion of enmity and the baraita of differences between priests
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Abba questions Rava about a tanna who does not consider enmity and thus the anointed for war does not serve at all. The Gemara then cites a baraita listing the differences between the High Priest and common priest, and specifies which laws apply to the anointed for war. It concludes that the tanna who lacks enmity applies it only to equals, but to a lesser priest enmity applies.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Abba's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Abba's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Abba asks Rava about the tanna who lacks enmity and therefore the anointed for war does not serve at all.

The Gemara cites a baraita listing the differences between the High Priest and common priest, and specifies which laws apply to the anointed for war, concluding with the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages.
The Gemara resolves that the tanna who lacks enmity applies it only to equals, but to a lesser priest enmity applies.

items.text: Tradition about Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the anointed for war's use of garments
items.text_en: Tradition about Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the anointed for war's use of garments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu taught a tradition in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, but Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi turned away. Some say it was Rabbi Chiya bar Abba who taught it. Rav Papa questions why they turned away from Rabbi Chiya bar Abba. When Ravin came, he reported that the matter was settled: the anointed for war may borrow the garments of the High Priest for consultation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu taught a tradition in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, but Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turned away from him.
Rav Papa questions why Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turned away from Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, since they could have simply told him that Rabbi Yochanan did not say that.
When Ravin came, he reported that the matter was settled: the anointed for war may borrow the garments of the High Priest for consultation, and a baraita supports this.

items.text: Procedure for consulting the Urim and Tumim
items.text_en: Procedure for consulting the Urim and Tumim
items.desc_en: The Gemara details the procedure: the questioner faces the priest, who faces the Divine Presence. The questioner asks, and the priest responds with 'Thus says the Lord.' Rabbi Yehuda says he need not say 'Thus says the Lord.' One may not ask aloud or merely think, but must speak like Hannah. One may not ask two questions at once; if asked, only the first is answered, as shown by David's inquiry.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing the procedure: the questioner faces the priest, who faces the Divine Presence, and the questioner asks while the priest responds with 'Thus says the Lord.'
Rabbi Yehuda rules that the priest need not say 'Thus says the Lord,' but only the direct answer.
The baraita rules that one may not ask aloud or merely think, but must speak like Hannah in her prayer, citing verses.
The baraita rules that one may not ask two questions at once; if asked, only the first is answered, as shown by David's inquiry about Keilah.

items.text: Laws of consulting the Urim and Tumim
items.text_en: Laws of consulting the Urim and Tumim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if one asks out of order, they must ask again in order, citing biblical verses. If the matter requires two questions, two are answered. The decree of the Urim and Tumim is irrevocable, unlike a prophet's decree.
