sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one asks the Urim and Tumim out of order, they are answered in order, and the questioner must repeat the question properly, citing the verse about Keilah.
The Gemara adds that if the matter requires two questions, two answers are given, citing David's double inquiry about the Amalekite raid.
The Gemara concludes that the decree of the Urim and Tumim is irrevocable, unlike a prophet's decree, citing the verse 'במשפט האורים'.

items.text: Why they are called Urim and Tumim, and the case of Gibeah
items.text_en: Why they are called Urim and Tumim, and the case of Gibeah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the names: Urim because they illuminate their words, Tumim because they complete them. It addresses why at Gibeah of Benjamin the Urim and Tumim did not complete the answer, concluding that the people did not inquire properly until the final time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Urim and Tumim are so named, and answers that Urim illuminates their words and Tumim completes them.
The Gemara raises the case of Gibeah of Benjamin where the Urim and Tumim did not complete the answer, and resolves that the people did not inquire properly until the final time when they did.

items.text: How the Urim and Tumim were made
items.text_en: How the Urim and Tumim were made
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish debate whether the letters of the tribes' names were protruding (boltot) or joined together (mitztarfot). The Gemara addresses missing letters by noting that the names of the patriarchs and the phrase 'Shivtei Yeshurun' were written there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Urim and Tumim were made, and presents the debate between Rabbi Yochanan (letters protruding) and Reish Lakish (letters joined together).
The Gemara objects that the letter 'tzadi' is missing from the tribes' names, and Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak answers that the names of the patriarchs (which include a tzadi) were written there.
The Gemara further objects that the letter 'tet' is missing, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the phrase 'Shivtei Yeshurun' (which includes a tet) was written there.

items.text: Who may consult the Urim and Tumim
items.text_en: Who may consult the Urim and Tumim
items.desc_en: A beraita teaches that only a priest who speaks with ruach hakodesh and has the Shechinah resting upon him may be consulted, citing the cases of Tzadok and Evyatar. The Gemara clarifies that Evyatar was not disqualified but rather assisted.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that a priest who does not speak with the Holy Spirit and the Shechinah does not rest upon him may not be consulted, citing the case of Tzadok and Evyatar; the Gemara clarifies that Evyatar was merely assisting.
The Gemara resolves that Evyatar was not disqualified but rather assisted the other priests in the consultation.

items.text: Only for the king, the anointed for war, and the Sanhedrin
items.text_en: Only for the king, the anointed for war, and the Sanhedrin
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that the Urim and Tumim are consulted only for the king, the anointed for war, and the Sanhedrin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Urim and Tumim are only consulted for a king, and Rabbi Avahu derives this from the verse, interpreting 'הוא' as the king, 'וכל ישראל אתו' as the anointed for war, and 'וכל העדה' as the Sanhedrin.
Rabbi Avahu derives from the verse that the Urim and Tumim are consulted only for the king, the anointed for war, and the Sanhedrin.

items.text: Mishnah: Yom Kippur prohibitions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Yom Kippur prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the five afflictions of Yom Kippur: eating, drinking, washing, anointing, wearing shoes, and marital relations. Exceptions are made for the king and bride for washing, and a woman after childbirth for shoes, according to Rabbi Eliezer, while the Sages prohibit. The shiurim for liability are given: a kotevet gasa for eating and a melo lugmav for drinking.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens the new chapter by listing the five prohibitions of Yom Kippur: eating, drinking, washing, anointing, wearing shoes, and marital relations.
Rabbi Eliezer permits the king and bride to wash their faces, and a woman after childbirth to wear shoes.
The Sages prohibit all these exceptions.
The Mishnah states the shiurim (measures) for liability: a kotevet gasa for eating, a melo lugmav for drinking, and that eating and drinking do not combine.

items.text: Gemara: Half-shiur on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Gemara: Half-shiur on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'forbidden' when eating on Yom Kippur is punishable by karet. Rabbi Ila or Rabbi Yirmeya answers that it refers to a half-shiur. The Gemara then discusses the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding whether a half-shiur is prohibited by Torah law or rabbinically, concluding that Reish Lakish agrees it is rabbinically forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah uses the term 'forbidden' when eating on Yom Kippur is punishable by karet.
Rabbi Ila (or alternatively Rabbi Yirmeya) answers that the Mishnah refers to a half-shiur (less than the full measure).
The Gemara questions how this answer works for the opinion that a half-shiur is permitted by Torah law.
The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan (half-shiur is Torah-prohibited) and Reish Lakish (half-shiur is Torah-permitted).
The Gemara resolves that even Reish Lakish agrees a half-shiur is rabbinically forbidden, so the Mishnah's term 'forbidden' is appropriate.

items.text: Half-shiur and oaths
items.text_en: Half-shiur and oaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the implication of half-shiur for oaths, citing a Mishnah about one who swears not to eat and eats forbidden items. Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan explain that the oath applies to permitted items included with forbidden ones. Reish Lakish says it only applies when one explicitly specifies a half-shiur according to the Rabbis, or in a general oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can be liable for an oath if half-shiur is only rabbinically forbidden, citing a Mishnah where one who swears not to eat and eats forbidden items is liable.
The Gemara asks why the oath-taker is liable at all, given he is already bound by the Torah prohibition against eating forbidden items.

sub.text: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
sub.text_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan explain that the oath applies to permitted items included together with forbidden ones, making the oath effective.
Reish Lakish says the oath only applies when one explicitly specifies a half-shiur according to the Rabbis, or in a general oath without specification.

items.text: Introduction of Rabbi Akiva's principle
items.text_en: Introduction of Rabbi Akiva's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Akiva's view that a person can prohibit himself with any amount, setting the stage for the discussion on half a shiur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Akiva's principle that a person can prohibit himself with any amount, setting the stage for the discussion on half a shiur.

items.text: Objection from oath of testimony
items.text_en: Objection from oath of testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if a person has a Torah permit, how can an oath take effect? It cites the Mishnah that the oath of testimony only applies to those fit to testify, excluding a king or a dice player, who are disqualified by rabbinic decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: since the person has a Torah permit, how can an oath of testimony take effect?
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that the oath of testimony applies only to those fit to testify.
The Gemara asks: what does this Mishnah exclude?
Rav Pappa answers: it excludes a king.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers: it excludes a dice player.
The Gemara objects: a dice player is fit by Torah law, yet the oath does not take effect on him, showing that rabbinic disqualification prevents the oath.
The Gemara resolves: there the verse says 'if he does not tell,' and this person is not capable of giving testimony at all.

items.text: Clarification of 'prohibited' vs 'liable to karet'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'prohibited' vs 'liable to karet'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that when the Mishnah says 'prohibited' regarding half a shiur, it does not mean there is no karet for a full shiur; rather, karet applies only to eating, drinking, and work, while prohibition applies to other acts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's use of 'prohibited' implies that wherever the term 'liable to karet' is taught, 'prohibited' is not taught.
A baraita is cited stating that although all forbidden acts on Yom Kippur are prohibited, karet applies only to eating, drinking, and work.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's 'prohibited' refers specifically to half a shiur, while a full shiur carries karet, but karet itself is limited to eating, drinking, and work.

items.text: Alternative explanation: prohibition on other acts
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: prohibition on other acts
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: the Mishnah's 'prohibited' refers to other acts like washing, anointing, wearing sandals, and marital relations, derived from the word 'Shabbaton'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation: the Mishnah's 'prohibited' refers to other acts, not eating and drinking.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbah and Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbah and Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef cite a baraita from the school of Rav that derives the prohibition of washing, anointing, wearing sandals, and marital relations on Yom Kippur from the word 'שַׁבָּתוֹן' (Shabbaton), meaning cessation.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on half a shiur
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on half a shiur
items.desc_en: The core dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds that half a shiur is prohibited by Torah law because it can combine with another half, while Reish Lakish holds it is permitted by Torah law since there is no full eating.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the core dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds that half a shiur is prohibited by Torah law.
Reish Lakish states that half a shiur is permitted by Torah law.
Rabbi Yochanan explains his position: since half a shiur can combine with another half to form a full shiur, it is considered prohibited.
Reish Lakish explains his position: the Torah prohibits eating (אכילה), and half a shiur does not constitute eating.

items.text: Proof and refutation regarding half a shiur
items.text_en: Proof and refutation regarding half a shiur
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan brings a proof from a baraita that half a shiur is included in the prohibition of 'all fat', but Reish Lakish deflects it as a rabbinic support. The Gemara then supports Reish Lakish by noting that if it were Torah law, a verse would not be needed for a doubtful case like a koy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita that includes koy and half a shiur in the prohibition of 'all fat' (כל חלב), challenging Reish Lakish's view that half a shiur is permitted from the Torah.
Reish Lakish deflects the baraita as a rabbinic enactment with a mere scriptural support (אסמכתא בעלמא), not a Torah-level prohibition.

The Gemara supports Reish Lakish by arguing that if half a shiur were Torah law, a verse would not be needed to include a doubtful case like a koy (כוי), since the Torah does not typically legislate for doubtful cases.

items.text: Clarification of the status of a koy
items.text_en: Clarification of the status of a koy
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a koy is considered a unique creature, and therefore a verse is needed to include it, just as a verse was needed to include it elsewhere due to its unique nature.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that a koy is a unique creature, and therefore a verse is needed to include it, just as Rav Idi bar Avin's statement about 'כל' required a verse for the koy because its unique nature differs from a mere ספק (doubt).

items.text: First baraita: Affliction must be passive like labor
items.text_en: First baraita: Affliction must be passive like labor
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'you shall afflict your souls' cannot mean sitting in heat or cold to cause pain, because affliction is compared to labor, which is a passive prohibition. Therefore, affliction must also be a passive state, not an active one.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'you shall afflict your souls' and derives from the juxtaposition with labor that affliction must be a passive state, not an active one like sitting in heat or cold.
The gemara objects: why not allow moving from sun to shade or vice versa to relieve discomfort, which would still be passive?
The gemara resolves: just as labor is a unified prohibition without subdivisions, so too affliction must be a single undivided state, not subject to distinctions.

items.text: Second baraita: Affliction parallels other prohibitions
items.text_en: Second baraita: Affliction parallels other prohibitions
items.desc_en: Another baraita derives that affliction must be something for which one is liable elsewhere, specifically piggul and notar, which are subject to karet.

sub.desc_en: A second baraita derives that affliction on Yom Kippur corresponds to things like פיגול (piggul) and נותר (notar), which are prohibited elsewhere with כרת (karet).

items.text: Expansion to include all forbidden foods
items.text_en: Expansion to include all forbidden foods
items.desc_en: Through a series of hermeneutical extensions using the repeated phrase 'you shall afflict your souls', the baraita includes tevel, neveilah, non-sacred food, terumah, and consecrated food, each time excluding a category that is less severe in terms of punishment or prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins by including piggul and notar (which incur karet) and then extends to include tevel (untithed produce) via the repeated phrase 'you shall afflict your souls'.
The baraita includes tevel (which incurs death at the hand of Heaven) and extends to include neveilah (carcass) via the repeated phrase.
The baraita includes neveilah (prohibited by a negative commandment) and extends to include non-sacred food (chullin) via the repeated phrase.
The baraita includes non-sacred food (chullin) and extends to include terumah and consecrated food (kodashim) via the repeated phrase, completing the series of inclusions.

items.text: Alternative derivation: Affliction is destruction of the soul
items.text_en: Alternative derivation: Affliction is destruction of the soul
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests an alternative approach: the verse 'I will destroy that soul' indicates that affliction is something that destroys the soul, namely eating and drinking. It clarifies that this is not referring to forbidden sexual relations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative derivation: the verse 'I will destroy that soul' shows that affliction is something that destroys the soul, namely eating and drinking.

The Gemara clarifies the meaning of 'and if it is your wish to say', explaining that it addresses a potential objection that the verse might refer to forbidden sexual relations, and concludes that it must refer to eating and drinking.

items.text: Derivation from verbal analogy and rejection of alternatives
items.text_en: Derivation from verbal analogy and rejection of alternatives
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives affliction as hunger from a verbal analogy with the manna. The Gemara rejects alternative derivations from the affliction of Laban's daughters or the Egyptian affliction, based on distinctions between communal vs. individual affliction and divine vs. human affliction.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches a verbal analogy: the word 'עינוי' (affliction) used here regarding Yom Kippur and in the verse about the manna in the desert both refer to hunger.
The Gemara asks why we do not derive the meaning of affliction from the verse 'אם תענה את בנותי' (If you shall afflict my daughters), which refers to marital relations rather than hunger.
The Gemara answers that we derive communal affliction (Yom Kippur for the public) from communal affliction (the manna for all Israel), not from individual affliction (Laban's daughters).
The Gemara asks why we do not derive affliction from the Egyptian affliction, which is interpreted as abstinence from marital relations, a communal affliction.

The Gemara answers that we derive affliction by the hand of Heaven (divinely commanded or caused) from affliction by the hand of Heaven, not from affliction by the hand of man (the Egyptian oppression).

items.text: Discussion on the nature of affliction and sight
items.text_en: Discussion on the nature of affliction and sight
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi debate whether affliction from the manna was due to lack of bread or not seeing it. Rav Yosef deduces a hint for the blind, and Abaye advises eating during the day. Reish Lakish applies the verse to the pleasure of seeing a woman over the act itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about the manna and presents the debate between Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi: one says affliction is lacking bread, the other says it is not seeing what one eats.
Rav Yosef deduces a hint from this that blind people eat but are not satisfied, supporting the view that sight enhances satiety.
Abaye rules that one who has a meal should eat it only during the day, so that he can see his food and be satisfied.
Rabbi Zeira cites the verse 'Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the soul' to support the importance of seeing food.
Reish Lakish applies the same verse to say that seeing a woman is better than the act itself, citing the verse about sight versus wandering.
The Gemara cites the verse 'For he gives his eye to the cup, he walks in uprightness' as a continuation of the discussion.

items.text: Two opinions on the effect of wine
items.text_en: Two opinions on the effect of wine
items.desc_en: Two anonymous opinions are presented: one says that when a person's eye is on his cup, all forbidden relations appear to him as permissible; the other says that all the world appears to him as a plain.

sub.desc_en: The first anonymous opinion states that when a person's eye is on his cup, all forbidden relations appear to him as a plain (i.e., permissible).
The second anonymous opinion says that when a person's eye is on his cup, the entire world appears to him as a plain.

items.text: Interpretations of verses by Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
items.text_en: Interpretations of verses by Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi debate the meaning of "D'agah b'lev ish yashchenah" and "Nachash afar lachmo." One says to remove worry from one's mind, the other says to share it with others. Regarding the serpent, one says even eating all delicacies tastes like dust, the other says one's mind is not settled until eating dust.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi debate the verse 'דאגה בלב איש ישחנה'; one says to remove worry from one's mind.
The other says to share the worry with others.
Regarding the serpent's food, one says even eating all delicacies tastes like dust.
The other says one's mind is not settled until eating dust.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei on God's mercy in curses
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei on God's mercy in curses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei contrasts human and divine punishment: a person who angers his friend descends with him to life, but God cursed the serpent, Canaan, the woman, and the earth, yet each still receives sustenance or pursuit.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei opens by contrasting human and divine punishment: a person who angers his friend descends with him to life, but God cursed the serpent yet its sustenance follows it everywhere.
Rabbi Yosei provides further examples: Canaan eats his master's food, the woman is pursued by all, and the earth sustains all.

items.text: Debate on 'fish' vs. 'forbidden relations' in the verse
items.text_en: Debate on 'fish' vs. 'forbidden relations' in the verse
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether 'the fish we ate in Egypt for free' refers to actual fish or forbidden relations. The Gemara supports each view with verses and resolves contradictions, concluding that both complaints existed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a dispute between Rav and Shmuel over the meaning of 'the fish we ate in Egypt for free' — one says actual fish, the other says forbidden relations, each citing a different word in the verse.
The Gemara resolves the objection against each view: for 'forbidden relations', 'eat' is a euphemism; for 'fish', 'free' means they were provided from ownerless sources via a miracle.

The Gemara supports each view with a verse: for 'fish', the verse 'a locked garden' shows restraint from forbidden relations; for 'forbidden relations', the verse 'a sealed spring' shows restraint only from those prohibited.

The Gemara concludes that both complaints existed: the verse 'Moses heard the people weeping by their families' supports the forbidden-relations view, but the fish view is also valid, so both were present.

items.text: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi on the taste of cucumbers and melons in the manna
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi on the taste of cucumbers and melons in the manna
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi debate whether the manna contained the taste of all foods except cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic, or whether it contained both taste and substance of all foods except these five, which had taste but not substance.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi debate whether the manna contained the taste of all foods except cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic.

sub.text: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi (second opinion)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi (second opinion)
sub.desc_en: The other sage argues that the manna contained both taste and substance of all foods except these five, which had taste but not substance.

items.text: Interpretations of 'gad' and 'lavan' in the manna
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'gad' and 'lavan' in the manna
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi says the manna was round like a tendon and white like a pearl. A baraisa compares it to flax seed. 'Acherim' say 'gad' refers to a teaching that draws the heart like water. Another baraisa says 'gad' tells (magid) Israel whether a child is nine months to the first or seven to the last. 'Lavan' means it whitens Israel's sins.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi interprets the manna as round like a tendon and white like a pearl.
A baraita supports Rabbi Asi by comparing the manna to flax seed in its stalks.
Acherim interpret 'gad' as a teaching (הגדה) that draws the heart like water.
Another baraita interprets 'gad' as telling (מגיד) Israel whether a child is nine months to the first husband or seven to the last.
The term 'lavan' (white) is interpreted to mean that the manna whitens Israel's sins.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei: The manna revealed hidden matters
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei: The manna revealed hidden matters
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei teaches that just as the prophet told Israel what was in holes and cracks, so the manna revealed hidden matters. Examples: two people coming to Moses for judgment, and a man and woman disputing, with the manna's location indicating the truth.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei opens by stating that just as a prophet revealed hidden things to Israel, so too the manna revealed hidden matters.
Rabbi Yosei gives the first example: two people disputing about a slave come to Moses, and the location of their omer of manna reveals who stole and who sold.
Rabbi Yosei gives the second example: a man and woman disputing about marital infidelity come to Moses, and the location of her omer of manna reveals who sinned against whom.

items.text: Three levels of righteousness in gathering and eating the manna
items.text_en: Three levels of righteousness in gathering and eating the manna
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves contradictions in verses about gathering the manna: for the righteous, it fell at their tent entrance; for intermediates, they went out and gathered; for the wicked, they wandered and gathered. Similarly, the manna was bread for the righteous, cakes for intermediates, and ground in mills for the wicked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between three verses describing how the manna was gathered and asks how to resolve it.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by assigning each verse to a different level of righteousness: the righteous found manna at their tent entrance, intermediates went out to gather, and the wicked wandered to gather.
The Gemara notes a contradiction between three verses describing the form of the manna and asks how to resolve it.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by assigning each form to a different level of righteousness: the righteous received bread, intermediates received cakes, and the wicked had to grind the manna in mills.

items.text: The manna came with women's ornaments and precious stones
items.text_en: The manna came with women's ornaments and precious stones
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda said in the name of Rav that the manna came with women's ornaments that were ground in a mortar. Rabbi Chama said it came with pot herbs. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan that the manna came with precious stones and pearls, as implied by the verse about the princes bringing shoham stones.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda said Rav (or Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda said Rav (or Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda said in the name of Rav (or alternatively Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina) that the manna came with women's ornaments that are ground in a mortar.
Rabbi Chama said that the manna came with pot herbs.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan that the manna came with precious stones and pearls, as implied by the verse about the princes bringing shoham stones.

items.text: The taste of the manna like 'shad' or 'shed'
items.text_en: The taste of the manna like 'shad' or 'shed'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that just as a breast (shad) gives an infant many tastes, so the manna had many tastes. Alternatively, it was like a demon (shed) that changes into many colors, so the manna changed into many tastes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that just as a breast (שד) gives an infant many tastes, so the manna had many tastes.
An alternative interpretation compares the manna to a demon (שד) that changes into many colors, so the manna changed into many tastes.

items.text: The meat requested improperly was given improperly
items.text_en: The meat requested improperly was given improperly
items.desc_en: A tradition from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: the meat that the Israelites asked for improperly was given to them improperly.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha that the meat the Israelites asked for improperly was given to them improperly.

items.text: When to eat meat and the timing of meals
items.text_en: When to eat meat and the timing of meals
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the manna narrative that one should eat meat only at night. It addresses an objection from Abaye that one should eat a meal during the day, resolving that the manna was eaten 'like daytime' (i.e., after nightfall but while still light). Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds that initially Israel scavenged like chickens until Moses fixed a set mealtime.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the manna narrative that one should eat meat only at night.
Abaye objects that one should eat a meal during the day, not at night.
The Gemara resolves that the manna was eaten 'like daytime' (i.e., after nightfall but while still light).
Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds that initially Israel scavenged like chickens until Moses fixed a set mealtime.

items.text: Three categories of sinners regarding the quail
items.text_en: Three categories of sinners regarding the quail
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between verses about the quail: the intermediate sinners died immediately, while the wicked suffered for a month.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two verses about the quail: one says the meat was still between their teeth, the other says they ate for a month.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing three categories: intermediate sinners died immediately, the wicked suffered for a month, and the righteous were unaffected.

items.text: The meaning of 'vayishtechu' and the slaughter of the quail
items.text_en: The meaning of 'vayishtechu' and the slaughter of the quail
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha offer homiletic readings of 'vayishtechu' (they spread out) as 'vayishchatu' (they slaughtered), teaching that Israel became liable for slaughter or that the manna came with something requiring slaughter. Rabbi objects, citing a verse that already mentions meat. A baraisa then explains that the verse 'as I commanded you' teaches the laws of slaughter for birds and animals, and 'shatuach' teaches that the manna came with spread-out items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'וַיִּשְׁטְחוּ' (they spread out) and presents Reish Lakish's homiletic reading as 'וַיִּשְׁחֲטוּ' (they slaughtered), teaching that Israel became liable for slaughter, and a Tanna in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha reads 'שָׁטוֹחַ' as 'שָׁחוּט' (slaughtered), teaching that the manna came with something requiring slaughter.
Rabbi objects to the homiletic reading, arguing that the verse already mentions meat (the quail) explicitly, so the homily is unnecessary.

A baraisa is cited where Rabbi explains that the verse 'וְזָבַחְתָּ כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוִּיתִיךְ' teaches the laws of slaughter for birds and animals, and 'שָׁטוֹחַ' teaches that the manna came with spread-out items.

items.text: Manna's taste for different ages
items.text_en: Manna's taste for different ages
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that the manna tasted like bread for youths, oil for the elderly, and honey for infants.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina resolves the three scriptural descriptions of manna (bread, oil, honey) by assigning each to a different age group: bread for youths, oil for the elderly, honey for infants.

items.text: The nature of the quail (selav)
items.text_en: The nature of the quail (selav)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains the word 'selav' homiletically: the righteous ate it in peace (shalvah), while the wicked found it like thorns (silvin). Rav Chanan bar Rava lists four types of selav, describing the best and worst, and notes that the last type is only edible in a mixture.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the discrepancy between the written form 'שָׁלֵיו' and the vocalized reading 'סְלָיו' and asks about the meaning of the word.
Rabbi Chanina explains homiletically that the righteous ate it in peace (שַׁלְוָה), while the wicked found it like thorns (סִילְוִין).
Rav Chanan bar Rava lists four types of selav, describing the best and worst, and notes that the last type is only edible in a mixture.

items.text: Anecdote about Rav Yehuda, Rav Chisda, and Rava
items.text_en: Anecdote about Rav Yehuda, Rav Chisda, and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rav Yehuda had wine, Rav Chisda had wood, and Rava's tenant brought him food daily. One day the tenant did not come; Rava heard a child reciting a verse and inferred that Rav Chisda had died, and that the food was meant for the student (Rava) instead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rav Yehuda had wine, Rav Chisda had wood, and Rava's tenant brought him food daily, but one day the tenant did not come.
Rava asks what is happening and goes up to the roof, where he hears a child reciting the verse 'I heard and my belly trembled'.
Rava infers from the child's verse that Rav Chisda has died, and that the food intended for Rav Chisda was now being eaten by the student (Rava) instead.

items.text: The dew around the manna
items.text_en: The dew around the manna
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina resolves a contradiction about the dew: there was dew above and below the manna, like something stored in a box.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two verses: one says the dew rose, the other says the dew descended.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina resolves the contradiction by explaining that there was dew both above and below the manna, like something stored in a box.

items.text: The meaning of 'dak mechuspas'
items.text_en: The meaning of 'dak mechuspas'
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan debate the meaning of 'dak mechuspas': one says it dissolves on the palm, the other that it is absorbed in 248 limbs. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that 'mechuspas' is written with a samekh, implying it is 'covered' (mechuseh pas).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the phrase 'דַּק מְחוּסְפָּס' (fine and covered) from the verse describing the manna.
Reish Lakish explains that 'דַּק מְחוּסְפָּס' means something that dissolves on the palm of the hand.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'דַּק מְחוּסְפָּס' means something that is absorbed in 248 limbs.
The Gemara objects that 'מְחוּסְפָּס' (with a samekh) would mean 'covered' (טוּבָא), not 'dissolved'.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the word is written 'מְחֻסְפָּס' (with a samekh), meaning 'covered' (מכוסה), supporting Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation.

items.text: Dispute over 'lechem abbirim' (bread of the mighty)
items.text_en: Dispute over 'lechem abbirim' (bread of the mighty)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva interprets 'lechem abbirim' as bread eaten by ministering angels. Rabbi Yishmael objects, citing that angels do not eat bread, and explains it as bread absorbed in 248 limbs. The Gemara then presents alternative interpretations of the verse 'and a peg you shall have on your belt' (Deut 23:14) in this context: Rabbi Elazar ben Parta says it refers to items that merchants sold them, which the manna counteracted; Rabbi Yishmael says it refers to items from overseas; and a final 'davar acher' is introduced but cut off.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Akiva's interpretation that 'lechem abbirim' is bread eaten by ministering angels.
Rabbi Yishmael objects to Rabbi Akiva, arguing that angels do not eat bread, citing the verse about Moses.
Rabbi Yishmael explains 'abbirim' as 'eivarim' (limbs), meaning bread absorbed in 248 limbs.
The Gemara asks how to reconcile the verse about a spade (Deut 23:14) with the idea that manna produced no waste, and answers that it refers to food bought from gentile merchants.
Rabbi Elazar ben Parta says that even food from merchants was counteracted by the manna, so the spade verse applies only after Israel sinned.
Rabbi Elazar ben Parta explains that after sinning, God made them walk three parasangs to relieve themselves.

sub.text: Supporting evidence from Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Supporting evidence from Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana testifies that the camp was three parasangs long, and a baraita explains that they relieved themselves only behind the camp.
The Gemara cites the Israelites' complaint that the manna would swell in their stomachs, implying it produced no waste.
Rabbi Yishmael reiterates his interpretation of 'abbirim' as 'eivarim' and explains the spade verse as referring to food from overseas.
The Gemara introduces an alternative interpretation ('davar acher') but cuts off before completing it.

items.text: Identifying Joshua as the 'man' for whom manna descended
items.text_en: Identifying Joshua as the 'man' for whom manna descended
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the 'man' in the verse about manna descending as Joshua, using a verbal analogy between 'man' here and 'man' in another verse about Joshua. It rejects Moses as the referent because the analogy uses the absolute form 'man' rather than 'the man'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Joshua as the man for whom manna descended, citing a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the word 'איש' here and in the verse about Joshua.
The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps the 'man' refers to Moses, as the verse says 'והאיש משה' (the man Moses).
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the verbal analogy must be between the absolute form 'איש' and 'איש', not between 'איש' and 'והאיש' (the definite form).

items.text: Why manna descended daily rather than annually
items.text_en: Why manna descended daily rather than annually
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's students ask why manna did not come once a year. He answers with a parable: a king who provided his son's sustenance daily so the son would visit him daily. Similarly, daily manna made Israelites dependent on God daily, and also ensured they ate it warm and avoided the burden of carrying it.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai why the manna did not descend for Israel once a year.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai answers with a parable of a king who provided his son's sustenance daily so the son would visit him daily.
The gemara applies the parable: Israelites with many children worried daily about manna, directing their hearts to their Father in Heaven.
Two additional reasons are given: they ate the manna warm, and to avoid the burden of carrying it.

items.text: The height of the manna: sixty cubits
items.text_en: The height of the manna: sixty cubits
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i claims the manna was sixty cubits high, deriving this from a comparison of the flood's fifteen cubits of water to the manna's descent through 'windows' of heaven. He argues that since the measure of goodness exceeds punishment, and the flood had four windows per door (eight total), the manna's height is four times fifteen cubits, i.e., sixty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i, sitting among the sages studying the manna portion, declares that the manna was sixty cubits high.
Rabbi Tarfon rebukes Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i for piling up baseless claims.
Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i defends his claim by interpreting the flood verse: the fifteen cubits of water above the mountains were measured after the waters had already risen to mountain height.
He argues that the measure of goodness exceeds punishment: the flood used 'ארובות' (windows), while the manna used 'דלתי שמים' (doors of heaven), implying more openings.
He calculates: each door has four windows, so the manna had eight windows, making its height four times the flood's fifteen cubits, i.e., sixty cubits.

items.text: The manna seen by all kings and David's cup
items.text_en: The manna seen by all kings and David's cup
items.desc_en: Isi ben Yehuda says the manna rose high enough to be seen by all eastern and western kings, citing Psalm 23:5. Abaye deduces from 'my cup is full' that David's cup in the future world holds 221 log. The Gemara rejects the comparison between the flood and manna, noting differences in duration and scope.

sub.desc_en: Isi ben Yehuda states that the manna rose high enough to be seen by all eastern and western kings, citing Psalm 23:5.
Abaye deduces from 'my cup is full' that David's cup in the future world holds 221 log, based on the gematria of 'רויה'.
The Gemara objects that the comparison between the flood and the manna is invalid due to differences in duration and scope.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i derives his height of sixty amot for the manna via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'פתיחה' (opening) used in both the flood and manna contexts.

items.text: The five afflictions of Yom Kippur correspond to five in the Torah
items.text_en: The five afflictions of Yom Kippur correspond to five in the Torah
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the five afflictions (including eating and drinking) correspond to five instances of affliction mentioned in the Torah: 'and on the tenth', 'but on the tenth', 'Sabbath of rest' (twice), and 'and it shall be for you'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the five afflictions (עינויים) of Yom Kippur correspond to what?
Rav Chisda answers that they correspond to five afflictions mentioned in the Torah: 'ובעשור', 'אך בעשור', 'שבת שבתון' (twice), and 'והיתה לכם'.

items.text: Drinking is included in the prohibition of eating
items.text_en: Drinking is included in the prohibition of eating
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah lists six afflictions, not five, and resolves that drinking is included in eating. Resh Lakish proves this from a verse where 'wine' is called 'eating'. Rav Acha bar Yaakov proves it from a verse where 'strong drink' is called 'eating'. The Gemara rejects alternative interpretations involving dipping or eating dried figs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah lists six afflictions when the Torah only mentions five, and answers that drinking is included in the prohibition of eating.
Resh Lakish proves from the verse 'וְאָכַלְתָּ... תִּירוֹשְׁךָ' that wine, a drink, is called 'eating'.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the verse refers to eating wine through a dipping sauce (אניגרון), not drinking it directly.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov proves from the verse 'וְאָכַלְתָּ... בְּיַיִן וּבַשֵּׁכָר' that strong drink, a beverage, is called 'eating'.

The Gemara objects that perhaps this verse also refers to eating the strong drink through a dipping sauce, but rejects this because 'שֵׁכָר' implies an intoxicating drink, and a baraita about eating dried figs and entering the Temple is cited.

items.text: Deriving wine prohibition from Nazirite
items.text_en: Deriving wine prohibition from Nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the prohibition of wine on Yom Kippur is derived from the Nazirite through a verbal analogy (gezerah shavah) on the word 'sheikhar'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the derivation of the wine prohibition on Yom Kippur by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'שכר' from the Nazirite, concluding that just as there it refers to wine, so too here.

items.text: Clarifying 'tirosh' as wine
items.text_en: Clarifying 'tirosh' as wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'tirosh' is wine, citing a baraita that a nazir who vows from 'tirosh' is forbidden in sweet things but permitted in wine, and resolves that 'tirosh' is indeed wine, but in vows we follow common language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'תירוש' (tirosh) is wine, citing a baraita that one who vows from 'תירוש' is forbidden in all sweet things but permitted in wine.
The Gemara objects that 'תירוש' must be wine, citing the verse 'וְתִירוֹשׁ יְנוֹבֵב בְּתוּלוֹת' (and tirosh makes maidens flourish), arguing it refers to a product of tirosh.
The Gemara resolves that everyone agrees 'תירוש' is wine, but in vows we follow common language, where people distinguish between 'תירוש' and 'יין'.

items.text: Etymology of 'yayin' and 'tirosh'
items.text_en: Etymology of 'yayin' and 'tirosh'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the different names for wine: 'yayin' because it brings wailing to the world, and 'tirosh' because one who engages with it becomes impoverished.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why wine is called 'yayin' and why it is called 'tirosh'.
The Gemara explains that 'yayin' brings wailing (יללה) to the world, and 'tirosh' indicates that one who engages with it becomes impoverished (רש).

items.text: Rav Kahana and Rava on 'tirosh' and wine
items.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rava on 'tirosh' and wine
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana notes a contradiction in the spelling of 'tirosh' and interprets: if one merits, it makes him a head; if not, a pauper. Rava similarly interprets 'yeshammach' as either gladdening or stupefying.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana notes the discrepancy between the written and read forms of 'tirosh' and interprets: if one merits, it makes him a head; if not, a pauper.
Rava similarly interprets 'yeshammach' as either gladdening or stupefying, concluding that wine and spices make one alert.

items.text: Deriving washing and anointing from Daniel
items.text_en: Deriving washing and anointing from Daniel
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that washing and anointing are considered affliction from Daniel's fast, where he refrained from bread, meat, wine, and anointing, and the angel said he afflicted himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that washing and anointing are called affliction, citing Daniel's verse where he refrained from bread, meat, wine, and anointing.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda brei d'Rav Shmuel bar Shilat
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda brei d'Rav Shmuel bar Shilat
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that Daniel's 'bread of desires' refers even to fine wheat bread, showing his self-affliction.
The Gemara proves that Daniel's actions are considered affliction because the angel said 'from the day you set your heart to afflict yourself, your words were heard.'

items.text: Deriving washing from anointing
items.text_en: Deriving washing from anointing
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah derives washing from a verse comparing water and oil, but the Gemara notes a baraita that uses the same verse for anointing as drinking. Rav Ashi resolves that washing is derived from the verse 'and I did not anoint' itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: having found anointing from Scripture, from where do we derive washing as an affliction on Yom Kippur?
Rav Zutra bar Rabbi Toviyah derives washing from the verse comparing water and oil: just as oil applied externally (אַבָּרַאי), so too water is external washing, not drinking.

sub.text: Gemara's objection – citation of a baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection – citation of a baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a baraita (תנא) derives the opposite: the same verse is cited to equate anointing to drinking, not washing, so Rav Zutra's derivation is contradicted.
Rav Ashi resolves that washing is derived directly from the verse 'וְסוֹךְ לֹא סָכְתִּי' itself, not from the water-oil analogy, thus avoiding the baraita's counter-derivation.

items.text: Explaining 'and I came by your words'
items.text_en: Explaining 'and I came by your words'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the angel's statement 'and I came by your words' as referring to the verse in Ezekiel about the seventy elders offering incense, which Daniel saw in a vision.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the angel meant by 'and I came by your words', citing the verse about the seventy elders offering incense in Ezekiel's vision.

items.text: Biblical proof that washing is an affliction from Ezekiel
items.text_en: Biblical proof that washing is an affliction from Ezekiel
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse from Ezekiel describing the idolatrous priests turning their backs to the Temple and bowing eastward to the sun. It explains that the phrase 'their backs to the Temple' teaches that they were exposing themselves and defecating downward, implying that washing is involved in the concept of affliction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Ezekiel verse about the idolatrous priests and interprets 'their backs to the Temple' as exposing themselves and defecating downward, implying that washing is an affliction.

items.text: Aggadic narrative: Gabriel and the angel of Persia
items.text_en: Aggadic narrative: Gabriel and the angel of Persia
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story where God tells Michael that Israel has sinned. Michael pleads for the righteous, but God decides to burn them. Gabriel is sent to take coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city. Rav Chana bar Bizna says that had the coals not cooled, no remnant of Israel would have survived. Rabbi Yochanan says Gabriel was punished for not following orders precisely, and the angel Dubiel of Persia was appointed in his place for 21 days, as referenced in Daniel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens the narrative: God tells Michael that Israel has sinned, Michael pleads for the righteous, but God decides to burn them and sends Gabriel to take coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city.

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida states that had the coals not cooled in transit from the cherub to Gabriel, no remnant of Israel would have survived.
Rabbi Yochanan reports that Gabriel was punished with sixty lashes of fire for not following the order precisely, and was questioned why he deviated from the command.
The Gemara concludes that the angel Dubiel of Persia was appointed in Gabriel's place for twenty-one days, as referenced in the verse about the prince of Persia opposing Daniel.

items.text: Gabriel's intervention to annul the decree against Israel
items.text_en: Gabriel's intervention to annul the decree against Israel
items.desc_en: Dubiel writes a decree of taxation against Israel and the rabbis. Gabriel, from behind the curtain, quotes a verse about the reward for those who toil in Torah. The Gemara then describes how Gabriel advocates for Israel, comparing Daniel's wisdom to all the nations. God allows Gabriel to enter, and he finds Dubiel holding the decree. Gabriel swallows it, or according to another version, erases the seal. This explains why in Persia some pay the tax and some do not.

sub.desc_en: Dubiel orders a tax decree against Israel and the rabbis, and it is written.
Gabriel, from behind the curtain, quotes a verse about the reward for Torah scholars' wives, but the heavenly court does not heed him.
Gabriel argues before God that Daniel's wisdom outweighs all the nations' sages.
God asks who advocates for Israel, is told it is Gabriel, and permits him to enter.
Gabriel finds Dubiel holding the decree and swallows it.
An alternative version states that the decree was written but not sealed, or that Gabriel erased the seal after swallowing.
The Gemara explains that this is why in Persia some pay the tax and some do not, and the angel of Greece later comes but is ignored.

items.text: Derivation that washing is an affliction from David's example
items.text_en: Derivation that washing is an affliction from David's example
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive that washing is called עינוי from the verse about Evyatar, where David says 'you afflicted yourself' (התענית). The verse about David's men says they were 'weary' (עייף), which is explained as being from lack of washing. However, the Gemara questions whether it might be from lack of shoes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative derivation that washing is called עינוי (affliction) from the verse about Evyatar, where David says 'you afflicted yourself' (התענית), and the description of David's men as 'weary' (עייף), which is explained as being from lack of washing.
The Gemara objects that the 'weariness' (עייף) might refer to lack of shoes rather than lack of washing.

items.text: Derivation that washing is an affliction from Proverbs
items.text_en: Derivation that washing is an affliction from Proverbs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak derives that washing is an affliction from the verse 'Cool water on a weary soul' (מים קרים על נפש עייפה). The word 'weary' (עייפה) implies affliction from lack of washing. The Gemara questions whether it might refer to thirst, but notes the verse says 'on a weary soul' (על נפש עייפה), not 'in a weary soul'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak derives that washing is an affliction from the verse 'מים קרים על נפש עייפה' (cool water on a weary soul), interpreting 'עייפה' (weary) as affliction from lack of washing.
The Gemara objects that the verse might refer to thirst rather than lack of washing.
The Gemara resolves that the verse says 'על נפש עייפה' (on a weary soul), not 'בנפש עייפה' (in a weary soul), indicating external affliction like washing rather than internal thirst.

items.text: Derivation that going without shoes is an affliction from David
items.text_en: Derivation that going without shoes is an affliction from David
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive that going without shoes is an affliction from the verse where David goes up the Mount of Olives barefoot (יחף). It questions whether this might be from a specific type of footwear (סוסיא ומרטקא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that going without shoes (נעילת הסנדל) is an affliction, citing the verse where David went barefoot (יחף) up the Mount of Olives.
The Gemara objects that David's barefoot state might have been due to wearing only סוסיא ומרטקא (light footwear or socks) rather than being completely without shoes.

items.text: Derivation that going without shoes is an affliction from Isaiah
items.text_en: Derivation that going without shoes is an affliction from Isaiah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives from the verse where Isaiah is told to remove his shoes (נעלך תחלוץ) and goes barefoot (יחף). The Gemara questions whether this might refer to patched shoes (מנעלים המטולאים), just as 'naked' (ערום) there means in worn-out clothes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives that going without shoes is an affliction from the verse where Isaiah is told to remove his shoes (נעלך תחלוץ) and goes barefoot (יחף).
The Gemara objects that the verse might refer to patched shoes (מנעלים המטולאים), just as 'naked' (ערום) there means in worn-out clothes, not literal nakedness.

items.text: Final derivation that going without shoes is an affliction from Jeremiah
items.text_en: Final derivation that going without shoes is an affliction from Jeremiah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers a final derivation from Jeremiah: 'Refrain your foot from being bare (מיחף) and your throat from thirst.' The verse connects barefootedness to affliction, and the Gemara interprets it as a warning to avoid sin so that one does not come to barefootedness.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's final derivation
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's final derivation
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives that going without shoes is an affliction from Jeremiah 2:25, which connects barefootedness (יָחֵף) to thirst, and interprets the verse as a warning to avoid sin so that one does not come to barefootedness.

items.text: Derivation that marital relations are an affliction from Laban's words
items.text_en: Derivation that marital relations are an affliction from Laban's words
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that marital relations are called עינוי from the verse where Laban says to Jacob: 'If you afflict (תענה) my daughters.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that marital relations (תַּשְׁמִישׁ הַמִּטָּה) are called an affliction (עִנּוּי)?

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the verses 'If you afflict' and 'If you take'
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the verses 'If you afflict' and 'If you take'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether both phrases refer to afflictions or one to marital relations and one to afflictions, concluding from the word order that 'If you afflict' refers to marital relations and 'If you take' to afflictions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that 'If you afflict' refers to marital relations and 'If you take' to afflictions, then rejects the alternative that both refer to afflictions because the verse writes 'and if you take' with a conjunctive vav.

The Gemara suggests that both phrases could refer to afflictions—one for his own afflictions and one for afflictions from the world—but rejects this because the verse writes 'If you afflict and if you take' in that order, not the reverse.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about marital relations as affliction
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about marital relations as affliction
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether marital relations themselves are called affliction, citing the verse 'And he lay with her and afflicted her'. Abaye responds that the verse refers to afflicting her through other sexual acts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether marital relations themselves are called affliction (עינוי), citing the verse 'וַיִּשְׁכַּב אוֹתָהּ וַיְעַנֶּהָ' (and he lay with her and afflicted her).
Abaye responds that the verse refers to afflicting her through other sexual acts (ביאות אחרות), not through marital relations themselves.

items.text: Baraita on washing and anointing on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Baraita on washing and anointing on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may not wash or anoint even part of the body, but if dirty with mud or excrement, or if sick or having scabs, one may do so normally. Additionally, a woman may wet one hand to give bread to her child.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general prohibition against washing or anointing any part of the body on Yom Kippur, with exceptions for one who is dirty with mud or excrement, or who is sick or has scabs.

sub.text: Baraita (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel via Tanna debei Menasheh)
sub.text_en: Baraita (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel via Tanna debei Menasheh)
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that a woman may wet one hand to give bread to her child, without concern.

items.text: Story of Shammai the Elder and the decree to feed with two hands
items.text_en: Story of Shammai the Elder and the decree to feed with two hands
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Shammai the Elder refused to feed with one hand, and the Sages decreed he must feed with two hands. Abaye explains the reason is due to the prohibition of 'shevut' (resting on Yom Kippur).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Shammai the Elder refused to feed a child with one hand, and the Sages decreed he must feed with two hands.
The Gemara asks why the Sages imposed this decree.
Abaye explains that the decree is due to the prohibition of שְׁבוּת (resting on Yom Kippur), which forbids even a semblance of labor.

items.text: Baraita on crossing water to greet a superior and the question of a teacher going to a student
items.text_en: Baraita on crossing water to greet a superior and the question of a teacher going to a student
items.desc_en: A baraita permits crossing water up to the neck to greet one's father, teacher, or a greater person. The Gemara questions whether a teacher may do so for a student, and cites Rav Yitzchak bar bar Chana's testimony about Ze'iri going to his teacher Rav Chiya bar Ashi, with Rav Ashi clarifying the roles.

sub.desc_en: A baraita permits crossing water up to the neck to greet one's father, teacher, or a greater person.
The Gemara raises a question: may a teacher cross water to greet a student?

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar bar Chana's testimony
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar bar Chana's testimony
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar bar Chana testifies that Ze'iri went to his teacher Rav Chiya bar Ashi, implying a teacher may go to a student.
Rav Ashi clarifies that in that case, Rav Chiya bar Ashi was the student and Ze'iri was the teacher, so the testimony does not permit a teacher going to a student.

items.text: Rava and Rav Yosef's rulings on crossing water for fruit guarding and Torah study
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Yosef's rulings on crossing water for fruit guarding and Torah study
items.desc_en: Rava permits the people of the other side of the river to cross to guard fruit, citing a supporting baraita. Rav Yosef permits crossing to come to the lecture but not to return, with Abaye objecting that this will cause future stumbling; an alternative version permits both directions.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits the people of the other side of the river to cross the water to guard fruit.
Abaye tells Rava that a baraita supports his ruling: fruit guards may cross up to their necks in water without concern.
Rav Yosef permits the people of Bei Tarbu to cross to come to the lecture but not to return.
Abaye objects that if only one direction is permitted, it will cause future stumbling when people hesitate to come.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's ruling
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's ruling
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Yosef permitted both directions, and Abaye explains that the return is permitted to prevent future stumbling.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda's ruling on crossing water for Torah study
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda's ruling on crossing water for Torah study
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda are standing on a riverbank, and Rami bar Pappa asks if he may cross to ask a halachic matter. Rav Yehuda rules that one may cross, provided he does not remove his hand from under his cloak; an alternative version attributes this to Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Rav Yehuda and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda stand on a riverbank, and Rami bar Pappa calls out from the other side, asking if he may cross to ask a halachic matter.
Rav Yehuda rules that one may cross, provided he does not remove his hand from under his cloak, citing the joint opinion of Rav and Shmuel.
An alternative version attributes the same ruling to Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda, citing a baraita.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and the derivation from Ezekiel's vision of the river
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and the derivation from Ezekiel's vision of the river
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that crossing water even on a weekday is limited, citing verses from Ezekiel's vision of the river: one may cross up to the ankles, knees, and loins, but beyond that is forbidden. The Gemara explains that a swift stream is different, and derives that one may not cross by swimming or in any boat, large or small.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that even on a weekday crossing water is limited, citing the verse from Ezekiel about crossing up to the ankles.
Rav Yosef continues citing the Ezekiel passage, showing that crossing is permitted only up to the knees and loins, but beyond that is forbidden.
Abaye answers that a swift stream (like Ezekiel's river) is different from still water, so the limitation does not apply to still water.
The Gemara derives from the verses that one may not cross the river by swimming, in a small boat, or in a large ship, as translated by Rav Yosef.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Pazzi and Rabbi Pinchas on the river's significance
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Pazzi and Rabbi Pinchas on the river's significance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Pazzi teaches that even the Angel of Death cannot cross the river, linking verses. Rabbi Pinchas in the name of Rav Huna of Tzippora describes the spring from the Holy of Holies, which grows from the size of locust horns to a thread, then a web, and finally a small flask at the entrance of the Temple courtyard.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Pazzi teaches that even the Angel of Death cannot cross the river, linking the verse 'בל תלך בו אניה שיט' (no ship of rowing shall go in it) with the verse 'משוט בארץ' (from roaming the earth).

sub.text: Rabbi Pinchas in the name of Rav Huna of Tzippora
sub.text_en: Rabbi Pinchas in the name of Rav Huna of Tzippora
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas, citing Rav Huna of Tzippora, describes the spring from the Holy of Holies that grows from the size of locust horns to a thread, then a web, and finally a small flask at the entrance of the Temple courtyard, citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teaching about the water.

items.text: Opening: The future spring and a hint about niddah
items.text_en: Opening: The future spring and a hint about niddah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about a spring flowing from the Temple, which will become a stream for purification. Rav Yosef derives a hint that a niddah must immerse up to her neck, but the halakha does not follow him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about a spring flowing from the Temple, which will become a stream for purification of those with ritual impurities.
Rav Yosef derives a hint that a niddah must immerse up to her neck, but the halakha does not follow him.

items.text: Crossing water on Shabbat and Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Crossing water on Shabbat and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about crossing water on Shabbat when one is wearing shoes (since on Yom Kippur there is no shoe issue). Nechemya testifies that Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Asi crossed a stream by wearing their shoes. Then it asks about sandals; Rav Rihumi testifies that Ravina crossed through clothing, and Rav Ashi says sandals are initially forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: on Yom Kippur there is no shoe issue, but on Shabbat when shoes are worn, what is the rule for crossing water?
Nechemya testifies that he saw Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Asi cross a stream by wearing their shoes (through clothing).
The Gemara asks: shoes are settled, but what about sandals?
Rav Rihumi testifies that he saw Ravina cross through clothing (wearing sandals).
Rav Ashi rules that sandals are forbidden לכתחילה (a-priori) for crossing water.

items.text: Story of Ravina and the Exilarch
items.text_en: Story of Ravina and the Exilarch
items.desc_en: The Exilarch came to Hagronya; Ravina did not attend the lecture. The next day, Rafram tried to embarrass Ravina, asking why he didn't come. Ravina gave excuses: his foot hurt, there was a stream, and he didn't know about Rav Ashi's ruling that sandals are initially forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: the Exilarch came to Hagronya, all the rabbis attended the lecture except Ravina.
The next day, Rafram seeks to embarrass Ravina before the Exilarch by asking why he did not attend the lecture.
Ravina answers that his foot hurt, and when asked why he did not wear shoes, he explains the pain was on the top of his foot.
Rafram asks why Ravina did not wear a sandal instead, and Ravina responds that there was a stream of water on the path.

Rafram asks why Ravina did not cross the stream by wearing the sandal in the manner of a garment, and Ravina responds that he did not hold of Rav Ashi's ruling that a sandal is forbidden לכתחילה (as an initial practice).

items.text: Laws of washing and cooling on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Laws of washing and cooling on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: Judah bar Gerogrot teaches that sitting on moist clay is forbidden on Yom Kippur. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi specifies moist clay that can be squeezed. Abaye adds that it is forbidden only if one intends to squeeze. Rav Yehuda permits cooling with fruits. Various Amoraim discuss cooling methods: with a gourd, a silver cup (full forbidden, empty permitted for silver, but Rav says empty is also forbidden due to danger), and earthenware is always forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Judah bar Gerogrot teaches that sitting on moist clay is forbidden on Yom Kippur.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi specifies that the prohibition applies only to moist clay that can be squeezed.
Abaye adds that the prohibition applies only if one intends to squeeze the clay.
Rav Yehuda permits cooling oneself with fruits on Yom Kippur.
Rav Yehuda himself would cool with a gourd (קרא).
Rabbah would cool with a gourd (יָנוֹקָא).
Rava would cool with a silver cup.
Rav Pappa rules that a full silver cup is forbidden but an empty one is permitted, while earthenware is always forbidden because it absorbs heat.
Rav objects that even an empty silver cup is forbidden due to danger (of scraping).

items.text: Practice of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with a towel on Yom Kippur and Tisha B'Av
items.text_en: Practice of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with a towel on Yom Kippur and Tisha B'Av
items.desc_en: Ze'eira bar Chama, host of many sages, tells Rav Yosef bar Yehoshua ben Levi about his father's practice: on Yom Kippur eve, he would soak a towel and wring it, then use it the next day to wipe his face, hands, and feet. On Tisha B'Av eve, he would soak it and pass it over his eyes. Rabbah bar Mari reports a similar practice but reversed for the two days. Rabbi Yaakov challenges Rabbi Yirmeya bar Tachlifa, saying he taught the opposite and was refuted with the law of squeezing.

sub.text: Ze'eira bar Chama to Rav Yosef bar Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Ze'eira bar Chama to Rav Yosef bar Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Ze'eira bar Chama tells Rav Yosef bar Yehoshua ben Levi about his father Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's practice: on Yom Kippur eve he would soak a towel and wring it, then use it the next day to wipe his face, hands, and feet; on Tisha B'Av eve he would soak it and pass it over his eyes.

Rabbah bar Mari reports a similar practice but reversed for the two days: on Tisha B'Av eve the towel is placed under the head and used the next day to wipe face, hands, and feet; on Yom Kippur eve it is wrung and used the next day for the eyes.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Tachlifa
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Tachlifa
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov challenges Rabbi Yirmeya bar Tachlifa, saying he taught the opposite and was refuted with the law of squeezing (סחיטה).

items.text: Does a sage need permission to permit firstborn animals?
items.text_en: Does a sage need permission to permit firstborn animals?
items.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Tachlifa reports that Rabbi Elazar was asked: does an elder sitting in the study hall need permission to permit firstborn animals? The question is whether the rule that the Nasi's house reserved this right applies, or if an elder is exempt. Rabbi Tzadok ben Chakola testified that Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, an elder, took permission. Rabbi Abba corrects: Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra was a priest, and the question was whether the halakha follows Rabbi Meir (who disqualifies a suspect from judging) or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (who trusts him for others). The answer was like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.text: Rav Menashya bar Tachlifa reporting Rav Amram reporting Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Tachlifa reporting Rav Amram reporting Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Tachlifa reports that Rabbi Elazar was asked whether an elder sitting in the study hall needs permission to permit firstborn animals.

The Gemara clarifies the underlying question: whether the rule that the Nasi's house reserved the right to permit firstborns applies, or whether an elder is exempt; Rabbi Tzadok ben Chakola testifies that Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, an elder, took permission.

Rabbi Abba corrects that Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra was a priest, and the real question was whether the halakha follows Rabbi Meir (who disqualifies a suspect from judging) or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (who trusts him for others); the answer was like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

items.text: Beginning of a new question: going out with a sandal of...
items.text_en: Beginning of a new question: going out with a sandal of...
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new inquiry about whether one may go out with a sandal of a certain type, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new inquiry about whether one may go out with a sandal of a certain type on Yom Kippur.

items.text: Stories about wearing sandals of reed-grass on Yom Kippur and public fasts
items.text_en: Stories about wearing sandals of reed-grass on Yom Kippur and public fasts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani and Rabbah bar bar Chanah report that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Elazar of Ninveh wore sandals of reed-grass on Yom Kippur and public fasts, respectively, and when asked about the other day, they said it is no different. The Gemara then lists other Amoraim who wore similar footwear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about wearing sandals of reed-grass on Yom Kippur, and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi wore such sandals on Yom Kippur and said the same applies to a public fast.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports that Rabbi Elazar of Ninveh wore sandals of reed-grass on a public fast and said the same applies to Yom Kippur.
The Gemara lists Rav Yehuda, Abaye, Rava, and Rabbah bar Rav Huna who also wore similar non-leather footwear on Yom Kippur or public fasts.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah about a wooden leg and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah about a wooden leg and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama raises an objection from a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir permits a amputee to go out with his wooden leg on Shabbat, but Rabbi Yosei forbids it, and it is taught that both agree it is forbidden on Yom Kippur. Abaye explains that the wooden leg has compartments for padding, and the prohibition is due to pleasure. Rava challenges this, arguing that if it is not a shoe, padding does not make it one, and pleasure without footwear is not forbidden on Yom Kippur, citing Rabbah bar Rav Huna's practice. He also notes that the latter clause of the Mishnah implies the first case is without padding.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama raises an objection from a Mishnah about a wooden leg, where Rabbi Meir permits and Rabbi Yosei forbids it on Shabbat, and both agree it is forbidden on Yom Kippur.
Abaye explains that the wooden leg has compartments for padding (כתיתין), and the prohibition on Yom Kippur is due to pleasure (תענוג).

Rava objects that if the wooden leg is not a shoe, padding does not make it one, and pleasure without footwear is not forbidden on Yom Kippur, citing Rabbah bar Rav Huna's practice, and notes that the latter clause of the Mishnah implies the first case is without padding.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation: the dispute is about a decree on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation: the dispute is about a decree on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rava concludes that everyone agrees the wooden leg is a shoe, and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei is about Shabbat: one opinion decrees that one might remove it and carry it four cubits, while the other does not decree.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that the wooden leg is universally considered a shoe, and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei is about a rabbinic decree on Shabbat lest one carry it four cubits in the public domain.

items.text: Children's exemptions on Yom Kippur and the rationale
items.text_en: Children's exemptions on Yom Kippur and the rationale
items.desc_en: A baraisa states that children are permitted all things except wearing sandals. The Gemara questions why sandals are different, as one might say people made them, but the same applies to washing and anointing. It answers that sandals cannot be done from yesterday due to the danger of scorpions, as Shmuel said. The Gemara then notes that the baraisa says 'permitted' initially, so it explains that for things that are not their regular upbringing, the Sages decreed, but for their regular upbringing, they did not. Abaye cites his mother's advice on a child's upbringing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that children are permitted all things on Yom Kippur except wearing sandals.
The Gemara questions why sandals are singled out, since washing and anointing are also human-made activities.
The Gemara suggests that washing and anointing could have been done yesterday, but sandals cannot.
The Gemara objects that sandals too could have been made yesterday.
The Gemara explains that sandals cannot be worn from yesterday due to the danger of scorpions, citing Shmuel's statement that wearing shoes brings one close to death.
The Gemara objects that the baraita says 'permitted' לכתחילה (the ideal standard), implying no prohibition at all.
The Gemara resolves that the Sages decreed only for things not part of a child's regular upbringing, but not for their regular upbringing.
Abaye cites his mother's advice on a child's regular upbringing, and notes that Rabbah bought cheap clay vessels for his children to break.

items.text: The king, bride, and woman after childbirth: exceptions to the prohibitions
items.text_en: The king, bride, and woman after childbirth: exceptions to the prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a king and a bride may wash their faces, and a woman after childbirth may wear sandals. The Gemara identifies this as the opinion of Rabbi Chananya ben Tradyon citing Rabbi Eliezer, against the first Tanna. It explains the reasons: for the king, because 'the king's beauty shall your eyes see'; for the bride, so she not be repulsive to her husband; for the woman after childbirth, for cold protection. Rav asks Rabbi Chiya about the duration for a bride, and he answers thirty days. Shmuel adds that if one is in danger from a scorpion, it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a king and a bride may wash their faces, and a woman after childbirth may wear sandals.
The Gemara asks which Tanna authored this Mishnah, and identifies it as Rabbi Chananya ben Tradyon.
A baraita is cited: the first Tanna prohibits washing for king and bride and prohibits sandals for the woman after childbirth, while Rabbi Chananya ben Tradyon citing Rabbi Eliezer permits them.
The Gemara explains the reasons: for the king, because 'the king's beauty shall your eyes see'; for the bride, so she not be repulsive to her husband.
Rav asks Rabbi Chiya for how long the bride is permitted to wash her face.
Rabbi Chiya answers that the bride is permitted for thirty days, as taught in a baraita.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation for the woman after childbirth
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation for the woman after childbirth
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the woman after childbirth may wear sandals for cold protection.
Shmuel adds that if one is in danger from a scorpion, wearing sandals is permitted.

items.text: Transition to the next Mishnah: the measure of a date-bulk
items.text_en: Transition to the next Mishnah: the measure of a date-bulk
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins the next Mishnah which states that one who eats a date-bulk is liable. Rav Pappa raises a question about this measure, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about the measure of a large date for eating on Yom Kippur.
Rav Pappa raises a question about the measure, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry about the date's definition
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry about the date's definition
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a question about whether the date is measured with or without its pit, and whether a bone the size of a barley grain is measured with or without its shell, wet or dry. The Gemara notes that Rav Papa and Rav Ashi each did not need to ask the other's question because their respective terms (גסה and לחה) clarify the matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about whether the date (כותבת) is measured with or without its pit.
Rav Ashi asks whether a bone the size of a barley grain is measured with or without its shell, and whether it is measured wet or dry.

The Gemara explains that Rav Ashi did not need to ask Rav Papa's question because the term 'גסה' (large) clarifies the matter, and Rav Papa did not need to ask Rav Ashi's question because 'לחה' (wet) is called a spike and 'שלא בקליפתה' (without its shell) is called a husk.

items.text: Rava's statement about the large date and a challenge
items.text_en: Rava's statement about the large date and a challenge
