Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya expounds the verse 'מִכֹּל חַטֹּאתֵיכֶם לִפְנֵי ה׳ תִּטְהָרוּ' to teach that Yom Kippur atones for sins between man and God but not for interpersonal sins until the fellow is appeased.
Rabbi Akiva adds that Israel is fortunate because their Father in Heaven purifies them, like a מִקְוֶה (ritual bath) purifies the impure.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between definite and suspended guilt-offerings
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between definite and suspended guilt-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'definite guilt-offering' (asham vadai) and not a suspended guilt-offering (asham talui). It offers two answers: either the Mishnah refers to complete atonement, which the suspended offering does not provide, or it refers to offerings that no other atonement follows, whereas a suspended offering is followed by Yom Kippur atonement, as per a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies 'definite guilt-offering' (אשם ודאי) and excludes a suspended guilt-offering (אשם תלוי), given that the latter also has atonement (כפרה) written regarding it.
The first answer explains that the Mishnah refers to offerings that provide complete atonement (כפרה גמורה), which the suspended guilt-offering does not.
The alternative answer explains that the Mishnah refers to offerings for which no other atonement follows, whereas a suspended guilt-offering is followed by Yom Kippur atonement.

A baraita is cited to support the alternative answer: those liable for definite sin-offerings and guilt-offerings remain obligated even after Yom Kippur, but those liable for suspended guilt-offerings are exempt.

items.text: Gemara: Yom Kippur atonement requires repentance
items.text_en: Gemara: Yom Kippur atonement requires repentance
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says Yom Kippur atones 'with repentance,' implying not without it. This seems to disagree with Rabbi, who holds Yom Kippur atones for most sins even without repentance. The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi, repentance requires Yom Kippur, but Yom Kippur does not require repentance (i.e., it atones without repentance for most sins).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says death and Yom Kippur atone 'with repentance,' implying not without it, and asks whether this contradicts Rabbi's view.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi holds that Yom Kippur atones for most sins even without repentance, except for three severe sins.
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi, repentance requires Yom Kippur, but Yom Kippur does not require repentance (i.e., it atones without repentance for most sins).

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'light transgressions' and a contradiction
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'light transgressions' and a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists both positive and negative commandments as light, since a positive commandment is lighter. Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah refers to a negative commandment that can be rectified by a positive act. The Gemara then raises a contradiction from a baraita listing light transgressions, which includes a full negative commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions both positive and negative commandments as light, since a positive commandment is lighter and should be obvious.
Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah refers to a negative commandment that can be rectified by a positive act (לא תעשה שניתק לעשה).
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that lists light transgressions as including a full negative commandment (לא תעשה גמור), not just one rectified by a positive act.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Is the prohibition of 'Lo Tissa' excluded from repentance?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Is the prohibition of 'Lo Tissa' excluded from repentance?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the sin of 'Lo Tissa' (taking God's name in vain) is excluded from repentance, citing Rabbi Yehuda's view that repentance atones for lesser sins but only suspends punishment for graver ones. A second source suggests that 'Lo Tissa' is uniquely unforgivable, but the Gemara concludes this is a dispute among Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether the prohibition of 'Lo Tissa' (taking God's name in vain) is excluded from repentance, citing a source that includes similar sins.
Rabbi Yehuda teaches that repentance atones for sins less severe than 'Lo Tissa', but for 'Lo Tissa' and similar sins, repentance suspends punishment and Yom Kippur atones.
A second source argues that 'Lo Tissa' is uniquely unforgivable, as the verse 'וְנַקֵּה' (He will not cleanse) applies only to taking God's name, while other negative commandments are cleansed.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on categories of atonement and the paradox of 'Nakeh' and 'Lo Yenakeh'
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on categories of atonement and the paradox of 'Nakeh' and 'Lo Yenakeh'
items.desc_en: A baraisa outlines that repentance atones for positive commands and negative commands that are breakable to a positive command, while Yom Kippur atones for kareis and court-imposed death penalties. Rabbi Elazar resolves the apparent contradiction between 'Nakeh' and 'Lo Yenakeh' by explaining that God cleanses those who repent but not those who do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that the dispute is among Tannaim, citing a baraita that distinguishes between different categories of sins and their atonement.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse 'וְנַקֵּה' (He will not cleanse) applies only to those who do not repent, while those who repent are cleansed.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's four divisions of atonement and the unique severity of Chillul Hashem
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's four divisions of atonement and the unique severity of Chillul Hashem
items.desc_en: Rabbi Matya ben Charash asks Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya about Rabbi Yishmael's four categories of atonement. The response details three categories: repentance alone for positive commands, repentance plus Yom Kippur for negative commands, and repentance plus Yom Kippur plus suffering for kareis and death penalties. For Chillul Hashem, all these only suspend punishment, and only death fully atones.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Matya ben Charash asks Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya about the four categories of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael taught, and Rabbi Elazar responds that there are three, with repentance accompanying each.
For one who violates a positive commandment and repents, forgiveness is immediate, as the verse says 'שׁוּבוּ בָּנִים שׁוֹבָבִים' (Return, wayward children).

For one who violates a negative commandment and repents, repentance suspends punishment and Yom Kippur atones, as the verse says 'כִּי בַיּוֹם הַזֶּה יְכַפֵּר עֲלֵיכֶם' (For on this day He will atone for you).

For one who violates kareitot (extirpation) or court-imposed death penalties and repents, repentance and Yom Kippur suspend punishment, and suffering purges the sin, as the verse says 'וּפָקַדְתִּי בְשֵׁבֶט פִּשְׁעָם' (I will punish their transgression with a rod).

For one guilty of חילול השם (desecration of God's name), neither repentance, Yom Kippur, nor suffering suffice; all suspend punishment, but only death purges the sin, as the verse says 'עַד תְּמוּתוּן' (until you die).

For one guilty of חילול השם (desecration of God's name), repentance, Yom Kippur, and suffering only suspend punishment, and only death fully atones, as the verse 'אִם יְכוּפַּר הֶעָוֹן הַזֶּה לָכֶם עַד תְּמוּתוּן' (This iniquity shall not be atoned for you until you die) teaches.

items.text: Amoraic definitions of Chillul Hashem
items.text_en: Amoraic definitions of Chillul Hashem
items.desc_en: Rav defines Chillul Hashem as taking meat without immediate payment in a place where credit is not customary. Abaye qualifies this, and Ravina notes that Mata Mechasya is such a place. Rabbi Yochanan defines it as walking four cubits without Torah or tefillin. Rabbi Yitzchak and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak add that causing others to be ashamed or saying 'May his Master forgive him' also constitutes Chillul Hashem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a concrete example of what constitutes Chillul Hashem (desecration of God's name).
Rav defines Chillul Hashem as taking meat from a butcher without paying immediately in a place where credit is not customary.
Abaye qualifies that Rav's example applies only in a place where merchants do not demand payment, but where they do demand it, there is no Chillul Hashem.
Ravina notes that Mata Mechasya is a place where payment is demanded, so Rav's example would not apply there.
The Gemara describes how Abaye would take meat from two partners, pay each a coin, then bring them together to settle accounts, avoiding Chillul Hashem.
Rabbi Yochanan defines Chillul Hashem as walking four cubits without Torah study or tefillin.
Yitzchak de'Bei Rabbi Yannai defines Chillul Hashem as any situation where one's reputation causes his colleagues to be ashamed.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak defines Chillul Hashem as when people say about someone, 'May his Master forgive him.'

items.text: The positive and negative aspects of Chillul Hashem through a person's conduct
items.text_en: The positive and negative aspects of Chillul Hashem through a person's conduct
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraisa explaining that one who studies Torah and interacts with people pleasantly causes God's name to be loved, while one who studies Torah but is dishonest or rude causes God's name to be profaned, as people speak ill of his learning.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita: one who studies Torah and serves scholars but conducts business honestly and speaks gently causes God's name to be loved, as people praise him and the verse says 'בְּךָ אֶתְפָּאָר' (in you I am glorified).

The baraita contrasts: one who studies Torah but deals dishonestly and speaks harshly causes God's name to be desecrated, as people say 'Woe to him' and the verse says 'עַם ה׳ אֵלֶּה וּמֵאַרְצוֹ יָצָאוּ' (these are God's people who left His land).

items.text: Homilies on the greatness of repentance
items.text_en: Homilies on the greatness of repentance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina teaches that repentance brings healing to the world. He resolves a contradiction between verses about 'wayward children' and 'healing your backslidings' by distinguishing repentance from love versus fear. Rav Yehuda resolves another contradiction by adding suffering as a factor. Rabbi Levi concludes that repentance reaches the Throne of Glory.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina opens with a homily that repentance brings healing to the world, citing the verse 'ארפא משובתם אהבם נדבה' (I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely).

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina raises a contradiction between two verses about repentance — one calling Israel 'wayward children' and the other promising healing — and resolves it by distinguishing repentance from love (אהבה) versus repentance from fear (יראה).

Rav Yehuda raises another contradiction between verses about repentance and adds suffering (יסורין) as a factor, and Rabbi Levi concludes that repentance reaches the Throne of Glory, citing the verse 'שובה ישראל עד ה׳ אלוהיך' (Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yonatan on the power of repentance
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yonatan on the power of repentance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that repentance is great because it overrides a negative commandment of the Torah, citing a verse from Jeremiah. Rabbi Yonatan adds that repentance brings redemption, as per Isaiah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that repentance is great because it overrides a negative commandment of the Torah, citing a verse from Jeremiah.
Rabbi Yonatan adds that repentance brings redemption, as per Isaiah.

items.text: Resh Lakish on repentance turning intentional sins into errors or merits
items.text_en: Resh Lakish on repentance turning intentional sins into errors or merits
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish first says repentance turns intentional sins into errors, then contradicts himself by saying it turns them into merits. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one is from love, the other from fear.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish opens by stating that repentance is great because it turns intentional sins into errors, citing a verse that calls an intentional sin a 'stumbling block'.
The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory statement from Resh Lakish that repentance turns intentional sins into merits, citing a verse about the righteous person who does justice.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that one statement applies when repentance is from love (turning sins into merits) and the other from fear (turning sins into errors).

items.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan on repentance lengthening life
items.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan on repentance lengthening life
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that repentance lengthens a person's years, citing Ezekiel.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that repentance lengthens a person's years, citing Ezekiel.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak on God's mercy versus human mercy
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak on God's mercy versus human mercy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak contrasts human behavior, where appeasement is uncertain, with God's willingness to accept verbal repentance, even for secret sins, and credits the penitent as if offering sacrifices.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabba bar Mari
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabba bar Mari
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak opens by contrasting human mercy, where appeasement is uncertain, with God's mercy.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabba bar Mari
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabba bar Mari
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak concludes that God accepts verbal repentance even for secret sins, credits the penitent with goodness, and considers it as if they offered voluntary sacrifices.

items.text: Rabbi Meir on repentance benefiting the entire world
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir on repentance benefiting the entire world
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that repentance of a single individual leads to forgiveness for the whole world, as per the verse 'I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely, for My anger is turned away from him.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir teaches that repentance of a single individual leads to forgiveness for the whole world, as per the verse 'I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely, for My anger is turned away from him.'

items.text: Definition of a penitent and the rule of concealing sins
items.text_en: Definition of a penitent and the rule of concealing sins
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda defines a penitent as one who faces the same temptation twice and avoids it. A contradiction between verses about concealing sins is resolved: public sins must be confessed, private sins may be concealed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes a penitent (בעל תשובה), and Rav Yehuda answers that it is one who faces the same transgression twice and avoids it.
Rav Yehuda demonstrates that the penitent must avoid the same woman, same time, and same place.
Rav Yehuda raises a contradiction between two verses: one praises concealing sin, the other condemns it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: a public sin must be confessed, a private sin may be concealed.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah in the name of Rav Nachman offers an alternative resolution: sins between man and his fellow must be confessed, sins between man and God may be concealed.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda on forgiveness for repeated sins
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda on forgiveness for repeated sins
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda states that a person is forgiven for the first three offenses but not the fourth, citing Amos and Job. The Gemara clarifies that this applies even to an individual, not just the community.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda states that a person is forgiven for the first three offenses but not the fourth, citing Amos 2:6.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds a second proof from Job 33:29, showing that God acts with a person two or three times.
The Gemara asks why the baraita needed to cite a second verse (Job 33:29) in addition to Amos 2:6.
The Gemara explains that the second verse is needed to teach that the rule of forgiveness for three offenses applies even to an individual, not only to the community; after that, he is not forgiven.

items.text: Confession of sins on Yom Kippur and the prohibition of repeating confession
items.text_en: Confession of sins on Yom Kippur and the prohibition of repeating confession
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that sins confessed on one Yom Kippur should not be confessed again unless repeated. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov argues that repeating confession is praiseworthy. The Gemara resolves the contradiction with Rav Huna's statement that repeating a sin makes it permissible.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach in a baraita that sins confessed on one Yom Kippur should not be confessed again unless repeated; if one confesses without repeating, he is like a dog returning to its vomit.

רבי אליעזר בן יעקב (Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov) argues that repeating confession is praiseworthy, citing the verse 'כי פשעי אני אדע וחטאתי נגדי תמיד' (For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the verse about the dog applies according to Rav Huna's statement.
Rav Huna states that once a person commits a transgression and repeats it, it becomes permitted to him.
The Gemara objects: Can it enter your mind that it is actually permitted?
The Gemara corrects: Rather, say it becomes to him as if it were permitted, i.e., he treats it lightly.

items.text: The requirement to specify the sin in confession
items.text_en: The requirement to specify the sin in confession
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava holds that one must specify the sin, citing Moses' confession. Rabbi Akiva disagrees, citing the verse 'Happy is he whose transgression is forgiven.' The Gemara explains Moses' specification as per Rabbi Yannai, who said that the abundance of gold and silver caused the sin.

sub.desc_en: The anonymous Tannaic statement rules that one must specify the sin in confession, citing Moses' confession that specified the sin of the golden calf.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava endorses the requirement to specify the sin, as per the cited verse.
Rabbi Akiva objects, citing a verse that praises one whose sin is covered, implying that specification is not required.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that Moses' specification was not to fulfill a requirement but to explain the cause of the sin, as per Rabbi Yannai.
Rabbi Yannai explains that Moses attributed the sin to the abundance of gold and silver God gave Israel, which caused them to make the golden calf.

items.text: Moses and David: publicizing versus concealing sin
items.text_en: Moses and David: publicizing versus concealing sin
items.desc_en: Moses insisted his sin be recorded, while David asked that his sin be concealed. A parable of two women punished in court illustrates: one who sinned and one who ate unripe figs of the Sabbatical year; the latter's sin was publicized to avoid misunderstanding.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces two good leaders, Moses and David, and contrasts their attitudes toward having their sins recorded.

sub.text: Supporting verses for Moses and David
sub.text_en: Supporting verses for Moses and David
sub.desc_en: Moses insisted his sin be recorded (citing the verse about his lack of faith), while David asked that his sin be concealed (citing the verse 'ashrei n'sui pesha').

A parable illustrates: two women were punished in court — one who sinned and one who ate unripe figs of the Sabbatical year; the latter's sin was publicized to avoid misunderstanding, analogous to Moses publicizing his sin.

items.text: Publicizing hypocrites and the fate of the wicked
items.text_en: Publicizing hypocrites and the fate of the wicked
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses publicizing hypocrites to prevent desecration of God's name, and that repentance of confirmed sinners delays punishment. It concludes with sayings about the tranquility of the wicked and the humility of judges Rav and Rava before entering court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that hypocrites are publicized to prevent חילול השם (desecration of God's name), and that repentance of confirmed sinners delays punishment even after the decree is sealed.
The Gemara offers aphorisms about the tranquility of the wicked ending in calamity, and records Rav's prayer before entering court, expressing humility and hope that his exit be like his entry.
The Gemara introduces Rava's similar prayer before going out to judge, but the text is cut off, indicating a parallel practice to Rav's.

items.text: Opening aggadic exposition on the fate of the wicked and righteous
items.text_en: Opening aggadic exposition on the fate of the wicked and righteous
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a series of aggadic statements contrasting the fate of the wicked, who are given leeway in this world but ultimately perish, with the righteous, who are judged strictly but merit eternal reward. It cites verses about Ahab and Moses to illustrate that divine favor in this world is not necessarily good, and that the righteous benefit their descendants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with an aggadic description of the wicked person who goes to his death willingly but does not benefit his household.
Rav Zutra cites a verse about the fleeting nature of wealth when he was carried on shoulders during the festival Shabbat.
The Gemara explains that it is not good for the wicked to receive favor in this world, citing Ahab as an example whose punishment was delayed.
The Gemara explains that it is good for the righteous not to receive favor in this world, citing Moses as an example whose death was decreed for lack of faith.
The Gemara states that the righteous merit reward for their descendants, citing Aaron's sons who were spared from burning due to their father's merit.
The Gemara states that the wicked cause their descendants to be liable, citing Canaan's descendants who were fit for appointment but suffered due to their father's guilt.

items.text: Principle of influencing the public
items.text_en: Principle of influencing the public
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that one who leads the public to merit will not sin, while one who leads the public to sin will find repentance nearly impossible. This is explained by the desire to avoid a situation where the leader and his disciples end up in different afterlives.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that one who leads the public to merit will not sin.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this principle.
The Gemara explains that the reason is to prevent the leader from being in Gehinnom while his disciples are in Gan Eden, citing a verse.
The Gemara adds the parallel case: one who leads the public to sin is prevented from repentance, so that he is not in Gan Eden while his disciples are in Gehinnom, citing another verse.

items.text: The one who says 'I will sin and repent'
items.text_en: The one who says 'I will sin and repent'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's statement about one who repeatedly sins with the intention to repent is analyzed. Rav Huna in the name of Rav explains that repeating a sin makes it seem permissible to the sinner, though not actually permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of one who says 'I will sin and repent, I will sin and repent.'
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats 'I will sin and repent' twice.
Rav Huna in the name of Rav explains that once a person commits a transgression and repeats it, it becomes permitted to him.
The Gemara objects: could it really enter your mind that it becomes actually permitted?
The Gemara resolves: rather, it becomes for him like something permitted (he treats it as permissible, though it is not).

items.text: Yom Kippur atonement without repentance
items.text_en: Yom Kippur atonement without repentance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Yom Kippur does not atone for one who says 'I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone.' The Gemara questions whether this contradicts Rabbi's view that Yom Kippur atones even without repentance, and resolves that the Mishnah refers to one who relies on Yom Kippur while sinning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone' does not receive atonement.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi's view that Yom Kippur atones even without repentance.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi says Yom Kippur atones for all sins whether or not one repents.
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi, the case is different because the sinner relies on Yom Kippur while sinning.

items.text: Interpersonal sins and Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Interpersonal sins and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chavu challenges Rabbi Avahu with a contradiction: the Mishnah says Yom Kippur does not atone for interpersonal sins, yet a verse implies that a judge (Elohim) can effect atonement. The Gemara resolves that the verse teaches that one must appease the other person, while for sins against God, repentance and good deeds suffice.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chavu's challenge to Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chavu's challenge to Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chavu challenges Rabbi Avahu by citing a contradiction: the Mishnah states that Yom Kippur does not atone for interpersonal sins, yet a verse (שמואל א ב:כה) says 'if a man sins against a man, the judge (אלהים) shall judge him,' implying atonement through a court.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the verse: the first clause teaches that one must appease the other person (the judge facilitates this), while the second clause teaches that for sins against God, only repentance (תשובה) and good deeds (מעשים טובים) suffice.

items.text: Laws of appeasing an offended party
items.text_en: Laws of appeasing an offended party
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that one who offends another, even verbally, must appease him. Rav Chisda adds that this must be done with three rows of three people each. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that one should not ask more than three times, and if the offended party has died, one must bring ten people to his grave and confess.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that one who offends another, even verbally, must appease him, citing a verse and explaining that if he has money he should give a gift, otherwise he should gather many friends to intercede.
Rav Chisda adds that the appeasement must be done with three rows of three people each, citing a verse that implies a public acknowledgment.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that one should not ask for forgiveness more than three times, and if the offended party has died, one must bring ten people to his grave and confess.

items.text: Stories of rabbis seeking forgiveness
items.text_en: Stories of rabbis seeking forgiveness
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates stories of Rabbi Yirmeya, Rabbi Zeira, and Rav, who went to great lengths to appease those they had wronged. Rav's attempt to appease a butcher ended tragically when the butcher accidentally killed himself, illustrating the seriousness of seeking forgiveness before Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya, who had a grievance with Rabbi Abba, sits at Rabbi Abba's door and is drenched by a maidservant's water, then quotes a verse about raising the poor from the trash heap.
Rabbi Abba hears, goes out to appease Rabbi Yirmeya, citing the verse about appeasing a friend.
Rabbi Zeira would repeatedly pass before the person he wronged to make himself available for appeasement.
Rav goes to appease a butcher on Yom Kippur eve, but the butcher rejects him.
The butcher accidentally kills himself with a bone while splitting a head, and Rav enters Rabbi's house.

items.text: Rav's attempt to appease Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Rav's attempt to appease Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav tried to appease Rabbi Chanina multiple times before Yom Kippur but failed. It questions how Rav could do this given the rule that one should not ask more than three times, and how Rabbi Chanina could remain angry given the principle that one who overlooks his traits is forgiven. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Chanina saw in a dream that Rav would become a leader, so he refused to be appeased so that Rav would go to Babylonia to teach Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav tried to appease Rabbi Chanina thirteen times before Yom Kippur but failed.
The Gemara questions how Rav could ask for forgiveness more than three times, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's rule.
The Gemara answers that Rav is different, and then questions how Rabbi Chanina could remain angry given Rava's principle that one who overlooks his traits is forgiven.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Chanina saw in a dream that Rav would become a leader, so he refused to be appeased so that Rav would go to Babylonia to teach Torah.

items.text: Mitzvah of vidui on Yom Kippur eve
items.text_en: Mitzvah of vidui on Yom Kippur eve
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the primary mitzvah of vidui is at nightfall, but the Sages said to confess before eating lest one become confused. Even after eating, one confesses again in case something went wrong. Additionally, one confesses at every prayer: Maariv, Shacharit, Musaf, Mincha, and Ne'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the primary mitzvah of vidui (confession) on Yom Kippur eve is at nightfall, but the Sages ruled to confess before eating lest one become confused during the meal.
The baraita adds that even after eating, one confesses again in case something went wrong during the meal.
The baraita concludes that one confesses at every prayer service: Maariv, Shacharit, Musaf, Mincha, and Ne'ilah.

items.text: Formulas for vidui and the essential confession
items.text_en: Formulas for vidui and the essential confession
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses where the individual and the prayer leader recite vidui, and records various formulas: Rav says 'Atah yode'a razei olam', Shmuel says 'Mima'amakei halev', Levi says 'U'vetoratecha katuv leimor', Rabbi Yochanan says 'Ribon ha'olamim', Rabbi Yehuda says 'Ki avonoteinu rabu', and Rav Hamnuna says a longer prayer. Mar Zutra notes that if one says 'Aval anachnu chatanu', that is the essential vidui, as Shmuel stood up when the prayer leader said it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the vidui is recited, answering that an individual says it after his prayer and the prayer leader says it in the middle.
The Gemara asks what formula is said, and Rav answers with 'You know the secrets of the world'.
Shmuel offers the formula 'From the depths of the heart'.
Levi offers the formula 'And in Your Torah it is written saying'.
Rabbi Yochanan offers the formula 'Master of the worlds'.
Rabbi Yehuda offers the formula 'For our iniquities are too many to count and our sins have grown too numerous to number'.
Rav Hamnuna offers a longer prayer expressing humility and a request for atonement without suffering.
The Gemara notes that this is the vidui of Rava for the entire year and of Rav Hamnuna Zuta for Yom Kippur.

Mar Zutra rules that if one says 'But we have sinned' (אבל אנחנו חטאנו), no further formula is needed, citing Bar Hamdudei's testimony that Shmuel stood up when the prayer leader said this phrase, proving it is the essential vidui.

items.text: Ne'ilah prayer: definition and dispute
items.text_en: Ne'ilah prayer: definition and dispute
items.desc_en: A Mishnah states that in three periods (fasts, ma'amadot, and Yom Kippur), priests lift their hands four times. The Gemara asks what 'Ne'ilat she'arim' means: Rav says it is an additional prayer, Shmuel says it is the 'Mah anu' prayer. An objection is raised from a baraita that lists five prayers with seven blessings each on Yom Kippur. The Gemara resolves that this is a dispute between Tanna'im: Rabbi Meir requires vidui at Ne'ilah, while the Sages say one may choose. This refutes Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that in three periods (fasts, ma'amadot, and Yom Kippur), priests lift their hands four times a day, including at 'Ne'ilat she'arim'.
The Gemara asks what 'Ne'ilat she'arim' (closing of the gates) refers to.
Rav says it is an additional prayer (צְלוֹתָא יַתִּירְתָּא).
Shmuel says it is the 'Mah anu' prayer (the prayer beginning 'What are we, what is our life').

An objection is raised from a baraita that lists five prayers with seven blessings each on Yom Kippur, including Ne'ilah as a full prayer, contradicting Shmuel's view that Ne'ilah is merely the 'Mah anu' prayer.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is between Tanna'im (early sages).
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir requires vidui (confession) at Ne'ilah, while the Sages say one may choose to include it, showing that the dispute about Ne'ilah's nature is a Tannaic dispute.
The Gemara concludes that Shmuel's position is refuted (תְּיוּבְתָּא).

items.text: Practice of Ulla bar Rav and individual recitation
items.text_en: Practice of Ulla bar Rav and individual recitation
items.desc_en: Ulla bar Rav led the prayer before Rava, beginning with 'Atah bechartanu' and ending with 'Mah anu meh chayeinu', and Rava praised him. Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan says an individual recites this after his prayer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Ulla bar Rav led the prayer before Rava, opening with 'אתה בחרתנו' and concluding with 'מה אנו מה חיינו', and Rava praised him.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's statement
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan adds that an individual recites this prayer after his own prayer.

items.text: Does Ne'ilah exempt Maariv?
items.text_en: Does Ne'ilah exempt Maariv?
items.desc_en: Rav says Ne'ilah prayer exempts Maariv, consistent with his view that Ne'ilah is an additional prayer. The Gemara questions this from Rav's own statement that Maariv is optional, and Rav clarifies he spoke according to the one who says it is obligatory. An objection is raised from a baraita listing five prayers on Yom Kippur, including Maariv with seven blessings. Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel says one prays a full eighteen blessings.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the Ne'ilah prayer exempts one from the Maariv prayer, consistent with his view that Ne'ilah is an additional prayer (צלותא יתירתא).
The Gemara questions Rav's ruling, citing his own statement that the הלכה (binding law) follows the one who says Maariv is optional (רשות).
The Gemara resolves that Rav's ruling was stated according to the opinion that Maariv is obligatory (חובה), not according to his own view.
An objection is raised from a baraita listing five prayers on Yom Kippur, including Maariv with seven blessings, and Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel says one prays a full eighteen blessings.

items.text: Opening dispute about ba'al keri immersion on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Opening dispute about ba'al keri immersion on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute about whether a ba'al keri may immerse all day or only until minchah. The first Tanna permits immersion until minchah, while Rabbi Yosei permits it all day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction by asserting that the dispute is between Tannaim.
The baraita states that all obligated in immersions immerse normally on Yom Kippur, with niddah and a woman after childbirth immersing at night.
The Tanna Kamma permits a ba'al keri to immerse only until minchah.
Rabbi Yosei permits immersion all day.

items.text: Contradictory baraita cited
items.text_en: Contradictory baraita cited
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that seems to contradict the previous one: it states that a ba'al keri immerses all day, and Rabbi Yosei says he cannot immerse from minchah onward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that reverses the positions: the first Tanna permits all day, and Rabbi Yosei restricts until minchah.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who has recited the Ne'ilah prayer and one who has not. The first baraita refers to one who has not yet recited Ne'ilah, so he may immerse all day; the second refers to one who has already recited Ne'ilah, so he may not immerse after minchah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one baraita refers to one who has recited the Ne'ilah prayer, the other to one who has not.

items.text: Debate about whether immersion at its proper time is a mitzvah
items.text_en: Debate about whether immersion at its proper time is a mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the rationale of the Rabbis who permit immersion after Ne'ilah, explaining that they hold immersion at its proper time is a mitzvah. Rabbi Yosei disagrees. A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei allows immersion even when a divine name is written on the skin, implying he holds immersion at its proper time is a mitzvah. The Gemara concludes that they dispute whether immersion at its proper time is a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if he has already prayed Ne'ilah, what is the rationale of the Rabbis who permit immersion after Ne'ilah?
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis hold that immersion at its proper time is a מצוה (commandment).
The Gemara infers that Rabbi Yosei must hold that immersion at its proper time is not a מצוה (commandment).
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei permits immersion even when a divine name is written on the skin, implying he holds immersion at its proper time is a מצוה (commandment).
The Gemara concludes that the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei is whether immersion at its proper time is a מצוה (commandment).

items.text: Identification of the baraita with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah
items.text_en: Identification of the baraita with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the baraita where Rabbi Yosei permits immersion with a divine name on the skin as being authored by Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah, who holds that immersion at its proper time is not a mitzvah, and that it is sufficient for the immersion to be performed at the last possible moment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the baraita with Rabbi Yosei's lenient position is actually Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.
The baraita states that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda holds that immersion suffices at the last moment, supporting the identification.

items.text: Baraita about one who experiences a seminal emission on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Baraita about one who experiences a seminal emission on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who experiences a seminal emission on Yom Kippur should immerse and then rub himself in the evening. The Gemara corrects the text to say he should rub himself before evening, implying that rubbing is a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis taught: one who experiences a seminal emission on Yom Kippur immerses and rubs in the evening.
The Gemara objects: rubbing in the evening is pointless, as the immersion already happened.
The Gemara corrects: say 'from the evening he rubs' (before immersion).
The Gemara explains that the baraita holds it is a מצוה (commandment) to rub.

items.text: Aggadic statements about one who sees a seminal emission on Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Aggadic statements about one who sees a seminal emission on Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: A tanna teaches before Rav Nachman that one who sees a seminal emission on Yom Kippur has his sins forgiven. A contradiction is raised from another baraita that says his sins are arranged. The Gemara resolves that they are arranged for forgiveness. Then a teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael says such a person should worry all year, but if the year passes, he is assured of a share in the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recited before Rav Nachman: one who sees a seminal emission on Yom Kippur has his sins forgiven.
The Gemara objects: another baraita says his sins are arranged (not forgiven).
The Gemara resolves: 'arranged' means arranged for forgiveness.
A teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael says such a person should worry all year, but if the year passes, he is assured of a share in the World to Come.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that one can know this because the whole world is hungry (for forgiveness) and he is satisfied.
When Rav Dimi came, he said that such a person increases life and causes others to increase (in merit).

items.text: Additional aggadic comments
items.text_en: Additional aggadic comments
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the person who sees a seminal emission on Yom Kippur is like one who is sated while the world is hungry. Rav Dimi adds that he will have long life and increase.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: one who sees a seminal emission on Yom Kippur should worry all year, but if the year passes, he is assured of a share in the World to Come.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says: know that the entire world is hungry and he is sated (i.e., his affliction is a sign of favor).
When Rav Dimi came, he said: he increases life abundantly and causes increase.
